# Isaiah 29-49

### CHAPTER 29

**V. 1.** *{Woe to Ariel, to Ariel, the city where David dwelt}* In this chapter is contained a sad prophecy against Jerusalem; and consequently, the whole state of the Jews, whereof that was the head city, threatening the destitution and destruction of either; yet concluded, as our prophet's usual manner is, with gracious promises of mercy, and restitution again.

*{Woe to Ariel, to Ariel*} Or, *O Ariel, Ariel*: as chap. 10.5. & 18.1. the word signifies, *a mighty lion*, *God's lion*, or, *a lion of God*: as, *mountains of God*, Psal. 36.6. and *trees of God*, Psal. 104.16. and so it seems taken, 2 Sam. 23.20. *two Ariels*; that is, *two mighty lions*, or *lion-like* men: and so also, 1 Chr. 11.22. but here, in a more peculiar manner, as consecrated to God's service, is the brazen altar of burnt offerings, so called, Ezek. 43.15,16. not, as some superstitious Jews, in regard of some relation it should have to the Lion in the Zodiac, but because it seemed as a *lion*, to devour the bodies of those beasts, that were by the fire, continually burning upon it, consumed into ashes, Lev. 6.9,12,13. for fire is said to devour, and to be fed with such matter, as is thereby consumed, Lev. 3.11,16. chap. 5.24. & 11.5. So rather, than as some, because morning and evening some beast was offered to it, as to a *lion*, for his daily diet, Num. 28.2–4. It is that, that is hereafter, ch. 31.9. called *God's chimney*, or *furnace*, put here, for the Temple, the place of it; the ruin whereof, is here threatened, together with the city of Jerusalem, wherein the Temple stood. And it may well be conceived, as spoken by way of compellation, *O Ariel*; because the verb, next following, is in the second person, as spoken to it, or those, that either attended it, or resorted to it for sacrifice; and for the more emphasis, the word is reiterated, as, *O Jerusalem, Jerusalem*, Mat. 23.27. and so, also, would some have the text taken here, as there; delivered by way of lamentation: *Alas, Ariel, Ariel*: as Jer. 13.27. But I rather follow the former, as seeming better to suit with the words ensuing.

*{the city*} Or, *of the city*; or, *in the city*: for the particle *in* is oft wanting; as chap. 28.7. that belong to it, or are situate in it, Ezr. 7.17. or, it may be read, following the received version; *and to the city*, supplying the copulative: as chap. 22.6. for the destruction of the city, as well as of the Temple, is denounced, v. 2. and so it would agree fitly with their exposition, who by the altar, suppose to be meant the Temple, and mount Moriah, on which it stood, 2 Chr. 3.1. by the city of David, mount Sion, where the king's court was, 1 Chr. 11.7. and so destruction, of both estates, together denounced. But I conceive it rather, to be added, by apposition, in way of explication; *O Ariel, thou city*: as if he had said, if you ask, what by *Ariel*, I mean, I tell you, it is the city of Jerusalem, therefore by way of anticipation, here so termed; because it was to be made as another *Ariel*, v. 2. See the like, ch. 24.10. And *the city*, put here for the inhabitants of it, whom, in the next branch, he directs his speech unto.

*{where David dwelt*} Or, *wherein*, or, *in which David dwelt*: because a defect not of the adverb, so much as of the preposition, and the relative according to the Hebrews' usual syntax, as, 1 Chr. 15.12. 2 Chr. 1.4.

*{dwelt*} Heb. *encamped*: whereupon, some render it, *which David encamped against*, 2 Sam. 5.6,7. others, *which David fortified*; because it is said of the fort of Sion, that David *dwelt in it, and called it the city of David, and built round about it*, 2 Sam. 5.9. but the word is used sometime simply, for *to dwell*, as Neh. 9.30. Mention is made of David, the rather, partly to mind them of him, from whom they had degenerated: as 1 King. 11.4,6,12. & 14.8. and partly to let them know, that no such relation, or external privilege should exempt them, from deserved destruction, Jer. 7.4,14. Mat. 3.9,10. See chap. 7.13.

*{add ye year to year; let them kill sacrifices*} Or, *proceed ye from year to year, in procuring, or causing your festival sacrifices to be slain*. Keep your yearly feasts, while you may, you inhabitants of Jerusalem, for you shall not keep them long, Exod. 23.14. Lam. 1.4. nor shall your vain confidence, in your sacrifices, long continue, Jer. 7.14,21. Yet I suppose this no sufficient ground, for their opinion, who hence gather, that this prophecy was delivered just two year before the siege of Jerusalem, by Sennacherib, and to extend itself no further, than that expedition, which some ensuing passages seem to control.

*{and year to year*} As ver. 14. ch. 52.1.

*{let them kill*} That is, say some, let the priests kill: but the word seems indefinite, *let sacrifices be slain*: *add ye—let them slay sacrifices*: that is, *cause sacrifices still to be slain*: as chap. 47.1. *thou shalt not add, they shall not call thee*: that is, *thou shalt no longer be called*: and Hos. 1.6. *I will not add, I will not have mercy any more*: that is, *I will not continue still to show mercy*: and Prov. 23.35. *I will add, I will further seek after it*: that is, *I will again seek after it still*. See v. 4.

*{kill*} Some of the Jewish critics suppose it, to be a standing verb, as they term it, in the form here used, and render the text therefore, *let sacrifices be slain*, as the direct grammatical construction of it; or, as others, whom the old Latin concurs with, *your feasts*, or *sacrifices, shall be cut off*, and fail, by occasion of the enemy's, either siege, or surprisal of the city, Dan. 11.31. Lam. 1.4. & 2.6. But most take it, for a passing verb, as in another form, it is used for *to cut*, or *to lop*, chap. 10.33,34. and those that so take it here, suppose it, to signify *to behead*, or, *to cut off the head of a beast*, because the Chaldee paraphrast so uses it, ch. 66.3. and some of ours so render it here.

*{sacrifices*} Heb. *feasts*: that is, *festival sacrifices*: *feasts* for beasts slain, and sacrificed at, and in their solemn feasts: as Exod. 23.18. Psal. 118.27. for they seem wide, who because the verb is used of *lopping*, or *cutting down of boughs*, or *branches*, chap. 10.34. would have by this term understood, not the beasts that were slain; but such boughs, or branches of trees, as at some of their festivals, they were wont to cut down to build them booths and arbors with, or to make use of otherwise, Neh. 8.15,16. Mat. 21.8. Howbeit, their conjecture is not improbable, who deem this prophecy to have been delivered, at the time of some solemn feast: the scope of the prophet, in this passage, being to check their jollity, and to control their security, and vain confidence, in the sacrifices then offered: so ch. 66.3. Jer. 7.21. Hos. 9.1. Amos 4.4,5. & 5.21,22.

**V. 2.** *{Yet I will distress Ariel, and there shall be heaviness, and sorrow: and it shall be unto me, as Ariel*} For all the jollity you now make, and enjoy in your festivals, and the safety, and security, that, in regard of these present performances, you promise to yourselves; yet neither shall you be able, by any force you can make, to rid yourselves out of the straits, that the enemy shall put you into; nor by any rites, performed by you, so to pacify God's wrath, justly incensed against you, as to cause him not to join with, and assist the adversary, in so pressing, and oppressing you, and your city.

*{Yet*} Heb. *And*. But so also, chap. 17.6.

*{I will distress*} Not the enemy only, but I myself by them, and with them. So they complain, Psal. 66.11,12. Lam. 1.5,12–15. & 2.1–8. & 3.1–17. and so ch. 22.5. ver. 3,5.

*{Ariel*} Not the city only, but my Temple also, and mine altar, Lam. 2.1,6,7.

*{heaviness, and sorrow*} There are two words in the Hebrew here, of the same notion, and arising from the same root, as if we should say, *mourning, and mournfulness*; or, *grief, and grievousness*. And it seems to have been an usual form of speech among them, whereby to express an extremity of grief and heaviness. For the same is found also, used, Lam. 2.5. rendered there, *mourning, and lamentation*. See the like hereunto, ver. 14. Such heaviness they should be in, as in regard of their own present distresses; so for the overthrow, in especial manner, of the Temple and the altar, as it follows there, Lam. 2.6,7. Or, as those that restrain this to Sennacherib's invasion; for their brethren slain abroad, in the cities of Judah, chap. 10.6. & 36.1.

*{and it shall be unto me, as Ariel*} That this passage has reference to the city of Jerusalem, before mentioned, ver. 1. is generally agreed. But it is diversely expounded; some read it, as in the time past, *because* (as chap. 64.5.) *it hath been unto me, as Ariel*; that is, *as a fierce lion*. See Jer. 12.8. Or, *it shall be as a fierce lion*, beset with shepherds, or hunters on every side. See chap. 31.4. Jer. 12.10. Ezek. 19.8. Others, *It shall be as Ariel*; that is, the city shall be in the same distress, that the Temple, and the altar shall be in. But this seems but a poor expression; for the city might be in distress, and yet not the Temple: whereas the Temple standing in the head, and heart of the city, that could not be in any distress; but the city, of necessity, must first so be. Others, therefore, the city shall be, on every side, encompassed with slain men; as the altar is wont to be, at some solemn festival, with beasts, brought for sacrifice, and the people that bring them, Psal. 26.6. & 118.27. or, it shall be encompassed with slain men, as the altar is wont to be with slain beasts; which they understand of men not slain without it, but round about it, by Sennacherib's forces, Psal. 79.2,3. Or, lastly, which I take to be the genuine sense, the whole city shall be as an *Ariel*, as the altar, and the place where it stands; it shall be all on a light-fire, all full of gore-blood, and the dead bodies of men slaughtered, after the surprisal of it, 2 King. 25.9. 2 Chr. 36.17,19. Psal. 74.7,8. Lam. 4.15.

*{unto me*} Because all this, as before, was showed, from God inflicted on them for their sins, ch. 10.5. So *the Lord's slain*, ch. 66.16.

**V. 3.** *{And I will camp against thee round about, and will lay siege against thee with a mount; and will raise forts against thee*} I will bring in an enemy that shall, on every side, besiege it, ver. 8. myself commanding them, as in chief, ver. 2. Joel 2.11,25.

*{will camp*} As before, *where David encamped*, ver. 1.

*{against thee*} A change of the person, as ch. 1.29. and elsewhere.

*{round about*} Heb. *as*, or, *in manner of a ball*, or, *a globe*. See ch. 22.18. A phrase, not unusual in other languages: for so they say *a globe of soldiers*, in Latin. Or, as some read it, *with a ball*. The particle, *with*, as in the next branch, supplied: that is, say they, *with a round camp*; for their camps used to be round. Which they gather from a word used, 1 Sam. 26.5.

*{lay siege*} Or, *lie in siege*; as Jer. 32.3. or, *beset thee*, as Psal. 139.5.

*{with a mount*} Or, as some, *a standing*; that is, say they, *a tower*, or, *gallery*, for soldiers to stand upon for assault. For the word, nowhere else found, has a notion of *standing* in it. But that agrees well enough to a *mount*. The other seems to come within compass of the next branch; and must be understood collectively, if it be admitted. See Ezek. 26.8,9.

**V. 4.** *{And thou shalt be brought down, and shalt speak out of the ground, and thy speech shall be low out of the dust, and thy voice shall be as one, that hath a familiar spirit out of the ground, and thy speech shall whisper out of the dust*} By these your distresses, your former pride shall be pulled down, Levit. 26.19. ch. 2.11–17. & 5.15. and you shall not talk scornfully, and carry yourself presumptuously, and insolently, as now you do, ch. 28.14,15. but shall be glad, in submiss, and base manner, to petition the enemy, ch. 10.3,4. fulfilled in part, as the Rabbins observe, in Ezekiah's message to Sennacherib, 2 King. 18.14. and his messengers' speech to Rabshakeh, 2 King. 18.26.

*{thou shalt be brought down, and speak out of the ground*} Heb. *thou shalt be laid low, shalt speak out of the ground*, or, *from off the ground*; and afterward, *out the dust*: that is, by an Hebraism, *thou shalt speak demissly or, dejectedly from off the ground, and out of the dust*. Like one that lies on the ground, in the dust; as poor prisoners, and captives are wont to do, chap. 47.1. & 52.2. For the phrase, see on ver. 1. and the like also, Hos. 9.9. *They have made deep, have corrupted themselves*: that is, *They have deeply corrupted themselves*. And 1 Sam. 2.3. a place parallel to this, *do not multiply, speak not so proudly*: that is, *speak no more so proudly*.

*{be low*} Be abated, and abased. See both words, this, and the former, likewise together, ch. 2.6. & 5.15.

*{as one that hath a familiar spirit*} Who used to mutter their spells, or give out their answers, in a low and obscure manner, many times, not intelligible. See ch. 8.19.

*{out of the ground*} Alluding, it may be, unto those caves and holes, out of which the Devil, sometime, inspired his agents, and uttered his oracles.

*{whisper out of the dust*} Heb. *peep*, or, *hiss*, chap. 8.19. Like the hissing of a serpent out of his hole, Jer. 46.22.

**V. 5.** *{Moreover the multitude of thy strangers, shall be like small dust, and the multitude of thy terrible ones shall be as chaff, that passeth away: yea, it shall be at an instant, suddenly*} All your helps, and strength, either from abroad, or at home, be they never either so many, or so mighty, shall fail you, shall stand you in no stead; for they shall like dust, or chaff, be also suddenly blown away, as with a whirlwind. Yet the Jewish commenters, whom some of ours also follow, understand all this, and what follows, ver. 6. not of the inhabitants of Jerusalem, but of the Assyrians, that beleaguered it. And of these, some expound it of the numberless number of them, and the swiftness of their approach, Job 27.16. Ezek. 26.10. Others, of their strange dispersion, and sudden destruction. To which purpose, see ch. 17.13. See the like, chap. 41.15,16. But the context seems to run the other way.

*{Moreover*} Heb. *And*; as ch. 8.1.

*{strangers*} Hired soldiers, from other parts, ch. 25.2.

*{small dust*} An emphatical expression: for the substantive itself, signifies *small dust*, distinguished from *dust*, in general, Deut. 28.24. and the adjective, properly, *ground to powder*, Numb. 16.12. See ch. 40.15. such as every puff of wind, soon disperses, Psal. 18.42.

*{thy terrible ones*} Some, *thine oppressors*; applying this, as *strangers*, before, to Sennacherib's forces; as ch. 25.4. Other, *thy tyrants*, or, *roisters*: understanding it of those great ones, among themselves, that domineered over the meaner sort, and in whose might, being also military men, they much confided, ch. 28.14,15.

*{as chaff that passeth away*} Not able to stand before the wind, Psal. 35.5. See Lam. 1.15.

*{it shall be at an instant suddenly*} Or, *for an instant*. Some expound it of the help and relief, that foreign forces, or others, besides their own, should afford them, which should not last long, but be suddenly blasted, Jer. 37.7. Others, of their affliction and distress, that it should in an instant be over, ch. 17.14. Others, of the enemy's expedition, in the execution, of God's judgments upon them, chap. 28.19. & 30.13. Jer. 4.20. & 6.26. & 15.8. and this seems most probable.

**V. 6.** *{Thou shalt be visited of the Lord of Hosts, with thunder, and with earthquake, and with great noise, with storm and tempest, and the flame of devouring fire*} In a most dreadful and direful manner will God execute his judgments upon you, as if heaven and earth conspired together, and all the elements concurred to the working of your ruin. This some understand of the destruction of the Assyrian forces, by the ministry of an Angel: of which, see ch. 30.27,28,30,31. Others, of the destruction of Jerusalem, by the Chaldeans, ch. 24.17,18. Lam. 1.12,13. & 2.1,5. see the like expressions, Psal. 11.6. ch. 13.13.

*{thunder*} Psal. 18.12–14. Rev. 8.5.

*{earthquake*} 1 Sam. 14.15. Psal. 18.7. ch. 2.19,21. Rev. 16.18.

*{noise*} Heb. *voice*: as Exod. 20.18. Rev. 8.5. thunder God's *voice*, Psal. 29.3–9. *great noise*, or *voice*, great cracks of thunder, Psal. 77.17,18. see ch. 30.30,31.

*{storm and tempest*} Or, *stormy tempest*: see ch. 4.9. both joined, as here: so Amos 1.14. Nah. 1.3.

*{flame of devouring fire*} Ch. 5.54. & 9.5. & 26.11. & 30.30. Lam. 2.3.

**V. 7.** *{And the multitude of all the nations, that fight against Ariel, even all that fight against her, and her munition, and that distress her shall be as the dream of a night vision*} This verse, and the next, some expound of the frustration of the vain hopes that Sennacherib had conceived of surprising Jerusalem, which suddenly vanished away, like a dream when a man awakes, Job 20.8. Psal. 73.20. see ch. 17.13,14. others of the eagerness, and insatiableness of the Chaldeans, in the pursuit and execution of their cruelty, against, and upon God's people: see ver. 8.

*{all the nations*} As some, the Assyrians, and their associates, c. 10.8. & 17.13. as others, the Chaldeans, and their complices, 2 King. 24.2. Jer. 1.15.

*{that fight*} Or, *war*, Zach. 14.12. or, *in troops assemble*: as Exod. 38.8.

*{against Ariel*} Jerusalem: see ver. 1,2,8.

*{distress her*} Ver. 2,3.

*{as a dream*} *They shall be as a dream*: that is, it shall be with them, as with a man in a dream: see the like, Mat. 13.24,45. & 18.23. & 20.1. & 22.2. & 25.1,14.

*{a night vision*} Heb. *vision of the night*, Job 4.13. & 20.8. & 33.15.

**V. 8.** *{It shall be, as when an hungry man dreameth, and behold he eateth; but he awaketh, and his soul is empty: or, as when a thirsty man dreameth, and behold he drinketh; but he awaketh, and behold he is faint, and his soul hath appetite: so shall the multitude of all nations be, that fight against mount Zion*} The prophet here more particularly declares, what manner of dream it was, that he intended, ver. 7. such an one, wherein a man being hungry and thirsty, has some imaginary refreshing and satisfaction, while he is asleep, which vanishes and proves nothing at all when he awakes. So did Sennacherib's dream, that he fed himself with, concerning the surprisal of Jerusalem, chap. 10.10,11. & 36.18–20. & 37.10,12. But the similitude sorts no less fitly, with the Chaldeans' insatiable cruelty, and thirst after blood, when they might seem to have been glutted with it, that they were still no less greedy of it, than a man, thirsty, is of drink, for all that which he seemed to have drunk in his dream, 2 Chr. 36.17. Jer. 51.35. most apparently verified in the spiritual Babylon, which though drunk again and again, with the blood of God's servants; yet unto drunkenness, still adds thirst, Deut. 29.19. Rev. 17.6. & 18.24.

*{he awaketh, and his soul is empty*} Or, *when he awaketh, his soul is empty*, as Prov. 6.12. ch. 40.31. *his soul*, for *himself*: he is still empty; he is never a whit fuller, for all he did eat in his sleep: so *my soul*, for *myself*, Psal. 57.4. *empty*: as, Ezek. 24.11.

*{but*} Heb. *and*: as ver. 9. ch. 51.6.

*{but he awaketh*} Or, *but when he awaketh, behold he is faint*, or, *athirst*: as Jer. 31.25.

*{his soul hath appetite*} He is as eagerly desirous of drink, as before; though in his dream, he seemed to have drunk largely: see the same phrase, Psal. 107.9.

*{so shall the multitude be*} So it shall be with them; as ver. 7.

*{mount Zion*} Jerusalem: as Psal. 48.11. ch. 3. ver. 17.

**V. 9.** *{Stay yourselves, and wonder, cry ye out, and cry*} The prophet having given warning of those heavy judgments of God, before mentioned, does in the next place complain of, and wonder at the strange stupidity, and deep security, of those among his people, that no whit regarded what had been threatened; but did still, as freely, as ever, abandon themselves unto all sensuality and excess: see the like, ch. 5.11,12. & 22.12,13. & 28.5–15.

*{stay yourselves, and wonder*} The prophet here, as most interpreters take it, turns his speech unto the pious party, inviting and inciting them, to admire at, and lament for, the obstinate persistence of a great party among them. The words are by some read, *They delay* (Psal. 119.60. to wit, to return unto God, by humiliation and reformation, Jer. 13.27.) *and wonder ye at it*; a defect of the pronoun; as ch. 28.20. For those that render them, *wonder, and wonder*, as Hab. 1.5. that is, wonder exceedingly, or, again, and again, mistake the latter word, being deceived with the affinity, that it has in sound with the former.

*{cry ye out, and cry*} So some other versions, but the former word, is never found in that notion; but constantly, in a signification of *delight*, or *sport*, Psal. 94.19. & 119.16,70. ch. 11.8. & 66.12. and some other therefore render it, *They take their pleasure*, or *sport it* (as Job 21.10,12. Amos 6.3–6. 1 Tim. 5.6. Jam. 5.5.) *but cry ye out*; lamenting their folly, Ezek. 9.4. Howbeit, some, would have both this, and the former, to be spoken unto the worse party, reading the words; *Stay still, and be stupid, riot and revel it*: yet not seriously, but in way of derision; as Eccl. 11.9. or, of them, as others, who thus render them, *They have blinded themselves, and are blind*: as chap. 6.10. & ver. 10. But the words here, and there, are not the same: There is in both branches, a pleasant run of words, which our English cannot so fitly express; somewhat like, as if it were said, *They stay, but stare ye; they riot, but roar ye*: but the words of staring and roaring, will not so well fit here.

*{they are drunk, but not with wine; they stagger, but not with strong drink*} They are dulled in their understanding, lulled asleep in their sinful practices, unsteady in their courses, as secure, as men drowned in drink; and by reason thereof, in a deep, or dead sleep; so ch. 19.14. See the same phrase in another sense, ch. 51.21.

*{but*} Heb. *and*; as as ver. 8,13.

*{not with wine*} This is not so much; or, not only with wine; but with a spirit of stupidity, which God, in his just judgment has cast them into, v. 10. see the like, Deut. 8.3. Jer. 7.22. Hos. 6.6. the negative is not absolute, but comparative: for to drunkenness and sensuality, they were, also, excessively given, ch. 28.7,8. there is in either branch a defect of the preposition: as chap. 28.28. expressed, chap. 28.7.

*{stagger*} As ch. 24.19. or, *stray*; as Gen. 4.14. Jer. 14.10. but here the former rather.

**V. 10.** *{For the Lord hath poured out upon you, the spirit of deep sleep, and hath closed your eyes*} One ground, and cause of their extreme stupidity and security, is here rendered; to wit, for their sin his just judgment, for their willful obstinacy, God had given them up unto a further degree of stupidity and blindness: by withdrawing that light from them, against which they had rebelled, Job 24.13. chap. 63.10. it is a just thing with God, when men willfully wink, to dash out their eyes, Joh. 3.2. & 9.39–41. Rom. 1.18,28. 2 Thess. 2.10–12.

*{the Lord hath poured out*} See the like, ch. 19.14. and the apostle's allegation of this place, Rom. 11.8.

*{poured out*} As the word is used, Exod. 30.9. Hos. 9.4. yet the Jewish doctors would have it rather here rendered, *covered*: as the notion of the word is, chap. 25.8. & 28.20. & 30.1. that it may answer the word used in the close of the verse. But the notions here, and there, are divers: for here the allusion is to some soporiferous potion, or medicine, that being ministered to a man, or sprinkled upon him, so as to bedew him, casts him into a deep sleep: whereas, there is to some film, that grows over the sight, or some veil, that covering the eyes, hinders the sight: that there is an eye, to ch. 19.14. (a place parallel to this) to this latter, ch. 25.7.

*{upon you*} A change of the person, as v. 3.

*{the spirit of deep sleep*} Or, *a spirit*: for there is no article in the text. In Hebrew there are three several words: whereof one signifies *to slumber*, chap. 56.10. Psal. 121.3. another, *to sleep*, Psal. 76.5. and 121.4. a third, to be in *a deep sleep*, Judg. 4.21. Psal. 76.6. and thence the word here used, and Gen. 2.21. & 15.12. 1 Sam. 26.12. Job 4.13. & 33.15. Prov. 19.15. the apostle uses a word, wherewith the ancient Greek rendered it, which properly indeed signifies *compunction*, according to the notion of the verb, whence it is regularly derived: but the authors of that version, as they coined many words, after an unusual stamp; so it is not unlikely, that they did the like with this, deducing it from a word, that signifies *night*, the time of sleep, thereby to express the word here used.

*{hath closed your eyes*} The word here used in the first light form, signifies to shut one's own eyes, ch. 33.14. in the first grave form, another's, so here. See ch. 6.10.

*{eyes*} Not of the body, but of the mind; as Num. 24.17. Deut. 28.2,4. Psal. 119.18. Eph. 1.18.

*{the Prophets, and your rulers, the seers hath he covered*} This heavy judgment of obduration and excaecation, has not befallen the meaner and common sort of people only: but the principal ones, also, in either state, as well ecclesiastical, as civil, that should have been as lights and guides to others.

*{the Prophets*} To wit, the false ones: yet so called: because they pretended and professed themselves to be such: so Jer. 5.31. & 6.13.

*{and your rulers, the seers*} Heb. *and your heads, the seers*; which some expound, *even your chiefest*, or *principal* (to wit, in your account) *seers*: *Head*, for *chief*: as Exod. 30.23. 1 Chr. 12.18. *Seers*, for *Prophets*: as ch. 30.10. others, *and your rulers, the seeing ones*: that is, the wisest and prudentest of them, ver. 14. *Heads*, for *rulers*: as Numb. 1.16. *seeing*, for *understanding*: as Prov. 20.12. or, *your rulers, the seers*: because the prophets, in those distracted times, took upon to rule and govern, Jer. 5.31. & 26.8.

*{hath he covered*} He has covered them, with that mist of spiritual blindness and darkness, Mic. 3.6,7. v. 14. Or, as I suppose, the words should be rendered, *the eyes of the Prophets, and of your princes, together, with the seers, hath he covered*, ch. 25.7. the word *eyes*, is supplied from the foregoing branch: the like whereunto, see Job 22.24. ch. 58.13. Dan. 4.33. Rev. 11.15.

**V. 11.** *{And the vision of all is become unto you, as the words of a book that is sealed*} A sad effect of this dreadful judgment: to wit, that all God's warnings and messages, delivered to them by his prophets, should no more be regarded by them: nor they conceive any understanding or benefit from them; than a man, though he can read, by a book, or letter tendered to him, so long as it is sealed up: or, a man that cannot read, whether it be sealed, or unsealed.

*{the vision of all*} To wit, of all God's prophets, whom he sends on messages to you: or all their messages and sermons, ch. 1.1. or, *every vision*, that is, all teaching; as Prov. 29.18.

*{of a book that is sealed*} As books sometime were, Dan. 12.9. Rev. 5.1. or, *of an epistle*, or *letter*: as 2 King. 5.4. & 10.1. Jer. 29.1. for such were commonly, as now, so then, sealed, 1 King. 21.8. Est. 3.12,13. & 8.8. as deeds and evidences also were, Jer. 32.11. See there which some suppose here to be alluded unto.

*{which men deliver to one that is learned*} Heb. *which they give it*: (a familiar and frequent redundancy, in that language: as Psal. 1.4.) *which they give* (that is, *which is delivered*, or *given*: as Gen. 40.13. Rev. 4.19. & ver. 12.) *to one that knoweth a book*, or *a letter*: that is skillful in the book, or letter, that is able to read it, or on it: *a knowing man*, for a *skillful*, or *cunning man*, Gen. 25.27. 1 Sam. 16.17,18. 1 King. 5.6.

*{saying, read this, I pray thee*} Heb. word for word; *cry this*: as ch. 40.6. Zach. 1.16,17. but it is used, also, commonly for *reading*, Deut. 31.11. Neh. 8.3,8. Jer. 36.6,23. because in reading, the voice is wont to be lifted up, that it may be the better heard, by those, for whom, or to whom, aught is read. Hence the *reading* among the Jewish critics, distinguished from the *writing*, when the letter of the text is read otherwise, than it is written: and thence also the Turks' *Alkoran*, or law, has its name.

*{and he saith, I cannot, for it is sealed*} For neither book, nor letter can be read, until the seal be broken up, Rev. 5.2–5. the whole sentence may thus be rendered: *which when it is delivered to one that can read, saying, read this, I pray thee: he saith, I cannot, because it is sealed*; See ch. 8.16. & 28.25.

**V. 12.** *{And the book is delivered to one that is not learned, saying, read this, I pray thee: and he saith, I am not learned*} Or, *And, when the book*, or *letter is delivered to one that cannot read: saying, read this, I pray thee; he saith, I cannot read*. So they of our Savior, *How knoweth this man letters, having not learned them?* Joh. 7.15. and of some of the apostles, it is said, they were *illiterate men*; that is, not trained up in school-learning, Act. 4.13.

*{delivered to*} Heb. *given upon*: but so the particle is used, Josh. 10.6. 1 Sam. 2.11.

*{that is not learned*} Heb. *that knoweth not to read*: and so afterward, *I know not to read*: that is, I cannot read, *knoweth not*, for *cannot*: as Jer. 8.12.

**V. 13.** *{Wherefore, the Lord said, Forasmuch, as this people draw near me with their mouth, and with their lips do honor me, but have removed their heart far from me: and their fear towards me, is taught by the precept of men*} Another cause, or reason is here rendered, of God's so severe proceeding in judgment: as before, their stupidity, sensuality, and security, ver. 9,12. so now their mere formality in God's service and worship, which they frequented and performed, only in regard of human, either tradition, teaching; or authority maintaining and enjoining it; see Mat. 15.8. Mar. 7.6.

*{Wherefore*} Heb. *And*; as ch. 8.2. or, *Moreover*, as ver. 5.

*{Draw near me with their mouth*} Worship me in hypocrisy, not in sincerity, with the outward man, and disposition of body: but not with the inward man, and affection of mind, ch. 48.1,2. & 58.2,3. Jer. 12.2. Ezek. 14.3,4. & 33.31. *mouth*, for *mouths*; and *heart*, for *hearts*: as *lie*, for *lies*, ch. 28.15. and so *precept*, for *precepts*.

*{but their heart*} Heb. *and*: as ver. 9.

*{their fear towards me*} That is, *worship of me*, *fear* for *worship*: as 2 King. 17.32,33.

*{is taught*} Is *taught them*: a defect of the pronoun: as ch. 13.8,15.

*{by the precept of men*} Either their religion is not according to my mind: but according to men's devices, consisting in the observation of human traditions, Jer. 7.31. Hos. 5.11. Mat. 15.3,9. Col. 2.22. or, all their devotion under their religious kings, was not hearty, but for their command only, 2 King. 23.22,26. 2 Chr. 27.2. Jer. 3.10.

*{of men*} Not sent by God, nor taught of him, say some, Jer. 23.16,17,21,32. but it seems to be more large, as was before showed.

**V. 14.** *{Therefore, behold I will proceed to do a marvelous work amongst this people, even a marvelous work, and a wonder*} A strange judgment denounced against them, for this their hypocrisy, and formality: so far, from being pleasing or acceptable to God, that it is most odious and abominable in his sight, ch. 1.11–15. & 66.3.

*{Behold*} As ch. 26.11. & 28.16.

*{I will proceed*} Heb. *I will add*, as v. 1. ch. 7.10. the syntax seems irregular, both here, and ch. 38.5. the verb being of the third person; the like whereunto, the Jewish critics observe, Psal. 6.2. Ezek. 9.8. Now, this to salve, some of them, render the words, *I am he that will add*. Others suppose it a participle, or a noun, as one of the same making, Psal. 16.5. *thou art maintaining*, or *the maintainer of my lot*: see on chap. 28.16.

*{to do a marvelous work*} Heb. *to do, or deal marvelously* as Judg. 13.19. chap. 28.29. Joel 2.26.

*{amongst this people*} Heb. *with this people*.

*{even a marvelous work*} The word, *even*, being not in the original, is here needless: the word is, according to some, a verb: and then the text runs thus, *I will further deal marvelously, dealing marvelously*: that is, *I will deal exceedingly marvelously*: such like repetitions, see ch. 24.3,16,19. but I take it, rather for a noun: because I find it so used, 2 Chr. 2.8. and the word coupled with it, there prefixed, here annexed, seems to require it. So taking it, the words may well be rendered, *I will deal marvelously with this people, by a marvelous thing, and a miracle*: for the word *work*, is not in the Hebrew text.

*{a marvelous work, and a wonder*} The words are two of the very same notion, and derived from the same root, or verb, even that here used, and may, for variety, be rendered, *a marvelous thing, and a miracle*, both used and joined, to express, more emphatically, the exceeding strangeness, of that God intended to do. See the very like, ver. 2. whether this so marvelous and miraculous business, be the infatuating of their wise counselors, and turning of their wisdom into folly: as 2 Sam. 15.21. or, the strange change and alteration, in the land and state, v. 17. is not certain.

*{for the wisdom of their wise men shall perish, and the understanding of their prudent men shall be hid*} Their wise men, and great politicians, whose counsels they so much rely upon, accounting them as oracles, 2 Sam. 16.23. shall be infatuated; and all their prudent, and provident plots and projects come to nought, chap. 19.11–14. v. 15,16. c. 31.1,2. Jer. 49.7. Obad. 8. Rom. 1.22. 1 Cor. 1.19,20. & 3.19,20. This the more strange; because done with that people, whose governors God had promised to endow with wisdom; but now threatens, for their unthankfulness and misdemeanors, to deprive them again of it: see ch. 28.3,21.

*{for*} Heb. *and*; as chap. 20.17. Howbeit, the copulative may well stand; and the meaning then be, that all the wisdom and policy, which their statesmen, the wisest of them, shall use to prevent, or avert this strange act that God intends, shall be utterly frustrate, ver. 16.

*{the wisdom*} Their state-skill, together with all their deep projects, v. 16.

*{shall perish*} As Jer. 18.18. & 49.7. Mic. 4.9.

*{shall be hid*} Heb. *shall hide itself*; as chap. 45.15. *hiding thyself*; but the reciprocal form, is sometime used for the passive, Num. 1.46. Judg. 20.15. either shall not appear, and show forth itself, whether for confusion, and uncertainty, what to act or devise, chap. 19.14. or for distraction and fear, to deliver their minds freely, Amos 5.13. Or, shall be covered over with that mist, or veil of stupidity, and blockishness, that God threatened to involve them in, ver. 10. or, shall depart from them; as Gen. 31.49. *when we shall be hid*: that is, *shall have departed*, and *be absent one from another*. So Joh. 12.36. *he departed, and was hid*: that is, absented himself from them; or, shall vanish away, and perish, be utterly lost: as some take the word, Prov. 28.28. It seems the same with the former branch, in other terms, and the prophet may well be deemed, in the use of the word, to have an eye to what follows, ver. 15. of their contriving and plotting things so closely, as to conceal them from God himself: as if he had said, You make account, to have your counsels hidden from God; and by his just judgment, they shall so be hid, that either they shall never come to light, or shall be utterly frustrate, and vanish away, if they do.

**V. 15.** *{Woe unto them, that seek deep to hide their counsel from the Lord; and their works are in the dark; and they say, who seeth us? and who knoweth us?*} These words may well be read, as by way of compellation, *O ye, that hide your counsel too deep for the Lord, whose doings are in the dark, and that say, who can see us? or who can know us?* The persons, here spoken of, seem those scoffing statesmen, that derided all that the prophets spoke; and by their wiles and shifts, made account that they were sufficiently, able to secure themselves, whatsoever should come, or howsoever it should fare with others, ch. 28.14,15,22. Nor is it unlikely, but that they would promise the like security unto others, with whom they were in esteem, as great wizards of state: but as God, before, threatened to infatuate them, and turn their wisdom into folly; so he now further tells them, that albeit, their devices and designs be so cunningly contrived, and so closely and covertly carried, that, in their conceit, they seemed to be deeper, and more abstruse, than God himself was able to descry and discover; yet they should no more be able, either to conceal themselves, and their plots, from him, or to bring to effect, aught, that he intended to cross them in, than the potter's clay is able to keep out of his sight, when he has it in his hand, or to mold itself into any other frame, than he is pleased to work it to.

*{Woe unto them*} Or, *Ye*. Of the compellation, see chap. 10.5. & 18.1. Of the change of the person, see Job 18.4. and chap. 30.19.

*{that seek deep to hide their counsel from the Lord*} That is, as some, that take counsel in secret with themselves only, not consulting with God, or seeking to him for direction, or assistance, chap. 31.1. But the words seem rather to intend somewhat else; and they lie thus in the text, *that make deep from the Lord, to hide counsel*. Where there are two Hebraisms, which being opened, will much clear the text. The former is, in *making deep to hide*: for *to make deep to hide*, is nothing else, but *to hide deep*; as, *to make deep to dwell*, is, *to dwell deep*, Jer. 49.8,15. See also, chap. 31.6. The latter is, in *making deep from the Lord*; for *to make deep from the Lord*, is, *to make too deep for the Lord*: to wit, to descry, or discover: as, *deep from hell*, or, *the grave; long from the earth: broad from the sea*: that is, *deeper than hell*, or, *the grave: longer than the earth: broader than the sea*, Job 11.8,9. The meaning then is plain, conceived according to their intent, or conceit, concerning their own contrivances: that think, or make account to hide your counsels so deep, that God himself cannot see them. So of Nabal his servants, *He is a son of Belial, from to speak*, or, *speaking to him*: that is, *He is such a son of Belial, that one cannot speak to him*: as our version well renders it, 1 Sam. 25.17. See also, chap. 25.1. There is, in the words, a metaphor, taken from the practice of those that dig deep to hide aught, that they would not have found out. See Prov. 20.5. Job 12.22. Psal. 64.6.

*{their works are in the dark*} Or, *whose doings are in the dark*; in secret, out of sight: as things that are stowed, or done in dark places cannot be seen without light, Psal. 11.2. & 64.2,4. Job 24.13–17. as if any darkness could hide from God, or any secret place exclude his eyesight, Job 34.21,22. Psal. 139.11,12. Prov. 5.21. & 15.3,11.

*{and say, Who seeth us? and who knoweth us?*} Or, *who can see?* or, *who can know us*: that is, can descry, or know what we do. Meaning that none could, no not God himself, Job 22.11–14. Psal. 10.11,13. & 64.5. & 94.7. the future, for the potential: as Job 38.31,32,33,34,35,37. and the copulative for the disjunctive: as Judg. 11.31. Job 31.5,7,9. ver. 16.

**V. 16.** *{Surely your turning of things upside down, shall be esteemed, as the potter's clay*} Heb. *Your turning upside down*, (as 2 King. 21.13.) or *rolling to and fro*, (as Hos. 11.8. or, *changing, and turning into new shapes*, (as Exod. 7.15. Levit. 13.3. 1 Sam. 10.6.) *if as the potter's clay it shall be accounted*. But the particle, *if*, is, in Scripture, oft used, not as a conditional, but as a note of asseveration, and assurance: as Prov. 3.34. & 23.18. So the Hebrew writers here expound it. Howbeit, I conceive the word rendered *if*, to be, here, rather an interrogative: as oft it is, Job 8.3. & 11.2. & 17.2. & 39.27. and the negative omitted oft, in such forms of interrogation, (that which has not hitherto, by any, been observed) ought to be supplied. So 1 Sam. 2.27,28. *Did I not appear to thy father's house? and did I not choose him? and did I not give to thy father's house?* Job 20.4. *Knowest thou not this of old?* where our version has supplied it: And Job 21.4. *Is not my complaint to man?* where our version has omitted it. See more hereof on Jer. 31.20. And so the words may be rendered: *Shall it not be accounted, as the potter's clay?* or, *as clay to the potter?* as if he had said, Yes undoubtedly, it shall. So this, in sense, comes fully home to the former: as the like twofold version, Psal. 63.6. And the meaning either way rendered, Your turning of things upside down, to conceal your intended courses, as men whelm a dish, or vessel, to keep what is in it, or under it, out of sight, Mat. 5.15. or, that which you roll up and down in your thoughts, devising how to contrive it, with the greatest cunning, and probability of success, to that purpose, casting it now into one frame, and then into another shape, until you have molded it to your mind: lies as open to God's eye, as the fashion of the pot of clay, does to the potter, when he has it before him, upon the wheel: and he is as able to quash it all, as the potter is to mar and alter the fashion of the vessel, when the making of it likes him not, Jer. 18.3,6. & 19.9,10. Job 12.22. & 26.6. Psal. 33.10,15. Prov. 15.19. Heb. 4.12,13. Yet there want not that render it, *Your turning*, or, *contriving*, of things, *is, as if the clay were accounted the potter*; or, *as if the potter were reputed as the clay*. And as others, again, *O your perverseness! as if the potter were accounted* no better, or no other, *than the clay*. But the former seems more natural; and is the more received, both with Jewish, and other writers.

*{for shall the work say of him that made it, He made me not? or shall the thing framed, say of him that framed it, He hath no understanding?*} Or, some render it; *for it is as if the work should say of the workman, He made me not; or the thing framed, should say of him that framed it, He understandeth me not*. That is, your vain imagination in supposing that you can conceal aught that you do, or devise from God, is even, as if the vessel, framed by the potter, should, if it could speak, say, that he is ignorant of the fashion of it, and by consequence deny, that ever he made it. For sure, if they did believe that God made them, they could not but withal conceive, that he cannot be ignorant of aught, in his own work, Psal. 33.15. & 94.8–11. & 139.1–5,13–15. 1 Chr. 28.9. Amos 4.13. See ch. 45.9,10.

*{for shall the work say*} Or, *for, it is, as if the work should say*. See the like concise forms, Josh. 2.12. Esth. 2.20. ch. 18.3. & 54.9. & 55.9. Howbeit, the particle, is used for an interrogative, ch. 36.19. and may so be here.

*{of him*} Heb. *to him*. So ch. 23.5. & 27.2.

*{or*} Heb. *and*: so ver. 15.

*{the thing framed*} The word is applied to the frame of man, both body and soul, Job 17.8. Psal. 103.14. and to the imaginations of man's heart, Gen. 6.5. Deut. 31.21. 1 Chr. 29.18. Properly, *potter's work*; but used, more generally, for any kind of *frame*, Hab. 2.18.

*{of him that framed it*} Or, *of its potter*. The word before used, to keep to the comparison, so ch. 64.8.

*{he hath no understanding*} Or, *he understandeth me not*. He knows not what my fashion is: applied to man, in regard of God, he knows not what I think, or do, Psal. 94.7. The pronoun is to be supplied, from the branch before going; as chap. 58.13. See the like defect, Job 16.8,9. and 29.11.

**V. 17.** *{Is it yet not a very little while, and Lebanon shall be turned into a fruitful field, and the fruitful field shall be esteemed as a forest?*} Heb. *Lebanon shall return to Carmel, and Carmel be counted for a wood*, or, *forest*. This some expound of a general devastation of the land; that mount Lebanon, being a place stored with goodly tall cedars, should become like *Carmel*, a place that had much arable ground, her cedars, and other tall trees being felled, and the *Carmel* of it, that is, their arable land, and places planted with vines, and other fruitful trees, should be so overgrown with shrubs, and wild plants, no man dressing, or manuring them, that they should seem to be as a forest. That, say they, which was effected by Sennacherib's army, overrunning the whole country, ch. 6.23,24. & 37.24. and came to pass, within a short time after this prophecy. See ver. 1. And the letter of the text seems to look this way. Yet others expound it parabolically, that the proud, lofty ones, like the cedars, should be pulled down; and low, and lowly ones, like the plants of Carmel, should be exalted: which, some of them, suppose fulfilled, in the breaking up of Sennacherib's camp, what time, the proud Assyrians were abased, and the Jews, in a very low condition, advanced, chapter 10.12,18,34. Others, in the Chaldean invasion, when the great ones, were either slain, or carried captive, and the poor sort only spared, 2 King. 25.6,7,12,18,21. chap. 2.12,13,17. & 6.15,17. & 7.21,22. & 40.5. Luk. 1.52. & 18.14. See ver. 20,21. Others again, refer it to the times of the Messiah, as importing a rejection of the Jews, and calling in of the Gentiles, that the Gentiles, who had been as savages, or as wild forests, fraught with barren and fruitless trees, should by spiritual managing and manuring, become orderly and fruitful; whereas the Jewish people that had been managed, and manured before; should grow wild and savage then. Now those all that thus expound this passage, seem to make it rather a commination, indeed than a promise, whereas, both by what here ensues, as also by chap. 32.15. where the very same is repeated, it appears, rather, to be a very gracious promise, of the great fertility and fruitfulness, that God would abundantly bless their land with, upon the restitution of their state, either after the Assyrian devastation, chap. 37.30,31. or after the Babylonian deportation, Jer. 31.12. or both: see chap. 4.2. So great, as some expound it, that the wild places, that now lay forest-like, untilled, should become as fertile, as those places that are, at present, manured, and yield the most fruit; and those places that are now most fertile, should then so abound with fruit, that they might well be reckoned, but as wild woods, in regard of what then they should be: Or rather, as with the Jewish commenters, I conceive it, that the woody, like *Lebanon*: that yielded nothing but matter for building and fuel, should then be tilled, as *Carmel*, to yield grain and fruit, affording plenty of food; and those that had been before such, as were now so tilled, should be so replenished with corn, and fruitful trees, that they should seem to be as a wood. See Psal. 72.16. This I suppose to be the first, proper, and literal sense of the words: which if any yet deem, further, to intimate the abundance of graces, in the kingdom of Christ, I shall not contend with him. See chap. 30.25,26. & 32.15. & 35.1,2.

*{a very little while*} Heb. *a little small*; as ch. 10.25. and it may seem to have reference to the Assyrian invasion, and the consequents thereof; both here and there, albeit, that some passages before, v. 2–8. seem to reach further.

*{Lebanon*} Of this mountain; see on ch. 2.13. It is sometime used for lofty, and stately places and persons, as there; and ch. 10.34. Jer. 22.23. but here for wild, and untilled places, as appears by chap. 32.15. where that is termed *wilderness*, that is here called *Lebanon*.

*{shall be turned into*} Heb. *shall return to*. He seems to allude to their *turnings*, and windings, v. 16. which should be frivolous, and frustrate; and to foretell, for the comfort of the faithful, another manner of *turning*, and change, that God himself would work for his; without any plots, or projects of theirs.

*{a fruitful field*} Heb. *Carmel*. The word primarily, signifies *a green*, or *full*: as some, ear of corn, Levit. 2.14. & 23.14. 2 King. 4.42. From whence, *grounds arable*, or *cornfields*, are thought to have been first so termed; though afterward it were enlarged to such lands, as were not sown with, or set apart for corn only, but tilled, and manured for other purposes, and planted with vines, fig trees, or olive trees, and the like: opposed therefore, to woods and forests, or wildernesses, that were suffered to run wild, or to lie waste, and were stored only, with fruitless trees, Cant. 2.3. chap. 10.18. & 16.10. and 32.15,16. and 37.24. And in regard of much ground of that nature, lying on, and about them, some places in the land of Judah and Israel, had that name, in more special manner, appropriated unto them, Josh. 15.15. & 19.46. chap. 33.9. See chap. 10.18.

*{shall be esteemed as a forest*} Heb. *shall be accounted for a forest*. Or, *be counted a forest*: shall seem to be such.

**V. 18.** *{In that day, shall the deaf hear the words of the book, and the eyes of the blind shall see out of obscurity, and out of darkness*} Our prophet here, after his usual manner, begins to close up his sermon with matter of comfort, in the better information and reformation of some that had been ignorant, and averse, v. 18. the confirmation, and abundant consolation of the godly, v. 19. the confusion, and destruction of those that had wronged and oppressed them, ver. 20,21. the vindication of them from their former shame and reproach, v. 22. the propagation, and enlargement of the church by conversion of many proselytes, ver. 23,24. All which seem to have been, in part, made good to that people, in those times, but was to be more plentifully fulfilled, in the kingdom of Christ.

*{In that day*} When these afflictions before-mentioned shall befall this people; as ch. 2.7. & 4.1. or, after the time, that these afflictions have befallen them, and the land and state reformed by them, the obstinate wicked ones being destroyed, and the residue reclaimed and refined, ch. 1.25,28. as ch. 4.2.

*{shall the deaf hear—and the eyes of the blind shall see*} This some expound, of those willfully blinded, and obstinate profane ones before-mentioned, v. 10,15. that howsoever now they neither believed, or regarded aught, that by God's prophets was foretold them; yet when things foretold were now fulfilled, they should be constrained to take notice of, and to acknowledge the truth of them, chap. 26.11. Ezek. 2.5. & 6.10. So it should be matter, not of mercy so much, as of judgment. But others, and so the most, rather understand it of a gracious work upon the souls of many, that being possessed with spiritual deafness, and blindness before, should then, being, by the Spirit of God, cooperating with the ministry of his messengers, cured, and recovered of these their former maladies, attend unto God's messages, conceive them aright, give all credit, and yield all obedience thereunto, Job 33.14–16,23–26. chap. 35.5. Luke 4.18. John 9.29. Act. 26.18. Eph. 1.18. Rev. 3.18.

*{hear*} *To hear*, both here, and elsewhere, in Scripture, is not barely to give one the hearing, as we use to say; as chap. 6.9. & 42.19,20. Mat. 13.14,19. Act. 22.12. but to hear with attention, with understanding, with belief, with obedience, Deut. 6.3,4. & 26.17. 1 Sam. 15.22. Mat. 13.9. Acts 26.14. Heb. 4.2.

*{of the book*} Or, *letter*; as v. 11. which this passage has an eye to, either of God's law; as Deut. 6.6. & 31.11. Josh. 1.8. or the message of God's prophets, more specially related to in that place. See ch. 30.20,21. neither should they be then, as a *book*, or *letter sealed up*; as before they had been, v. 11.

*{shall see out of obscurity, and out of darkness*} That is, coming *out of obscurity*, or *a mist* (see chap. 8.22.) *and out of the dark*. See the like defective speech, Ps. 45.8. ch. 38.17. being brought out of that spiritual mist and darkness, wherein they were before involved, ch. 9.2. & 25.7. & 49.6. Luke 1.77,79. & 2.32. Col. 1.12,13. 1 Pet. 2.9. Yet those that apply this to the obstinate, partly, by *darkness*, understand that darkness, that they endeavored to hide their projects in, ver. 15.

**V. 19.** *{The meek also shall increase their joy in the Lord*} The sincerely godly, and faithful ones, shall have abundance of joy and comfort, having both escaped and survived those grievous calamities, and being freed from the oppression of those ungodly great ones now rooted out, who were formerly a terror to them, ver. 20,21. Psalm 58.10,11. and 68.1–3. chap. 35.10. and 66.10,11. Acts 9.31.

*{The meek also*} Heb. *And the meek*; as ch. 22.9.

*{meek*} Such are the sincere godly; though, therefore the rather, meanly esteemed in the world, Psalm 25.9. and 37.11. Mat. 5.5. Gal. 5.23. therein conformable to Christ their head, Mat. 11.29. & 21.5.

*{shall increase their joy*} Heb. *shall add joy*: *to add to*, for *to increase*; as ch. 26.15. they shall have joy upon joy, abundance of joy, ch. 61.10. Joh. 15.11. Phil. 4.4. 1 Pet. 1.6,8. 1 Joh. 1.5. a defect of the pronoun, as ch. 13.22.

*{joy in the Lord*} Or, *through the Lord joy*: for so lie the words in the original; through him, that is, by means of his mercy, and goodness showed to them (as ch. 26.13.) they have much joy: and so it imports the cause, or means, whereby they attained unto this their joy, Ps. 21.1,2. or they have much joy, that is, abundance of spiritual joy; as implying the ground, or the subject matter and quality of it; Ps. 32.11. & 63.14. & 97.12. Phil. 3.1. the order of the words seems to lead to the former.

*{and the poor among men shall rejoice in the Holy One of Israel*} The same, in effect though in other terms, with the former.

*{the poor among men*} Heb. *the needy*, (as chap. 25.4. & 22.7.) *of Adam*, that is, *of man*, or *mean man*. See chap. 2.9. *the poor of men*, as *the wise of women*, Prov. 14.1. that is, *the wise among women*: and *the poor of the people*, for *the poor among the people*, Exod. 23.11. or, *the poor of men*, that is, *the poorest of men*; as *the base of men*, that is, *the basest of men*, Dan. 4.17. and *the bad of the heathen*, for *the worst of them*, Ezek. 7.24. See chap. 14.30. the most poor and needy, even of the meaner sort of men, that were formerly spoiled, and made a prey to the great ones, chap. 3. v. 14,15. for among them also, God has his, and has a special care of them, Psal. 9.18. & 10.14,17,18. & 12.5. and 40.17. Matth. 5.3. and 11.5. Luke 6.20. 1 Cor. 1.26,29.

*{the Holy One of Israel*} See ch. 1.4.

**V. 20.** *{For the terrible one is brought to nought*} Those are destroyed, that were before a terror to them, v. 5. see ch. 16.4.

*{and the scorner is consumed*} The crew of the scorners and mockers is wasted away. See chap. 28.14, 22.

*{and all that watch for iniquity are cut off*} Heb. *watchers of iniquity*, that study how to do mischief, Psalm 36.4. Mich. 2.1. and watch opportunity to put it in execution, as wild beasts lie in wait to prey and spoil, Psalm 10.9. Jer. 5.6.

**V. 21.** *{That make a man an offender for a word*} The verb in its first light form signifies, *to sin*; in its first weighty form, *to expiate or take away sin*, Num. 19.19. Psalm 51.8. in its second light active form, first, and properly, *to make one sin*, himself, Eccles. 5.6. or some other, 1 Kings 14.16. & 15.30. so most frequently; but sometime, also, in a less proper sense, *to make one guilty*; either by accusing, or condemning, as guilty, be it rightfully, or wrongfully. Now of this use of the word, albeit, I meet not, as yet, with any instance in Scripture, save this here only; yet I doubt not, but that it may well be warranted; first, by the use of another of the like notion, that signifies properly, *to make wicked*; but is thus very frequently, and familiarly taken, Deut. 25.1. Job 9.20. & 10.2. Prov. 7.15. chap. 50.9. & 54.17. and secondly, by the common use of its opposite; which signifying properly, *to make just*, Dan. 12.3. Yet is most commonly used, for *to acquit, assoil, pronounce, or defend as guiltless*, and free from offense, Exod. 23.7. Deut. 25.1. 1 Kings 8.32. Job 27.5. Psalm 82.3. Chap. 50.8. See ch. 5.23. where the condemning of one unjustly, is said to be a *taking of his righteousness from him*: Nor do we in any other sense use the word *justify*; nor the apostles in their writings, that word otherwise, for the most part, that answers the Hebrew term, Rom. 3.28. & 4.2. & 5.1. & 8.33. Gal. 2.16. Now in regard of the twofold notion, and use of the word, some taking it here, in his first and proper sense, would have the false prophets meant, who by their words and lies, made men to sin, Jer. 23.16, 17, 26, 27. Ezek. 13.10, 19, 22. But the prophet seems not here to be dealing with such, save as they might also be evil instruments, in the bad practices here spoken of, and the most therefore, both Jewish, and ours, understand it of great oppressors, and other wicked ones, their complices; or herein like them, that for a word slipping, from a man unawares, or some speech of his, perverted and misconstrued by them, would be ready to question him, molest him, bring him into trouble, and either procure, or pronounce a sentence and doom against him, as a delinquent, Jer. 18.18. & 20.10. Mat. 22.15. and 26.61. Luke 11.53, 54.

*{and lay a snare for him, that reproveth in the gate*} A metaphor from the practice of fowlers, that set springs and gins for birds, Psal. 91.3. Prov. 6.5. and so do these, for God's prophets, their teachers, devising which way to ensnare them, and create trouble to them; yea, take their lives from them, out of their extreme malice, and deadly hatred, that they bear them, for their seasonable and wholesome reproofs, which they cannot abide, Mat. 22.45, 46. and 22.15, 16, 18. and 26.3, 4, 14–16. and 27.18. Luke 23.2. Acts 9.29. and 23.24, 25.

*{that reproveth in the gates*} That is, in public; for the gates of their cities, were places, wherein there was usually much confluence of people; in regard, that both matters of judicature, and other public affairs, were there commonly transacted, Deut. 17.5. and 21.19. and 22.15, 24. 2 Kings 7.17, 18, 20. as also, *the gates of the Temple*, were places of much concourse, 1 Sam. 2.22. 2 Kings 20.4. Jer. 26.10. for which cause, the prophets, also, delivered God's messages in the gates sometimes of the Temple, Jer. 7.2. sometimes of the king's house, and of the city, as well as in the Temple, Jer. 17.19. and 22.2. and I rather, therefore, concur with those, that render the words according to our version here, *and lay a snare for him, that reproveth in the gate*; than with those, that would have them read, *they lay a snare in the gate, for him that reproveth*: especially finding the very same elsewhere, *they hate him that reproveth in the gate*, Amos 5.10.

*{and turn aside the just for a thing of nought*} That pick quarrels against men and in judgment, prosecute and cast them, being otherwise guiltless; either for matters of no moment, or worth (as 1 Sam. 12.21.) or for things that are not: for nothing (as Job 6.18.) without any weighty or just cause, Ps. 69.4, 5. or, as others, that by vain and frivolous pretenses, and falsehoods, turn aside, or cause to go the wrong way, the cause of the righteous; as ch. 41.29. Of the word, see ch. 24.10.

*{turn aside*} Heb. *make to decline*; and in matter of judicature, it is applied sometime to the party questioned, sometime to the carriage of his cause: when to the party questioned, it imports to wrong him, and, causelessly, *to cast, or condemn* him, Prov. 18.5. *it is not good to accept the person of the wicked, or to overthrow, or depress, or cast the righteous in judgment*: and ch. 10.2. *to turn aside, or force aside the needy from judgment*: and again, *they turn aside the poor in the gate, from their right*, Amos 5.12. & Mal. 3.5. *that turn away the stranger*, to wit, from his right: when to the cause, or the course of judicature, it implies, *a perverting* of the right, and even carriage of the business, Exod. 23.6. *Thou shalt not pervert the judgment of thy poor in his cause*: and *cursed be he that perverteth the judgment of fatherless, stranger, or widow*, Deut. 27.19. and, *To turn aside, or pervert the right, or judgment of a man*, Lam. 3.35. and Prov. 17.23. *A wicked man taketh a gift out of the bosom, to pervert the ways of judgment*: to which purpose, that also seems to be intended, Amos 2.7. of *perverting, or turning aside the way, or course of the meek*: to wit, by oppressing and over-swaying them in matter of judicature. All which laid together, induces me to conceive, that as there is an ellipsis, or defect, of the word *judgment*, signifying a *judiciary proceeding* in that injunction, Exod. 23.2. *Thou shalt not speak in a cause declining, or turning aside to great ones*; that is, to *make judgment declined, or to turn aside* (for that the word is to be supplied there, appears by ver. 9. above related) so that in most of the places, if not all, before produced, where the person alone is mentioned, the same word is to be supplied not by annexing it, as our version does, Amos 5.12. and Mal. 3.5. to the close of the sentence, but by inserting of it in the body of it, *that pervert, or turn aside the poor, and the stranger*, that is, *the judgment of the poor, and the stranger*, and the like: as it is expressed, Deut. 27.19. & Lam. 3.35. the word may well be rendered, according to the native notion, and proper use of it; either *to divert, or turn aside*, and then it is a metaphor taken, either from the forcing of man or beast, out of his course or way; as it is used of Balaam's beating his ass *to turn her aside again*, Num. 22.23. & Ps. 125.5. *those that turn aside to crooked ways*: and chap. 30.11. *go out of the way, turn aside out of the path*; and so it is, to cause a diversion from a direct way, and straight line of justice and equity, in the carriage of a man's cause: or it may be rendered, *to depress, or over-sway*; as it is used oft, for *to incline, or bow down*, Gen. 24.14. Ps. 31.2. Prov. 5.1. & 7.21. Amos 2.8. and so it may be in allusion to the use of a balance, such as Justice is wont to be deciphered, holding in her hand, that which seems glanced at, Psal. 58.2. as being an over-swaying, or swaying down the balance of judgment or justice the one way, the wrong way, (whereas it ought to hang even and level) to the prejudice of the guiltless party. A learned annotator renders the words a new way, *they make the just to decline into the waste, or desert*; that is, by setting snares for him, in the gate; so that he cannot (without hazard of life) enter the city, they enforce him to betake himself unto waste places, and to live as an exile in the wilderness, as David wished he could; Psal. 55.7. Jeremie, that he might, Jer. 9.2. yea, as David, and others, sometime were constrained to do, 1 Sam. 24.1. & 26.3, 19, 20. Heb. 11.38. and indeed the word here is applied sometime to waste places, but not put for them. See Jer. 4.23. but the received version seems the genuine, and more familiar.

**V. 22.** *{Therefore, thus saith the Lord, who redeemed Abraham, concerning the house of Jacob; Jacob shall not now be ashamed: neither shall his face now wax pale*} The reproach and contempt which God's people formerly endured, and the fears and terrors that they were formerly exposed unto, what by the adversary from abroad, or by the great men that oppressed them at home, shall be utterly removed, chap. 25.8. & 54.4. & 61.7.

*{Wherefore*} Considering how they have been formerly wronged, as well at home, as from abroad, verse 20, 21. Psalm 12.5.

*{thus saith the Lord*} As ch. 51.22.

*{who redeemed Abraham*} Or, *rescued and delivered*; so is the word ordinarily used, 2 Sam. 4.9. 1 Kings 1.29. Psal. 55.18. & 107.2. that called him from, and brought him out of an idolatrous place and people, Gen. 12.1. Job 24.2, 3. though that Abraham himself, ever was an idolater, does not thence appear: or, that rescued him out of, and preserved him from many dangers and distresses, that he was exposed unto, and might have otherwise been surprised with, by means of those strange people of several countries, through which he traveled, and among whom he sojourned, Gen. 12.3. & 15.1. Ps. 105.12, 14, 15. See Gen. 48.16.

*{concerning*} Heb. *unto*: See ch. 37.33.

*{the house of Jacob*} The Jewish people, his family descended from him their father, ch. 2.5.

*{Jacob*} This some understand of the person of Jacob: Jacob, who if he were alive, would be ashamed to see his children fallen from God, shall now have no cause of any such shame. But by *Jacob*, is here meant, rather, Jacob's posterity, the *house*, or family of *Jacob*, before mentioned. See ch. 9.8. & 14.1.

*{not now*} As formerly, ch. 7.2. & 30.5.

*{be ashamed*} Heb. *blush*, Ezra 9.6. Jer. 6.15. for shame, Psalm 44.15.

*{his face wax pale*} Heb. *white*: for though the verb be nowhere else in Scripture read; yet the nouns derived from it, are elsewhere found, and so signify, Dan. 7.9. Est. 1.6. & 8.15. *pale, for fear*, Jer. 30.6. though some make this the same with the former, understanding both of shame, and Joel 2.6. *blackness, or swartness* of face, is made an effect of extreme fear.

**V. 23.** *{But when he seeth his children, the work of mine hands in the midst of him, they shall sanctify my name, and shall sanctify the holy one of Jacob, and shall fear the God of Israel*} To the removal of their former reproach, shame and fear, is a further blessing added, that should much enhance their forementioned joy, v. 19. the consideration of a large increase of an holy issue, that God should bless his church with, not such ignorant, formal, and profane ones, as it consisted of formerly; but an understanding people, new molded, bringing honor to his name, and serving him sincerely, according to his will and word; for whom it shall have abundant occasion of blessing of God, for blessing it with such increase.

*{But*} As chap. 2.6. yet some, *For*: as chap. 28.27. and of these, some thus render the words, *For he seeing, or in his sight, his children, the work of my hands in the midst of him, shall sanctify my name*: and the reading seems not improbable. Howbeit I never find, this form so used in an absolute notion.

*{when he*} That is, *Jacob* himself, say some; as ver. 22. but I suppose it taken, both here, and there, for the posterity of *Jacob*, the Jewish church and State, considered, as a body. For howsoever it be true, that the church of professors consists and is made up of those particular persons, that profess the true service of God in Christ; and the church of sincere faithful ones, is constituted of those particular persons, that are truly converted, and sincerely sanctified; yet as the one, or the other make up an entire body, whether political, or spiritual; so is the church, consisting of those particular persons of either sort, said to be, as a mother to them; and those particular persons that make up that body, are said to be, as children unto it, ch. 54.1. & 60.4, 5. Gal. 4.26, 27.

*{seeth his children*} As of Christ, *he shall see his seed*, Chap. 53.10. or *his children in his sight*, as before, his children, the true race of Jacob, Psa. 24.6. Gal. 6.15, 16. that walk in the steps of faithful Abraham, John 8.39. Rom. 4.12.

*{the work of my hands*} Psal. 138.8. ch. 43.21. & 60.21. Eph. 2.8. the regenerate, John 1.13. James 1.18. 1 Pet. 1.3, 23. a kind of new creature, Psal. 51.10. 2 Cor. 5.17. Gal. 6.15.

*{in the midst of him*} *with him*, or *among him*: as chap. 19.1, 3. for he speaks here of Jacob, as there of Egypt: of either, as of a body, for State: which shows, that by Jacob, here cannot be understood the person of Jacob, but his posterity.

*{they*} To wit, *Jacob*: before, *he*; now *they*: a passage from number to number; as ch. 14.1. whereby the term appears to be collective; unless we follow the latter mentioned version.

*{shall sanctify my name*} They shall honor me for this favor, and by their religious carriage, *sanctify my name*, which, by the profane, and irreligious demeanor of others, had been so exceedingly defiled, and polluted among them before, Ezek. 20.39, 41. & 22.26. & 36.20. Amos 2.7. Mal. 1.6, 7. Rom. 2.24.

*{and shall sanctify*} Or, *yea, they shall sanctify*, as ch. 3.9. because it is but a repetition of the same thing, for the more vehemency. Howsoever there want not some, that distinguish them, reading the text, *when he seeth his children—sanctifying my name*, or *how they sanctify it; then shall they sanctify*, etc. but the words run more easily the other way.

*{the holy one of Jacob*} As, *the holy one of Israel*, verse 19.

*{and shall fear*} Serve and worship, with fear and reverence, Psal. 2.11. & 5.7. Hos. 3.5. Heb. 12.28.

**V. 24.** *{They also that erred in spirit shall come to understanding; and they that murmured, shall learn doctrine*} Such as were untractable, and unteachable before, shall then become pliable, and voluntarily yield themselves to the word of God's prophets, and the work of his Spirit, as ready and willing to be instructed, and new molded by either, Psal. 110.3. ch. 11.6–9. ver. 18. Rom. 6.17.

*{that erred in spirit*} That were possessed, and led away by a spirit of error, as all are by nature, Psal. 58.3. & 95.10. ch. 53.6. until the Spirit from above be poured forth upon them, chap. 32.15. to enlighten their minds, Eph. 5.18. 2 Cor. 4.4. Heb. 6.4. & 10.32. and to lead them into all necessary saving truth, Luke 1.79. Joh. 14.26. & 16.13. 1 John 2.20, 27.

*{shall come to understanding*} They shall not be like those, that either refuse to be taught, and to learn aught, Psalm 35.33. & 82.3. Jer. 9.6. or are ever learning, but never attain to any degree of sound knowledge, chap. 28.9–11. 2 Tim. 3.7. Heb. 5.12. Hebr. *shall know understanding*: as Pro. 4.1. that is, *shall have understanding*: as the like is rendered, Job 38.4. or, *shall be able to understand*; as Neh. 10.28. *every knowing understanding one*: for so the text there is, *every one able to understand*; as in the same chap. ver. 3. *understanding to hear*, for, *able to hear with understanding*: *to know* for *to be able*, as chap. 28.11.

*{they that murmured*} Such as were formerly ready, out of discontent and impatience, or out of a crossness of spirit, and untoward disposition, 1 Tim. 1.25. to be ever, and anon, repining at, and murmuring against the passages of God's providence, and messages of his ministers, Exod. 16.2. & 17.3. Num. 11.1. Deut. 1.27. Psal. 116.25. 1 Cor. 10.10. Some apply it unto the Jews, that murmured at the calling, and coming in of the Gentiles, Matth. 20.11. Luke 15.28–30. Acts 11.2, 3. & 13.45. & 22.21, 22. as 1 Thess. 2.16.

*{learn doctrine*} The word signifies, properly, such a *lesson*, or instruction, as is by teaching, *received* from another. The word is used, Deut. 32.2. Job 11.4. Prov. 1.5. & 4.2. & 16.23. where it is sometime rendered *learning*, and it is so called, because in teaching and *learning*, there is a kind of *giving* and *receiving*, Prov. 1.3, 4. & 8.10. & 9.9. Yet some of the critics would have it, properly, to signify *a pleasant*, and delightful *speech*, that easily finds acceptance, because used of the harlot, (whose *lips drop like an honeycomb*, and her language is *smoother than oil*, Prov. 5.3.) Prov. 7.22. where it is rendered, *fair speech*. To which purpose they allege also, Prov. 16.21, 23. So it should be, that which the apostle calls *an acceptable speech*, or, *a lesson worthy of all acceptation*, 1 Tim. 1.15. & c. 4.9. But the former reason seems the sounder. See Luke 8.13–15. Acts 2.41. & 8.14. & 11.1. & 17.11.

### CHAPTER 30

**V. 1.** *{Woe to the rebellious children, saith the Lord, that take counsel, but not of me, and that cover with a covering, but not of my Spirit, that they may add sin to sin*} It was the usual manner of the Jewish State, and people, and that sometime, under the better sort of their kings, when they were annoyed, or invaded, or expected some such matter from some neighboring nation, or other, instead of staying themselves upon God, and his protection, as, by his prophets, he advised them, to seek for succor and assistance to some foreign State, to the Syrians, against the Israelites, 2 Chr. 16.2, 3. to the Assyrians against the Syrians, 2 King. 16.7. Hos. 5.13. & 7.11. & 12.1. to the Egyptians against the Assyrians, one while, Chap. 20.5, 6. 2 Kings 18.21. Hos. 12.1. against the Chaldeans, another while, Jer. 2.18, 36. & 37.5. Ezek. 29.6, 7. In this kind they were faulty, as well in Esay's, as in Jeremie's time, by fleeing either into, or unto Egypt; and seeking shelter there, or succor thence. Against those that were thus delinquent, does the prophet, principally, bend himself, both in this chapter, and in the next. In the former part of this chapter, he reproves them sharply, first, for taking courses of their own, to secure themselves, and confiding therein, without seeking to God: withal, showing what the success and issue of such their courses should be, ver. 1.7. And secondly, for their opposing of God's prophets, that dissuaded the one, and forewarned them of the other, ver. 8.14. and standing out willfully, against those advices, that, by them, God had given, for their indemnity and safety, verse 15, 17. In the later part, he passes for the comfort of God's people, to gracious promises. First of protection of his faithful ones, in those troublesome times, verse 18, 19. Secondly, of future favors, upon their reformation and amendment, v. 2–26. and the destruction of the adversary, by whom they had been afflicted, and straitened, ver. 27–33.

*{Woe to*} As chap. 29.15.

*{the rebellious children*} *Children*, because of the Jewish nation; God's adopted people, and professing themselves so to be, Deut. 32.6, 9. chap. 1.2. and 43.1. and 44.1, 2. and 64.8. Jer. 3.4, 5. *rebellious*, or *refractory*, or *unruly*: (as Deut. 21.18. Hos. 4.16. where *a backsliding heifer*, seems no very fit epithet) because refusing to be ruled by God, and obstinately addicted unto ways and courses of their own, Deut. 32.5, 15. chap. 1.2. and 63.10. and 66.3. Jer. 3.14. and 5.23.

*{that take counsel, but not of me*} Heb. *to make counsel*, or *in making counsel*: that is, holding a consultation: as noting that wherein they showed themselves to be such: as chap. 3.8. Heb. *and not of me*: and so in the next branch; and chap. 29.13. that consult; but will not have God of their counsel, Josh. 9.14. refuse to consult with him, as their duty was to do, chap. 8.19.

*{that cover with a covering, but not of my Spirit*} Heb. *to cover*; or, *in covering*, (as before) with a *covering*; as chap. 22.17, 18. The same word, chap. 25.7. and 28.20. that take courses to secure themselves, other than I, by my Spirit, direct them unto. See ch. 4.5. & 28.15. & 29.15.

*{that they may add sin to sin*} Heb. *sin upon sin*: as 2 Chron. 28.13. Ezra 10.10. That is, thereby adding sin to sin. Of which manner of speech, see on chap. 3.8. and Jer. 7.18. *adding sin to sin*, that is, proceeding, and going on still in sinful courses: as chap. 29.14. or proceeding from one sinful course to another: and heaping up excesses one upon another: as chap. 29.19. Numbers 32.14. Whereas by their wicked ways, they had before provoked me unto wrath, instead of seeking to me, by repentance for the same, they add to their former evil carriage, a new sinful course, by ways of their own, contrary to mine admonition and advice, endeavoring to shift off, or shelter themselves against my judgments, ready to seize on them; for their former sins. See somewhat the like, 1 Samuel 12.19. Luke 3.19, 20. Those that refer this to the times of Zedekiah, expound it, adding to their treachery and perjury, in rebelling against the King of Babel (in regard whereof, also, they would have them here termed rebellious) Ezek. 17.13, 15. by distrust of God, and confidence in human helps. But whether the word translated *rebellious*, will so well sort with this exposition, I am somewhat doubtful: of the application of the Prophecy, to those times; more anon. Meanwhile if we shall descend to particulars, we may as well expound the *adding of sin to sin*; their adding of sin, in seeking aid now from Egypt, against the Assyrians, to their former sin, in seeking the like from Assyria, against the Israelites, and the Syrians, 2 Chr. 28.16. But I conceive the words to be more general: as the like, Deut. 29.19.

**V. 2.** *{That walk to go down into Egypt, (and have not asked at my mouth) to strengthen themselves in the strength of Pharao, and to trust in the shadow of Egypt*} In these words, the prophet more particularly, declares what the counsel and course was, that he condemned in them, and for which he denounced a woe against them verse 1. to wit, their running into Egypt, and relying on that State for shelter and safeguard. Now this, many of our interpreters turn over to Zedekiah's time. And it is true, that in those days both before the surprisal of Jerusalem, they sought to Egypt for succor, Jere. 37.7. Ezek. 17.15. as also after it, upon the death of Gedaliah, they fled thither for shelter, Jer. 43.4–7. But the prophet seems rather to bend his speech against those of his own times, who under Ezekiah, also were faulty in this kind, to wit, in having recourse unto Egypt, and relying on it for safety and assistance, against the Assyrian forces; as appears plainly, ch. 20.5,6. see there. Nor does aught appear to me, in this whole sermon, concluding, with the fall of Senacherib, as all grant and agree in, that may not very fitly, accord with those times.

*{walk to go down into Egypt*} That is, *journey, or, travel* (out of their own land) *to go into Egypt;* as 2 Sam. 19.20. *Am come down to meet the King.* The word *walking,* applied usually to travelers, Gen. 32.1. and that of *descending, or going down;* as here; so Gen. 26.2. chap. 52.4. of passing from place to place, without any special reference to the situation of places, or any peculiar notion of descent included, Judg. 15.8. 2 Sam. 19.26. See Chap. 38.8. And there is no necessary implication therefore (which the Rabbins would have) of their land, being higher than the land of Egypt. Into Egypt it is not unlikely, that many fled out of divers parts of Judea; upon Senacheribs irruption: and no less probable, that from some of the principal in the State, if not not from Ezekiah himself, some message also, was sent thither, and motion made for aids from thence, ver. 4. when it appeared, that the Assyrian, by the presents sent him, would not be appeased, 2 King. 18.13–17.

*{and have not asked my mouth*} Or, *but* (as ver. 1.) *ask not counsel of me,* or, *consult not with me,* what they should do; as Josh. 9.14. either by Priest; as 1 Sam. 23.9,10. or by prophet; as 1 Kin. 22.7. See 2 King. 1.3.

*{to strengthen themselves in the strength of Pharaoh*} Or, *by the strength;* as Psal. 78.26. A defect of the Pronoun; as chap. 13.8,15.

*{the shadow*} That is, *the covert.* Of which ver. 1. *shadow,* for *protection;* as Judg. 9.15. Eccles. 7.12. Cant. 2.3. A metaphor, taken either from hens, or other fowl, that secure their young, by overshadowing them with their wings, Psal. 17.8. & 91.1,4.
