Mat. 23.37. or from goodly fair trees, that afford shelter against heat and storm, unto man and beast, that come under their spreadings, Lam. 4.20. Ezek. 31.6. Dan. 4.12,14.

**V. 3.** *{Therefore shall the strength of Pharao be your shame, and the trust in the shadow of Egypt your confusion*} Or, *And your trust* (a defect of the pronoun; as Psal. 45.3.) *in the shadow of Egypt your ignominy,* or, *disgrace;* as Psal. 71.13. Heb. *And the strength of Pharao, &c.* as Jer. 1.17. & 6.11. Or, *For the strength, &c.* as chap. 13.8. & 16.2. rendering a reason of woe denounced, ver. 1. to wit, The ill success of these their counsels and courses: which should turn all to their confusion and shame; when they should by experience, find to their grief and smart, that they were altogether unable to do them any good, verse 5. See Chap. 20.5,6. & 30.6. Jer. 37.7. & 38.22.

**V. 4.** *{For his Princes were at Zoan, and his Ambassadors came to Hanes*} Or, as some render it, *when* (as Joel 2.20.) *his Princes had been at Zoan, and his Ambassadors had arrived at Hanes: his Princes, and his Ambassadors:* That is, say the Jewish Commenters, either the kings, or the peoples. Some of the chief about the king sent in embassage to the King of Egypt, to crave his assistance against the Assyrian; as they before had sent to the Assyrian, to obtain peace, 2 King. 8.14. but with as sorry success in the one, as in the other ch. 33.7. See the like of Hoshea, 2 King. 17.4. See also ch. 57.9. & Hos. 12.1.

*{Zoan*} A famous city in Egypt. See chap. 19.11.

*{came to*} Heb. *touched at.* Or, *reached unto;* as Psal. 88.7.

*{Hanes*} Another city of Egypt, called also, *Tahapanes,* Jer. 2.16. See more of it there. And *Tahpanhes,* Jer. 43.3,8.

**V. 5.** *{They were all ashamed of a people, that could not profit them, nor be an help, nor profit, but a shame also, and a reproach*} When they came into Egypt, they sped so ill, that they returned with nothing but shame and disgrace; and so was fulfilled what was foretold; v. 3. Spoken here in the wonted prophetical strain, as a thing already past and done.

*{They were all ashamed*} Heb. *Each, or every one,* (to wit, of those that went, or were sent, say the Rabbins; but we may well add both of them, that were sent, and of those also, that sent them) *was ashamed.* So the word is most frequently used, in an immanent, or standing notion, Jer. 2.26. & 8.9,12. & 10.14. & 48.20. & 50.2. Ezek. 9.52. Joel 1.10,12. Zach. 9.5. & 10.11. Nor see I therefore, why some late learned Interpreters should render it here in a transitive, or passing sense; *He* (that is, the king, say they,) *shall shame them all;* that is, all his people, or all those of Jerusalem. Though the verb be sometime found in an active use; but then mostly, if not wholly, in a notion, not of *shaming,* but of *drying up;* as Psal. 74.15. Ezek. 17.24.

*{that could not profit them*} A defect of the relative, as chap. 10.2,3. Heb. *will not,* or, *shall not profit.* But the future is oft used potentially. So 1 Sam. 12.21. Jer. 2.11. Yet some render it, *would not profit them.* Psammetichus then King of Egypt, say they, would not break with the King of Assyria, whom he had formerly made peace with; and refused therefore to afford them any succor, or assistance against it. But these are mere conjectures, having no ground from story sacred, or other. More likely it is, that the Egyptian king, whoever he were, that then was, either dared not, by seeking to succor them, provoke so potent and prevalent a king as the Assyrian then was, having surprised, and carried captive, the other ten Tribes before; or if he made any attempt, it came to as little effect, as the aid that was afterward, out of those parts, sent to the support and succor of Zedekiah, Jer. 37.7. See verse 7.

*{nor be an help, nor profit*} Heb. *nor for help, nor to profit.* Beginning a new branch, not coupled to the former; as if he had said more fully, with supply from the former; of a people, I say, neither fitted for help, nor able to be any way useful to them: and not that alone; but that would be a foul shame, and disgrace unto them, in not answering their expectation, Chap. 20.6. See Jerem. 2.36.

**V. 6.** *{The burden of the beasts of the South: Into the land of trouble and anguish, from whence come the young and old lion, the viper, and fiery flying serpent, they will carry their riches upon the shoulders of young asses, and their treasures upon the bunches of camels, to a people that shall not profit them.*} The prophet proceeds to tax their extreme folly, in taking so much pains, and undertaking such toilsome and dangerous journeys, through the deserts of Arabia; to transport their goods and treasure into Egypt, either there to secure them; or thence to procure, and hire aids, from those, that should not be able to stand them in any stead.

*{The burden*} Some, at these words, would begin a new sermon, because the several prophecies, many of them, so begin: as chap. 21.1,11,13. but the continuation of the subject matter: and the sequel of the context, is such, as affords no probability for any such conceit. By the word, some would have understood, *a burdensome prophecy;* as chap. 13.1. and so the Greek, rendering it, *a vision.* But others rather take it in its proper sense, for *a burden:* as chap. 46.1. a place parallel to this.

*{of the beasts of the South*} Some, *for the beasts of the South:* that is, a burdensome prediction, for those brutish persons that toil and moil like beasts, to convey their goods to them, from whom there is nothing, but mischief and misery to be expected. And there is another word indeed, frequently used for *brutish men,* that signifies *a beast,* Psalm 73.62. & 91.6. Prov. 12.1. & 30.2. Jer. 10.10,14. but that here is used very seldom so, if ever, for those two places, Job 18.3. Eccles. 3.18. duly weighed, come not home here. By *beasts of the South,* therefore understand, the beasts hereafter mentioned, that carried their chattels and treasure into Egypt, which lay South from the land of Judah, Jer. 13.19. said here to be a burden to them, as the Babylonian Idols were to the beasts that bore them away, chap. 46.1. Some would have the word *burden,* taken here absolutely, rendering the text, *as for the burden of the beasts of the South:* or, *that travel Southward:* and the like construction is found, Psalm 18.30. & 104.17. Hos. 9.11. But the text may be read, admitting a trajection, not unusual, and joining it with the carriages afterward specified; *a burden for beasts, traveling Southward,* or bound for the South, *shall they carry,* to wit, *their riches, &c.* See the like trajections, Job 23.9. & 35.12. Psal. 17.7,13. & 89.50. & 90.11. & 140.11. chap. 29.23. & 41.27. Jer. 15.18,21.

*{into the land of trouble and anguish*} Heb. *into a land of affliction or, distress and anguish,* Prov. 1.27. that is, as some, into Egypt, alluding in the former word to the name thereof, wherewith it has some affinity in the Hebrew: and minding them of what hard usage they had there formerly found, Exod. 1.11,13,14. Deut. 4.20. & 16.3. and what only they might be sure from thence to expect. But others read the words, *by,* or *through a land of affliction and anguish:* for so also is that particle oft used, as Gen. 22.6. & 13.17. Est. 9.2. Psalm 19.4. chap. 37.29,34. & 42.3. that is, through that vast wilderness, that lay between the land of Judah and Egypt, which they passed through before, when they came thither from Egypt, and which they then found to be such, as is here related: See Deuter. 8.15. & 32.10. Jerem. 2.2,6. Yet some conceive; that in these terms, is described that narrow passage or neck of land lying between the red Sea, and the midland, by which they were to pass, ere they could enter into Egypt: but hereof there is no great probability, that neck of land being not so narrow, as should cause any such difficult passage, as the prophets words here imply.

*{from whence come the young and old lion, the viper, and fiery flying serpent*} Heb. *the Lion, and Lion from them,* that is, *from those parts:* or *from which parts:* the positive for the relative, as Job 33.15. Jer. 2.6. and a defect of the verb, as 2 Kings 6.32. Rom. 4.17. Now all this, divers Interpreters apply also to Egypt, expounding the words, some of the beasts, that were there adored, some of the wild beasts and serpents that abounded in Africa, and those parts of it, that neighbored upon Egypt. Others, again, not of any beasts, but of the Egyptians themselves, people, in condition, like to such beasts, and that should unto them prove such. See chap. [11].6,8. But to run to allegories, where a plain and proper sense, even offers itself, is unsafe: that such creatures as these were very rife, as well in the deserts of Arabia, as of Africa, cannot be doubted, much less denied. See Deut. 8.15. Of their way to Egypt, I conceive all this to be spoken, as not only tedious and difficile for want of needful accommodations, but as dangerous also, in regard of such harmful creatures as these, abounding in those parts, and from thence also, infesting the countries near to them.

*{the young and old lion*} There are two words here used, which both signify *a lion;* but with some difference, as is supposed; whether the one, *a young;* the other, *an old* one, as our version renders them, is uncertain. But of the several terms, wherewith *lions* are in Scripture designed, see the notes on Job 4.10.

*{the viper*} Or, as some, *the Basilisk;* a serpent so called, from a word that signifies, as some say, *to hiss,* Chap. 42.14. but the word there signifies, rather, *to cry out,* as a woman in travail: and another thence derived, the Rabbins are said to use, not for the *hissing* of serpents; but for the *bleating* of sheep; it is found also, Job 20.16. chap. 59.5. See there.

*{the fiery flying serpent*} Such as were in the wilderness, that the Israelites passed through, in their way to Canaan, Num. 21.16. Deut. 8.15. see Chap. 14.29.

*{they will carry their riches*} Or, *chattels,* so termed; because mens strength seems to lie in their wealth. These they carried into Egypt, some in likelihood, that fled their country upon the Assyrians approach, there to secure them: see Chap. 15.7. as those also, no doubt did, that fled into Egypt, upon the dispersion of the people, after the murder of Gedaliah, for fear of the Chaldeans, Jer. 43.5–7. Others, sent by the State, to procure help and aids against the enemies invasion.

*{upon the shoulders of young asses*} Heb. *shoulder:* as Chap. 46.7. the place that burdens bear most upon, Gen. 49.14,15. ch. 10.27. *of young asses;* of much use in these parts, as well for burden, as for saddle, Gen. 32.15. & 49.11. Judg. 10.4. & 12.14. Ch. 32.24. see chap. 21.7.

*{and their treasures*} Which some would distinguish from their *Chattels,* and restrain to their *Coin* or *Bullion;* but the one term is of as large extent, as the other: see Chap. 2.7. & 23.18. & 45.3.

*{upon the bunches of camels*} Heb. *bunch:* the word is nowhere else found in Scripture; and those Jewish Critics do but dally with us, that would have it so termed, because when galled with burdens, it was healed with *honey;* in regard that the words that signify either, arise from one root: the word is rather, by some other of them, deemed to be an Arabic term, for that camels, with the Arabians, were of more use ordinarily, than with any other people, Chap. 60.6,7. Jer. 49.29,32. they had, some kind of them, one; some, two bunches apiece, and were very useful for carriage, in regard of the great weight they were able to bear; but especially with those that were to travel through waste places, because they would continue long without water: see Chap. 21.7. From this their bunched body, arose that proverbial speech, of driving, or drawing *a camel through a needles eye,* Matth. 19.24. instead whereof, the Jewish Rabbins have another not unlike it, *to thread needles with Elephants.*

*{to*} Heb. *upon:* but so also used, Chap. 29.12. See ver. 1.

*{a people that shall not profit them*} Or, *cannot:* as verse 5. a defect of the relative; as verse 5. of the pronoun; as Chapter 29.19.

**V. 7.** *{For the Egyptians shall help in vain, and to no purpose*} Heb. *And;* as verse 3. *in vain, and to no purpose.* Heb. *in vanity, and inanity: vanity, even that which cannot profit,* Jer. 16.19. and *a vessel of inanity,* or *emptiness,* Jer. 51.34. that has nothing but wind in it; both here conjoined, to show what manner of relief, or succor, it was like to be, that the Egyptians should afford them. Yet hence it appears, that somewhat they attempted; as that from them, somewhat was expected, from chap. 29.5,6. So Jer. 37.7,8.

*{Therefore have I cried, concerning this, Their strength is to sit still*} Or, *Therefore do I cry unto her.* Either I the Lord (the prophet now speaking in the person of God, as verse 8.) Or, I Esay, do give them warning, and foretell them, with as much earnestness, as I can; as Prov. 1.24. Chap. 58.1. & 65.12. in the name of God, and by command from him; that it is their wisest course, and will prove their surest strength, quietly and patiently to rest, and to depend upon God, his protection and assistance; and not run to and fro, hunting after foreign helps, either from Egypt, or any other, v. 15. Chap. 28.12. Jer. 2.18,36. Hos. 5.13.

*{concerning this*} That is, concerning Egypt, and seeking to her for aid; as some of the Jewish Commenters: so is the particle used Chap. 29.16. or, as other of them, *to her,* to this city Jerusalem; or, *to the daughter of my people,* as the prophets use to speak, cha. 22.4. Jer. 26.14.

*{strength*} Heb. *Rahab:* a name given to Egypt, as is commonly supposed, from her power and pride: see Chap. 51.9. which term, the prophet, is by some, deemed here the rather to use; as implying, that this course, which he here advises them unto, would be a better and surer means of strength to them, than any that Egypt was able to afford. Yet can I not easily assent to the learned Annotator, who would have the text thus rendered; Therefore have I called here (that is, Egypt) *Rahab hem shabeth.* I have given Egypt this name, which signifies, *Rahab is a cessation;* the Egyptian power is ceased.

*{to sit still*} Not neglecting any lawful means of defense, which they are nowhere forbidden to do (save where God determined to give deliverance by miracle, and to manifest his might the more, enjoined a waving of them, Judg. 7.2,8,16,17.) nor condemned for so doing, 1 Kings 20.22. 2 Chro. 14.6,8. & 26.9–15. & 32.2–6. but not seeking assistance from other strange people, contrary to the charge herein given them by God; but relying upon him, as able, by such means, sufficiently to secure, as it pleased him, to assign, or afford them, 2 Chr. 32.7,8. Some think there is an allusion here, either to the words of Moses, Exod. 14.14. or of Jehaziel, 2 Chro. 20.17. *stand still:* the word *still,* being not in the text here is added, to make the sense, to us, more plain. Howsoever, hence it seems to me, to appear, that this prophecy has not reference to Zedekiahs time, for there, albeit, they were admonished, that Egypt should not relieve them: yet were they not advised, as here *to sit still,* but to go out, and yield themselves unto the enemy, Jer. 38.2,17,18.

**V. 8.** *{Now go, write it before them in a table, and note it in a book, that it may be for time to come, for ever, and ever.*} The words of God to the prophet, by whom, having forewarned them of the evil, that they would bring upon themselves, by looking abroad, and advised them of the surest course, that they could take for their own security and safeguard, he now wills him, to put in writing, what he had delivered unto them, that it might remain, as upon record, for a testimony against them, of their disobedience and distrust.

*{go*} See chap. 20.2. so Gen. 11.3. Jer. 35.22. & 50.5. for there is, no necessity, as some would have this term intimate, that the prophet should be abroad, when God set him this task, and that he was willed to get him home to accomplish it.

*{write it*} This prophecy, or that which follows, ver. 8. but the former rather: see chap. 8.1.

*{before them*} Heb. *with them.* This some conceive, as if God commanded the prophet to go out of his house, and commit to writing openly, in some public place, in the view of the people, what he had before by word of mouth delivered: which conceit, crosses that, which was by some others, over curiously picked out of the term before going, of Gods sending the prophet home to do it there. Others, that God enjoined him to write it, having not yet published it, to be read *with them,* in their presence. I conceive, that it may well be rendered, *write it on a table* to be *with them:* that is, that it may abide among them, to mind them, when these things now foretold them, do accordingly fall out, what they had been warned of before. For I cannot concur with those, who suppose it meant, not of the people: but of other his prophecies, that this should be written together *with them,* as Jeremy was enjoined to write all his former prophecies, or the substance of them at least together: and after, to add some other thereunto, Jer. 36.2,32. However, both in the former, *it:* and in this *them,* the pronoun is put for the noun, as chap. 17.10.

*{in a table*} Or, *on a table:* as Exod. 32.15,16. to be hung up, or fastened to the wall, or on a post, or pillar, as Laws and Decrees were anciently, in some public place, where everyone might take notice of it: so Hab. 2.2.

*{note it in a book*} Heb. *delineate,* or, *describe it on a book,* as ch. 49.16. Ezek. 4.1. engross it in a book, that it may remain upon record, for a monument to posterity, as on a table before, for them at present: so Deut. 31.19. Job 19.23,24.

*{for time to come*} Heb. *for an after day.* So Prov. 31.25.

**V. 9.** *{That this is a rebellious people, lying children, children that will not hear the Law of the Lord*} Or, *For it is a rebellious people:* either declaring the subject matter, that was to be recorded; or, the reason, rather, why God would have it to be recorded, as Deu. 31.19,20,21,27. the pronoun, for the verb substantive, as ch. 43.10. Ezek. 2.5.

*{a rebellious people*} Heb. *a people of rebellion:* as, *children of rebellion,* Num. 17.10. and, *an house of rebellion,* Ezek. 12.2. See Deu. 31.29. chap. 48.8.

*{lying children*} Either faithless and dissembling; or false and counterfeit children, such as carry not themselves as children, nor answer the expectation of him, by whom they have been adopted, Deut. 32.5,20. chap. 1.4. & 57.4. & 63.8,10.

*{that*} A defect of the relative: as ver. 5,6.

*{will not hear*} Endure to hear, Psalm 58.4,5. Jer. 6.10. or, hearken to and obey, chap. 28.12. Jer. 6.16,17. & 44.16. Zach. 7.11,12.

*{the Law of the Lord*} The commandment of God, delivered by Moses, as some, forbidding them to return into Egypt, Deu. 17.16. & 28.68. ch. 31.1. or rather, the instructions and admonitions of Esay, and other Gods messengers sent unto them, v. 10. see chap. 1.10. & 5.24.

**V. 10.** *{which say to the Seers, See not, and to the Prophets, Prophesy not unto us right things, speak unto us smooth things, prophesy deceits.*} That forbid Gods messengers to preach unto them, unless they will preach such things to them, as please them, and soothe them up in their sins, by promising peace and prosperity to them, though they go on in their sinful courses. See Mic. 2.6,11. a place parallel to this: and Jer. 11.21.

*{the Seers, see not*} The same with the next branch, only the terms divers, in sound, and letters: but in sense and notion the same: see chap. 1.1. & 2.1.

*{right things*} Heb. *straight,* agreeable to equity, Amos 3.10. chap. 59.14. they desired not to have the truth of God, or their duty to God, taught, or told them: such teaching was too harsh for their tender ears; it crossed their corruptions: nor could they endure to have those courses contradicted, which themselves had pitched upon, or were addicted unto; nor to hear Gods judgments denounced against them, for their persisting in the same, Jeremy 43.2. hence that scoffing demand, *what is the burden of the Lord?* Jerem. 23.33.

*{smooth things*} Heb. *smoothnesses;* as Psal. 12.2,3. that is, flatteries; sermons of peace, prosperity and pleasure; and that strain the false prophets therefore wholly addressed themselves unto; because they saw it pleased the people, chap. 56.10,12. Jer. 4.10. & 6.14. & 8.10. & 23.17. Ezek. 13.10,18,22. hence that *smoothing,* or *slicking* of their tongues, Jer. 23.31.

*{prophesy*} Heb. *see,* as before.

*{deceits*} Or, *illusions,* Job 16.3. not that they so termed them, but that they were so indeed, Jer. 5.31. & 23.16,25,26,32. Ezek. 13.7,8.

**V. 11.** *{Get ye out of the way, turn aside out of the path*} Take another course, than that you now do; be not so strict, and precise in your preachings, Mich. 2.6. the same thing in divers terms.

*{cause the holy one of Israel to cease from before us*} Or, *from us;* as chap. 21.15. & 31.8. & 37.6. talk not so much to us of *the holy one of Israel,* (a term then very rife in the mouth of Gods messengers; chap. 1.4. & 5.19,24. & 10.20. & 12.6. & 17.7. & 29.19,23.) molest us no more, with so many messages from him: see Job 21.14. Some render the words, *make the holy one of Israel turn out of the way, that he may cease from before us,* that he and we may not meet, to trouble us in our way, but we may walk as we list: but this seems a little too much strained.

**V. 12.** *{Wherefore thus saith the holy one of Israel*} He proceeds to foretell what for this their extreme impiety should befall them; and he makes his introduction unto the denunciation of it, with that title that scoffed at, and desired not to hear, ver. 11.

*{Because ye despise this word*} You set light, by the word of warning, admonition, and advice now given you, from God, by the mouth of his messenger, v. 7,15.

*{and trust in oppression, and perverseness, and stay thereupon*} You trust to your shifts, and your means, compassed by wrong dealing, thereby making account to secure yourselves. See Chap. 28.15.

*{oppression*} Or, as some, *fraud:* see Psalm 62.10. and chap. 33.15. Howbeit, some learned Critics suppose the word here used, by a transposition of letters, to be put for another word, that signifies *perverseness;* the rather, because this, and the next, are found both joined, as here, together, Prov. 2.15. and the like transposition is found in many other words; as in that for a *sheep,* Lev. 14.21. & 17.3. in that, for a *garment,* Exod. 22.9,23. and others.

*{perverseness*} Heb. *a perverted, or cross way,* or *course,* it is rendered *froward,* Prov. 2.15. & 3.32. & 14.2. a defect of the subject; as *vile,* for, *vile grapes,* chap. 5.24. *burning,* for *burning fire,* Jer. 36.22. *untempered,* for *untempered mortar,* Ezek. 13.11. such cross courses, by which they departed from God, (as the word imports, from whence it comes, used Prov. 3.21.) leaving him, and his advice, to cleave to courses of their own, ver. 11.

*{stay thereupon*} Trust thereunto, as of strength sufficient to support you; a metaphor taken from a staff, wherewith a man stays himself up: see chap. 3.1. & 10.20. & 50.10.

**V. 13.** *{Therefore this iniquity shall be unto you, as a breach ready to fall, swelling out in an high wall, whose breaking cometh suddenly at an instant*} The ground of the denunciation was in verse before-going; the subject matter of it follows in this, and the next. The shifts and devices that you trust to, shall all fall to pieces, and yourselves perish irrecoverably together with them.

*{this iniquity*} This your vain confidence, and the wealth so gotten (Luke 16.9.) which you trust to, ver. 12. Psal. 52.7.

*{as a breach ready to fall*} Heb. *as a rupture* (Neh. 6.1. Job 16.14.) *falling,* so *perishing,* for *ready to perish,* chap. 27.13. but here rather, *threatening a fall,* as some render it; because the rupture, or breach, cannot be said properly *to fall:* or, as others, *a rupture of a falling wall,* or *a wall ready to fall,* supplying the word used, Psal. 62.3. another than that which hereafter follows; as *the flower of a fading plant,* Chap. 28.4. a defect of the subject: see v. 12. This your insolency, and arrogancy, is but a forerunner of your fall, Pro. 16.18. & 18.12.

*{swelling out*} As *blains,* or *blisters,* do on mens bodies, which are hence so termed, Exod. 9.9,20. the Latin terms it *bellying wall,* whence the proverb, *take heed of overcharging a wall with a belly,* because such are prone to burst.

*{in an high wall*} The less able to stand for the weight it bears, and the more dangerous in its fall, Mat. 7.27. I suppose they sit here beside the cushion, who conceive in these words, an allusion to be unto men crushed to pieces, by the fall of a wall; as 1 Kings 20.30. Luke 13.4. See Psal. 62.3.

*{whose breaking*} Or, *breach:* that is, rending asunder in the fall, for the former rupture within, and the giving out thereupon, before mentioned, go both of them, before the fall, and foreshow what would ensue.

*{suddenly at an instant*} Chap. 29.5.

**V. 14.** *{And he shall break it, as the breaking of a potters vessel, that is broken in pieces, he shall not spare, so that there shall not be found in the bursting of it, a sherd to take fire from the hearth, or take water withal from the pit*} All your plots and projects; and all the stays you trust to, shall be so quashed and dashed to pieces, that nothing shall come of them, that may do you any service, or be in the least manner useful to you, much less yield you that security that you expect from them.

*{he shall break it*} He, that is, *God,* say some; *the enemy,* say others, true of both, but neither here needful, the word being taken indefinitely; *he shall break it,* that is, *it shall be broken:* and that is enough to express the prophets mind: so ch. 9.6. Jer. 23.6. Amos 4.2. Mic. 3.4. Hab. 3.17.

*{it*} That is, the iniquity, v. 13. that you trust to, and all the designs that you build thereupon, chap. 29.16. Howbeit, some refer it to the wall before mentioned v. 13. which when it falls, is with the fall of it so shattered and battered, that it is with it as with an earthen bottle that is burst all to shivers.

*{as the breaking of a potters vessel*} Heb. *according to the breach* (as chap. 13.19. or, *as with the breach* (as chap. 22.17,18.) *of a bottle of the potters:* as Jer. 19.1. as an earthen bottle, when it falls to the ground, or is thrown upon the pavement, is wont to break all to shivers, so as it cannot be pieced together, or made up again: see Jer. 19.11.

*{broken in pieces*} Or, *to shivers,* Mich. 1.7. with Chapter 27. verse 9.

*{he shall not spare*} Or, *which one spareth not;* to make the connection the clearer, a defect of the relative, as v. 5,6,9. which a man the owner of it, or other, has no regard to, what becomes of it; or throws away, on purpose, to break it: or, *that is not spared,* no regard being had to it, as before.

*{so that*} Heb. *and,* as chap. 10.19. Jer. 14.19.

*{there shall not be found*} Or, *there remaineth not;* as Chap. 13.15.

*{in the bursting of it*} Or, *among the shivers,* or broken pieces of it, to wit, of the bottle.

*{a sherd*} Job 2.8.

*{to take fire*} As Prov. 6.27. & 25.23. whence the name of *tongs,* to take fire with Exod. 35.3.

*{The hearth*} For which another word, Psal. 102.3. Both from burning, chap. 33.14.

*{To take up*} This word is used, of liquor, (as the former of fire) Haggai 2.16. *to draw out,* in this notion nowhere else found.

*{the pit*} Made of purpose for receipt of water, Jer. 14.3. from an Ethiopic term, says one, that signifies to gather together, Mat. 13.2. & 18.20.

**V. 15.** *{For thus saith the Lord God, the holy one of Israel*} Or, *Thus said,* This is the advice, that God, whom you list not to hear named, gave you: see ver. 11,12.

*{In returning, and rest shall ye be saved; in quietness and confidence shall be your strength*} Your only means of strength and safety is by resting quietly on God, and trusting to his protection, and not seeking for shelter, or relying upon reliefs from abroad, v. 7.

*{in returning*} Or, *by returning,* to wit, unto God, by repentance, Jer. 3.1,12,14. & 4.1. Or, as some rather, *by quietness:* for it is a noun, not a verb: and howsoever the verb of *returning,* be commonly used of *repenting:* yet does no noun, or verbal thence deduced, signify *repentance,* in Scripture, as by almost a general mistake, is commonly imagined: the one, to wit, *teshubah,* is used of other *returns,* of the times of the year, 2 Sam. 11.1. 1 Kings 20.22. of speech, in way of answer, Job 21.34. & 34.36. from journey home 1 Sam. 7.17. of return by repentance, in Scripture nowhere: howsoever, the Rabbins do commonly so use it, as where they say, that it was one of those *seven* things, that were made before the world began: the other, to wit, *Meshubah,* in which the *mem* is no preposition, but a mere ministerial, or formative letter, is never used, as the Hebrew Critics, but in way of reproof, and is so far from signifying repentance or conversion to God, that it ever imports *aversion* from, or rebellion against God, Jer. 2.18. & 3.22. & 5.6. & 8.5. & 14.5. Hos. 11.7. & 14.5. and the reason is, because the verb whereof both come, signifies, as well *to turn from,* as *to turn to,* yea in one form it is no otherwise used than *to turn away,* and *revolt,* cha. 57.17. Jer. 3.14,22. & 8.5. & 31.22. & 49.4. or, *to turn away,* and *make to revolt,* chap. 47.10. one place only is ambiguous, Pro. 1.32. where some render this word, *aversion:* others, and so the most of the Jewish, *ease,* or *rest:* and this, the rather, because *tranquility* follows: from whence also, some so render the word *shubah* (nowhere else found) here, where it is joined with two other words of the selfsame notion, and comes very near home to the term of sitting still, ver. 7. to which also the use of the verb, whence it comes, is by good Writers deemed in many places to incline, as among others, Psalm 23.6. *I shall sit quietly in the house of God,* Num. 10.36. at the sitting down of the Ark, *Cause to rest, O Lord, the many thousands of Israel,* and Psalm 23.3. *he quieteth my soul,* or *maketh me to rest,* and Jer. 30.10. & 46.27. *Jacob shall rest, and be quiet and at ease,* where it is joined in both places, with the same word, that this is knit unto here. Yet some other interpret it, of *turning* from their purpose, of seeking, or sending to Egypt. But that of *rest,* and keeping quiet, seems best to sort with the context. See Chapter 7, verse 4.

*{shall ye be saved*} Or, *may ye be saved;* in a potential notion, this is the only way of safety for you, if you be content to embrace it.

*{in quietness*} See chap. 7.4.

*{confidence*} In trusting to God, and depending upon him, 1 Chr. 1.20. 2 Chr. 13.18. & 16.8,9. Psalm 34.22. & 37.40. & 125.1. ch. 26.3,4. See the contrary chap. 7.9.

*{strength*} As verse 7. though another word here used.

*{and ye would not*} Or, *yet ye would not;* as ch. 29.2. You would not accept of Gods gracious offer, nor follow his advice: see Pro. 1.25. Mat. 23.37.

**V. 16.** *{But ye said, No; for we will flee upon horses; therefore shall ye flee: and we will ride upon the swift; therefore shall they that pursue you be swift.*} You make account to secure yourselves better another way, to wit, by posting apace upon swift beasts, if any enemy appear, out towards Egypt; but this shift of yours will not stand you instead: for your enemies will be too swift for you, they will pursue you, and overtake you, before you get thither.

*{But*} Heb. *And;* as chap. 29.13.

*{Ye said*} Or, *ye say:* You think with yourselves: as Psalm 14.1.

*{No:*} We will not so do, Jer. 6.16,17. & 44.16.

*{for*} Or, *but:* as chap. 39.23.

*{We will flee upon horses*} Heb. *horse;* as afterward, *a swift one,* escape by help of them: see Hos. 14.13. yet some render it, *we will flee to horses,* as *to a people,* vers. 6. to the help of horses, which Egypt was stored with chap. 31.1. so Psa. 20.7. but the branch following, carries it rather, the former way; *swift* beasts, as he sometime said, being for *flight,* rather than for *fight.*

*{flee ye shall*} This some refer to Zedekiahs flight, Jer. 39.4. Others, to the flight of Captain John with his Complices afterward into Egypt, Jer. 43.5,7. But it is not unlikely, but that many of them also, so endeavored to do upon Sennacheribs approach: though some expound it, *ye shall flee indeed,* that is, you shall be carried captive, and exiled: and it is true, that in Greek and Latin, *flight* is used, for exilement enforced: but not so, I suppose, in Hebrew; and the next branch goes the other way.

*{on swift ones*} Heb. *on a light,* that is, *swift one;* as chap. 19.1. *Swift,* for *swift beast,* or *swift horse,* as some, to make the gender agree, a defect of the subject, as verse 22,13. and *swift one,* for *swift ones;* as before, *horse,* for *horses;* and *beast,* for *beasts,* as Jon. 4.11.

*{they that pursue you shall be swift*} The enemy shall make after you, and match you, if not exceed you in swiftness: so that the swiftness of your horses, be they never so swift, shall not stand you in any stead, chap. 5.26. Jer. 4.13. Lam. 4.19. Hab. 1.8. Psalm 33.16,17. Amos 2.14,16.

**V. 17.** *{One thousand shall flee at the rebuke of one: at the rebuke of five shall ye flee*} A small company of the enemy shall be able to put you all to flight: see Deut. 32.30.

*{shall flee*} Supplied out of the following branch: see the like, chap. 13.13. & 18.7.

*{the rebuke*} Not verbal, but actual, the *assault,* or *onset:* as Psa. 76.6. yet seldom in this notion used, but of God: but here made choice of, to show what a small matter should then dismay them, and cause them to turn the back to the foes, notwithstanding all their confident conceits at present.

*{five*} A small and inconsiderable number, Lev. 26.8.

*{shall ye flee*} Or, *shall ye all flee:* for that seems to be supplied: as 1 Sam. 30.8.

*{until ye be left, as a beacon upon the top of a mountain, and as an ensign on a hill.*} That is, as most understand it, until a very small remnant of you be left, being, through Gods mercy, reserved, after that the main bulk and body of you, has, through Gods just judgment, been cut off and destroyed, chap. 1.9. & 6.13. & 10.12. & 17.6,9. & 37.32. But I suppose rather (for he speaks not here of killing and destroying, but of chasing and putting to flight) the meaning to be, that they should be so dispersed, that they should not be able to rally, or bring their troops into a body again, or to be any considerable company of them, in any one place together; but that they should, being scattered one from another, be found straggling, here one, and there another, as a *beacon,* or the like, that stands alone on some hill by itself. Hither belongs that of *coming out against an enemy one way,* and *fleeing seven ways* before him, Deut. 28.7,25.

*{left*} Either left alive, escaping: as Chap. 17.9. and so Luke 17.35,36. or *forsaken,* left alone, without company: as cha. 1.8. & 6.12. each one shifting, as in such flight, and fighting, for himself.

*{as a beacon*} Heb. *a mast,* chap. 33.23. Ezek. 27.5. but here used for such a tall pole, as our maypoles, resembling a mast, erected on an hill, or set up in some eminent place, for some special public use, as from thence to give warning of the approach of some hostile troops, or the like: for it seems but weak, that some here have, of setting up the mast of a ship on some foreland, where the ship had itself miscarried: nor is it so probable, that hereby should be understood, *a tree bereft of branches* or *boughs:* or, *a tree,* or two, left for *masts,* or *standers,* or *seamarks,* or *waymarks,* when all the rest of the wood about it, has been felled.

*{on the top*} Heb. *head:* as chap. 2.2. & 17.6.

*{as an ensign on a hill*} Of which, see on chapter 13.2. but in this place it seems to intend no other, than such as was in the former branch intimated: so it is used, Num. 21.8. of the pole, on which Moses pitched the serpent of brass: an emblem of solitariness in this place.

**V. 18.** *{And therefore will the Lord wait, that he may be gracious unto you; and therefore will he be exalted, that he may have mercy upon you*} Here begins the latter part of this sermon, containing matter of comfort, for the constant, and convert faithful, laid down in gracious promises, referred to two heads; the one, concerning the deliverance and restitution of Gods people, v. 18–26. the other, concerning the destruction of the Assyrian, their enemy, verse 27–33.

*{And therefore*} Or, *Yet therefore;* as chap. 29.2. or, *And yet,* or *Notwithstanding:* as chap. 51.21. Jer. 16.14. & 30.16. for all this, if it have reference to what went before: or, *therefore;* for this end if it have reference to what follows, in all that God does in this kind, he intends nothing but grace and mercy unto those that be his, either that continue still faithful to him, or are reclaimed and amended by these judgments upon them: see 2 Chro. 15.3,6.

*{will the Lord wait*} That is, as some, he *respites,* and suspends the execution of judgment, at present, expecting your reformation and repentance, that he may not proceed in rigor against you, Gen. 6.3. Jer. 3.12. & 8.4–6. & 26.2,3. Ezek. 18.31,32. & 33.11. 1 Pet. 3.20. 2 Pet. 3.9. or, as others rather, he will stay and delay the putting an end to these troubles, for some time, expecting a seasonable time to show mercy, when men being humbled and amended by them, are fitted for the receipt of it, chap. 10.20. & 17.7,8. & 27.8,9. verse 22. This the rather, because the *waiting* afterward commended, has relation hereunto. For as for those that take it transitively, as some of the Jewish doctors do, *the Lord will make to wait,* that is, will cause you to wait and depend upon him, they seem to force the text aside, out of its plain path.

*{will he be exalted*} That is as some he will *keep aloof,* for a time, until the season of showing mercy come, Psalm 10.1. but I find nowhere the word is so used, rather God, who seemed to sit still, and not regard what was done, while the enemy prevailed, will at length raise up himself, and advance his own name, both in the destruction of the enemy, and the deliverance of his people, Psalm 46.10. Chap. 33.10.

*{upon you*} That have kept constantly with him, or have sincerely returned to him, ch. 1.27. & 59.20.

*{for the Lord is a God of judgment*} *Judgment,* is in Scripture taken, sometime, for a strict, severe, and exact execution of justice on Delinquents, as chap. 28.17. And so is God, *a God of judgment,* in regard of obstinate wicked ones, Exod. 34.7. Psalm 146.7. cha. 5.16. and so some would have it here. Sometime, again, it is put for *moderation* and *discretion;* as Psalm 112.5. such as God uses in the chastisement of his children, opposed to wrath, or rage, rather, and rigor of Justice, chap. 27.8. Jer. 10.24. and 30.11. and so it is here to be understood, He is a God, that does all things with wisdom, moderation and discretion, especially in his carriage towards, and dealings with his children. See chap. 28.24,29.

*{Blessed are all they that wait for him*} While he waits to show himself gracious unto them: That are content to wait quietly, depending upon him for deliverance, not running out, this way, and that way; and seeking by indirect courses, to relieve, or secure themselves; but expecting it from him, when to him, it shall seem seasonable to send it, Psalm 33.20,21. and 40.1. 1 Chr. 8.17. and 28.16. and 49.23. Daniel 12.12. Hab. 2.3. Zeph. 3.8.

**V. 19.** *{For the people shall dwell in Zion at Jerusalem: thou shalt weep no more*} He proceeds to show wherein God would be gracious, and merciful to them, to wit, in making Jerusalem a place of refuge, and safeguard for them; and upon their supplications to him, in returning such gracious answer, not by verbal promises only, but by actual performances, as should put an end to all their, both fears and tears. See chapter 37. The words may be read, *For a people in Zion shall sit still,* (as verse 7. or *sit quietly,* and safely (as Psal. 23.6. See verse 15.) *and in Jerusalem;* as some render it. See chapter 10.12. A company of Gods people, that either before, were abiding in Jerusalem, or repaired thither out of other parts of Judea, upon the Assyrian invasion; for shelter and succor, shall through Gods gracious protection, sit there in safety, chapter 37.35. Or; which I conceive to be the genuine sense; *For thou the people* (I mean) *of Zion, that abide,* or *dwell in Jerusalem, shalt weep no more.* Of which change of the person, see 1 Kings 22.28. Job 17.10. and 18.4. Which last is a fit parallel to this, thus read; and shows that such interchanges are found, as well in the Indicative mood, as in the Imperative, to which some Grammarians would restrain them. It is word for word there, *Tearing his soul in anger, shall the land for thee be left?* For, *O thou that tearest thyself in thine anger, shall the Land for thee be left:* and here, *People in Zion shall dwell,* or, *abideth in Jerusalem: Thou shalt not weeping, weep;* for, *O thou people of Zion, that dwellest,* or, *abidest in Jerusalem, thou shalt no more* *weep. People in Zion,* for *people in Zion:* As *mountains in Gilboa,* for *mountains of Gilboa,* 2 Sam. 2.21. The defect of the relative, here supplied, is so common, as nothing more. See ch. 28.12,26,29. Ver. 5,6,9,14. That of the copulative, usual also, (as Chap. 17.14. & 27.4.) is not here material; because it varies not in this regard, either the sense, or the syntax. See Chap. 10.24.

*{thou shalt weep no more*} Heb. *thou shalt not, weeping weep;* as Jer. 22.20. As formerly you did, Chap. 33.7. See Chap. 25.8. & 35.10.

*{he will be very gracious unto thee, at the voice of thy cry; when he shall hear it, he shall answer thee*} See the complement hereof, 2 Chr. 32.20,21. ch. 37.4,6,7,15,21,22,35,36.

*{he will be very gracious unto thee*} He, the Lord; as v. 23. Heb. *will dealing graciously, deal graciously with thee.* The word, so repeated, has an emphasis in it, as before.

*{at the voice of thy cry*} Heb. *of thy crying:* as ch. 57.13.

*{when he heareth it*} Heb. *as* (that is, so soon as) *he heareth it.* Or, *so soon as he heareth:* for the Hebrew Critics suppose the pronoun to refer to the person hearing, not to the thing heard: but then there must be a defect of the word *it,* to be supplied, as ch. 28.20,28. and oft elsewhere.

*{he will answer thee*} Heb. *he hath answered thee.* The present tense for the future: as ch. 20.16. Mic. 7.8. he will grant your request: do what you require, for you: as Ps. 118.5. & 143.1. See ch. 58.9. & 65.24.

**V. 10.** *{And though the Lord give you the bread of adversity, and water of affliction, yet shall not thy teachers be removed into a corner any more; but thine eyes shall see thy teachers*} The effect follows, both of the distress that God had brought them into, and of his gracious deliverance of them, out of it again: (as Ps. 66.11,12.) to wit, that they should then look after, and attend to their teachers, who should freely admonish them, which they had formerly refused to do, ver. 20,21. and surcease their former idolatrous courses, abandoning, and abolishing whatsoever had any relation thereunto, v. 22.

*{And though the Lord give you*} A defect of the discretive; as, Job 19.26. Though others render it, *The Lord indeed will give you.* And some of the Rabbins, *And when,* or *after that the Lord hath given you: and thy teachers shall not be removed.* See the like construction, Ruth 2.9. Howbeit, because the words are, by some, deemed to contain matter of promise, rather than menace; they read them far otherwise than our version, and the most, exhibit: the Belgic version thus, *And the Lord will give you bread in adversity, and water in affliction.* The particle, as oft, wanting. So ch. 26.8,18. Jer. 5.7. and 11.23. That is, he will in your greatest straits, supply you with some competency of necessaries, 1 Kings 17.6. Psalm 33.19. and 34.10. See chap. 33.16. And this I should rather incline to, the syntax being familiar, and suiting well with the context, than that which another learned writer exhibits, *I will make your adversity bread, and your affliction water:* I will make your afflictions to be as food to you. But the frequent use of the proverbial form, seems much to strengthen the received reading.

*{bread of adversity, and water of affliction*} Or, *bread of straits, and water of affliction;* for *oppression,* which our margin has, sorts not so well here. It seems to have been a proverbial form of speech, importing short and sorry fare, or diet. Such as those use to have allowed them, that are shut up in prison; and such as those are put to, in time of a siege, that are mured up in some city, especially when all the country about them has been plundered, and spoiled by the enemy; the case of Samaria, 2 Kings 6.25. and of Jerusalem, as in the Chaldean siege, Jer. 38.9. & 52.6. Albeit, not so extreme in the Assyrian invasion, Chap. 2.27. and 36.1,12. Of the phrase, see Deut. 16.3. 1 Kings 22.27. 2 Chr. 18.26. Meanwhile they seem to run far beyond the mark, that put this off to the Maccabees times: and those that would alter the received construction, because the word *water,* is not in a contract, but in an entire form, might have observed, that so it is also, in those places of the sacred story pointed to, where the syntax is, without contradiction, the same.

*{yet*} Heb. *and.* But so Chapter 29.20. verse 18. Howbeit, in this place, it may seem to be more fitly (if at all here expressed) rendered, *then,* as Chap. 24.3. See the beginning of the verse.

*{shall not thy teachers be removed into a corner any more*} The word, here used, and nowhere else found, (as many other in this prophet, which makes his writings the more difficult) is derived from one that signifies, sometime *the wing* of a fowl, ch. 10.14. Sometime *the skirt* of a garment, Num. 15.38. sometime, *the corner,* or *border,* the utmost part of a land, ch. 11.12. Hence divers expositions of the word in this place, some rendering it, as our version, *driven into corners.* But such kind of corners, or hidden and secret places, the word seems not to signify. Others, *driven away,* or *run away* into remote parts; which they understand of seeking after foreign people for relief, Proverb. 17.24. Others, *thy teachers* shall not hide their faces with the *skirt* of their garment; as men are wont to do, that they may not see them, or be seen of them, whom they regard not, or by whom they are not regarded, 2 Kings 3.14. Others, lastly, they shall not flee from you, but stay by you; they shall not be *on the wing,* either driven, or called away, and removed far from you, Psal. 55.6,7. And this most follow, as implying, that though God kept them in straits, and held them to hard meat, for some space of time, yet during that time they should not want of his prophets, Esay, and others, to instruct them. This is true, but I conceive it not to be the prophets meaning in this place; wherein he seems rather to relate how it should be with them, when by this hand of God that had been upon them, they were now reclaimed, to wit, that their teachers should not be inhibited, and thrust away by them, as formerly they had been, v. 10,11. for those words, *any more,* do evidently relate to what had before time been with them. And I shall crave leave to add a further notion, which I suppose may have place here. I took away, says the Assyrian, the wealth of the world, like eggs out of a birds-nest, and *none dared move the wing* against me, ch. 10.14. in allusion whereunto, to wit, to the manner of fowls, which with the wing are wont to strike at, and put by the hand, that offered to take eggs, or chickens from under them, the prophet here making use of an unusual word, might say, *Your teachers shall not be winged,)* as divers, but in another sense, render it) that is, *wing-beaten,* (as *cudgeled,* for beaten with a cudgel) thrust aside, and put away, by such as distaste what they deliver. But this I submit to the judgment of others.

*{thy teachers*} That is, say some, Ezekiah, and his godly Princes, that set them, at first, into the good way of God, 2 Kings 29.5–12. & 30.2,5–9,12. Others, Esay, and the other religious priests and prophets. But because there is an ambiguity in the word: and it is used, sometime, for *rain,* that is, cast forth and shed abroad, Joel 2.23. sometime, for *an archer,* that sends out shafts, 2 Sam. 11.24. sometime, for *a teacher,* that pours out, and distills doctrine like rain, Deut. 32.2. Chap. 9.14. Prov. 5.13. Some of the Hebrew Commenters, (nor want there that concur with them) would have the meaning to be, that their *rain* should not be restrained, or kept from them, that the ground being watered, they might then again have plenty, instead of that scarcity, which they were afflicted with before. And because it might be objected, that the word is plural: whereas neither this, nor another of the same lineage, are in this notion ever found, but singular, This, to put by, they observe, that the verb which it is joined with, is singular: and that there may be an irregularity in the form of the word. But the words next following, ver. 21. carry it the former way. And as for the incongruity of the number, it is a thing so common, as nothing more, in a distributive way, to join a noun plural, with a verb singular; *thy teachers,* for *any one* of them. So Exod. 17.12. Est. 9.23. Ps. 73.7. Joel 1.20. And the speech is emphatic, not any of your teachers, be he never so mean, shall be slighted, rejected, or disregarded by you. Besides, that the blessing of rain, and seasonable showers, comes after apart, ver. 23.

*{but*} Heb. *and:* as ch. 28.7.

*{thine eyes shall see thy teachers*} *Thy rain,* say some; but of that, before: and *thy rain,* is a phrase unusual in Scripture. This most expound, of having with them, and enjoying their teachers. And the word, *seeing,* in Scripture, is not seldom so used, Psal. 34.12. ch. 29.23. & 33.17. Jer. 17.6. so that they should not complain of a want of them; as in some ages they have done, Psal. 74.9. Amos 8.11,12. Howbeit, I conceive the meaning here to be, (delivered, in way of opposition, to their wonted carriage) that they should look after their teachers, with due respect and regard, whom they had looked away from, and rejected before. *Your eyes see,* is an emphatic phrase in Scripture, Gen. 45.12. Josh. 24.7. But it is here yet more emphatic; *Thine eyes shall be seeing;* you shall be frequently, yea, continually eyeing of them, and looking after them, as those on whom you depend for instruction, and direction, as 2 Chr. 20.21. Ps. 123.1,2. So Solomon admonishes his son, never to have his eyes off his precepts, Prov. 3.21. & 4.21.

**V. 21.** *{And thine ears shall hear a word behind thee, saying, This is the way: walk ye in it, when ye turn to the right hand, and when ye turn to the left*} These words also, as the former, are, by most, understood of a promise of direction, that God would afford them, by his Word and Spirit, in the time of their afflictions, before mentioned, ver. 20. And they suit well with that direction, whereby God is wont, in all estates, so to guide his, that they may walk evenly, and uprightly, in those ways, that tend to heaven and happiness, Ps. 25.9,12,14. Chap. 35.8. & 59.21. Joh. 16.13. Yet I adhere rather to those who conceive this to be spoken of the new disposition, and demeanor of Gods people; who as they should have their eyes now set upon their teachers, whom they expected instruction from, Luk. 4.20. so their ears should be ready to hearken to, and follow such directions, for the ordering of their lives, as from them they should receive. See ch. 29.18.

*{thine ears*} Now opened, ch. 51.5.

*{shall hear*} Hearken to: which before they refused to do, ch. 18.12. v. 9.15.

*{a word behind thee*} Alluding to a Pedagogue, says one, that following the children, whom he has charge of, calls to them, and minds them of the way, when he sees them going out of it. To a Shepherd, says another, that driving his sheep before him, whistles them in, when he sees them ready to stray.

*{this is the way*} *The right way*. The way that you should go, Psal. 25.9. Jer. 6.16.

*{when ye turn to the right hand, and when ye turn to the left*} Heb. *when ye right hand it, and when ye left hand it*. But, *and*, is here for, *or*; as Job 31.5,7,9. It seems to have been a proverbial form of speech, by the common use of it, Gen. 13.9. and 24.49. 1 Sam. 6.12. 2 Sam. 2.22. & 14.19. Job 23.9. chap. 9.19. & 54.3. Taken from passengers, that journey on the road, or the king's highway, leading to some place of note, whither they are bound; which they must not leave, but keep precisely to it, because if they go out of it, over hedge or ditch, they trespass upon, upon those, into whose lands they break, or on whose ground they tread; if they strike into any lane, or bypath, on either side, they cast themselves behindhand in their journey; and unless they get timely into it again, are not like to attain the place they intend, Numb. 20.17. Deut. 2.27. It is, both here, and elsewhere, applied to the straight way of God's precepts, whether laid down in his law, in general, or delivered in special, by the mouth of his messengers; which is precisely to be observed, without declining any way from it, Deut. 5.32. & 17.11,20. & 28.14. Josh. 1.7. & 23.6. 2 Kings 22.2. 2 Chr. 34.2. Prov. 4.27. They seem to swerve from the genuine sense of the phrase, who, by *right hand*, here understand prosperity, by the *left hand*, adversity: for prosperity and adversity, are not the ways that men turn aside into, in leaving God's way, but companions rather with them in their way, be it good or bad; or affections indifferent in themselves, neither morally good nor bad, of the way that they walk in, chap. 26.8. The meaning is plain, that we ought not to swerve any way, from any course, that God directs us to, by his word. See Job 23.10–12. Psal. 18.21,22. & 119.1,33–37,101,102,128.

**V. 22.** *{Thou shalt defile also the covering of thy graven images of silver, and the ornament of thy molten images of gold*} Another effect of their change, and argument of their amendment; the defacing of their idols, with all their appurtenances, Deut. 7.5. 2 Kings 23.4,8.

*{defile*} Not only convert them to a profane, or common use, as some would have it; (there is another word for that, Deut. 20.6. 1 Sam. 21.4.) but use it in a disgraceful manner; as Deut. 9.21. 2 Kings 18.4. So 2 Kings 23.8,13,24.

*{the covering*} The plates of silver, or leaves of gold, or the like, wherewith their images were overlaid, being not all of massy metal: so Exod. 38.17,19. Num. 16.38,39. See Chapter 40.19. Jeremy 10.4,9.

*{of thy graven images of silver*} Or, *thy silver graven images*. See Chapter 2.20. both for this and the next. *Graven images*, and *molten* ones, put here for images of all sorts; as Deut. 27.17. chapter 42.17.

*{the ornament*} Or, *coat*: vestment, garment; as Exod. 28.5. & 39.5. Which was oft-times of very rich and costly matter, as was that made all of beaten gold, which Denyse, the Sicilian tyrant, took off from an image of Jupiter, and gave him a cotton coat instead of it; affirming that the other was too heavy for summer, and too cold for winter, this more suitable for either season. Cicero *de natur. Deor.* lib. 3. and *Valer. Maximus*, lib. 1. c. 1.

*{thou shalt cast them away, as a menstruous cloth, thou shalt say unto it, Get thee hence*} You shall hate and abhor, not only your idols themselves, but whatsoever had any relation to them, and testify the sincerity of your conversion to God, by the abandoning and abolishing of them, see ch. 27.9.

*{cast them away*} Heb. *disperse*, or *scatter* them; being broken and torn to pieces. See Jer. 22.28. Exod. 32.20. 2 Kings 23.4,6,12.

*{as a menstruous cloth*} Heb. *one sick of her infirmity*, Lev. 12.2. & 15.33. There is, therefore, a defect of the substantive in regiment: as chap. 17.5. & 41.24. supplied, chap. 64.6. and to be supplied here, that it may answer to the word *coat*, or, *vestment*, before. You shall reckon it, as a most abominable thing, and accordingly dispose of it, or deal with it.

*{unto it*} *them*, before; *it*, now: that is, to each of them. None so rich, or precious, that you shall desire to retain, Deut. 7.25. For the syntax, see the like, Job 12.7.

*{Get thee hence*} *Go out*, or, *Be gone*. A speech of indignation, and detestation, Mat. 4.10. & 16.23. Get you gone, I have nothing further to do with you; there is a divorce between you and me. An allusion it may well be to somewhat of that kind, wherein the word is used, Deut. 24.2. Jer. 3.1. See Hos. 14.8.

**V. 23.** *{Then shall he give the rain of thy seed, that thou shalt sow the ground withal; and bread of the increase of the earth, and it shall be fat and plenteous*} As they shall manifest the sincerity of their return to God, by the destruction of their idols: so shall God declare his reconcilement unto them, by blessing their tillage, with a rich and plentiful return of increase: see ch. 37.30. 2 Chr. 31.10. See also, Ezek. 34.26,27. Joel 2.23,24.

*{Then*} Heb. *And*: as ch. 24.23. when they do the one, then will God do the other, Hosh. 2.17,21,22.

*{shall he*} Or, *will he*; the Lord: the pronoun, for the noun: as v. 19. Exod. 34.28. 2 Kings 25.4.

*{give the rain*} Or, *give rain*, Deut. 28.3,4,11,12.

*{of thy seed*} Or, *for thy seed*, or *to thy seed*: to water it, and bring it up: *the rain of thy seed*, for *rain for thy seed*: as *the rain of your land*, for *rain for your land*, Deut. 11.14.

*{and bread*} Or, *and* he will give *bread*: supplying it from the former branch: as Prov. 9.7. See 2 Cor. 9.10. or, *and* for *thy bread*; referring this also to *rain*; *rain* for *thy bread*, that is, for your bread-corn: as Job 18.5. ch. 28.28. 2 Cor. 9.10. and this, the rather, to carry on the tenor of the context the more evenly: *thy bread*, as *thy seed*: the pronoun thence supplied: as Psalm 45.3.

*{of the increase of the earth*} Or, *from the revenue of the ground*: for so is the word rendered, chap. 23.3. and signifies whatsoever comes out of the ground.

*{and it shall be fat and plenteous*} Or, *that it may be*, to make it so: as chap. 8.21. Mal. 1.9. Heb. *fat, and fat*: for both words have a signification of *fatness*, that is, *exceeding fat*: which applied to corn, or grain, does intimate the richness, fulness, fairness, and weightiness of it; and consequently, argues it the fitter for food, and able to give the stronger nourishment: so Gen. 27.28,39. Deut. 32.14. *the fat of the kidneys of corn*, and *fat pasture*, 1 Chr. 4.40. & Ezek. 34.14. thus, *fat*, through *God's footsteps dropping down fatness*, Psalm 65.11.

*{In that day shall thy cattle feed in large pastures*} God will afford plenty of food, and of all necessaries, not for man alone, but for beasts also: not for yourselves only, but for your cattle, Psalm 36.6. & 65.12,13. & 104.13–15. & 147.8,9. This branch, of right, belongs unto the next verse; as being jointly with it, concerning provision for their cattle.

*{in that day*} At the same time, as chap. 28.5.

*{shall thy cattle feed*} That is, each of them: for the noun is plural, the verb singular, as chap. 26.19.

*{in large pastures*} Heb. *in a pasture enlarged*: being not pent up, and straitened, as, in the time of the siege, they had formerly been: the word signifies, sometime, *a lamb*, or *ram* rather, see chap. 16.1. (where taken collectively, as here) Psalm 37.20. so called of *frisking* and *skipping*, 2 Sam. 6.14,16. as lambs, or rams, are wont to do, Psalm 114.4,6. sometime *a pasture*, wherein cattle use so to play and sport themselves, Psalm 65.13. especially, when having been pent up before, they come now to be enlarged, in pasture where running at large, they may range freely, and disport themselves at pleasure, and having scope enough, they may feed the more plentifully, and battle the better: see ch. 15.17.

**V. 24.** *{The oxen likewise, and the young asses, that ear the ground shall eat clean provender, which hath been winnowed with the shovel, and with the fan*} As their grain shall be rich, so it shall be very plentiful, which both seldom concur: there shall be so great abundance of it, and such plenty of provisions, that the laboring beasts shall eat, as pure corn, as men are usually wont to feed on themselves or such, says one, as at other times they used to reserve for their steeds: see Psalm 72.16.

*{likewise*} Heb. *and*; or *also*: as v. 22. or *even*: as ch. 1.6. or, *yea*: as ch. 29.23. for there is an emphasis in it.

*{oxen, and young asses*} Both these they used in earing their grounds ch. 32.20. though they might not draw both together, Deut. 22.10. alluded to, 2 Cor. 6.14.

*{clean provender*} So some of the Jewish writers on this place, affirming the word, in Arabic, to signify corn, *good and pure*: though others say, that in that language it is used for a small kind of pease, which the Latins call *cicer*, whereof *Cicero* had his name; we *Chick pease*, or *Chiches*. Others render it, *savory*, or well relished, because it comes very near to that word, that signifies, *leaven*, or *leavened*. Others again, *sharp*, because the word has some affinity with that which we call *vinegar*. The word being nowhere else found, becomes, here, therefore, the more ambiguous: but what *corn*, or *grain*, should have to do with *leaven*, or *vinegar*, I am not able to conceive; let me add what, peradventure, may with some be deemed, as likely as either of these: the root from whence it comes, signifies sometime, *to use harshly, to oppress*: whence *an oppressor*, or one that deals harshly, Ps. 71.4. and one oppressed, or harshly dealt with, ch. 1.17. which word, and this, differ but in one letter; and that letter, in either, wherein they differ, admits a mutual interchange. I suppose therefore, it may well signify corn, beaten and threshed out: for *threshing* is oft used in a notion of *oppression*, or *harsh usage*, ch. 25.10. Amos 1.3. Hab. 3.11. and *threshing*, or beating out of grain, is called a *chastising* of it, ch. 28.26. By the word then here used, I understand corn *threshed* out from the ear, or the straw: for of the cleanness of it, from the chaff, or other trash mixed with it, comes after in the winnowing; so the meaning should be, that their beasts should eat, not chaff, or straw, as they used to do, chap. 11.7. & 65.25. nor corn in the ear, or husk with the straw, or beaten out, but mixed still with baser seed, that had grown among it, or other like trash, as when they tread the mow, they might do, Deut. 25.4. but grain threshed out from the ear, and straw, and winnowed from the chaff and dust, accurately dressed, as if it were for themselves to eat at their own boards: which way soever it be taken, there is a defect of the subject, *clean*, or *savory*, or *sharp*, or *threshed*, for such *grain*, or *grain* so used; as *standing*, for *standing corn*, ch. 17.5.

*{provender*} Or, as some render it *for provender*: or, *instead of provender*: the word *belil* here used is so taken also, Job 6.5. & 24.6. (though they have another word besides, *for provender*, more frequently used, Gen. 24.25,32. & 42.27. & 43.24. Judg. 19.19.) and has in it a notion of *commixtion*, or *confusion*; as *Babel* coming from the same root has: and *provender* is so termed, because it consists commonly of divers sorts of corn, or pulse, mingled together, as in our horse-bread; of the grain, not severed as yet from the chaff: in regard whereof, our prophet, who is wont to be very accurate in the choice of his words, may seem the rather here to have used it.

*{that hath been winnowed*} The word signifies, primarily *to disperse*, or *scatter*, Lev. 26.33. Job 18.15. Prov. 15.7. and then *to winnow*, Ruth 3.2. Jer. 21.2. because in winnowing, and the chaff is dispersed, whence that proverbial form of speech, *as chaff before the wind*, Ps. 35.5.

*{with the shovel, and with the fan*} The former word is nowhere else used; in regard whereof, the signification is the less certain: but our Jewish masters tell us, that it signifies *a shovel*: so called, because by it, the corn is lift, or cast up against the *wind*, to sever the chaff from it: and some of them suppose a twofold manner of cleansing corn intimated, either both severally used about the same grain, as passing through two dressings, the one, first by the *shovel*, and the second after by the *fan*: or the one used at sometimes, and the other, at some other times, as occasion and opportunity was: and then the text should be rendered, by way of disjunction, *with the shovel*, or *with the fan*; either with the one, or the other: as Chap. 17.8. Others make but one sort of dressing implied, performed, partly, by the *shovel*, wherewith the grain is cast up; and partly by the *fan*, or *screen*, that receives it from the shovel: the latter word derived from the verb here used, is found, also, Jer. 15.7.

**V. 25.** *{And there shall be upon every high mountain, and upon every high hill, rivers and streams of waters, in the day of the great slaughter, when the towers fall*} A prosecution of the former promise, of a plentiful measure of seasonable showers, for the watering of their land, to make it the more fertile and fruitful, ver. 23. the want of it (not the abundance of it, as with us oft) being the ordinary cause of dearth in those parts, Deut. 28.12,13,14. 2 Sam. 21.1,10. 1 Kings 17.1. & 18.5. Jer. 3.3. & 5.24. & 14.2,3. Amos 4.7,8. The meaning then is, that God would send them such *a rain of liberalities*, as it is Psalm 68.9. such a large and liberal quantity of it, that the higher grounds shall run down with floods and streams of it, wherewith both themselves, that are wont to be driest, and the lands below them, should be abundantly watered, Judg. 1.15. Ps. 104.10. & 133.3. for, I suppose them to be wide here, who following a Jewish commenter, understand all this of storms and tempests, that should fall upon the Assyrian forces, quartering upon the hills near to Jerusalem: see v. 30.

*{high*} Or, *lofty*: as ch. 2.15.

*{mountain*} Of Judah, Ezek. 36.8–12.

*{high hill*} Heb. *lifted up*: as ch. 2.12.

*{rivers and streams of waters*} Or, *rivers with streams of water*. (For though the word be in a plural form, yet the notion of it is singular, as Chapter 1.30,39.) floods divers ways (so the word properly signifies, Gen. 10.25.) streaming down with water: see Chapter 44.4.

*{in the day*} *At*, or *after that time*, as ch. 4.1,3. the time more particularly designed; when it should thus be, to wit, after the overthrow given to Sennacherib, Ch. 37.30.

*{of the great slaughter*} That God shall make of the enemies of his people, that had put them to such frights before in the camp of Sennacherib, Chap. 37.37. See the like, chap. 34.5–7. Ezek. 39.17–20. Rev. 19.17,18.

*{when the towers fall*} *Towers*, properly great ones: for thence have they this name; and from thence arises some variety of reading, 2 Sam. 22.51. & Psalm 18.50. put here for great ones in state and place: as Chap. 2.15. Sennacherib's great Princes, that fell, no doubt, many of them, among the rest of his forces, ch. 10.8,33. See v. 31. Though many refer all this to the slaughter of the Babylonians, by the Medes and Persians, Chap. 13.15–18. & 14.21. and the fall of Babel's stately towers, Jer. 50.27,30. & 51.25,40,53,58. But the following discourse from vers. 27. carries it strongly the other way.

**V. 26.** *{Moreover the light of the moon shall be as the light of the sun, and the light of the sun shall be sevenfold, as the light of seven days*} This passage most of the Jewish interpreters expound of the days of Messiah, after the slaughter of Gog and Magog, Ezek. 39. And many of ours herein swerve not much from them, understanding it, some, of the great glory of the church here upon earth, in the times of the gospel, being mightily enlarged, and with spiritual endowments abundantly enriched, ch. 11.9. Joel 2.28,29. Mat. 28.28,29. Mar. 16.15,16. John 7.38,39. Acts 2.17,18,23. the luster whereof should be such, that it should far exceed the brightness of the celestial luminaries, ch. 24.23. or should far surpass that, which in foregoing times it had, 2 Cor. 3.7–18. See chap. 32.15. & 60.17. others, of the glorious condition of the church triumphant in heaven, chap. 65.19,20. Mat. 13.43. 1 Cor. 15.40,43. Rev. 21.10–23. But I rather concur with one of those Jewish commenters, and some others of ours, who conceive it to be meant of the great joy and gladness, that the people of God, coming out of those straits, that before they were held in, and freed from those fears that formerly enthralled them, should now be surprised with, and possessed of, upon their sudden and unexpected deliverance, out of those their grievous distresses, by the destruction, in an instant, of those forces, that lay so near them, and pressed so hard upon them, that there seemed no possibility of escape: see ch. 17.14. & 37.3. v. 29. *light* is commonly put for *joy* and *gladness*, Esth. 8.16,17. Ps. 97.11,12. & 112.4. *darkness*, for *grief, heaviness*, and *dread*, ch. 8.22. & 9.1,2. & 50.10. Amos 5.18,20. and as when men are in much grief and fear, the heavens themselves are said to be darkened, and the sun to be set with them, c. 13.10. Ezek. 32.7. Amos 8.9. so are the heavens, and those heavenly bodies said to shine forth, more than ordinarily, bright upon persons and people, when they are taken with extraordinary joy, which then commonly most exceeds, when their dangers and distresses have been extraordinary great, and their deliverance out of them, very sudden, ch. 58.10.

*{Moreover*} Heb. *And*, as ch. 29.5.

*{the light of the moon*} There is another word more commonly used for the *moon*: this here, and ch. 24.23. given to her from her *whiteness*, that is, brightness and beauty, Cant. 6.10. and save in these places, is not found.

*{as the light of the sun*} That is, as some, constant, not variable, with full and wane; but rather, for splendor, equal to it, which it otherwise comes far short of: 1 Cor. 15.41. nor is the word, for the *sun*, here, the common name of it; but a term given it from its *heat*, accompanied with *light* and luster, Job 30.26,28. Ps. 19.4. Cant. 6.10. ch. 24.23. no oftener found, save in that of Job, than the former.

*{as the light of seven days*} Wherein the world was made, and man stood, say some, as being now restored to its original excellency, much eclipsed by man's fall. But neither was there any sun the three first of those seven days, Gen. 1.16,19. nor is the time of man's fall certain, and the prophet plainly expounds himself, and shows his meaning to be, that the daylight should, through their excess of joy, seem such unto them, as if *seven days* of bright sunshine, were put all into one; a certain number for an uncertain: as Gen. 4.15. Job 5.19. Ps. 79.12. ch. 4.1.

*{in the day that the Lord bindeth up the breach of his people, and healeth the stroke of their wound*} When God repairs again those breaches that the Assyrian had made in the state of the Jewish people, ch. 37.30,31. & 38.6.

*{in the day that*} Or, *when*: as Gen. 3.17. Ruth 4.5.

*{bindeth up the breach of his people*} As a wound is wound up, to close it, Luk. 10.34. or bones that have been broken, or disjointed, being set again, are bound up, that they may fasten the better, chap. 3.7. Hos. 6.1.

*{breach*} As v. 13. c. 7.6.

*{healeth*} A metaphor; from the curing of a diseased or wounded body, to the restoring and settling of a distracted and distressed state: so ch. 19.22. & 57.19. Jer. 33.6.

*{the stroke of their wound*} Or rather, *the wound of their stroke*; or *their wound of stroke*, that is, the wound made in them, that is, in their state, by a stroke: for the latter word, of frequent use, signifies *a stroke*. Ch. 14.7. & 27.7. rendered *a sore*, chap. 1.6. the former *a wound*, though nowhere else found, yet the verb, whence it is derived, signifying *to wound*, Job 5.18. Ps. 68.21. and the affix, though annexed to the latter; yet in construction, ordinarily has reference to, and goes with the former: of which, see on chap. 2.20. Two words much of the same sense, or notion, are oft joined together, as here: so Num. 14.5. Deut. 8.15. & 32.13. Ps. 145. v. 5.

**V. 27.** *{Behold, the name of the Lord cometh from far, burning with his anger, and the burden thereof is heavy*} At this verse begins the last part of this chapter, concerning the destruction of Sennacherib, and his forces, and the great joy that God's people should have thereupon. With the same, are divers chapters and sermons concluded: as chap. 10.33,34. & 14.24,25. & 17.12–14. & 31.8,9. & 33.13,14. In this verse, and the next, is God described, as coming like some Potentate in state and pomp, but withal, in much fury, and indignation, furnished with instruments of torture and torment, to execute an heavy doom, either upon some rebellious people of his own, or upon some robbers, that from other parts, breaking in upon his people, have made much havoc of them, and spoiled a great part of their country.

*{Behold*} See the like entrance into the same subject, Chapter 10.33.

*{the name of the Lord*} That is, the Lord himself; as we use to say, the *King's Majesty*, for the King himself. So Psalm 20.5. & 116.13. chap. 18.7. & 50.10. or, as some, God worthy of all *renown*, and praise; *name*, for *renown*; as Gen. 6.4. & 11.4. or his *power*, to be showed in the execution of justice and vengeance, Ps. 99.3. chap. 59.19. Mal. 1.14. or, so comes, that the very *name*, or *fame*, of his coming, daunts his foes, Jer. 6.24. but the first is the plainest and the best: nor was there any fame of his coming, before he came.

*{cometh from far*} That is, as some, comes suddenly, unexpected, while he is deemed yet to be far off, Ps. 10.1. Amos 6.3. as men oft that have been traveling return from remote parts, when they are thought to be far off, and are least of all looked for, Mat. 24.44. Mar. 13.34,35. or, as others, from heaven, whence he sent his Angel to destroy the Assyrians, ch. 37.36. a place remote from the earth, Ps. 103.11. See ch. 13.5.

*{burning with his anger*} Or, *at the nose*: so the word signifies properly, Psal. 115.6. Ezek. 8.17. applied to God, by a figurative speech taken from man, whom anger puts into an heat, and such heat discovers itself, usually, in that part. See ch. 13.13. Or, *his nose*, or *anger, burneth*, Heb. *burning*.

*{and the burden thereof is heavy*} Heb. *heaviness*, as Prov. 27.3. his anger, wheresoever it lights, will prove *heavy*, that is, grievous, as Gen. 50.10. or *heaviness*, that is, *grievousness* itself, as chap. 21.15. & 42.25. most grievous; and there is then a defect of the pronoun, as chap. 27.9. or, as our margin, following therein, the Hebrew commenters, and some others, *and with grievousness of flame*: for so the word is sometime used, for a lifting up of fire, by flame and smoke, Judg. 20.38,40. and, as some, also, Jer. 6.1. he comes fuming at the nose with fire and smoke, see Psal. 18.8. or knitting this to the latter version of the former, *his nose*, or *face, burneth*, or *burning*, and (as Jer. 17.4,10,11.) *with a grievous flame*.

*{his lips are full of indignation, and his tongue as a devouring fire*} Or, *is as a devouring fire*, Exod. 24.17. *fire from his mouth*, Psal. 18.8. see Psal. 50.3. & 97.3.

**V. 28.** *{And his breath as an overflowing stream*} Or, *is as a stream*, or *flood overflowing*, Heb. *his spirit*: *spirit*, for *breath*: either of fire to consume, as Dan. 7.10. or, of water, to drown, as ch. 28.15,17,18. Rev. 12.15. or the prophet passes from one similitude to another, as ch. 28.17. and again afterward in this verse.

*{shall reach to the middle of the neck*} Or, *that reacheth to the middle of the neck*, a defect of the relative; as v. 14. Heb. *that divideth unto the neck*, or *by the neck*; as the same particle is used, Ezr. 10.17. that reaching unto the neck, divides by it, the upper part, to wit, the head, yet above water, from the rest of the body remaining under water; a type of a dangerous, and almost desperate condition, chap. 8.8. In which place, yet because the King of Assyria is said so to overflow the land of Judah; some, therefore, conceive the words to be spoken of by him, reading the words, *as a flood*, or *stream, overflowing him, that divided to the neck*, that is, overflowing him, totally, over head and ears, as we say, who did lately, with his forces, overflow the whole land and state of Judah, even to the neck, so as no part of it, save Jerusalem, the head city, seemed to be above water.

*{to sift the nations with a sieve of vanity*} Heb. *to shake to and fro*, as chap. 11.15. & 13.2. here more specially, as corn is shaken and tossed to and fro in a sieve, Luk. 22.31. but the use of a sieve, ordinarily, in such case, is to shake out the dross, or lesser and lighter seed, and retain the full and weighty grain, Amos 9.9. but this sifting, the prophet tells us, should be another manner of sifting, *a sifting with a sieve of vanity*; such a sifting, as did shake to and fro, what was sifted in it, till it came even to nothing; to drive them to nothing, by that, whereby he only purges his own people, ch. 27.8,9. or to sift them in such a sieve, as retains nothing, but lets all run through, to make an utter riddance of them. See somewhat the like in allusion to *fanning*, Jer. 4.11. the word rendered, *a sieve*, is nowhere else found in Scripture; in regard whereof, some of the Jewish critics question the signification of it, and would have it to signify rather, some part of horse harness, because of the *bridle* that follows: but they produce no proof, for such use of it; and beside what was before observed, of the prophet's passing from one trope to another, the word is oft found, thus used, in the Jewish doctors; as in that of one of them, concerning four sorts of scholars, or hearers, some like to *a sponge*, that sucks all in alike; some like an *hourglass*, or *water-glass* (such as anciently they were) that takes in at the one end, and puts out at the other (alluded to, Heb. 2.1.) some, like *a winebag*, that letting go the wine, and keeps only the dregs; (he might as well have said, *a bolter*, that bolts out the flour, and keeps in the bran) some, to *a sieve*, that lets go the trash, and keeps in the corn.

*{the nations*} Those of several countries, that served under Sennacherib.
