Others, *days over and above a year;* that is, some space of time more than a year: a few days, say some; as Gen. 24.55. more than a few, say others: but within two years; as 2 Chr. 22.15,19. But the main doubt here is, whether the term of time, here described, concern the entrance into the calamities, here foretold, or the continuance thereof with them. Some suppose the former, and hence gather, that this prophecy was delivered about the twelfth year of Ezekiahs reign, some two year before the Assyrian invasion, when all seemed quiet, and well grounded for future firm peace, the neighboring adversaries subdued, and both church and state settled, 2 Kings 18.7,8. 2 Chr. 32.1. Others suppose, rather, the meaning to be, that this calamity, caused by the Assyrian incursion, under Sennacherib, should continue for more than a year, very near two; but should within that compass, be circumscribed. And indeed that so it was, may appear by computation of the times: for in the fourteenth year of Ezekiah, Sennacherib invaded the land of Judah, 2 Kings 18.13. and not long after his departure, Ezekiah being at death's door, had with promise of recovery, and of security against the Assyrian, or any other adversary, a lease-parol of his life, made him from God, for fifteen years, then to ensue: and sealed solemnly both, with a strange and unheard of miracle, chap. 38.1,5,6,8. Now Ezekiah reigning but twenty and nine year in all, 2 Kings 18.2. there cannot well be two entire years, between the thirteen years before the access of Sennacherib, and the other fifteen after his departure. And I concur therefore with those, who conceive, in these words, to be contained, a just limitation of that calamitous time, that lasted during the abode of the enemy in their land. See the like ambiguity, Chap. 16.14.

*{for the vintage shall fail; the gathering shall not come*} The enemy entering your land, shall make havoc of all, and so overspread the whole country, Chap. 7.19. & 8.8. that you shall have, neither opportunity, nor ability to get aught in, of the fruits of the earth; as no doubt, while the Assyrian forces continued among them, little vintage or *fruit-gathering* could be had with them. See Ch. 1.7.

*{the vintage shall fail*} The vineyards shall, either be spoiled by the enemies, ere the time of cutting the grapes, or then seized upon by them.

*{the gathering*} Of other fruits, Mic. 7.1. whence *the feast of gathering,* when their fruits were all gathered in, Exod. 23.16. and 34.22.

**V. 11.** *{Tremble ye women that are at ease, be troubled ye careless ones: strip ye, and make ye bare, and gird sackcloth upon your loins*} Break off your secure, and reckless courses, and betake yourselves to lamentation, and humiliation. See ch. 22.12.

*{women that are at ease*} See v. 9. But *women* is not here in the text: yet not unfitly inserted, as supplied from v. 10. before; the adjective is here also feminine.

*{strip ye*} Of your better raiment, and ordinary apparel, as in time of mourning they were wont to do, Exod. 33.5.

*{make ye bare*} See ch. 20.2,3.

*{gird sackcloth*} An emblem of mourning, being the ordinary mourning weed. See Ch. 15.3. and though wanting here, yet well supplied from ch. 22.12. It is made a badge also of a mean condition Chap. 3.24. Howbeit, I concur not with those, that suppose here intimated, a fitting of themselves for servile employments, as being to be taken captive by the enemy, and made drudges. Who also therefore render the words without supply, *gird up your loins;* as Luk. 12.35. See Chap. 47.2. But the particle, *upon,* which they observe not, intimates a defect to be supplied, of that wherewith they were to be girt.

**V. 12.** *{They shall mourn for the teats, for the pleasant fields, for the fruitful vine*} The cause and ground of the lamentation before prescribed them, the spoil, and loss of their pleasant and fertile lands and grounds; the pleasure they had wont to take in them, and the fruit and benefit that they received from them.

*{They shall mourn*} Or, *Men shall mourn;* or *Lamentation shall be made.* Heb. *mourning* they shall be, that is, *mourning shall be:* the participle put indefinitely. The word is used for mourners, at solemn burials, Eccl. 12.5. See further on the next word.

*{for the teats*} That is, as most, for their fertile fields and vineyards, which as *teats,* yielding abundance of milk, nourished and fed them: whence their land was said to flow with milk, Ezek. 20.6. as others, for want of milk in their teats to nurse their poor infants with, Lam. 2.11. & 4.3,4. But one of the Jewish doctors, whom I rather here concur with, reads the words, *Beating upon their breasts: teats,* for *breasts:* as we use the word *breasts,* for *teats:* and so render it, Chap. 28.9. the usual manner being in solemn mournings, and much heaviness, to beat upon their breasts. See Mic. 2.7. Luke 18.13. and the word here rendered *mourning,* is most commonly in the Latin version, expressed by a term, that properly so signifies. So the text would be rendered, *There shall be beating upon the breasts.* So rather, than with a learned writer, as an epithet of the word *teats* or *breasts, for the mournful breasts,* as, *dry breasts,* Hos. 9.14. Of the word *teat,* see on ch. 28.9.

*{for the pleasant fields*} Heb. *fields of desire,* or delight. See Ch. 2.16. Jer. 3.14. *for them,* that is, for the spoil, want & loss of them: as c. 24.11. *for wine,* see Lam. 4.9. there is a pleasant affinity of sound here, between the words rendered *teats* & *fields:* which our English cannot express.

*{for the fruitful vine*} *Vine,* collectively, for *vines:* as ch. 24.7. See the like use of the particle, 2 Sam. 11.26. Zach. 12.10.

**V. 13.** *{Upon the land of my people shall come up thorns and briers, yea, upon all the houses of joy, in the joyous city*} At these words the prophet seems, closely, and (as we may so say) abruptly to pass from the relation of that spoil of the country, that for some short time should be very shortly made of it, by the Assyrian invasion; unto the prediction of a far greater and more general devastation, and of far longer continuance, that in future times should further befall their land, in the Chaldean invasion; under Nebuchadnezzar, described in this verse, and the next. So that it is, as if the prophet had said, I told you before of some trouble that would befall you for a year and a day, (as we use to say) or for days, not a few after the year's end: but I am now further to acquaint you with a far greater calamity that hereafter will befall your whole country, and shall last longer, by much, than that. See the like passage from the destruction of Judah's two adversaries, the kings of Israel and Syria, to the invasion of Judah itself, by the king of Assyria, without any express connection, so much as a copulative, as in this place: chap. 7.16,17.

*{land*} As chap. 1.7.

*{my people*} As ch. 22.4.

*{thorns and briers*} As ch. 7.23,24. & 34.13. Hos. 9.6.

*{yea*} Or, *also:* as a Jewish critic here expounds it: and so most take it; as also some of ours render it, chap. 15.9. & 16.8. Not your land only, but your pleasant houses, and palaces, as well in the city, as the country, shall undergo the like sad and rueful condition, being both alike wasted, and with the like overgrown. Howbeit, some render it, *burning:* as it is taken, ch. 3.24. understanding it, of the burning of the houses and palaces of Jerusalem by the Chaldeans, 2 King. 25.9. 2 Chron. 36.19. Neh. 1.3. & 2.3. Some take it for a causal particle, as relating the procuring cause of this mischief, *because over all the houses of merriment the city revels,* or *rejoices,* because she is so full of nothing but reveling and excess, ch. 5.11–13. & 22.2,13.

*{houses of joy*} Or, *pleasant,* or *merry-houses:* so termed, either because they took much delight in them; as Sion is said to be *the joy of the whole land,* Psal. 48.2. Whence some would have temple and palace, both situate on that mount, here to be meant; or, because they were at present full of mirth, and merriment in them, as misdoubting no trouble near. See ch. 13.12. Amos 3.15. Briers and brambles shall grow in the waste places, where such houses had before stood, but were now by the enemy either burned down, or defaced and demolished: as ch. 13.22.

*{in the joyous city*} Or, *the reveling city.* For the words seems to import here, as elsewhere, some excess; as ch. 5.15. *he that revels* it: and, chap. 24.8. *the noise of the revelers is at an end.* By the city thus termed here, some understand Samaria; and of that land, some of the Jewish commenters understand all this. But that seems not so probable. Others, even of them also, understand Jerusalem; unto whom the same term is given, and her inhabitants taxed for their faultiness herein, chap. 22.2,13. Others take it more generally, in a collective sense, *city,* for *cities:* as chapter 25.2. and understand by it, in general, the several cities throughout the whole land of Judah. See the same term also used, Zephan. 2.15.

**V. 14.** *{Because the palaces shall be forsaken, the multitude of the city shall be left*} As if he should say, no marvel if those places be with such trash overgrown, when they are wholly abandoned by those people, that did formerly therein abide.

*{Palaces*} Heb. *Palace.* The king's house burnt down by the Chaldeans, 2 Kings 25.9. or if taken collectively, for *Palaces,* such goodly and stately buildings, as were more like princes' palaces, than private men's dwellings, ch. 13.22.

*{forsaken*} Or, as the Tigurine, and some other, *disjected, dissipated, destroyed,* as they suppose also the word to be taken, Ezek. 31.12. See ch. 33.23.

*{the multitude*} Or, *noise:* such as a multitude makes, ch. 31.4. See ch. 22.2. Lam. 1.1.

*{shall be left*} See ch. 6.11,12. but there seems here an inversion of the words: *the multitude of the city shall be left,* for, *the city shall be left of its multitude:* for that is sure the meaning, not, that *a multitude shall be left in the city.* See the like, ch. 57.10.

*{the forts and towers shall be for dens for ever*} As the fairest buildings shall be demolished, so the highest towers and strongest forts shall be dismantled, and lie waste, as well the one, as the other.

*{the forts*} Or, as some render it here, *the cliff.* For the word is singular, (which our translators deemed to be taken collectively, as the Jewish commenters also take it,) and is elsewhere rendered *a tower,* 2 Kings 5.24. and, *a strong hold,* Mic. 4.8. it seems to have been the proper name of a place within Jerusalem, about Mount Sion, in which many dwelt, and was encompassed with a wall. See 2 Chron. 27.3. & 33.14. Neh. 3.26,27. & 11.21. in all which places, the name *Ophel,* is in our version retained; and so I conceive it may well be here, and then it must be meant of Jerusalem; though the same term be used of a tower or fort about Samaria, 2 King. 5.24. Howbeit, there want not some learned critics, who suppose the word *Ophel,* to signify dwelling houses, cut out of the rocky ground, such, as much about Jerusalem was, and so called of a word, that signifies *cloudy* and *dark,* not as Jerome says of the tower *Ophel,* because it reached to the *clouds;* but because they were *obscure* and *dark.* But this I suppose to be a very groundless and improbable conjecture: besides that the word that signifies *mist,* or *darkness,* ch. 29.18. is of another root. This *Ophel,* and *ophel* a mist, differ as much, as *Ab,* a father, and *Ab,* a cloud.

*{towers*} Heb. *tower,* or *watchtower.* See ch. 23.13. & Jer. 6.27. Yet the word there used, coming near to our *Beacon,* differs in a vowel from that here used, & nowhere else so read; that it may seem to have been, as the former, the name of some other, place thereabout, that which Jerome, from some Jewish doctors, avouches; but on what ground; I know not: for in their commentaries we now commonly have, I find it not.

*{for dens*} Or, *caves:* as chap. 2.19. 1 Sam. 13.6. but here *dens;* because such intended, as wild beasts use to lurk and lodge in; and those that conceive the word *ophel* to signify such houses, as was before said, suppose that the wild beasts now took up their lodgings in those stony caves, so cut out, which men had before inhabited. But of that before.

*{a joy of wild asses*} That running at large, Job 39.5. Jer. 2.24. shall there play and disport themselves, where people used to take their pleasure, and make merry together before; for thereto he alludes here. See ver. 13.

*{for ever*} That is, *for a long time:* for about seventy years; if the prophecy be of the Babylonian captivity, Jer. 25.11,12. Dan. 9.2. for the word here used, does not always import an everlasting perpetuity, but some long space of time only: See chap. 14.20. & 25.2. And the doctors' critical observation, as well here, as elsewhere, fails, that would have the word here used, where it is full written, as here it is, to signify *eternity.*

*{a pasture of flocks*} Places for sheep and goats to graze on. See chap. 17.2.

**V. 15.** *{Until the Spirit be poured upon us from on high*} This sermon as others, both before and after, the prophet concludes with gracious promises of the restitution of God's people, being purged, by their foregoing afflictions, and God's ample benediction upon them. See chap. 30.4.

*{until the spirit be poured upon us*} Until God be pleased to send forth a gracious gale of his Spirit, that breathing mildly and gently upon us, may restore all to a flourishing estate and condition again with us. See, Psal. 104.30. chap. 44.3. Some refer it unto the restitution of them, from their long thralldom in Babylon. See Ezek. 37.5,6,9,10,14. Others, (among whom also some of the Jewish masters) to the times of the Messiah, and the plentiful effusion of God's Spirit in those days. See Joel 2.28. Zach. 12.10. Act. 2.17,18,33. I will not deny, but that it may comprehend either. Yet I suppose, it withal includes, and was in part fulfilled in Ezekiahs time also, and the restitution of the Jewish state after the defeat of Sennacherib; and the words following imply as well a temporal change, as a spiritual; though this typified by the former. And there may seem also some allusion, by way of opposition, to another kind of Spirit before poured upon them in judgment, Chap. 29.10. or to such as that rather, Hag. 1.9. as for those that expound it of *the Spirit of judgment and burning,* Chap. 4.4. I cannot accord with them, because that seems to imply a foregoing work in the purging of the people; and fitting of them for what is promised in this place.

*{be poured*} So the word is used, Gen. 24.20. Ch. 53.12. Howbeit, because the word signifies sometime, and most commonly *to make bare,* ch. 3.17. ver. 1. some render it, *shall be made bare,* that is, *revealed,* or in a conspicuous manner poured out, as ch. 30.30. & 52.10. & 53.1. But this seems somewhat over nice.

*{from on high*} From God above, Psalm. 18.16. & 102.19. & 144.7. or from Christ, residing now in heaven, Act. 2.33. & 3.21. Eph. 4.8,11.

*{and the wilderness be a fruitful field, and the fruitful field be counted for a forest*} Or, and *then the wilderness shall be a fruitful field,* &c. as ch. 30.29. This some expound of the equality that should be among them, after their return from the Babylonian captivity, the greater and wealthier sort being then brought low, and the meaner sort made even with them; to which purpose, also they apply that, chap. 40.4. But the words seem rather to import a general fertility, that should be in all places throughout the land; of which, as also of other expositions of this passage, see on chap. 29.17. See also Ezek. 34.26,27.

*{the wilderness*} Or *waste:* such as divers were in the land of Judah, 1 Sam. 17.28. & 23.15,25. & 24.2. Chap. 35.1. & 40.3. Mat. 3.1.

*{be counted for a forest*} That is, be as a forest: as chapter 40.15.

**V. 16.** *{Then judgment shall dwell in the wilderness, and righteousness remain in the fruitful field*} Heb. *And judgment.* There shall be upright dealing, and due execution of justice, without partiality, in all parts of the land: see v. 1,2. Jer. 31.23. ch. 60.21. The whole land being described by a distribution of it into two parts, *the wilderness* (consisting of woods and plains, on which their cattle, great and small, were kept, 1 Sam. 25.15,21. Luk. 15.4. & many towns & habitations were near to them, & upon them, as Zacharies, Lu. 1.39,40,80.) & the *Carmel,* consisting of such grounds, as were either eared and tilled for corn and grain, or planted with vines olives, and other fruitful plants; opposed here, to the *wilderness:* of which, see more, on chap. 29.17. For those seems to stray far from the prophet's mind, who by *judgment* understand here, God's vengeance executed upon the Assyrians, by justice his goodness, and mercy to the Jews. See ch. 1.27. & 33.5.

**V. 17.** *{And the work of righteousness shall be peace, and the effect of righteousness, quietness, and assurance for ever*} The fruit and benefit that shall redound to the state and people, by this due execution & observation of justice, to wit, that they shall enjoy a constant tenor of peace, prosperity, quietness, and assured safety. See Ps. 72.2,3. Rom. 14.17. Jam. 3.18. The same thing, in effect, is in both branches implied.

*{peace*} That is, *prosperity:* whereof peace is both a procuring cause, Ps. 122.7. & 133.3. and a principal part, Ps. 119.165. Ch. 26.3. & 48.18. & 54.13. & 66.12.

*{quietness and assurance*} Or, *confidence.* See ch. 26.4. & 28.26. which may well be referred, not only to the settled tranquility, that they shall, then enjoy, living both free from fear of war, and hostile incursions from abroad, and from jars and broils at home amongst themselves; but a religious composure of mind also, resting quietly now upon God alone, and depending on him, with confident assurance of protection from him, Chap. 10.20. & 17.7. See chap. 30.15.

*{for ever*} Ch. 26.4. See ver. 14. as long as Ezekiah lives, say some, ch. 33.6. & 39.8.

**V. 18.** *{And my people shall dwell in a peaceable habitation, and in sure dwellings, and in quiet resting places*} A further description of that security and safety, that God shall in those times afford his people, in the several places of their abode, Lev. 26.5,6. ch. 4.5. & 26.1,3. & 33.20. Ezek. 34.25–28.

*{a peaceable habitation*} Heb. *an habitation* (as Exod. 15.13.) or, *a fold* (as 2 Sam. 7.8.) *of peace,* as *a land of peace,* Jer. 12.5. and *an habitation of righteousness,* Jer. 31.23.

*{sure dwellings*} Heb. *dwellings of assurances,* or *confidences,* that is, of most assured confidence: such as wherein a man is, or may be fully sure of safety and rest secure. See Prov. 1.33.

**V. 19.** *{When it shall hail coming down on the forest, and the city shall be low in a low place*} Those that thus render the text, knit this passage to the end of the verse foregoing; and indeed if it be thus read, it makes out no entire sense; as if it were said, *they shall sit safe, when it haileth on the forest:* or; as some; *howsoever it hail, when the forest goes down, and the cities abroad are ruined.* Others, to make the sense entire, render it, *But it shall hail, when it falleth upon the forests;* or *when it doth hail, it shall come down upon the forest, and the city shall be brought very low,* or *be utterly abased.* They that read the text thus, either way, expound it, some, of the ministry of the gospel thundering upon the consciences of wicked castaways, and throwing them, at length, down into hell, 2 Cor. 10.4–6. Hebr. 4.12. & 6.4–8. & 10.26–29. Matthew 11.23. Others, of God's judgments, that should now be bent against, and spent upon the wicked of the world, poured forth upon those that live without the pale of the church, and should ruinate their cities: or, as some, dividing their whole country into forests, or woods, not peopled; and city, places replenished with inhabitants (as the land of Judah before into land, *wild* and *tilled,* ver. 15.) it shall (as that plain where Sodom stood, Gen. 19.24.) be all utterly destroyed: or, as some other again, their country, that is as full of towns and cities, as a forest is of trees, shall be totally ruined. See Josh. 10.11. Psal. 11.6. chap. 10.33,34. & 28.2,17. & 30.30. There is yet another reading with those, that apply this to Jerusalem; then, say they, shall God's people enjoy this peace and safety, *when God hath hailed upon the forest* (that is, upon the land of Judah, wherein much woody ground was) and laid the city very low, that is, pulled down the pride of Jerusalem: this being the end for which God brought in the enemy upon them, not to destroy, but to humble them, Chapter 2.12–17. & 3.16. & 5.15. & 29.4. And these be the chief expositions, that most writers of note do give of this verse; from all whom, I must crave leave to dissent; and taking the text asunder, to deliver mine own thoughts of either branch apart, according to some hints given by two of the Jewish commenters; the one, concerning the former; the other, in the latter.

*{when it shall hail coming down on the forest*} Heb. *And it shall hail,* or *he shall hail in descending on the forest;* or as others, *in the descent of the forest.* Which, whether way we read, will come all to one. But some suppose the word rendered, *in descending,* or *in descent;* to be, not an infinitive, with a particle prefixed, but one entire word, a noun feminine, signifying *hail:* of which form, they give divers instances; and these thus read the words, *And it,* or *he, shall hail with hail the forest:* the meaning whereof, one of them very fitly gives, That God will preserve the fruits of the earth for them, that they shall not with storm and tempest be spoiled; and will therefore, in his providence, so dispose occurrences of that kind, that when storms of hail come, they shall light on the wild waste or forest, where it can do little hurt, and not on their corn grounds, or vineyards, or the like, where it might do much mischief, Ps. 78.47. & 105.32,33. and the prophet might well allude unto the division that God made with that hideous judgment between the land of Goshen, and the rest of Egypt, Exod. 9.22–26.

*{and the city shall be low in a low place*} That is, as most here take the Hebrew phrase, *with abasing be abased:* as chap. 22.18. or *utterly abased,* chap. 26.5. But they that thus render it, observe not the article prefixed to the word here used, and only cut shorter by the mid vowel here, than elsewhere; which as it sorts not so well with the word *abasing,* for which it is nowhere used (though the verb it comes of, be commonly so taken) so it is always joined with it, when it signifies (as it always does) *the low* ground, or *the vale,* distinct both from the hill, Deut. 1.7. Josh. 9.1. & Jer. 17.26. and from the plain too, 2 Chr. 26.10. whence *the cities of the lower* grounds, or *the vale,* opposed to those situate on *the upper* grounds, or *the hills,* Jer. 32.44. & 33.13. I render the words, therefore, after one of the Jewish scholiasts, *the city* (that is, *cities,* as chap. 25.2,3.) *shall be low,* or *beneath in the low* grounds, or *in the vale,* that is, as the Jew rightly understands it; Such shall be the tranquility and the security of those times; and through assurance of God's protection, so safe and so fearless shall they be, that they shall neither need, nor desire to build upon the hills and higher grounds only, that were places of greater strength, and better able to hold out against an enemy, Judg. 1.34,35. but should build towns and cities in the low grounds and the vale, where they might seem to be more exposed to peril and damage, by the irruption of any adversary, and indeed should be, if any such should invade the country, 2 Chr. 28.18. See 2 Chr. 20,29,30. & 32.22. so that in this passage, is a note of the security foretold and promised, v. 18.

**V. 20.** *{Blessed are ye that sow beside all waters, that send forth thither the feet of the ox and the ass*} The last benefit here foretold and promised, is God's blessing upon their labors, in earing and tilling their land, in causing it to return them a large and liberal increase, chap. 30.23,24. See ver. 15. And this is well subjoined to what went before: for the cities situate in the lower grounds (men, in times of peace, regarding wealth, more than strength; and revenue, than defense) were much better watered, and the grounds about them commonly more fertile, as we see it with us also, than those above upon the higher parts of the hill. God therefore promises, that as they should have opportunity, to till those rich and well watered grounds, so by his blessing upon their labors therein, they should receive rich crops from them, that should make them happy men, Lev. 26.3–6. Deut. 28.3,4,8. Ps. 144.13,15. If any, further, suppose hereby to be typified, God's spiritual husbandry in the ministry of the gospel, accompanied with his blessing, to the great joy and comfort of his ministers that labor therein, Mat. 13.8,13. Luk. 8.8,15. 1 Cor. 1.6–9. & 9.9,10. 1 Thes. 2.19,20. & 3.8,9. of which opinion, I find most to be; I oppose them not. Yet deem this to be the first, proper, and genuine sense; which, those that waive, decline the purpose and intention of the prophet in this place.

*{beside all waters*} So the particle is used, Exod. 14.9. Psal. 106.7. & 137.1. Eccl. 11.1. where that is, at least, alluded, that is here intended, to wit, that grounds well watered, yield much increase, ch. 35.6,7. Howbeit, I suppose none, either necessity, or probability, of that which some imagine, that the prophet should have any special eye here to the waters of Egypt, and the fertility of that soil, ch. 19.7. & 23.3.

*{sending thither the feet of the ox and the ass*} Putting in, these laboring beasts to ear the ground, and fit it for receipt of seed, Ps. 144.14. See c. 30.24. or, as some, to feed on the corn grown up, but green still, as an ordinary herbage, in regard of the great plenty of it, not turning them out into the common or waste, but sending them also into the field. See ch. 7.25. & 30.24. or to keep it down, when it begins to grow too rank; as in marsh grounds, new broken up, especially, is with us not unusual: Either of these, better than that of the ass, to bring in the corn, and the ox to thresh it out, Deut. 25.4. What dreams the Jewish dotards fetch out of these words, concerning their two Messiahs; the one, of the house of Joseph, the *ox,* Deut. 33.17. the other, of the house of Judah, the *ass,* Zach. 9.9. themselves, for the same, well deserving the title, that Jacob gives Issachar, Gen. 49.14. See on ch. 11.13.

### CHAPTER 33

**V. 1.** *{Wo to thee that spoilest, and thou wast not spoiled; and dealest treacherously, and they dealt not treacherously with thee: when thou shalt cease to spoil, thou shalt be spoiled; and when thou shalt make an end to deal treacherously, they shall deal treacherously with thee*} This chapter of the same nature and subject with the next foregoing, consists of three heads, artificially interwoven, one within another: the distresses of God's people, their delivery out of it, and the destruction and overthrow of the adverse party. In the entrance, the prophet directs his speech to the enemy, foretelling & forewarning him, of what should befall him, to wit, that as he had made a spoil of others, and dealt perfidiously with them, when he had no just cause given him, to deal in that manner with them; so when the time set him for power and liberty so to do, shall expire, he should in like manner, as with others he had dealt, by others also be dealt with himself.

*{wo to thee*} Or, *O thou:* as chap. 10.5. & 18.1. You the Chaldean, Nebuchadnezzar, as some, Chap. 14.4. & 21.2. Hab. 2. 5,8. or, as others rather, the Assyrian, Sennacherib. See v. 8.

*{and thou wast not spoiled*} Or, *when thou wast not spoiled:* as chap. 30.20. when others did not spoil you, Jer. 34.1. Zach. 12.2.

*{and dealest treacherously*} Heb. *art dealing treacherously.* So did Sennacherib with Ezekiah, 2 King. 18.14.17.

*{and they dealt not treacherously with thee*} Or, *when* (as before) *thou wast not treacherously dealt with.* See the like form of speech, ch. 53.2. Gen. 40.15. Job 19.26. But here may a doubt be made: for did not Zedekiah deal treacherously with Nebuchadnezzar, when he rebelled against him, 2 Kings 24.20? and Ezekiah the like with Sennacherib, when he rebelled also against him? 2 Kings 18.7. I answer, Zedekiah indeed did so, because he was set up by Nebuchadnezzar, and had sworn allegiance to him, 2 Chr. 36.13. Ezek. 17.15–19. and hence it may be gathered, that Nebuchadnezzar is not here intended. But of Ezekiah, it cannot be so said: for neither was he, by the Assyrian, advanced to the crown; nor does it appear, that he ever engaged himself to him, though his father, it seems, upon the assistance by the Assyrian afforded him against the Syrian and Israel, to continue amity with him, had agreed, for some yearly contribution to be made him, which Ezekiah, at his coming to the crown, refused to make good; and is therefore said to have rebelled against him, because he refused to be under that heavy yoke of contribution any longer; which how great it had been, may appear by that vast sum that Ezekiah sent to make his peace again with him; and which, though by Sennacherib accepted, yet perfidiously he proceeded still in hostile manner against him, 2 King. 18.14–17.

*{when thou shalt cease to spoil*} When your time, by God prefixed, is once expired, you shall be bereft of your power, and others shall spoil you. So of the Babylonian, Jer. 25.12,14. Hab. 2.8. as you had formerly dealt with others, so shall others deal with you, Judg. 1.5. Jer. 50.16. Mat. 7.1. Rev. 13.10. & 16.6.

*{shall deal treacherously with thee*} That is, say some, the Chaldeans shall deal treacherously with the Assyrians; and the Medes and Persians afterward with the Chaldeans. For the former branch of *spoiling,* it may well be granted, that as the Assyrians spoiled God's people, so the Chaldeans spoiled the Assyrians; and the Medes and Persians in like manner spoiled the Chaldeans. But for *treacherous dealing,* though the Chaldeans, before subject to the Assyrians, (see 2 Chron. 33.11.) might in such kind be faulty, yet it appears not, how the Medes and Persians should come to be charged with disloyalty toward the Chaldeans. It seems rather meant of Sennacherib, against bonds of allegiance, as well civil as natural, slain by his own sons, ch. 37.38.

**V. 2.** *{O Lord be gracious unto us; we have waited for thee: be thou their arm every morning, our salvation also in the time of trouble*} A prayer conceived, in the person of God's faithful people, entreating him, that since that they did by faith and patience depend upon him, expecting what issue he would be pleased to give, in the time of those present troubles, he would vouchsafe such succor and deliverance, as to other of his, he had formerly in the like cases afforded, Ps. 9.10. & 18.4,5. & 44.1,2. See ch. 26.16.

*{we have waited for thee*} See ch. 8.17. & 25.9. & 26.8. & 30.18. Ps. 22.4,5.

*{be thou their arm every morning*} Thus read, it should be a passage from person to person: as ch. 1.29. See ver. 4. or, as some would have it relating to the person of the church, as a mother presenting her children in her arms unto God their Father, to be taken into his protection: but it may better be read, *be thou, who wast their arm every morning, our salvation also:* a defect of the relative, as ch. 30.5,6,9.

*{their arm*} Their mighty and powerful support, succor, and safeguard, Ps. 89.21. & 136.12. Jer. 17.5. *an arm to them,* that is, to our forefathers, to your people in times past, Psal. 18.4,5. & 44.1. the pronoun, for the noun: as Gen. 15.13. Exod. 34.28.

*{every morning*} Heb. *by mornings;* that is, speedily or constantly: as Job 7.18. Ps. 73.14. & 101.8. & 143.7. Lam. 3.22.

*{salvation*} See ch. 11.2.

**V. 3.** *{At the noise of the tumult the people fled; at the lifting up of thy self the nations were scattered*} Or, as some, conceiving it to be a continuation of the former prayer; *Let the people flee, let the nations be scattered:* as Ps. 62.1,2. As others, *they shall flee,* they *shall be scattered:* as a prediction of the overthrow to be given to the Assyrian forces, consisting of sundry nations that served under Sennacherib, in way of answer to the people's prayer, 2 Chr. 32.20,21. But the manner of the prophets is to speak of things future, as past.

*{at*} Heb. *from:* as noting the cause, or ground of their flight and dispersion. So Ps. 18.12,15.

*{the noise of the tumult*} That was in the Assyrian camp, upon the descent of the angel, ch. 30.30,31. & 31.8,9. & 37.36,37. of the word here used, See ch. 29.5. & 20.4.

*{the lifting up of thy self*} As a judge, say some, to sit on the bench; or rather, as a warrior in fight, rousing up himself, and lifting up arm & hand to smite his foe, Ps. 118.16. See v. 10. In both branches, is implied how easily God is able to overthrow his adversaries; his bare voice, or hand lift up, is enough to do it, without striking any stroke, ch. 30.31.

**V. 4.** *{And your spoils shall be gathered, like the gathering of caterpillars: as the running to and fro of locusts, shall he run upon them*} One effect of the overthrow, by the angel, given the Assyrians, to wit, the spoiling of their camp, deserted by them, falling into the hand of the Jewish people. So v. 23.

*{your spoils*} Heb. *spoil:* as Deut. 22.14. that is, as most, the *spoils* of the Assyrians, that left and lost them, unto whom the prophet now bends his speech; as ch. 8.4. Zach. 14.1. Yet some, *Your spoil,* that is, of you the Jews; because they became owners of it: as *David's spoil,* or *prey,* 1 Sam. 30.20. though they seem to go out of the way, that understand it, of the *spoils* taken by the Assyrians, from the Jews, ch. 10.6.

*{shall be gathered*} As is usual after a defeat, 2 Chron. 20.25.

*{like the gathering of caterpillars*} The word is said to signify a kind of worm, in shape like a locust, but without wings: joined therefore with the locust is it, 1 King. 8.37. Psal. 78.46. and is so called of a word, that signifies *to devour,* or *consume,* Deut. 28.38. because they make spoil and havoc of all that is green, where they come, Exod. 10.15. Psal. 105.35. Joel 1.4. & 2.25. Some therefore expound it, Your spoils shall be as easily gathered, as the caterpillar devours herbs and grass. See ver. 23,24. Others, You shall be pillaged, and left as bare, as locusts and caterpillars use to leave the places where they have been, Joel 2.5. Others, You that as locusts and caterpillars, have destroyed and pillaged others, shall now be destroyed, and laid on heaps yourselves, and your spoils gathered together, as such vermin are wont to be. See Exod. 8.13,14. chap. 17.11. Howbeit, some suppose an allusion to those holes, wherein such vermin lodge themselves, and lay their eggs, in winter, where they may easily be taken up together, and so destroyed; and to eggs taken in a nest, are spoils compared, ch. 10.13,14. Yet this seems not to be so probable in this place.

*{like the gathering*} As such use to be gathered: a defect of the note of similitude: as ch. 28.1. expressed, Mic. 7.1. or, *with the gathering:* as ch. 24.22. either comes in sense to the same.

*{as the running to and fro of locusts, shall he run upon them*} The word rendered *locusts* is used generally, elsewhere, for *ditches* made to receive water, 2 Kings 3.16. Jer. 14.3. And so both some of the Jewish writers, and the old Latin, here, also, render it. The Rabbis expounding it of the noise that the Jews should make, going out to spoil the Assyrian camp, like the noise of water, running down into *ditches,* ch. 17.12,13. Others of the Assyrians gathered together into the valley of Tophet, as locusts or caterpillars swept into *a ditch,* there to be covered with earth, and destroyed, ch. 30.33. But the most deem it, a Syrian term, signifying *locusts,* and with little alteration, so also used, Amos 7.1. Nah. 3.17. And so taking it, some expound it, of the Assyrians, like *locusts,* overrunning the land, and laying it all waste, before the defeat given them, Joel 2.2,3. Others, of the angel falling in upon the Assyrian camp, and routing it as a company of *locusts* do upon a ground, which they suddenly depasture, Ps. 105.34,35. Others lastly, of the people pillaging the Assyrian camp; and running to and fro in it, and among the spoil they there meet with, as men, say some, that run up and down, to gather up the *locusts;* or, as others more probably, as the *locusts* themselves run to and fro in the corn, Joel 2. So the words would be read, as they are in the Hebrew; *According to the running to and fro of locusts running among it;* or, *by those that after the manner of locusts running to and fro, shall run to and fro among it;* to wit, the *prey,* or *spoil,* in the foregoing branch mentioned. See the like phrase, Chapter 1.7. and 13.19. a defect of the preposition noting the efficient: as Chap. 26.9. So in the next verse.

**V. 5.** *{The Lord is exalted*} Or, *will be exalted,* ver. 10. He will in glorious manner manifest his might, and gain much honor to himself, not only by the overthrow of his enemies, Ch. 2.11,17. & 12.4. & 59.19. but yet further, also by the restitution of his people, and settling them in a well-ordered, and firmly grounded state again, ver. 5,6.

*{for he dwelleth on high*} In the highest heavens: from whence he is able to pour down evils unavoidable, on the heads of those whom he hates: Psal. 2.4,5. & 11.4,6. & 33.10,11,13. & 93.4. & 115.3. chap. 24.18. and 57.15. But the words may, according to the Hebrew, be well thus read; *For he that dwelleth* (Heb. that is, *dwelling:* as Chap. 57.15.) *on high, will fill Zion with judgment, and righteousness:* and thereby gain abundance of honor to himself, Ps. 99.2,4,5.

*{he hath filled Zion with judgment, and righteousness*} Or, *he will fill Zion;* that is, Jerusalem; as Ch. 30.19. ver. 15. with *judgment,* say some, executed upon the enemy, and *righteousness,* that is, *goodness;* as Ps. 112.7. & 103.17. 2 Cor. 9.9,10. or, *faithfulness,* in performance of his promises; as 1 John 1.9. to his people, Chapter 1–27. Or, rather, with due execution of justice and judgment, in the state now refined, and restored to its ancient purity, ch. 1.21,25,26. See ch. 32.1,16.

**V. 6.** *{And wisdom, and knowledge shall be the stability of thy times, and strength of salvation*} Or, *The stability of thy times, and strong safeguard sufficient, shall thy wisdom and knowledge be;* the pronoun supplied from the former words, as ch. 58.13.) O Ezekiah: for to him the prophet here directs his speech; as foretelling by what graces in him, and his exercise thereof, the state should, in settled peace and safety, be established, during his days.

*{wisdom and knowledge*} See ch. 11.2. 2 Chr. 1.10.

*{the stability*} So the word is used, Exod. 17.12.

*{of thy times*} As Ps. 31.15. The time of your reign, ch. 39.8.

*{strength of salvation*} That is, *saving strength,* or *strong safeguard.* Heb. *salvations:* that is, *all manner of,* or *all sufficient salvation;* as 2 Sam. 22.51. Ps. 28.8. The words may well thus be rendered, *Thy wisdom and knowledge* (that is, your wise, and prudent carriage) *shall be,* (that is, shall procure to you; as John 12.50. & 17.3. Rom. 7.7.) *for thy times,* (during your days, chap. 39.8.) *firmness of strength of salvations,* that is, firm, strong, and all-sufficient safeguard. See the like continuation of regency, ch. 10.12. & 25.12. See also of this settlement of the state, under Ezekiah, ch. 32.17,18.

*{the fear of the Lord is his treasure*} Or, *shall be.* Heb. *it.* The pronoun for the verb substantive; as Ps. 44.4. Eccl. 1.5,10. Est. 7.5. ch. 43.10.25. The true service, and worship of God, Hos. 3.5. Heb. 12.28. shall be as dear unto him as any treasure, Psal. 19.9,10. & 119.72. or shall bring wealth to him, and enrich him, Ps. 112.1,2. & 128.1,5,6. Prov. 14.26. & 15.6. See Ezekiahs zeal in settling, and advancing the true worship of God, 2 Kings 18.3–6. 2 Chr. 29. & 30. & 31. and the great wealth that God endowed him with, 2 Chr. 32.22,23,27,29.

**V. 7.** *{Behold their valiant ones shall cry without; the ambassadors of peace shall weep bitterly*} The prophet, the more to amplify and magnify the greatness of God's goodness in the delivery of his people, which he comes afterward to relate, v. 20. and to show the opportunity and seasonableness of it, makes way thereunto, by declaring the great difficulties, and deep distress they were in, until it pleased God to send it: which is here two ways laid forth; First, by the uneffectual issue of all means used, to pacify the over-powerful enraged adversary, v. 7. And secondly, the spoil and waste he had made of the whole land, none being able to make head nor place to stand out against him, ver. 8,9.

*{Behold*} See ch. 29.14. & 30.27. & 32.1.

*{the valiant ones*} The word *Erel,* here only used, and not elsewhere, in Scripture, comes near to the word *Ariel,* chap. 29.1. and accordingly, many here diversely expound it. For first, because the altar is sometime termed *Ariel,* Ezek. 43.15. therefore so some take *Erel* here; reading the words, *Behold their Erel, shall they cry without:* that is, the Assyrians, in mockery, *Behold their altar;* intimating, that their sacrifices thereon offered, should now stand them in no stead. Others, because *Ariel* is sometime put for Jerusalem, and the temple, wherein the altar stood, Chap. 29.1,2. do by Erel, understand that city, and temple also, reading the words thus, *They shall cry for their Erel,* that is, for their city, and for their temple, and altar there, to see them so distressed, or destroyed. See ch. 29.1,2. Others again, because Ariel signifies *a mighty Lion,* or *a Lion of God;* and is put sometime, for *a mighty,* or *a Lionlike* man, 2 Sam. 23.20. thus render it, *each most valiant among them, shall cry out:* the noun singular taken collectively, or distributively, and joined with a verb plural; as Chap. 26.19. But the most, (and that most probable) say, the word signifies *an herald,* that uses to *cry aloud* like *a lion,* Chap. 21.8. Dan. 3.4. and whose speech carries power with it, as speaking in the person of his sovereign, whose messenger he is, and delivering his mind and message, Prov. 19.12. & 20.2. Eccl. 8.4. And hence the word is used among the Talmudists, for *an Angel,* whom that name is given to, both in Hebrew (the very word used in the next clause) and in Greek because they are God's *messengers,* Psal. 103.20. & 104.4. Heb. 1.7,14. So that the words hence, may well be read and rendered, *their messengers,* understanding thereby, either those that Ezekiah, and the state, sent with presents, unto Sennacherib, at first to stay him, if it might be, from proceeding further, as misdoubting that he had not power sufficient to oppose him, Luke 14.31,32. See 2 Kings 18.14. or those other, that afterward he sent to parley with Rabshakeh, when the Assyrian forces were now come nearer the city, Chap. 36.3.

*{cry*} *Cry out.* Through extremity of grief, as a woman in travail, Chapter 26.17. because they could not obtain that for which they were sent, to wit, any terms of peace without rendition, ch. 36.15,16.

*{without*} Either without the city, whither they were sent to meet with Rabshakeh, Chapter 36.3. or, abroad openly in the streets, not able to conceal their heaviness; but coming into, and passing along the city, with their garments rent, in mournful manner ch. 36.22.

*{the ambassadors of peace*} Not that brought tidings of peace; as ch. 25.7. (for they could not speed in their treaty) nor, as some would have it, that labored to have peace, upon any terms, made with the Assyrian, complotting, and complying underhand with him; as of Shebna, some surmise; (see on ch. 22.15.) but those which were sent with commission, to entreat of peace if, on any terms reasonable, it might have been compassed.

*{weep bitterly*} Heb. *with bitterness.* A defect of the preposition; as v. 5. See ch. 22.4.

**V. 8.** *{The highways lie waste; the wayfaring man ceaseth*} As in dangerous times, in a land pestered with soldiers; foreign forces especially, few dare travel to and fro; and those that are, by necessity, enforced so to do, shun the common roads commonly, as the most dangerous, and betake themselves to blind & less beaten byways, Judg. 5.6.

*{the wayfaring man*} Or, *passenger.* Heb. *passing by the way,* as Job 21.29. Lam. 1.12. & 2.15.

*{ceaseth*} Heb. *resteth:* for thence the *Sabbath;* because of that rest, cease from work, Gen. 2.2,3. So ch. 14.5. & 24.8.

*{he hath broken the covenant*} He, that is, the people of Judah, say some, have broken their covenant with God, and now suffer for it, God, by the enemy's sword, revenging the breach of his covenant, Lev. 26.15,25. Others, God himself, of whom the people complain, as not keeping the covenant he had made with Abraham and David, Psalm 89.28,34,39. But it is rather, the enemy Sennacherib, that he speaks of, who had received from Ezekiah, in way of composition, the sum by himself assigned him, and yet still proceeded in hostile manner against him, 2 Kings 18.14,17. See on v. 1.

*{he hath despised the cities*} Or, *he scorneth cities:* both by surprising and sacking of them, and by insulting over them, ch. 10.9,10,14. & 36.1,19,20. So Hab. 1.10.

*{he regardeth no man*} Neither any man, high or low; nor God neither, ch. 10.8,14. & 36.8,9. So Hab. 1.10. *he regardeth none,* either to keep faith to them, or to make spare of them; but breaks faith with them, and makes havoc of them, ch. 10.7. v. 1.

**V. 9.** *{The earth mourneth and languisheth*} Or, *The land mourneth, it languisheth:* being overrun by the Assyrian forces. See chap. 24.4.

*{Lebanon is ashamed, and hewn down*} Or, *Lebanon is shamed,* as bereaved of her trees, cut down for the service of Nebuchadnezzar, to make warlike engines for his sieges: see ch. 14.8. & 37.24. *it is hewn down;* which of the trees is proper, of Lebanon itself, not so: Or, as some, *it is withered away:* which being spoken of trees cut down, is not so fit: or, as others, *it languisheth:* but that we had in another word before. I suppose, we may well render it, *it is decayed.* The word is nowhere found, but here, and chap. 19.6. where it is rendered *withereth;* but may as well there also be, *is decayed.*

*{Sharon is like a wilderness*} *Sharon,* the name of a fertile and pleasant region, lying in the tribe of Gad, beneath mount Lebanon, and adjoining unto Bashan, as appears by, 1 Chr. 5.16. (howsoever some would place it in Ephraims portion, and some in Zebulons) there had David his herds of cattle fed, 1 Chr. 27.29. which argues the fatness of the soil, and the *roses of Sharon* were in request, Cant. 2.1. which argues the pleasantness of the place. See ch. 35.2. It is supposed to be the same with *Lashsharon,* mentioned, Josh. 12.18.

*{Bashan and Carmel shake off their fruits*} They have the fruit and leaves of the trees growing on them, shaken off, and beaten down by the enemy's rude soldiery: the word is used afterward, v. 15. or they are as waste, as a tree that has shed fruit and leaves, ch. 1.30. despoiled of all the fruit that the rich soil with them yields, like a fig tree that casts his untimely figs, when it is shaken with a stiff wind, Rev. 6.13. Yet some render the word *bray,* or *roar,* because of the lion's *roaring;* it is used, Jer. 51.38. and the Talmudists use it, for the *braying* of an ass or a camel: of *a waste howling wilderness;* but in another sense Moses speaks, Deut. 32.10. The former seems better here.

*{Bashan and Carmel*} Two other places, not unlike the former: of the former; see chap. 2.13. 1 Chr. 5.12,16. Psal. 22.8. Of the latter, see ch. 10.18. & 29.17. Jer. 4.26. Now because Sharon and Bashan were not in the land of Judah, but in some of the other tribes: some would have them here to be put figuratively, not for those particular places, but as *Carmel* is oft used, for places in Judah, like unto, and of the same condition with them; which though it be not improbable; yet it is not unlikely, that those places suffered much from that vast army of the Assyrians in their passage. Howsoever, the prophet's scope is to show, that the land was generally laid waste, as chap. 1.7,8. & 10.18. For as for those, that suppose the whole land, by the four boundaries of it, here described, *Libanus* on the North, *Sharon* on the West, *Bashan* on the East, *Carmel* on the South; I doubt whether their geography can be made good or no. I should concur rather with those, who suppose, that by these places, Sennacherib made his way unto Judea: for *Carmel,* says Tacitus in his history, lib. 2. stood between Judea and Syria. See Pliny l. 5. c. 19.

**V. 10.** *{Now will I rise, saith the Lord: now will I be exalted: now will I lift up my self*} *Now will I arise,* to help and deliver my people, when they are in these inextricable straits, see v. 2. Then it is most seasonable for God to strike in, when all seems given up for lost and gone, when all human helps and hopes utterly fail; man's extremity, being his opportunity, Ps. 11.3,4. & 12.5. & 78.65. & 119.126. ch. 37.3. & 59.16. See ver. 3,5. ch. 30.18.

**V. 11.** *{Ye shall conceive chaff, ye shall bring forth stubble:*} Your frivolous projects & designs, wherewith you Assyrians grow great, and whereof you promise to yourselves great matters, shall all be frustrate, and unable to produce aught: it shall be, as if you had sown chaff instead of grain, and stubble had come up of it instead of corn: see somewhat the like expressions, Job 4.8. Psal. 7.14. Prov. 22.8. ch. 59.4. *chaff and stubble,* for light stuff of no worth, or combustible matter; such as any puff of wind may soon blow away; any spark of fire suddenly set on a light flame, ch. 5.24. & 41.2,15,16.

*{Your breath, as fire shall devour you*} Or, *your Spirit a fire, that shall devour you:* a supply of the note of similitude in the one, as v. 4. of the relative in the other, as v. 1.

*{your breath*} Or, *Spirit,* as Job 15.13. the fire that you have blown and kindled, to burn others with, shall consume yourselves, as Dan. 3.22. or, your wrath and rage against God and his people, breathing out reproaches and blasphemies against either; or, the haughtiness of your hearts, or stoutness of your stomachs, shall prove your own overthrow, your own ruin and confusion; and shall be, not as wind only, to blow away all your vain projects, but as fire to devour yourselves, (Jer. 5.13,14.) by incensing the wrath of God against you, and procuring, from his hand, your utter destruction. ch. 10.11,12,16,17. & 37.3,4,23,29,36. Ps. 76.10,11. The Jewish doctors, some of them, reading the text, *in your Spirit the fire shall devour you,* thence gather, that the Assyrians had their inward vitals burnt up with the stroke of the angel, their bodies still standing bolt upright. But that is one of their groundless figments.

**V. 12.** *{And the people shall be as the burnings of lime*} Heb. *burnings of lime;* that is, as chalk that is burnt to make lime: see chap. 27.9. Some read it, as if they were cast into limekilns, as 2 Sam. 12.31. but so large a supply needs not; that of the note of similitude is sufficient, as v. 11. so here, and in the next clause.

*{as thorns cut up shall they be burnt in the fire*} Or, *with fire,* as Jer. 37.8. *as thorns* not growing, or green, that are not so easily kindled, but *cut up,* and sear, that will soon take fire, and are burnt oft times in the same place, where they lie, or if not there, elsewhere: see 2 Sam. 23.6,7. Ps. 80.16. ch. 27.4,11. By these similitudes, he describes that fatal blast, wherewith so many thousands were suddenly smitten in the Assyrian camp, and destroyed, as if they had been burnt up with fire, See ch. 10.16,17. & 30.27,28,30,33.

**V. 13.** *{Hear ye that are afar off, what I have done; and ye that are near, acknowledge my might*} God, by the prophet, calls upon all people, far and near, to take notice of, and seriously to consider of this remarkable judgment of his, executed upon the Assyrians: see c. 18.3. thereby also implying, that the vengeance taken on them should be such, and so notorious, that it should be talked of far and near, ch. 59.19.

*{acknowledge*} Or, *take notice of,* Heb. *know:* see ch. 1.3. Jer. 3.13.

**V. 14.** *{The sinners in Zion are afraid; fearfulness hath surprised the hypocrites*} What the ground of this fear should be, or who they be that should be thus surprised with it, is much questioned. Some, and so the most, understand the words of the wicked inhabiting Jerusalem, thus surprised and possessed with fears and frights; either upon the access of the Assyrian, mistrusting God's promises, and misdoubting his power, as not able to protect them against so potent an adversary, that by fire and sword carried all away before him: as Chap. 7.2,9. or being terrified with apprehension of that dreadful execution done upon the Assyrians; (as Psalm 119.119,120. Hab. 3.16.) and complaining of God's rigor and severity, with Cain, Gen. 4.13. and fearing lest the like vengeance should light also upon them. So Num. 16.34. 1 Sam. 5.10,11. & 6.19,20. Others would have it spoken of these wicked ones, the Assyrians, that lay near to Jerusalem, such of them, as had escaped, and survived the great overthrow of their countrymen and complices, inciting one another in all haste to be gone, as there being no staying by it, or standing out against such a God. So the Egyptians, Exod. 14.25. But this seems not to suit well, either with the words of the text, or with that which after ensues. I rather therefore take the words the other way, and concur with the first.

*{in Zion*} In Jerusalem: as ver. 5. *by,* or *about Zion,* is too harsh here.

*{are afraid*} Or, *shall be afraid:* as v. 5,6,7.

*{fearfulness hath surprised*} As Ps. 48.6. or *shall surprise* them, as before.

*{hypocrites*} Or, *profane,* or *flagitious* ones. See ch. 9.17. & 24.5. Those profane, that derided and jeered God's prophets formerly, when these judgments were by them foretold and denounced, ch. 22.13. shall now, when they perceive the enemies approach, and see that which before they would not believe, much of it fulfilled, shall then be clean out of heart, and at their wits' end.

*{who among us shall dwell with devouring fire? who among us shall dwell with everlasting burnings?*} That is, as some, with God, who is a consuming fire, when he is once incensed; and whose wrath once kindled, burns without stint or end, Deut. 4.24. & 9.3. & 29.23. & 32.22. Ps. 85.5. & 89.46. Heb. 12.29. or rather, as others, with the Assyrian forces which like a consuming fire wasted and devoured all before them, as those locusts, Joel 2.3.

*{who among us*} The words, or thoughts, at least, of those distrustful wicked wretches, and in the text therefore *say they,* or the like, would as a supply, be inserted: as Job 8.18. Neh. 13.25. ch. 22.13. & 26.19.

*{who among us shall dwell*} So the particle is used, Ezra. 2.65. for *among,* or *of.* But more commonly, yea, most usually, it has another notion with it, and is rendered, *for us,* Ps. 124.1,2. with Rom. 8.31. chap. 6.8. ver. 21. and so the best of the Jewish commenters here take it; reading the words *who will gather for us:* for so the word rendered, *dwell,* sometime signifies; as Psalm 56.6. and 59.3. and 104.2. In this prophecy, thrice together in one verse Chap. 54.15. and that there, as also in the Psalms, used of warlike preparations. They therefore conceive the meaning to be this, Who is able to stand for us, and to gather forces together sufficient to make head, and to protect us against so great an army, as the Assyrian brings with him, that has already overrun, and laid waste the whole land; chap. 36.1. I shall add one other reading, and so leave it. The word, here used, signifies, oft times, also *to fear;* as Job 19.29. Ps. 22.23. & 33.8. Hos. 10.5. So I conceive it may be here taken, and the words thus rendered, *Who of us can but fear a devouring fire?* such as the Assyrian army is. The negative in interrogations is oft times implied, and to be supplied; as Job 20.4. and 21.4. whereof see on Jer. 31.20. Thus read, the context would most clearly, and evenly run.

*{with devouring fire?*} The word *with,* is not in the text: and *against,* may be supplied, as well, as *with,* as Ps. 53.5. ch. 32.2. *a devouring fire,* is attributed to the enemy here, as to the locusts, Joel 2.3. Yet I doubt whether any allusion be here, (as some conceive) to that sacred fire, (adored anciently, by many people, in those parts, as having some kind of deity) that was carried before their kings. Of the Persian kings, see Xenophon, in the life of *Cyrus,* lib. 8. and of the latter Roman emperors, Herodian, *in Commodus,* and in *Pertinax.*

*{everlasting burnings*} This those that understand the passage of God, expound of those everlasting burnings in hellfire, Matth. 3.12. & 25.41. Mark 9.44. Yet with some allusion unto that fire, that burnt night and day upon the altar, Chap. 31.9. Levit. 6.2. in which place another word of very near affinity to this, is used. Howbeit, the word itself, properly seems to signify *an hearth,* on which fire is made, so it is rendered, Psal. 102.3. nowhere else found, save here and there: and some therefore here so render it, *hearths of perpetuity,* that have fire ever on them, or never lack burning. And this others understand, also, of the Assyrians' fury and rage, that was never satisfied; but as the fire that has never enough, Prov. 30.16. was incessantly spoiling, and making havoc, of countries and people, Ch. 10.7. See ch. 14.6. So *hatred of antiquity* or *perpetuity;* for inveterate hatred, or hatred long continued, Ezek. 25.15. See chap. 32.14. Yet neither do I conceive any allusion here to any such *eternal fire,* as they termed it, which, at first, kindled from heaven, was continually kept burning on their *everlasting hearths* (so they styled them) among the Magi in the Eastern parts, some small portion whereof was borne anciently, before the Asian kings, as Ammian reports, l. b. 23. which way soever the words be rendered, whether, *who among us can abide,* or *dwell,* (to wit, in safety) *with a devouring fire,* with *continual burnings?* or *who can gather* forces *for us* against such? or *who can* but *fear* such? they may well be the words of profane and wicked persons distrusting God's providence, and power to defend and protect them against the Assyrians: as if they should say, The prophets tell us, that God will protect this city, and deliver it out of the hands of the Assyrians, and we need not therefore to look after any aids from abroad: but who is there among us, that is able to raise forces sufficient to withstand them? or who is there of us, that can do other than fear; or that can promise himself safety; when he sees all the land on a light fire about him, against one that continually burns up all before him? A learned late writer, would have the context thus cut out, *who of us shall abide? the fire devoureth, who of us shall abide? the burnings are everlasting.* But I suppose, he walks herein by himself.

**V. 15.** *{He that walketh righteously, and speaketh uprightly; he that despiseth the gain of oppressions, that shaketh his hands, from holding of bribes; that stoppeth his ears from hearing of blood, and shutteth his eyes from seeing evil*} The prophet's answer to those distrustful persons' question; declaring who they are, that need not on such occasions be dismayed, but may contentedly rest on God, with hopeful expectation of assured protection, and undoubted safety; nor such indeed as they were, but such as were truly religious, and made conscience of their ways: of whom he gives a large description and portraiture to life in this place. See somewhat the like, Ps. 15. & 24.4.

*{walketh righteously*} Lives so: as Ps. 26.11. & 119.1. man's life and conversation being in Scripture compared to *a way,* and *a walk,* Ps. 1.6. Eph. 2.10. & 4.1.17. & 5.8. Heb. *in righteousnesses;* in a continued course of righteousness; and just dealing of all sorts, Ps. 106.3. ch. 56.1,2.

*{speaketh uprightly*} Heb. *evennesses,* or *uprightnesses.* See ch. 26.10. & 45.19.

*{despiseth*} As 1 Sam. 15.23. ch. 30.12. or; *refuseth:* as ch. 7.15,16. see ch. 31.7.

*{gain of oppressions*} Or *deceits:* but that rather, as Pro. 28.16. gain, by such courses gotten: as Lu. 16.9. *the mammon,* or *wealth of unrighteousness,* by unjust means procured, and compassed. See ch. 30.12.

*{that shaketh his hands from holding of bribes*} That is, as some, if a bribe chance to come into his hand, he shakes it off, as Paul did the viper, Acts 28.3,5. or rather, *he shaketh his hands from receiving,* (as it is rendered, Prov. 4.4.) or *taking hold of* (as Prov. 5.5. & 28.17.) *of a gift,* or *a bribe:* as Deut. 16.19. when it is offered and tendered to him; for it is not so much the holding or keeping of it, (which Judas himself durst not do, Mat. 27.3,5. it burnt like a spark of hellfire in his hand) but the taking of it, that the godly keeps his hands free from.

*{stoppeth his ears*} Ps. 58.4.

*{from hearing of blood*} Heb. *bloods;* that is, murder, cruelty, or any courses, or counsels tending thereunto; any the least motion to such purpose, he endures not to hear. See ch. 1.15.

*{shutteth his eyes*} Ch. 29.10.

*{from seeing of evil*} The very sight of evil in others is an eyesore to him, Ps. 119.158. Hab. 1.3,13. 2 Pet. 2.7,8. or, he carefully shuns such objects, by the sight whereof, he may be enticed, or induced to any evil, Job 31.1. Psal. 119.37. Mat. 5.28.

**V. 16.** *{He shall dwell on high, his place of defense shall be the munitions of rocks: bread shall be given him; his waters shall be sure*} The man described, as before, shall be as safe, as if he were in a fort impregnable, not to be taken by any force; and sufficiently furnished with store of provisions to hold out any siege.

*{on high*} Heb. *in heights,* or *high places,* chap. 58.14. such as are commonly deemed most safe, Psal. 18.33. he shall be as safe, wheresoever he be abiding, though his dwelling place be in the vale, as if he were seated on the highest rock, or hill, that is. See ch. 32.18,19.

*{his place of defense shall be the munitions of the rocks*} Or, *his high place,* or *high fort,* (as the word properly signifies. See Psal. 9.9. chap. 25.12.) shall be *rocky holds;* either founded on a rock, Mat. 7.24. or cut out of a rock, chap. 22.16. See both joined together, Ps. 18.2. & 31.3. impregnable, not for height only, but for strength too, such as *rocks* are, Judg. 15.8. & 20.45. Job 39.28. Prov. 30.26.

*{bread shall be given him*} Heb. *his bread shall be given.* Such *bread;* that is, such *provision* (see 1 Kings 4.22. Neh. 5.14.) as he shall desire, or shall have need of, (as ch. 32.6.) shall be afforded him, 1 King. 17.6. Jer. 37.21.

*{his waters shall be sure*} Or, *his water,* (for the word is in notion, singular, though in form plural. See Chap. 3.1.) that is, his drink; (for that was in those parts, the usual ordinary drink, Gen. 24.13,14,18,19. Joh. 4.7,9,11.) such as he shall have need of, shall not fail him. See the contrary; Job 6.15–20. Jer. 14.3. & 15.18. Chap. 32.6.

**V. 17.** *{Thine eyes shall see the King in his beauty, they shall behold the land that is very far off*} A further benefit and blessing, that such should enjoy, the sight of their king, and state, settled in prosperity and glory: and liberty to travel abroad unto the remotest parts of the land without danger or disturbance, in safety.

*{see the King*} That is, God, say some, in beatifical vision, Job 19.26,27. Mat. 5.8. Heb. 12.14. 1 Joh. 3.2. or Christ coming in glory, with comfort and joy, Mat. 16.27,28. & 24.30. Acts 1.11. Rev. 1.7. But the course of the context carries it to King Ezekiah, whom after the defeat of Sennacheribs forces, the persons above described, v. 15. (unto whom the prophet now turns his speech) should behold, not dejected, and in a submiss and low manner stooping, and seeking to an insolent tyrant, 2 King. 18.14. ch. 10.4. ver. 7,8. nor in sackcloth, and mourning weeds, as before in time of their distress, Chap. 37.2,3. but restored to his former state and dignity, yea, raised up to a far greater degree of honor and magnificence, than he ever in any former time enjoyed, 2 Chr. 32.22,23,27–29.

*{they shall behold*} *They,* that is, *thine eyes* (it is no change of the person, for the word is feminine) *shall behold,* or *see,* that is, *visit;* as 2 Sam. 13.6. *behold,* would do better in the former branch; *see,* in this.

*{the land that is very far off*} Heb. *the land of far distances,* Jer. 8.19. that which some understand of ambassadors repairing to Jerusalem out of countries far remote, 2 King. 20.12,14. 2 Chron. 32.22,23. ch. 39.1,3. but that the text will not well bear. But the meaning is, you shall not now remain mured up in Jerusalem, or in any other place of defense, as formerly, not daring to stir out for fear of being snapped up and surprised by the enemy, ver. 8. Lam. 5.9. but you shall be at full liberty to look abroad, and to travel safely and quietly all over your land, to the remotest parts of it, Psalm 31.8. and 119.45. Yet there want not those who understand all this spoken, not to the just, before described; but to some great ungodly one, and in particular to Shebna, as telling him, that the day should come, when he should see his sovereign, whom he now scorned and vilified, as a petty prince, in regard of Sennacherib, (see ch. 8.6.) in great state and magnificence, when as himself should be either exiled, or carried captive into a strange country, as was also foretold of him, chap. 22.18. But the former suits much better with the tenor of the prophet's speech.

**V. 18.** *{Thine heart shall meditate terror: where is the Scribe? where is the receiver? where is he that counted the towers?*} This some understand of their terrors and affrightments that they were in, while Sennacheribs forces were masters of the field, and they were now preparing to fortify the city against his approaches; as foretelling in what distractions they should then be, for the present, chap. 22.7–11. & 37.1,2. Others, of their calling to mind afterward, and with some delight now considering, what fears they had formerly been possessed with, and what speeches among those distractions had fallen from them; or insulting, as some think, over the enemy, now overthrown and dispersed, and demanding of Sennacherib, what is now become of his great officers, that he made use of in his camp: and this seems to be not improbable. Though I do not concur with those, who suppose this, and that of the apostle, 1 Cor. 1.20. to be of one and the same sense; which to make good, the old Latin translation has most unreasonably strayed here from the text.

*{where is the Scribe*} The words, as some, of people full of distraction, asking where is this officer, and that officer, to look after his charge. See ch. 22.7–11. or, as other, demanding where the enemy's officers now are. See ch. 51.13. and thus far it is not unlike to that, 1 Cor. 1.20. See somewhat the like also, ch. 19.12.

*{The Scribe*} Of the *Scribes* office among the Jews, See chap. 36.3. the old Latin renders it, *the lettered,* or *learned* man: as the word is used of Ezra, Ezra 7.6. But it seems to have been the title of some officer in the camp: some would have it to be one of the Council of War: Others, one that kept a record, and took account of the captives. I conceive it rather to be such an officer, as the *Muster-master* is with us.

*{the receiver*} Heb. *the weigher:* nor, as the old Latin; *he that weigheth the words of the Law.* But the *tribute-gatherer,* or the *paymaster,* so called, because they both received money by weight, Gen. 22.16. Jer. 32.9.

*{he that counted the towers*} Or, *counteth,* or *surveyeth,* or *surveyed:* he that surveyed the towers, or other parts about the city, as some, how to make the city most defensible, by slighting some of them, and strengthening the rest, ch. 22.10. or, as others, rather, such artists and engineers; or others, in the Assyrian camp, as took notice of such forts, as were to be assaulted, to consider what courses were to be taken for the more easy and speedy surprisal of them: as also, of what towers and galleries were to be raised and used for the taking of any fort or city: see on ch. 26.1. v. 20. For the old Latin translator is here most ridiculous, rendering it, *the teacher of little ones;* whereas the word signifies, *a great tower,* or *fort,* a *tower,* or *fort,* from its *greatness* so termed: whence the diversity of reading, 2 Sam. 22.51. & Psal. 18.50. Howbeit, some understand all this, as the words of discontented persons, despairing of any likelihood or possibility, of maintaining a siege against Sennacheribs forces; there is neither order taken, nor provision made, for the defense of the city; nor soldiers to muster, nor money to pay them, nor forts wherein to lodge them. But I concur rather with those, that understand them of the Assyrian officers.

**V. 19.** *{Thou shalt not see a fierce people; a people of a deeper speech than thou canst perceive; of a stammering tongue, that thou canst not understand.*} Or, as some, *Look not upon* such a people; consider not the Assyrians, what a fierce and rude people they are, as Shebna, and some others, tell you, whereby to affright you, as if you could not but fall into the hands of such, and be at their mercy, if you stood out against them. But the received reading agrees better with the sequel of the context; as promising deliverance from the Assyrians, and giving them assurance, that they should not return to molest them again. See ch. 38.6.

*{not see*} Within the walls of Jerusalem, ch. 37.33. or, not see them again within your land, after you are once rid of them, as Exod. 14.13. you shall no more be vexed with such cruel strange people, they shall have no more access to you, ch. 16.4.

*{fierce*} As *of a fierce countenance,* Deut. 28.50. Dan. 8.23. yet some of the Jewish critics render it, *a barbarous* people, Ps. 114.1. by the change of a letter; the like whereunto they give instance of, in a word used for *a chamber:* and others of them deem it, a foreign term, of no family in their language.

*{of a deeper speech than thou canst perceive*} Heb. *of depths of lip from hearing;* or *more than to hear: depths* or *profundities:* as Prov. 9.18. *depths,* or *profundities of lip,* for speech or language, deep, profound, or not intelligible, as Ezek. 3.5,6. *lip,* for *language,* as Gen. 11.1. Zeph. 3.9. *from hearing,* that they cannot be heard or understood: of the phrase, see on chap. 23.1. & 28.20. *to hear,* for *to understand:* as ch. 36.11. whence also it appears, that the Jewish people did not commonly understand the Syrian tongue, which both the Assyrians and the Chaldeans ordinarily used, Dan. 2.4. the pronoun, though not amiss supplied, yet is not in the original; so, Job 15. ver. 7.

*{of a stammering tongue*} Or, *ridiculous,* or *barbarous,* rather: such, say the Jewish doctors here, as all languages are, besides the Hebrew; as the Greeks had the like esteem of all languages, save their own, Rom. 1.14. yea, such as any language seems to be unto him, that understands it not, 1 Cor. 14.11. See ch. 28.11. Deut. 28.49,50.

*{that thou canst not understand*} Heb. *whereof understanding is not:* for there is a want, not of the pronoun only, as before, but of the relative also, as v. 1,11,20.

**V. 20.** *{Look upon Zion, the city of our solemnities*} See how safe, and whole, Jerusalem is still, notwithstanding all the vain and presumptuous vaunts and menaces of the insolent enemy, that he would do thus, and thus, unto her, chap. 10.11. so Psal. 48.12,13. *walk round about Zion, and tell her towers; mark well her bulwarks, and her palaces:* and see if any one of them be wanting, or any breach, or flaw, made in any one of them, for all the enemy's might, multitude, and boastings, ch. 37.33. See ver. 16.

*{Zion*} Jerusalem, as ver. 5.

*{the city of our solemnities*} Or, *solemn assemblies,* or *meetings,* which were there held. See chap. 1.14. & 14.13.

*{thine eyes shall see Jerusalem a quiet habitation*} Free from those disturbances, wherewith she was formerly disquieted, Chap. 30.17,18. Ps. 128.6.

*{a tabernacle that shall not be taken down*} Or, *removed,* as some render it: the word is nowhere else found. But a learned writer refers it to an Ethiopic root, that signifies *to bear,* as a beast does man or burden, Mat. 21.7. Mark 11.2,7. The city is compared to a tabernacle, as ch. 54.2. yet not like to that tabernacle made by Moses, which was from time to time taken down, and removed from place to place, as they journeyed in the wilderness, Numb. 4.5. and 10.17. but as the temple built by Solomon, that stood constantly firm and fixed, Ps. 78.69. a type of the safety and stability of the church, Ps. 46.5. & 48.8. & 125.1. Mat. 16.18.

*{not one of the stakes thereof shall ever be removed, nor shall any of the cords thereof be broken*} No one tower, or palace, or part of it, shall be in the least degree impaired. See above, Ps. 48.12,13. an allusion to those cords, wherewith the curtains of the tent, or pavilion, supported with a pole, pitched in the midst of it, being fastened unto pins, or stakes, driven into the ground, do keep them tight, and so help to uphold it, ch. 54.2.

*{not one of the stakes thereof shall be removed*} Or, *no stake whereof shall be removed.* Heb. *the stakes thereof shall not go:* the noun is singular, the verb plural; which justifies, *not one,* in our version. See Ch. 26.19. and *to make to go,* is *to remove,* Job 19.10. as, *to go,* here, *to be removed,* plucked up, and pulled out of its place; the possessive, for the relative, as v. 21. Exod. 18.20. Job 3.3. Ps. 11.4.

*{Stake*} Or, *pin:* the word properly signifies *a nail,* or *a pin,* such as we use to hang things on, chap. 22.23,25. Ezek. 15.3. then such *pins,* or *stakes,* of what matter soever, as were used about tents, Exod. 27.19. Judg. 4.21.

*{for ever*} As ch. 13.20. & 25.8.

*{nor shall any of the cords thereof be broken*} Or, *and whose cords shall none* of them *be broken.* Heb. *and all the cords thereof shall not be broken: all not,* for *not any:* as Ezek. 18.22,24. See v. 14.

**V. 21.** *{But there the glorious Lord will be unto us a place of broad rivers, and streams; wherein shall go no Galley with oars, neither shall gallant ship pass thereby*} In this verse and the next, the prophet shows by whose powerful support and safeguard, the city should attain and enjoy this constant and assured safety, by God alone, and his protection of it, Chap. 26.1,3. Psal. 46.5. & 48.8. Zach. 2.5. compared here to a broad river, that is of much use and strength to a city; but withal, of so stiff and strong a current: that neither ship or galley, of any enemy, shall be able, with help of wind, or oars, or both, to get up thereby to it, to molest or annoy it; and the prophet seems to allude to, and meet with the conceit of those, that thought meanly of Jerusalem, because it had no such great river near it, as Niniveh and Babylon had, which the Assyrian boasted of, and to which he is compared, ch. 8.7. or such an one as Egypt had of Nilus, wherein they so much confided, Ezek. 29.3. but a small rivulet, or two only; which though they might afford water sufficient for the city, Psal. 46.3,4. Yet they had no great breadth of channel, to bear any great vessel, or ran with any strong stream, nor could afford much strength or defense to the city. See Chap. 8.6. But God, says the prophet, shall instead of such a river, as Euphrates, or Nilus, afford more security and safety unto us, than any such river did, or could do unto them; he will himself be such a river to us, so broad, and of so strong a stream, as neither the king of Assyria, nor any other enemy shall be able to pass. See Ezek. 47.5. or, as some expound it, he will make this city and land as Mesopotamia, that was environed with the branches of the one, as Egypt that was fenced and fed, and enriched with the streams of the other.

*{there the glorious Lord will be unto us*} Or, as some render it, *the Lord* will be, (or, will appear, will show himself) *glorious,* or *magnificent for us;* because the epithet is not wont to go before his master, or owner, in the Hebrew: or, will do *gallantly* for us; for so the word is afterward here rendered, to wit, in the overthrow of our enemies.

*{a place of broad rivers and streams*} Or as some, *in place,* that is, instead of such *rivers* and *streams* as Eccl. 3.17. a defect of the copulative; as Ch. 31.13. Heb. *broad, of hands,* or *spaces;* as the word is used, ch. 22.16. Ps. 104.25.

*{wherein shall go no galley with oars*} Heb. *no ship of oar shall go in it,* Of the syntax, see on v. 20. *ship* or *oar,* for, bark, vessel, or galley, rowed with oars. See Ezek. 27.5,6,26,29. *shall go,* that is, *pass:* as Ps. 104.26. *there go the ships.*

*{nor gallant ship*} The term given before to God. God, as he has done gallantly for us, in our present delivery; so he will for the future, so engage himself for our safety, that no enemy of what power soever, shall he be able to approach us, to disturb our peace, Ps. 91.4,9,10.

**V. 22.** *{For the Lord is our Judge, the Lord is our Law-giver, the Lord is our King, he will save us*} God alone has interest in us; to him alone we belong; and so long as we continue loyal to him, our sovereign, and walk according to the laws, by him prescribed us, we shall be sure of his protection and safeguard, Deut. 26.17–19. & 30.19,20. & 33.12,26–29. Ps. 81.8,9,13–15. ch. 48.17–19.

*{our Judge*} To right us against those that wrong us, Psal. 7.6,8,11. & 9.4. & 26.1. & 75.7. & 94.2. he seems to have some reference to those judges, that God raised up for the rescuing of his people out of the hands of their oppressors, Judg. 2.16. Acts 13.20.

*{our Law-giver*} Heb. *Statute-maker,* Gen. 49.10. a title given to God more especially, in regard of his people, unto whom he had prescribed such statutes and ordinances, as he had not to any other, Ps. 147.19,20. See Deut. 33.2,21. Jam. 4.12. of the term, see chap. 10.1.

*{our King*} He, and not the Assyrian, who yet has formerly tyrannized over us, ch. 26.13. and would still so do. See Ps. 44.4. & 74.12. & 89.18.

*{he will save us*} As a sovereign protects his subjects, that continue loyal to him, and live according to his laws, Ps. 7.8. & 72.4,12–14. See ch. 25.9.

**V. 23.** *{Thy tacklings are loosed; they could not well strengthen their mast; they could not spread the sail*} The prophet here returns again, to foretell the defeat given to the Assyrian forces; whereof somewhat before, v. 3. addressing his speech unto them, or to Sennacherib their chief commander, and he compares his vast army, here, to a great galleon, in distress at sea, and so incessantly pursued and driven with furious blasts of boisterous winds, that she is not able to bear sail, or keep up her mast, and cannot therefore but miscarry: and this resemblance he may the rather seem to have made choice of, because he had spoken before of goodly great ships, with top and topgallant, v. 21.
