See ch. 2.16. So that it is, as if he had said, Your shipping, O Assyrians, is, or shall be, wrecked; you have miscarried, or shall miscarry, as by shipwreck. See Psalm 48.7.

*{Thy tacklings are loosed*} So the old Latin, and divers other later versions; but that signification of the verb here used, is questioned; nor is there any place produced, where it is so used. The margin has it; *They have forsaken thy tacklings;* and so some other, *they shall leave thy tacklings,* or *thy tacklings shall be left:* they shall be let go, and give over, by those that should manage them; an argument of evident danger, and great likelihood of wreck approaching, when the mariners, as despairing of safety, give over the managing of their tackle, and leave the ship, to shift, as it may, for itself, Act. 27.30,40. And the word here used, does not unusually signify so *to leave,* or *give over,* Exod. 23.11. Judg. 6.13. 1 Sam. 10.2. Psal. 27.9. Prov. 17.14. Chap. 2.6. But some other render it, with the ancient Greek, *Thy tacklings are split* or *broken;* or, that which follows thereupon, they are *dissipated,* driven to and fro with the wind, or thrown about aboard the ship, as they conceive the word to be used, Chap. 32.14. Ezek. 31.12. See ch. 16.8. which way soever we take it, it seems opposed to that which he had said before of the city, compared to a tent, that no stake, or cord of it, should be stirred, verse 20. whereas of the enemy's army, compared to a ship on the other side, he says, that no mast or tackle of it should hold. For I cannot accord with those, that of a *tent,* or *pavilion,* expound this whole passage; by *mast,* in the next branch, understanding the pole pitched in the midst, to bear it up. See ch. 30.17. and much less with that, which a learned annotator exhibits, who renders it, as spoken to Sion, *Thy sorrows are cast:* you have no longer cause to be sorry: that the word signifies as well pains, as cords, Job 21.17. Ps. 18.4. & 116.3. is undoubted; but how that suits here, appears not.

*{they could not well strengthen their masts*} *They,* that is, the *tacklings,* which failing, the mast cannot stand.

*{well*} Heb. say some, *the straightness of the mast:* that is, they could not keep the mast upright: supposing the word here used, to be a noun substantive; but it is hard to find a place where it is so used. Others make it not a noun, but an adjective and render it, *they could not hold,* or *keep the mast straight,* or *upright:* and the word indeed seems so to be taken, Gen. 42.11,19. Prov. 15.7. Eccl. 8.10. nor do they miss of the true sense of the place, that here so understand it. Yet, because (as was intimated on ver. 21.) the adjective is seldom set before its substantive, in Hebrew: it is conceived rather to be an adverb, here, as our English translators took it, when they rendered it, *well:* as also, it oft elsewhere signifies *well,* or *aright,* Exod. 10.29. 2 Kings 7.9. Jer. 8.6. & 23.10. for, as for those, that would have it a note of similitude, though it be commonly so used, Gen. 9.7,9. 1 Ps. 1.4. Yet that has no place here; as little in mine apprehension that, which the forementioned learned writer suggests, *the basis of the mast,* that is, says he, of the standard, whereon the banner was to be displayed in the field; which God would not suffer to be fixed, much less the banner to be upon it displayed: but the prophet seems to be here in a diverse resemblance.

*{could not strengthen*} Heb. *they shall not:* for, *they could not,* or *they shall not be able to strengthen,* or *hold fast,* or *keep firm:* the indicative form, in a potential notion: as Num. 23.10. Deut. 4.28. Neh. 6.6. Job 9.3. & 14.4. Est. 5.14. ch. 10.19. & 26.18. Dan. 3.15. with 17. so also in the next branch.

*{they could not spread their sail*} Heb. *the sign,* or *flag,* or *ensign,* as the word most commonly signifies, and so divers interpreters, after the old Latin, here render it; understanding the word, some, of *a flag,* set on the top of a tent, or pavilion, to show whom it belonged to: Others, of the *banner* displayed in fight in the field: Others, of the *flag on the* top of the mast of a ship, which none of them, seem to fit well here. And others, therefore, lastly, after the Chaldee paraphrast, with the Jewish commenters, render it, as ours, here, the *sail:* the meaning of the words being, that their tackle was all so split, and torn, and dissipated, as well those that should keep the mast upright and steady, as those also, that should hold and guide the sail, that neither mast nor sail could do them any service; and their ship therefore destitute of all such necessary furniture, must needs be swallowed up of the sea.

*{Then is the prey of the great spoil divided*} Or, *then shall the prey* (as Gen. 49.27.) *of a great spoil be divided.* The spoil of the Assyrians' camp, after the defeat given them, and their sudden flight thereupon, ch. 32.8,9. divided among the Jewish people, as the Syrians, 2 King. 7.16. and of those of Moab and Ammon, 2 Chr. 20.25. and, as after a wreck of some great carvel, or carrack, laden with abundance of rich commodities, the coasting people are wont to seize on such of them: as on drift, come floating to the shore: see v. 4.

*{prey of a great spoil*} Or, as some of the Jewish critics, *prey,* and *much spoil,* or *spoil in abundance:* see ch. 9.7. a defect of the copulative: as ch. 32.13. See 2 Chro. 28.8.

*{the lame take the prey*} Or, *shall take the prey.* Heb. *prey,* or *prey on the prey,* as ch. 10.6. Ezek. 38.12,13. the lame shall do as the lepers did, 2 Kings 7.8. The weakest and most impotent shall be able enough to make spoil of them; as the Jebusites bragged that they could do with David and his, 2 Sam. 5.6,8. or, shall among the rest, seize on the prey, when the enemy is fled and gone, Ps. 68.12. ch. 37. v. 36,37.

**V. 24.** *{And the Inhabitant shall not say, I am sick*} No one inhabitant of Jerusalem, shall have cause to complain of any infirmity, contracted by the siege or invasion of Sennacherib; their health, or ability of body, shall not (as by long and strait sieges is usual) be in the least degree impaired: See Psal. 105.37. Others, the weak shall take heart; or, they shall have incolumity, health and strength, restored to them, Psalm 103.3. chap. 35.6. But the former is, I take it, more agreeable to the scope and drift of the prophet's discourse.

*{the inhabitant*} To wit of Jerusalem, v. 20. *inhabitant,* for *inhabitants:* as Chap. 5.3. Yet here rather distributively, than collectively, as there: *the inhabitant shall not say,* for *no inhabitant shall say:* see v. 21.

*{I am sick*} As 1 Sam. 30.13. or *feel pain:* as Prov. 23.35. or *am weak:* as Judg. 16.7,11.

*{The People that dwell therein shall be forgiven their iniquity*} Or, *the People dwelling therein, being discharged of iniquity:* for so it runs word for word in the Hebrew. *Discharged,* or *disburdened of iniquity:* as Psalm 32.1. or, as it may well be rendered, *having iniquity taken off them;* or, *from them,* 2 Sam. 12.13. Psalm 103.12. being by the hand of God upon them, refined and reformed; and God, upon their repentance, now reconciled unto them, Chap. 1.25.27. and his wrath, by their sins formerly incensed, remitted wholly, and removed, ch. 38.27. & 43.25. & 54.7–10. & 57.17,18. Jer. 31.34. a defect of the pronoun: as ch. 13.15.22.

### CHAPTER 34

**V. 1.** *{Come near, ye nations, to hear, and hearken, ye people; let the earth hear, and all that is therein, the world and all things, that come forth of it*} Whether this chapter, and the next, belong to the prophecy, or sermon, recorded in the foregoing chapter; as some would have it, or contain another several one, is not altogether so certain. Yet the former seems not improbable. Howsoever, this chapter, for the subject matter of it, agrees much with Chap. 24. and the next, with Chap. 25. this being a prophecy of the destruction of the enemies of God's people: the next, of the restitution of the church. And this he makes entrance into, by a summons of all nations, yea, of all creatures: as Chap. 1.2. to take notice of, and consider, what he was about to do, as with one nation before, ch. 33.13. so now to all of them that had been enemies to his people; implying thereby, that what was here denounced, did nearly concern them all, and the several places of their abode.

*{all that is therein*} Heb. *the fullness thereof:* as chap. 42.10. Psal. 24.1.

*{the world*} The habitable world: as Mar. 16.15. or, the world that yields aught (as the word properly imports) for the food, and use of man or beast, opposed to the waste that is altogether barren, and devoid of aught, such as that, Jer. 17.6.

*{all things that come forth of it*} Heb. *all the offsprings,* or *proceeds of it,* ch. 22.24. & 42.5.

**V. 2.** *{For the indignation of the Lord is upon all nations, and his fury upon all their armies*} Or, will be *against:* as Gen. 40.2. & 41.10. God intends to proceed in wrath and vengeance against all those nations, that had been enemies to his people: or, as some, all the wicked of the world, in general. But these seems to enlarge it overmuch; as well, as those on the other side to over-narrow it, that restrain it to the king of Assyria, and his subjects or associates. See ch. 24.1. & 26.21. Joel 3.2. v. 8.

*{indignation*} Or, *boiling wrath;* for the word properly signifies *a bubble.* Hos. 10.7. (where it seems not so well rendered *scum: froth,* were better there, than *scum:* for which another word is, Ezek. 24.6,11.) such as are wont to rise on the top of the water, when the pot boils upon the fire, ch. 64.2.

*{fury*} Or, *fervent wrath,* from a word, that signifies *heat,* Ps. 19.5. & 39.3. whence the sun is so termed: chap. 24.24.

*{all their armies*} Heb. *each army of them;* that have waged or do wage war against his people. See ch. 24.21.

*{he hath utterly destroyed them, and hath delivered them to the slaughter*} Or, *he will utterly destroy them,* (*make an anathema of them.* Josh. 6.17,21. See ver. 5.) *and will deliver them* (Heb. *give them,* as Jer. 15.9.) *unto slaughter.* He has passed such a doom of destruction upon them, as sure to be put in execution, as if it were executed already. ch. 14.26,27. Joh. 3.18.

**V. 3.** *{Their slain also shall be cast out*} To be devoured by birds and beasts, (the multitude of the slain being such, that they shall want either person to bury them, or places to bury them in; or, people in detestation of them, casting their corpses out to lie and rot aboveground, Jer. 7.33,34. & 22.19.) as themselves had formerly dealt with God's people, Ps. 79.2,3. Jer. 34.20.

*{and their stink shall come up out of their carcasses*} Heb. *and their carcasses, the stink of them shall ascend,* or *go up:* a nominative put absolutely: as Psal. 18.31. & 104.17. See Exod. 8.14. ch. 66.24. Amos 4.10. Joel 2.20.

*{and the mountains shall be melted with their blood*} They shall run down with streams of blood, as with water, chap. 30.25. as if they were even dissolved into blood. See chap. 64.2,3. nor need we, with some interpreters, by *mountains,* understand here heaps of carcasses, piled up like hills, as those that Sampson made of the Philistines, Judg. 15.16. It is an hyperbolical form of speech, used in like manner of great plenty, of anything coming from the mountains, and the plants there growing, or the beasts there grazing. So, *the hills shall flow with milk,* Joel 3.18. and, *the hills shall melt with wine,* Amos 9.13.

**V. 4.** *{And all the host of heaven shall be dissolved. and the heavens shall be rolled together as a scroll, and all their host shall fall down, as a leaf falleth from the vine, and as a falling fig from the fig tree*} So great shall their fear and terror be, and so strange and dreadful the judgments of God inflicted upon them, that the whole frame of the creature shall seem to be dissolved, and the world to be at an end. See the like, ch. 13.10,13. & 24.21. Rev. 6.13,14. Yet neither do I concur with those, that understand these words of the general doomsday, though such things then shall be, 2 Pet. 3.10,11. no more than those in the Revelations are to be so understood; many things, in the course of the context, both there, and here, showing, that they cannot so be meant, and much less with those, who suppose no more to be meant, than the thickening and darkening of the air, by such abundance of foggy vapors and exhalations, ascending from the gore-blood and putrefied carcasses, and the production of divers meteors, consisting of such, that shoot to and fro, like stars, and fall at length to the ground. The one go too far, and the other fall far too short. It is the manner of God's prophets, in their descriptions of some extraordinary judgment, to set it forth in such colors, as if they were deciphering the face of that last universal judgment, whereof, such are, in some sort, resemblances and forerunners. See Dan. 7.9,10. Joel 3.12–16. as, on the other side, the restitution of God's people after some grievous calamity, and long affliction, is wont to be shadowed and set forth in such terms, as have caused many to be mistaken in them, conceiving no other, than the general resurrection, at the last day, to be therein described. See Chap. 26.19. Ezek. 37.2,13. Dan. 12.1,2.

*{host*} See Gen. 2.1. ch. 24.21. & 40.26.

*{shall be dissolved*} Heb. *pine,* or *waste away,* Lev. 26.39. Ezek. 24.23. & 33.10. Zach. 14.12. See ch. 3.24. & 5.24. the verb is plural, because the noun is collective. See 2 Pet. 3.10.

*{rolled up as a scroll*} Heb. *as a book.* and so Rev. 6.14. alluding to such books, as were then in use, called *rolls,* or *volumes.* See Chap. 8.1. so that as it could not be seen what was written in those books, when they were so rolled up; no more should the stars now, as they might formerly, when the heaven was spread abroad, Psalm 104.2.

*{their host*} The stars, Rev. 6.13.

*{a leaf falleth*} Or, *as leaves fading, fall:* as ch. 64.6. Jer. 8.13. for so the word properly imports; as the leaves of a vine, when they are withered fall. See ch. 1.30. & 28.1.

*{as a falling fig*} The like defect of the substantive, see ch. 28.4. where a *fading,* is for, *a fading plant:* such green figs as come first; but shed after a while, when others begin to put forth. See Rev. 6.13. The old Latin, and some of our versions supply *leaf,* or *leaves,* from the former branch, but the gender is feminine, which help to strengthen (as also does that of the Evangelist) the former, but some would have it taken neutrally, as is the feminine oft in Hebrew, and then it may include both.

**V. 5.** *{For my sword shall be bathed in heaven*} A description of the great slaughter that shall be made, ver. 2. and the persons that shall be slaughtered.

*{my sword*} Spoken in the person of God. *his sword,* for his power manifested in the execution of justice, Deut. 32.41. Jer. 50.35–37. Ezek. 21.1,9.

*{bathed*} Imbrued in blood: as Jer. 46.10. Heb. *drunk:* as Rev. 17.6. or *soaked,* see v. 7. or *satisfied:* as Ps. 36.8. Pro. 7.19. Jer. 31.14,23. v. 6.

*{in heaven*} According to a decree passed concerning it in heaven, Ps. 119.89. See v. 16. Though some of the Jewish commenters read it, *my sword in heaven,* or, *that is in heaven, shall be made drunk.* Which is yet more probable, than what another of them has, of slaying the great potentates first, that sit aloft, as in heaven, chap. 14.13,14. and after that, the inferior ones, that sit far below them, as on the ground, Psal. 113.7,8. See chap. 24.21. or, what some of our, following the old Latin, that reads the words in the time past, *My sword hath begun to rage*, as drunken men use to do, Prov. 20.1. *in heaven*, that is, in my church, among mine own people, Ezek. 9.6. 1 Pet. 4.17. styled *heaven* in Scripture, Rev. 4.1. & 12.1. and thence shall descend to those without the church, called the earth, Rev. 12.12. See Jer. 25.15,16,18,29.

*{behold it shall come down upon Idumea, And upon the people of my curse, to judgment*} The people and persons, whom this sword is to make slaughter of, are more specially the Edomites, and together with them, such other nations, as were destinated to destruction.

*{behold*} As ch. 10.33.

*{come down*} From heaven; as ch. 30.30. Rom. 1.18.

*{upon*} *Come down upon,* for, *coming down* light *upon:* as Exod. 19.20. *The Lord descended upon the Mount,* for *descending,* abode *on it.* Of which manner of speech; see ch. 13.12. & 38.17.

*{Idumea*} Heb. *Edom:* that is, *Esau.* See Gen. 25.30. & 36.8. here put for his posterity, and their country. See ch. 21.11. as the Moabites, ch. 25.10. so here and Chap. 63.1. the Edomites are marked out, as two of the principal enemies of God's people. See Ps. 137.7. Lam. 4.21.

*{and upon*} Or, *even upon:* as Ezra 1.8. if the Edomites be in this latter branch also intended. See v. 6.

*{the people of my curse*} Heb. *cherem,* Josh. 6.17. Greek, *anathema,* 1 Cor. 16.22. it signifies a thing devoted to destruction, Deut. 7.26,27. See v. 2.

**V. 6.** *{The sword of the Lord is filled with blood, it is made fat with fatness*} An intimation of a very great slaughter.

*{sword of the Lord*} As Jer. 47.6. See ver. 5.

*{is filled*} Or, *shall be filled with blood;* shall drink its fill of blood, v. 5. ch. 15.9.

*{it is made fat with fatness*} Or, *it shall be fatted with fat;* it shall eat abundance of fat: a resemblance taken from some greedy glutton or other ravenous creature, that has gotten, and eaten his, or its fill of fat beasts.

*{and with the blood of lambs and goats, with the fat of the kidneys of rams*} Or, *even with,* &c. for he relates more particularly what *blood,* and *fat,* before, he meant.

*{of lambs, goats, and rams*} Men of all estates and ranks: but these seem here mentioned, as of the meaner sort; for the greater sort follows, ver. 7. and it seems somewhat over nice, that some have of the common people, priests, and wealthy ones. Howbeit, it may well be questioned, whether the word *carim,* translated *lambs,* might not rather be rendered, *bellwethers:* as it is by some, not amiss rendered, *leaders of the flock,* or *sheep,* 1 Sam. 15.9. to the soldiery especially, the words seem to have reference: as Ezek. 39.18. & Rev. 19.18. and to those, that had some command among them. See on ch. 16.1.

*{fat of the kidneys*} Which they lie enwrapped in, Levit. 3.8. Deut. 32.14.

*{for the Lord hath a sacrifice in Bozrah, and a great slaughter in the land of Idumea*} What he called *a slaughter* before, ver. 2. and hereafter again, he now calls *a sacrifice.* For the word signifies as well *to slay,* as *to sacrifice,* Gen. 31.54. 1 Sam. 28.24. 1 King. 1.9,19. Howbeit, there seems an allusion here, to the beasts offered in sacrifice, whose blood, and fat, was reserved, as for God, unto whom they were sacrificed, Levit. 7.23–27. See ch. 1.11. Deut. 32.38. & to those solemnities, in which so great abundance of them was slain, 1 Kings 8.63. 2 Chr. 29.31–35. & 30.24. to which some also add, as implying that God's vengeance executed on his enemies and on the enemies of his people, is as pleasing to him, as any sacrifice whatsoever, ch. 1.24. Jer. 46.10.

*{Bozrah*} The Edomites' chief city, chap. 63.1. Jer. 49.19,13. so termed, not, as the Greeks, who by an inversion of the letters, call it, *Byrsa,* as if it had its name, from an *ox hide,* that should encompass the ground it stood on, being cut out into thongs; (for the word is the same, with the name of that place, of which they tell us such a tale,) but from the fortifications and strength of it, bearing that name, as the word imports, chap. 20.15. & 25.2. & 27.10.

*{Idumea*} As v. 5.

**V. 7.** *{And the unicorns shall come down with them, and the bullocks with the bulls*} The great potentates, and mighty commanders, by these greater cattle, and wild beasts, resembled, shall be pulled down, and slain, as well as the rest, Psalm 22.21. Jer. 50.27. Rev. 19.8.

*{unicorns*} Not such horned creatures like horses, as our painters usually portray; or wild asses, which some tell us of, with one straight horn in the forehead. Whereof, see Aristotle, in his *history of living creatures,* l. 2. c. 1. Elian, l. 4. c. 52. & l. 16. c. 20. & Pliny, l. 8. c. 21. & l. 11. c. 37. for such in these days, nowhere found, are deservedly deemed figments: and the horns we have, called *unicorn's horns,* are well known to be the horns, not of land beasts, but of sea creatures; one, the principal of them, kept, as a royal monument with us, taken out of the head of a vast-bodied creature, found dead, and floating in the sea; another of less note, broken off from the head of the like sea creature, that had run it through the ship's timber, and there left it behind her; but as some guess the *rhinoceros,* a vast beast, for shape, not unlike to the elephant, whom he is reported to fight with, but instead of his trunk, furnished and armed with an horn, of no great length, rising from his nose, as engrafted on it, (whence he is so termed) and slanting somewhat back toward the head of the beast; whereof cups are made, and set in silver of no great size, nor slightly esteemed only for rarity: and this way most of our interpreters go; from whom our margin here renders it, *rhinocerotes.* But other stick at it, for two reasons especially: First, because this beast is not found, but in India, and in the remotest parts thereof; nor is it likely, that it was commonly known among the Jews, as this creature appears to have been, by the frequent mention of it, Num. 23.22. Deut. 33.17. Job 39.9,10. Psalm 22.21. & 29.6. & 92.10. and that bred also with them, as may seem by Psalm 29.6. and again because, (to let pass what is said of its, not *horn,* but *horns,* Deut. 33.17.) the beast here mentioned, is elsewhere spoken of, as having goodly, lofty, and stately horns, Deut. 33.17. Psalm 92.10. which of the rhinoceros cannot be well said. Some therefore of the Jewish writers, suppose it to be that, which the Latins term *Bubalus,* the Italians, *Bufalus:* with us, some a *buffalo;* some a *buff;* from whom, again, some of ours, somewhat dissenting suppose it rather to be that kind of *wild ox,* which the Latin writers call *Urus,* partly, because they find this in Scripture joined commonly with *oxen,* and *bulls,* whereby they conceive it to be some beast of that kind; Deut. 33.17. Psal. 22.12,21. & 29.6. and partly, because that, as this is of special note for strength, Num. 23.22. for horns, Psal. 92.10. and for untamable fierceness, Job 39.9,10. so these, are all reported also to be in the *urus* eminent. For besides his remarkable strength, and bigness, wherein some of them are reported, not to come much short of elephants; his horns are said to be so large, that drinking cups, or vessels rather, of great capacity are made of them; and withal, his untamable fierceness to be such, that being taken in pits, they will be slain sooner, than mastered; and though coming into men's hands very young, they will rather be starved, than tamed. See Cæsar of the *French war,* l. 6. & Pliny l. 8. c. 15. & l. 11. c. 9. but this of the *urus,* and that former of the *Bubalus,* may well be reconciled, if we shall observe what Pliny informs us, that the name *Bubalus* was among the common sort of people, given to the *urus,* even in his days. See on ch. 51.20.

*{come down*} An allusion to beasts struck down, and laid along by the hand of the huntsman or the butcher.

*{with them*} Together with the meaner sort, mentioned v. 6. See Ps. 68.30.

*{bulls*} The word is used for such as are of most excellency and eminency in their kind, whether of horse, *steeds,* as we term them: & so Judg. 5.22. Jer. 8.16. & 47.3. or, neat, *bulls,* and so here: as also, Psalm 22.12. & 59.13. & 68.30. Jer. 50.11.

*{and their land shall be soaked with blood, and the dust thereof made fat with fatness*} That which was before said of the sword, employed in the slaughtering of them, verse 5,6. is here said of the ground, receiving the blood, and the fat of the slaughtered. See verse 5.

*{their land*} The Edomites' country, verse 6.

*{soaked*} Heb. *drunken,* says our margin: but the word is used for *watering,* in a plentiful manner, Psalm 65.10. Prov. 11.25. Chap. 55.10. and 58.11. watered with abundance thereof, as with water.

*{the dust thereof*} Heb. *their dust:* as, *their land.*

*{made fat with fatness*} Cloyed, and thickened with fat, See verse 6.

**V. 8.** *{For it is the day of the Lord's vengeance, and the year of recompenses for the controversy of Zion*} It is the time that God has appointed for the righting and avenging of wrongs done by them, to his people.

*{the day of the Lord's vengeance*} So ch. 63.4. for they strain the words exceeding far, or pervert it rather to a clean contrary sense, that would have it sound, nothing but matter of love, and kind affection and retribution of good in lieu of evils and afflictions, formerly sustained, see ch. 61.2.

*{the year of recompenses*} Or, *retributions,* as, *the days of retribution,* Hos. 9.7. taken in the worse sense, for retribution of penalty, for wrong done: as chap. 35.4. & 59.18. Jer. 51.56.

*{for the controversy of Zion*} The controversy that he has against you for the wrongs that you have done her, as, *the quarrel of my covenant,* Levit. 26.25. for the quarrel that I have against you, for the breach of covenants. *Zion,* for, Jerusalem: as ch. 1.8. and Jerusalem, for the whole state of Judah, ch. 33.20. whereunto the Edomites had from time to time been very injurious, and done them much mischief, Psalm 137.1,2. Lam. 4.22. Ezek. 25.12. Amos 1.11. Obad. 10. See ch. 45.24,25. & 47.3,6. Mic. 7.9,10.

**V. 9.** *{And the streams thereof shall be turned into pitch, and the dust thereof, into brimstone; and the land thereof shall become burning pitch*} A rhetorical description of extreme devastation, in way of allusion to the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah, Gen. 19.24. Deut. 29.23. Rev. 19.20. & 20.10.

**V. 10.** *{It shall not be quenched night nor day; the smoke of it shall go up for ever*} This devastation of Idumea shall last long; as of cities burned down, the smoke, embers, and ashes, do a long time continue. See Jer. 7.20. Rev. 14.11. & 18.18. & 19.3.

*{from generation to generation, shall it lie waste*} That is, for many generations. See v. 17.

*{it shall lie waste*} Heb. *be wasted:* as chap. 60.11. *shall be opened,* for, *shall stand open;* and Neh. 1.3. *is broken,* and *are burnt,* for, continue broken and burnt.

*{none shall pass through it, for ever and ever*} Heb. *ever of evers.* See the like note of extreme desolation, Chapter 60.15. Jerem. 9.10,12.

**V. 11.** *{The cormorant and the bittern shall possess it; the owl also, and the raven shall dwell in it*} Such creatures, only, as haunt waste places, shall be, and abide there. See the like, ch. 13.18–22. & 14.23. Zeph. 2.13,14. Rev. 18.2.

*{cormorant*} Or, as some, *the pelican;* it is reckoned among the unclean birds, Deut. 14.17. Levit. 11.18. and noted for one, that keeps in waste places, Ps. 102.6. Zeph. 2.14. It seems, to be a waterfowl, and is supposed to be so termed, for swallowing down fish, shellfish especially, till by the heat of his gullet, or stomach, being in a manner concocted and made to open, he then *casts up* again, and so picks the fish out of the shell. Aristotle, *history of living creatures.* l. 9. c. 10. Pliny, l. 10. c. 40. Tully, *of the Deity,* l. 1.

*{bittern*} See on ch. 14.23.

*{possess it*} So, he will *make it a possession,* ch. 14.23.

*{the owl*} An unclean fowl, Levit. 11.17. Deut. 14.16. so called, because it shuns the clear daylight, and flies abroad, in the *evening,* or *twilight;* as the adulterer does, Job 24.15. it is rendered, *the great owl,* in Levit. & Deut. See v. 12.

*{raven*} An unclean fowl, also, Lev. 11.15. Deut. 14.14. that feeds upon carcasses and carrion, Prov. 30.17. Rev. 19.17,18.

*{dwell*} Instead of the former inhabitants, ch. 13.22.

*{and he shall stretch out upon it, the line of confusion, and the stone of emptiness*} It shall by line and level, be designed and laid out, to be an horrible desolation, and a waste wilderness: and in vain therefore for them, to attempt the restoring of it again, Mal. 1.4. a metaphor taken from the manner of masons and workmen, who when they are to take down some part of a building, are wont, by line and level, to mark out how far, or how much of it, is to be pulled down. See the like, 1 King. 21.13. Lam. 2.8.

*{he shall*} God shall, or, taking the word indefinitely, such a line shall be stretched out upon it: as ch. 22.8. & 33.1.

*{stones*} Or, *plummet,* or, *level,* as we call it, from the Latin, *Libella,* a stone, plummet, or other weighty thing, hanging on the line, or cord, to keep it right and straight, Zach. 4.10. See also, ch. 28.17. & Amos 7.7,8.

*{confusion, and emptiness*} The words are the same, used of that confused and formless shape of the lower part of the world, in its first production, Gen. 1.2. See ch. 34.10. Jer. 4.23.

**V. 12.** *{They shall call the Nobles thereof to the Kingdom, but they shall not be there, and all their Princes shall be nothing*} There shall be none of their nobles or princes left, to take the government upon them, if it were offered unto them. See ch. 3.6.

*{They shall call, the Nobles thereof to the Kingdom*} The particle *to,* is not in the text, and some therefore read it, *The Kingdom shall call the Nobles thereof,* to wit, to afford conduct, or defense to them: but the noun, and the verb, so joined, agree neither in number, nor person, and that particle is oft wanting, ch. 23.5. Ps. 45.7. Howbeit, the like irregular syntax is in the next verse. And a learned writer renders it, *The Nobles thereof shall call for a Kingdom, when there is none there;* that they might, under a king, enjoy their honors and places: so is the copulative used, Jer. 34.1. Neh. 2.13. Job 21.22.34.

*{nobles*} The word properly signifies *white* ones, Eccl. 10.17. Jer. 27.20. so called, because such are wont to go in *white,* that is, fair, goodly, and gorgeous apparel, Eccl. 9.8. Luk. 7.25. Rev. 3.4. & 7.9,13,14.

*{and*} Or, as some, according to that latter reading, *but:* as ch. 29.13.

*{nothing*} As chap. 40.17. & 41.12. or, *none:* as Amos 6.10. 2 Sam. 9.3.

**V. 13.** *{And thorns shall come up in her Palaces, briers and brambles in the fortresses thereof*} As in the places where such buildings formerly stood, when they lie ruined, is wont to be, chap. 32.13,14.

*{And thorns shall come up*} Or, *thorns also:* as ch. 32.7. Some render it, *a multitude of thorns,* because the noun is plural and masculine; the verb singular and feminine.

*{in her palaces*} The particle *in,* is wanting: as chap. 26.8. and 28.7.

*{And it shall be an habitation of dragons*} Ch. 13.22. & 35.7. Jer. 9.10,22. & 49.33. & 51.37. noted for abode in wastes, Job 30.29. Mal. 1.3. of the word, see ch. 27.1.

*{and a court for owls*} As if he had said, owls shall keep court there, alluding to the courts, that were usually before great men's houses, 2 King. 20.4. See ch. 35.7.

*{owls*} Or, *ostriches,* as some would have it, see Lam. 4.3. Heb. *daughters of the owl,* as it is commonly almost, generally styled: as Levit. 11.16. Deut. 14.15. and elsewhere: it may be, because less than those other kinds, mentioned, ver. 11,14,15. This, and the *Tannin,* in the branch next before, are found joined together, ch. 43.20. as creatures, both abiding ordinarily in the wilderness.

**V. 14.** *{The wild beasts of the desert, shall also meet with the wild beasts of the island*} Heb. *Zijim,* and *Ijim:* of which, see chap. 13.21,22.

*{and the satyr shall cry to his fellow*} Or, *his mate,* v. 15. one to another: as Gen. 11.3,7. See ch. 13.21.

*{the screech-owl also shall rest there, and shall find for her self a place of rest*} There being nobody to disturb her, chap. 17.2. Jer. 7.33.

*{screech-owl*} Or, *night-raven:* our margin, *night monster:* some of the Jewish doctors would have it to be *a chameleon,* that lives by the air: Others of them, *an evil spirit,* that haunts waste places (Mat. 12.43.) and our old Latin renders it *Lamia,* somewhat to that purpose; but the doting Talmudists tell us, that it is the name of Adam's first wife, made of the same mold with him, before Eva, Gen. 1.27. who because she would not be ruled by him, ran away from him, and became an evil spirit; whereupon also they write on a parchment, which they fasten over the door of the new married couple, *Adam Evah, out Lilits.* The word is nowhere else found in Scripture: it seems, by the name, to be some night bird; for as another of the like kind, ver. 11. was so called of the *evening:* so is this, as being a night-haunter, of the *night.*

*{rest*} Or, *rest her.* Heb. *make to rest;* or *place her rest:* the word is in like manner used, ch. 51.4. Jer. 31.4.

*{a place of rest*} Heb. *rest,* simply: as Gen. 8.9.

**V. 15.** *{There shall the great owl make her nest, and lay, and hatch, and gather under her shadow*} What creature this should be (the word being nowhere else read) the Jewish doctors agree not: some of them would have it the same with that rendered *a bittern,* ver. 11. (concerning which, see on chap. 14.23.) because the names differ but in a letter; and that such, as interchanges in Chaldee forms, especially, oft with the other. But other of them, deny that, and say it is another kind of bird: nor is it probable, that the prophet should mention the same twice. Our old Latin, following the Greek renders it, *an hedgehog:* some other, *an ouzel,* or her solitariness, supposed, by some, to be in Latin, called *merula.* The word having no known stem, or stock, it is hard given any certain, sentence of it: for whereas some would have it so termed, of *skipping,* or *hoping,* Cant. 2.8. the radical letters agree not, they differ as much, as *ats, hasty;* and *az then:* Howbeit, in the Arabic, the word of *leaping,* or *skipping,* is said to be so written, as this here, with *az:* whence, in Avicenna, is found the name of a serpent, so called, because it is wont to *spring up* from the ground, to fasten upon man or beast; which some therefore suppose to be here meant. That which might seem very probable, the words coming so near, the one to the other, *kippoz,* and *kippazab,* but that the text seems not so willing to admit it, ranking this among fowls; and describing the manner of her breeding, and brooding her young, in terms particular to that kind. I should suppose, therefore, if I may be so bold, to deliver my conjecture in so doubtful a business, that the serpent mentioned by Avicen, had its name from the fowl here spoken of, and the manner of its motion.

*{lay*} Heb. *deliver:* so ch. 66.7.

*{hatch*} Jer. 17.11.

*{gather*} Brood, her young ones, Mat. 23.37.

*{under her shadow*} Her wings, that shade and protect them, Ps. 91.1. Mat. 23.37.

*{there shall the vultures also be gathered*} Meet and flock together, as about a carcass such are wont to do, Matth. 24.28. Luke 21.37.

*{vultures*} It is found among the unclean fowl, Deut. 14.13. and and with the name a little altered, Lev. 11.14. where the old Latin renders it, *the kite:* some other, the *falcon,* so called of its *swift flight,* Deut. 28.49. Jer. 48.40. & 49.22. but the ancient Greek, as our here, and there, *a vulture:* so called of its color, because black as ink, Jer. 36.18.

*{each one with her mate*} Heb. *a woman:* and, or with, *her friend,* or *familiar,* Exod. 11.2. Jer. 9.20. a defect of the particles: as Ps. 5.4. See ver. 14,16.

**V. 16.** *{Seek ye out of the book of the Lord, and read*} Look into the book of the law, say some, wherein these curses are recorded; or, as others, when the day comes, of the execution of this judgment, take the book of this prophecy into your hands, and read over this passage; and see if any of these be found wanting here: or, these shall as certainly be found all there, as if they were, by name, entered each of them into a roll of record: and there you might be sure to find them, could you but have the sight of that book. Such like phrases, alluding to rolls and registers, are frequent in Scripture, Exod. 32.32,33. Ps. 56.8. & 69.28. ch. 4.3. Mal. 3.16.

*{no one of these shall fail*} Either of the several kinds: as Mat. 4.23. Luk. 11.42. or of the whole number, and tale of each kind, entered into God's lists: as ch. 40.26.

*{none shall want her mate*} There shall none of them be alone: but store of each kind, ver. 14. or, none shall be without her mate, that they may there breed, and replenish the country with such kind of wild creatures: as Gen. 7.2. Heb. *a woman*, or *each one, and her familiar, they shall not visit*: that is, *miss*, or *want*, as the word of *visiting* is used, Num. 31.49. 1 Sam. 25.15. in regard whereof, some render it, *a woman, and her mate, they shall not miss*; that is, neither the one, nor the other, shall be found missing, either in God's roll, by those that can come to the sight of it, or in the country designed unto them; and so it should, in effect, be the same with the former.

*{for my mouth it hath commanded, and his Spirit it hath gathered them*} An emphatical redundancy of the pronoun added to the noun: as Chap. 8.13. & 48.6. Or, *my mouth, it is, that hath commanded* (or given order to have this done) *and his Spirit it is* (whose mouth commanded it) *that will gather them together*, there to inhabit: the pronoun, for the verb substantive; as Eccl. 1.5, 10. Chap. 43.10, 13. a defect of the relative, as Chap. 33.1, 11, 19. and a passage from person to person, as ver. 5, 6. Chap. 33.4, 6, 17. he has given out a commission for it; and as by a secret instinct will bring them together, as he did sometime to Noah, Gen. 7.9. See Chap. 10.6. Joel 2.11.

**V. 17.** *{And he hath cast the lot for them, and his hand hath divided it, unto them, by line*} Or, *he will cast the lot for them, and his hand will divide it to them by line*. He will share it out to them, and divide it among them, as an inheritance, whereof many are coheirs; or a possession, wherein many are joint purchasers, is wont to be divided by line and lot, Psal. 16.5, 6. Mic. 2.5. the *line* being first used for the meting out of the parts; and the *lot*, for assigning of each one, out of the parts so set out and bounded, his share: so was the land of promise shared, Num. 26.53–56. Josh. 13.7. & 14.1, 2. & 18.4, 6. which the prophet may seem to allude unto, to wit, that as God had by line and lot, divided the Canaanites' country to his people: so he had, in like manner, divided the Edomites' land unto these wild and savage creatures, to inherit and possess it forever, or for many descents: for so it follows.

*{they shall possess it for ever, from generation to generation shall they dwell therein*} Heb. *to generation and generation*, that is, *for many generations*: as chap. 60.15. See ver. 10.

### CHAPTER 35

**V. 1.** *{The wilderness, and the solitary place, shall be glad for them, and the desert shall rejoice, and blossom as a rose*} This chapter, and the former, are, questionless, two parts of one, and the same sermon, and have coherence evident enough, the one, with the other; that being of the dreadful destruction of the enemies of God's people, and the utter desolation of their lands: this, of the joyful and glorious restitution, exultation, and exaltation of God's people, thereupon ensuing, and opposed thereunto. So chap. 14.1, 2. & 25.1–9.

*{wilderness*} The land of Judah, that had before, by the enemy overrunning it, been made like a wilderness, Chap. 1.7. & 8.23, 24. & 14.17. & 32.12–14.

*{solitary place*} Or, *waste*. Heb. *dryness*, that is, *land of dryness*, or *drought*; as Psal. 63.1. chap. 32.2. & 14.18. and there may be in the word, an allusion to the name of *Sion*, thence derived. See Jer. 30.17.

*{shall be glad for them*} For the judgments of God, executed upon her malicious enemies, and her deliverance from their cruel oppressions. Psalm 48.11. & 98.10.

*{the desert shall rejoice*} Shall revive, recovering of her former devastations, and look as with a cheerful and pleasant surface again, Psalm 96.12. & 98.8. chap. 51.3. & 52.9.

*{blossom*} Or, *flourish*: for the land or ground is not so properly said to blossom, nor the *rose* neither, Psal. 72.7. chap. 27.6. Hos. 10.4.

*{as a rose*} Cant. 2.1. so *as a lily*, Hos. 14.5. where the same verb is used.

**V. 2.** *{It shall blossom abundantly, and rejoice even with joy and singing*} As the land, so the state also (for by the recovery of fertility and pleasantness to the land, is shadowed out also the flourishing condition of the state. See Chap. 4.2.) shall have a new face, shall put on a new habit. Whereas it was pensive and mournful before, it shall now abound with joy, Psal. 126.1, 2. ver. 10. Chap. 61.10. whereas formerly it was in a dejected and rueful condition, it shall now flourish exceedingly, and be more glorious, than before these calamities befell it. See on Chap. 33.17.

*{blossom abundantly*} Heb. *flourishing, flourish*: as Levit. 13.12. but to another purpose there.

*{rejoice even with joy*} Heb. *exult, even with exultation*; or, as some render it, *even with exultation, shall it exult*: a defect of the particle: as Chap. 33.7.

*{and singing*} Or, *and singing* it shall sing; for the verb is an infinitive, and implies, frequently, a defect of the indicative, or, imperative, or rather includes either of them in it. Exod. 20.8. where the word is, *Remembering*, for, *Remembering remember*, Eccles. 9.11. *I returned, and seeing*, for, *seeing saw again*. So Ezek. 1.14. Jer. 14.5. *singing sing*, for sing abundantly. So Psal. 132.16. See Jer. 31.12. & 51.48.

*{the glory of Lebanon shall be given unto it, the excellency of Carmel, and Sharon*} It shall now be, for stateliness; like Lebanon; a mountain full of lofty cedars, for wealth and beauty like Carmel and Sharon, two places of special note, for fertility and pleasantness. See Chap. 27.6. & 29.17. & 32.15. & 33.9.

*{they shall see the glory of the Lord, and the excellency of our God*} Either his people shall see it: as Chap. 33.17. & 52.8. & 66.18. or men shall see it; others also shall see it, and take notice of it; as well as they: as Psal. 98.3. Chap. 40.5. or taking the word indefinitely, the glorious majesty and power of God, shall be most conspicuously shown and seen, as in the destruction of the enemies of his people, and the overthrow of their lands and states; so in vindication of his people, delivery of them from their former distresses, and raising them to such a flourishing and glorious estate; that were in so great contempt before, Chap. 33.5, 10. & 40.5. & 59.19.

**V. 3.** *{Strengthen ye the weak hands, and confirm the feeble knees*} The prophet having before declared, both what judgments God intended to inflict on the enemy; and unto what estate he is resolved to raise up his people: hereupon he exhorts, and incites them to hearten and encourage one another, God's ministers especially, the weak and feeble-minded ones, with faith and patience, to expect the fulfilling of these gracious promises, Heb. 12.12.

*{weak hands*} Hands that hang down, Job 4.3. See chap. 13.7.

*{feeble knees*} Knees, for feebleness, ready to fall. So the word imports, Job 4.4.

**V. 4.** *{Say to them that are of a fearful heart, Be strong, fear not*} Be not out of heart, or dismayed, in regard of your present pressures, Chap. 40.1. & 43.1.

*{fearful*} Heb. *hasty*: as Chap. 32.4. prone to fear; opposed to *confidence*, Chap. 28.16.

*{behold, your God will come with vengeance, even God with a recompense; he will come, and save you*} God will, ere long, come to execute judgment on your enemies, and to work your deliverance.

*{behold*} As Chap. 30.27.

*{your God*} Whom your enemies jeer you with; demanding where he is, or what is become of him, Deut. 32.37. Psal. 42.3. & 115.2.

*{will come*} Though it seem long before he come, as the physician to the patient, that lies in pain; and relief to those that are in distress, Psal. 6.3. & 10.1. & 13.1. and the wicked think he will never come, Chap. 5.19. Zeph. 1.12. yet he will surely come, and that ere long, Chap. 30.27. & 40.10. & 66.15. Hab. 2.3. Heb. 10.37.

*{with vengeance*} To take vengeance on your enemies and oppressors, Chap. 34.8. & 59.17, 18. a defect of the particle *with*, both here, and in the next: as Chap. 34.15.

*{recompense*} Or, *retribution*. See Chap. 34.8.

*{he will come, and save you*} Or, *when he cometh, he will save you*; as Chap. 30.20. Ruth 2.9. See Chap. 33.22. & 50.1. performed, and made good, in part, in many gracious deliverances; at sundry times, from divers grievous calamities, from the Assyrian yoke, and from the Babylonian bondage, Chap. 37.35. & 38.6. Jer. 30.8, 10. but perfectly fulfilled in Christ, Chap. 9.5, 6. Mat. 1.21.

**V. 5.** *{Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened*} The great and manifold benefits, comforts, and blessings, that by those deliverances, should accrue to God's people, as well spiritual; as corporal.

*{Then*} When by the foregoing afflictions, God's people being now fitted for mercy, God shall be pleased to afford it, Chap. 1.25. & 4.2, 4. & 48.10.

*{the eyes of the blind shall be opened*} They that were before most stupid and brutish, shall now evidently see what affection God bears to his people, what care and regard he has of them, Psal. 58.11. & 126.2. or, those that were spiritually blind before, shall now, being enlightened, see, conceive, and understand, both the mystery of godliness revealed in God's Word, and his mercy and goodness manifested in his works, Psal. 34.5. & 107.43. & 119.18. See Chap. 29.18. & 32.3. & 42.7. & 43.8. fulfilled, corporally, in cures wrought by Christ, Mat. 9.27. & 11.5. & 12.22. & 20.30. & 21.14. Joh. 9.6, 7. spiritually, in the ministry of the gospel, by the efficacy of his Spirit, Act. 26.18. 2 Cor. 4.6. Eph. 1.18. Rev. 3.18.

*{and the ears of the deaf shall be unstopped*} They shall now listen to the Word of God speaking in his book, and by his messengers; that had no list to hearken unto either, before, Chap. 29.18. & 30.20, 21. & 32.3. & 50.5. Psal. 40.6. Job 33.16. fulfilled in Christ's time, both corporally, Mat. 11.5. Mar. 7.32. and spiritually, Act. 2.37, 41. & 8.6, 14. & 13.42, 48. & 16.14.

*{opened*} There is a pleasant consonancy between this term and the former; which our English cannot express.

**V. 6.** *{Then shall the lame man leap as an hart*} Even those that are lame shall get up, and go forth, to see the overthrow given the enemy, and gather some part of the spoils, Ch. 33.23, 24. or men shall be cured of such spiritual defects, in their souls, whereby they were disabled unto sincere, upright, constant, and cheerful walking in God's ways, Jer. 6.16. fulfilled in Christ's time, both corporally, Mat. 11.5. & 15.30. & 21.14. Joh. 5.8, 9. Act. 3.2. & 8.7. & 14.8. and spiritually, Rom. 6.4. & 8.1. Gal. 5.25. Eph. 4.8.

*{as an hart*} As men are wont to leap and spring up, upon sudden occasion of joy, Luk. 1.41, 44. Act. 3.8. or, walking both nimbly and steadily, in the good ways of God, Psal. 18.33. & 119.32. Heb. 12.13.

*{and the tongue of the dumb sing*} Those that have least tongue, or had no tongue at all, to aught that is good, Mat. 12.34. yet shall then, for joy, sing, and chant out the praises of him, that had done so great things for them. Chap. 26.1. & 32.4. ver. 2. fulfilled in the times of the gospel, both corporally, Mat. 9.32, 33. & 12.22. & 15.30. Luke 1.64. and spiritually, Mat. 21.16. Luke 2.20. & 19.37. & 24.50. Acts 3.8, 9. Rom. 15.11. Col. 3.16.

*{for in the wilderness shall waters break out, and streams in the desert*} One main ground of their joy, and their singing for joy, the great alteration that shall be, for the better, in the Jewish land and state. That which was a waste wilderness before, shall now be a well watered, and consequently, a fruitful and pleasant place. See ver. 1, 2. Chap. 30.23, 25. & 33.15. A type of the spiritual watering, whereby such persons and places become fertile and fruitful, that were barren of all grace and goodness before, John 7.38, 39. 1 Cor. 3.6–8. See the like promise to another purpose, chap. 43.20.

*{shall break out*} Heb. *shall be cloven*; that is, shall flow out from the earth, being cloven. So Psalm 74.15.

**V. 7.** *{And the parched ground shall become a pool, and the thirsty land springs of water; in the habitation of dragons, where each lay, shall be grass with reeds and rushes*} The same thing in other terms.

*{parched ground*} Heb. *heat*, chap. 49.10. or, *scorching heat*, for it has affinity with two words, that signify *to scorch*, or, *burn*: *scorching heat*, for, ground scorched with *heat*; as in the next branch, *thirst*, for, a land of *thirst*; a thirsty land: as also, Deut. 8.15. and, *dryness*, for a land of *dryness*; a dry land, ver. 1. The word, save in two places, this, and that other, is not found.

*{shall become*} Heb. *shall be for*, or, *unto*: as chap. 32.15. See chap. 41.18.

*{springs*} As Chap. 49.10.

*{the habitation of dragons*} Whose abode is in waste places. See Chap. 34.13.

*{where each lay*} Heb. *her couch*, or *resting place*: as it is rendered, Prov. 24.15. Jer. 50.6. where they, or each of them, lay. See the like form of speech, chap. 2.20. 2 Kings 5.13.

*{grass with reeds and rushes*} So the particle is used, Ezra 1.5. Jer. 19.13. or rather, *a court for reed*, or, *cane, and rush*: for either word, though collective, yet is singular. The word here used, does signify, most commonly, *grass*, chap. 15.11. & 40.6, 7. but sometime, also, *a court*, or, large open place, wherein grass usually grows. So in another form very frequently; but in this also, ch. 34.13. and so here.

*{reed*} Or, *cane*: for so the word is; and as yet remains in Greek, Latin, ours, and divers other languages. See ch. 19.6. & 36.6. & 42.3.

*{rush*} That uses to grow in moist and miry places, near to pools and plashes, Job 8.11.

**V. 8.** *{And an highway shall be there, and a way; and it shall be called the way of holiness; the unclean shall not pass over it; but it shall be for those*} Having related the flourishing condition of the land and state with God's people, in the words beforegoing; because all that were of little worth, unless it might be quietly enjoyed, and were to continue such: he adds here another benefit, that God's people should be blessed with, to wit, peace and safety, chap. 32.18. & 33.20. described hereby freedom of passage from place to place, ch. 33.17. and the exclusion of such as might annoy or disturb, chap. 29.20. & 32.5, 6. & 33.19.

*{shall be there*} In the lands of God's people.

*{an highway, and a way*} A common roadway, and a causeway the one for man, with beasts and carriages; the other, for foot passengers: or, *a causeway, and a way*; that is, *a way cast up*: for so the word here, and nowhere else found, imports, *a causeway*, or, *cast-way*: as also another of the same family does, more commonly used, chap. 7.3. & 40.3. & 49.10. both coming from a word that signifies *to cast up*, chap. 62.10. Jer. 18.15. in ways used for firmness and sureness. Of the form of speech, see chap. 4.5. Howbeit, I suppose the word, or words here used, to be taken collectively, for *ways*, or *causeways*; as chap. 40.3. the ways shall not be neglected and lie waste, as formerly they did, chap. 33.8. Lam. 1.4. but shall be kept in due repair, and fitted for the conveniency of passengers, who shall travel freely and safely by them.

*{it shall be called*} Or, *it shall be* simply: See on chap. 32.5. & 62.12.

*{the way of holiness*} Or, *a way of holiness*, that is, *an holy way*; as *hill of holiness*, for *an holy hill*, Psalm 15.1. and *city of holiness*, for *an holy city*, chap. 48.2. or, *the way of the Sanctuary*: the way of the Temple; so it is called, as a place of *holiness*, Psalm 20.2. Ezek. 42.14. See ver. 10. or, *the way of men of holiness*, that is, *of holy men*: a way, for such alone, to walk or travel in, a type of the way to heaven, Mat. 7.13, 14. *holiness*, for *holy men*; as *peace*, for *peaceable men*, Psalm 120.7. *charity*, for *charitable*, Prov. 10.12. *righteousness*, for *righteous*, as most, chap. 41.2.

*{the unclean shall not pass over it*} Or, *by which the unclean shall not pass*: the positive for the relative; as chap. 30.6. & 47.4. unclean people, that is, strangers, such as the Assyrians, Syrians, Ethiopians, and Egyptians, shall have no more access to the land of Judah, to pass to and fro in it, as formerly, Lam. 1.10. nor shall the passage to God's house be pestered with unclean persons of their own, the state being now refined and reformed, chap. 1.25, 26. & 60.21. & 62.12. Revel. 21.27.

*{but it shall be for those*} To wit, for those saints, or holy ones. See ver. 9. the pronoun, for the verb substantive, as Eccl. 1.5, 10. Job 28.28. the pronoun, for the noun, as chap. 33.2. Heb. *and*, for *but*; as chap. 29.13. or, *and*, for *for*; as chap. 29.14. and so some here, but reading the words another way, thus; *for he* shall be *with them* (as ver. 7.) or shall be *to them*, to wit, a guide; he shall accompany them, conduct, and guide them, as he did the Israelites in their traveling to Canaan, Exod. 13.21, 22. & 33.14–17. that they may neither miss their way, nor miscarry in it, Psalm 23.3, 4. & 25.8, 9. & 119.130. Luke 1.79. And a learned late writer, notwithstanding the pause, takes in hither from the next branch; *but he shall be walking the way with them*, He, that is, God, shall go along with them, and accompany them in their way. Howbeit, I incline rather to the former reading, for that which follows, v. 9.

*{the wayfaring men, though fools, shall not err therein*} The way shall be so plain, and easy to find, being a causeway cast up, and so straight, and right on, without windings and turnings, such as other crossways are wont to have, Psalm 125.5. Prov. 2.13, 15. that even the simplest that are (of whom it is made a note, that *they know not the way to the city*, Eccl. 10.15.) shall not miss of it, or, through want of skill, stray from it, especially having such a guide at hand, as occasion is, to direct them, chap. 30.21. & 59.21.

*{the wayfaring men*} Heb. *one going*, or *walking the way*, or *in the way*; as chap. 65.2. taken collectively.

*{though fools*} Heb. *and*, which those that go the last way above mentioned retain: but so, chap. 41.5. or, *even fools*, as chap. 1.6.

*{therein*} Wanting; as, *thereof*, chap. 27.9. So Deut. 8.12. Jer. 6.16.

**V. 9.** *{No lion shall be there, nor any ravenous beast go up thereupon; it shall not be found there*} The plainness of the way, and freedom from men ill disposed and ill affected, was before: here is now security given, in regard of fierce or ravenous beasts, that might annoy passengers, and either destroy, or disturb them, in their passage to and fro.

*{no lion*} This passage some expound of men, for fierce and ravenous disposition, like to such wild creatures, as chap. 11.6–9. but of such, he seems to have spoken before. Others, of the Devil, that roaring lion, ravenous wolf, and red dragon, 1 Pet. 5.8. John 10.12. Rev. 12.3, 9. but it seems rather, as the words sound, and as Job 28.8. conceiving it to be understood of the removal, or restraint of such noisome and noxious creatures, as use to grow numerous in those places, that through want of inhabitants lie waste, Exod. 23.29. and had so done in many places of the land, in all likelihood, during the time of the forepassed pressures, where the inhabitants had, by the enemy, been driven from their dwellings: but it is here said, that now they should be rid of such, and no longer infested with them: see the like promise, Lev. 26.6.

*{nor ravenous beast*} Heb. *ravenous of beasts*: the word properly signifies, *a burglar*, one that breaks into houses, to rob and spoil, or murder and mischief, Ezek. 7.22. & 18.10. Hosh. 4.2. Mic. 2.13. more generally rendered, *robbers*, Jer. 7.11. alluded to, John 10.1, 8, 10. here used, for any ravenous creature, such, among wild beasts, as these are among men: *ravenous*, or *ravener* (for the word is substantive) *of beasts*, that is, not one, that in a ravenous manner makes havoc and spoil of other beasts; (though such commonly so do;) but one among beasts, that is so qualified, or that so practices; as, *choice of firs and cedars*, is not the choice that others make of cedars; but the choice ones among them, chapter 37.24. Jeremiah 22. verse 7.

*{shall go up thereon*} Or, *shall pass along thereby*: for so the word is oft used, without special notion of ascent, 2 Sam. 2.1. & 5.19, 20. chap. 36.10. See chap. 38.8. Howbeit, the word may seem to have somewhat more than so in it here; and to have some reference to the condition of the way before mentioned, being said to be a causeway, or a way cast up, and so raised to some height, ver. 8. as if he had said, that though wild beasts might lurk in some by-places out of the way; yet none of them should be so bold, as to come upon the causeways, to impeach travelers in their passage.

*{it shall not be found there*} Or, *it shall not be there*: as chap. 13.15. & 51.3. none of those ravenous creatures shall haunt the highways, as Judg. 14.5. 1 Kings 13.24. Prov. 26.13. alluded to, Jer. 5.6.

*{but the redeemed shall walk there*} The ways shall be free and safe, for those that God has reserved for himself, and delivered out of the foregoing straits and distresses. See v. 8.

*{but*} Heb. *and*, as ver. 8.

*{redeemed*} Or, *reserved*, *rescued*, *delivered*; as Psal. 107.2. chap. 51.10. & 62.12. & 63.4.

*{walk*} Or, *go*, *travel*, as ver. 8.

*{there*} Or, *therein*; as Deut. 8.12. wanting in both places: but here supplied from the former branch.

**V. 10.** *{And the ransomed of the Lord shall return, and come to Zion with songs, and everlasting joy upon their heads*} Those that God shall have delivered, either from the Assyrian invasion, or the Babylonian bondage, both types of the spiritual deliverance of God's people by Christ, shall with expressions of much joy, repair after their wonted manner, to the set place of God's solemn service, being freed from their former tears and fears, and settled in an estate of continued joy and safety.

*{ransomed*} The word is in signification the same with that used, v. 9. as appears plainly, both here, and chap. 51.10, 11. the word signifies first, and properly, *to redeem*, or *buy out*; as Exod. 13.13. & 34.20. Num. 18.15–17. Job 5.20. but it is commonly used, in a more general notion, for *rescuing*, or *delivering* out of danger or distress, by any means or course whatsoever, Deut. 9.29. 2 Sam. 4.9. Psalm 55.18. & 34.22. & 78.42. chap. 29.22.

*{shall return, and come to Zion*} Shall return from captivity, or come back from those places, whither they had fled formerly for fear of the enemy. See Chap. 1.27. and 10.22. or *shall return and come*, that is, *shall again repair* (after their wonted manner, as the phrase is usual, Gen. 26.18. Psalm 78.41. Mal. 1.4.) *to Zion*, that is, to Jerusalem, where there was no free passage before, as chap. 23.20. or to the house of God, the Temple there situate; as Psalm 84.7. Chap. 2.2.

*{with songs*} Or, *with a singing noise*; or, *with a noise of exultation*: so the word properly signifies, Chap. 14.7. & 48.20. ver. 51.11. See ver. 2. either with such mirth as they repaired with to their sacred solemnities. See Chap. 30.29. or with solemn songs, penned on purpose for their present deliverance, Psalm 32.7. Chap. 26.1. & 38.9, 20.

*{and everlasting joy upon their heads*} Or, *and* with everlasting joy. See Jer. 2.37. or, *and everlasting joy* shall be *upon their heads*; the verb wanting, as Chap. 51.11. supplied, as Chap. 61.7.

*{everlasting joy*} Or, *lasting joy*, Heb. *joy of an age*, or *of perpetuity*, as Chap. 61.7. joy of long continuance here, Chap. 32.17. and to all eternity hereafter, John 16.22.

*{upon their heads*} Heb. *head*; as Chap. 51.11. on the head of each of them, as a precious crown, 2 Tim. 4.8. James 1.12. Rev. 2.10. & 4.4. & 7.9. or a garland, evergreen, and never fading, 1 Pet. 1.5. & 5.4.

*{they shall obtain joy and gladness*} Abundance of joy, chap. 51.3, 11. fullness of joy, in the light of God's favor; manifested in these, and the like gracious works wrought for them; but much more complete, in the immediate enjoyment of his glorious presence hereafter; the one being, as a type or shadow, so a forerunner, and earnest of the other, Psalm 4.7. & 16.11. & 89.15, 16. & 126.2. 1 Pet. 1.8. 1 Joh. 1.5.

*{and sorrow and sighing shall flee away*} The former griefs and groans, proceeding from their heavy foregoing pressures shall utterly vanish, and be clean forgotten, as if they never had been, Chap. 25.8. & 30.19. John 16.21. Rev. 21.4.

### CHAPTER 36

**V. 1.** *{Now it came to pass in the fourteenth year of King Ezekiah, that Sennacherib the King of Assyria, came up against all the defensed cities of Judah, and took them*} The relation of Sennacherib's invasion of the land of Judah, together with the deliverance of the city of Jerusalem, and the destruction of a great part of his army, and the shameful flight of himself with the residue, and the murder of him, at home, by the hands of his own sons; is here inserted, out of the records, in the books of the Kings, and Chronicles, in this chapter and the next; both to clear some of the foregoing prophecies, and to confirm, and seal up the truth, both of the predictions therein contained, of those evils that were to befall the Jewish nation, for their sins; as also of the promises delivered in them, concerning God's protection and deliverance of his faithful people among them, and of the comminations of the defeat and overthrow, therein denounced, against their adversaries, chap. 10. & 14.24, 25. & 17.12–14. & 24. & 25. & 30–35. See the like relations, to the like purpose, inserted in the prophecies of Jeremy, Chap. 39. & 52. And this story, see 2 King. 18.13. & 19. & 2 Chr. 32.

*{Now*} Heb. *And*; as 2 Chr. 36.22. chap. 7.1. for with the copulative, the Hebrew oft begins new narrations. So Ezr. 1.1. Neh. 1.1. Jon. 1.1.

*{it came to pass, that*} Heb. *it was*: with a defect of the particle carrying on the relation: as Chap. 7.1.

*{in the fourteenth year*} About eight years after the surprisal of Samaria by Salmaneser, and the deportation of the ten tribes. See 2 Kings 18.10, 13.

*{of King Hezekiah*} See Chap. 1.1.

*{Sennacherib*} Heb. *Sancherib*. Herodotus, who makes mention of him, lib. 2. calls him, *Sanacharib*.

*{King of Assyria*} This Sennacherib seems to have succeeded Salmaneser in the Assyrian empire, either immediately, as most think, or mediately, as may well be deemed, Sargon coming between. See Chap. 20.1. Herodotus styles him, *King of the Arabians, and Assyrians*; not of the Arabians only, as Joseph the Jew misrelates him, lib. 10. c. 1.

*{came up*} A term used of military expeditions, See chap. 7.1.

*{against all the fenced cities of Judah*} In pursuit of the conquest, that his predecessors had made, Salmaneser of Samaria; and Sargon of Palestina, (Chap. 20.1.) he attempted now against Judea, upon pretense of the contribution withheld by Ezekiah, which unto Tiglath-Pileser had, in former times, been paid in yearly, by Ahaz his father, 2 King. 16.7–9. & 18.7.

*{and took them*} That is, either took the most of them; not all simply, (for some of them he had not yet taken: See Chap. 37.4, 8.) but all in a manner, some few only excepted, that seemed as nothing, in comparison of the rest: as those universals are frequently taken; see Chap. 64.6, 7. Jer. 6.28. and 9.2. or, *he came up against them all, and took them*, for, *he came up against them all*, with a purpose *to take them*: as, *Balak arose, and warred against Israel*, for, *rose* with a purpose *to war against Israel*, Josh. 24.9. against whom yet he never actually warred, Judg. 11.25. his purpose was to surprise them all, whatsoever the issue were: and this way that seems to look, and to lead, that we find, 2 Chr. 32.1. where it is said, that *he encamped against the fenced cities, and thought to take them to himself*. Howbeit, the former seems to suit better, both with the matter of the story, and the drift of the relation. Otherwise, no mention should be of the taking of any. Beside, that his *purpose*, there mentioned, may have a more special reference, not so much simply to the *taking* of them, as to the taking of them, *to himself*, that is, to have, and hold them, as his own; wherein he fell short of what his intent and purpose was. And he names expressly, *the fenced cities*, both here and there: as Chap. 25.2. to intimate the general overrunning, and subduing of the whole country before him. For those of less strength must of necessity yield, when those of defense were unable to hold out. See chap. 33.8.

**V. 2.** *{And the King of Assyria sent Rabshakeh from Lachish, to Jerusalem, unto King Hezekiah; with a great army*} See 2 King. 18.17. 2 Chr. 32.9.

*{the King of Assyria*} Sennacherib, 2 Chr. 23.29.

*{Rabshakeh*} 2 King. 18.19. mention is made of two others joined with them, to wit, *Tartan* (of whom, see also, chap. 20.1.) and *Rabsaris*; (of which name, see Jer. 39.3.) but those other two are here omitted, and notice is only taken of Rabshakeh; either because the principal man, in the commission, though last named, in the relation; or, as is most likely, because he was the principal speaker, and the best skilled of them, it may be, in the Jews' language, 1 King. 18.19. whether the term *Rabshakeh*, be the proper name of the man, or the title of his place; (as of *Rabsaris* is deemed) importing the *chief butler*, or, *cupbearer* to the king, is not very certain. For as for the Jewish tradition, that he should be an apostate Jew, (which some of them gather, because he spoke their language, ver. 13. and because they rent their garments, upon his blaspheming, v. 22. whereof see more there; weak grounds to build that conceit upon) and that he should be the prophet Esay's son, in relation to whose apostasy, the prophet should name his other son, that continued loyal and constant to his father's God, and in his faith, *Shear-jashub*, Chap. 7.3. it may justly be deemed, as many other of the like, a fancy of their own framing.

*{from Lachish*} A city of Judah, (of which, see Josh. 10.3, 32. & 15.39.) against which he lay encamped, 2 Chr. 32.9. and where Ezekiah's messengers found him, when they came to him, and there made an agreement with him, 2 King. 18.14. contrary whereunto, he now sends Rabshakeh from thence with forces, either to seize on him, or to besiege him.

*{to Jerusalem*} The head city of the kingdom, (see chap. 1.1.) which unless it should, upon the sight of his vast army, and his summons sent with it, surrender, he was resolved to besiege.

*{with a great army*} Heb. *heavy*. So also, 2 King. 18.17. See Chap. 32.2.

*{and he stood by the conduit of the upper pool, in the highway of the fuller's field*} Of this place, see on chap. 7.3. & 22.9.

**V. 3.** *{Then came forth unto him*} By the king's appointment, ver. 21. whom they had summoned to a parley, 2 King. 18.18. it being neither honorable, nor safe, for him, to go out to them himself in person.

*{Then*} Heb. *And*: as chap. 30.29.

*{Eliakim Hilkiah's son, who was over the house*} Or, *high steward*, advanced now to that office, which Shebna formerly held, as was by this our prophet foretold should be, Chap. 22.20, 22.

*{and Shebna the Scribe*} Or, *secretary*, who had been *over the house*, or *high steward*, before, Chap. 22.15. and this seems to be the first step to his utter downfall, foretold, and threatened, ch. 22.19. Of the office, see 2 King. 4.3. Besides, hence it is not improbably conjectured, that this man Shebna, was either a stranger born, or of base and ignoble birth, for that there is no mention at all made of his parentage, when as of the other two, the one before, and the other after him, there is. See Chap. 22.16.

*{and Joah Asaph's son, the Recorder*} Or, *remembrancer*: it seems to have been an office, not unlike to our *Master of Requests*. See 2 Sam. 8.16. alluded unto, ch. 62.6.

**V. 4.** *{And Rabshakeh said unto them, Say ye now to Hezekiah, Thus saith the great King, the King of Assyria; what confidence is this wherein thou trustest?*} He begins this message, that he would have them deliver, from his master, to Ezekiah, with his master's lofty title, *The Great King*; which the Assyrian kings then arrogated, as having the largest extent of any known monarch, and the Chaldean kings took up, after them, having dissolved their empire; (but indeed is the style best beseeming him, who is absolute Lord, and King of heaven and earth, Ps. 47.2. & 48.2. Mal. 1.14.) thereby to terrify King Ezekiah, as afterward to affright his people, ver. 13. And his main drift throughout his whole speech, is to show, that Ezekiah, could not have any ground of hope, to be able to stand out against so great a potentate, as his grand master was, either from any power of his own, or from any other to be expected from abroad, either from man, or from his God.

*{I say (sayest thou) (but they are but vain words) I have counsel and strength for war*} In these words, his intendment seems plain to be this, to upbraid him with vanity, and condemn him of folly, if he suppose himself able to match, much more, if to out-go his master, either in policy, or in power, being so defective in either: but the manner of speaking, being very concise, makes the sentence not so clear.

*{I say (sayest thou)*} These words, *sayest thou*, must of necessity be supplied, if we retain the reading, which the text here exhibits. But in the History of the Kings, 2 King 18.20. it is, not, *I say*, but, *Thou sayest*; the letters the same, and the points or vowels also, all save one; and this if we follow, no supply at all will need. *Thou sayest*, that is, you may say, peradventure; though it be folly for you so to do: an indicative form in a potential sense: as Num. 23.10. Neh. 6.6. Est. 5.14. Job 37.23. Chap. 26.9,18. Yet some would have it spoken by Rabshakeh in his own person, or in the person of his king, *I say*, it is *but a vain thing*, for you to say, or think thus, or thus: or, as some of our former versions; *I said, surely, thou trustest in vain words*: supplying that of *trust*, from ver. 4. But I rather take it to run here, as in the story whence it is taken.

*{but they are but vain words*} Heb. *a word of lips*; that is, say some, a word, that comes from the *lip* only; that which he could not speak from the heart; as being conscious to himself, of his own deficiency in either: so it should be, not unlike that, ch. 29.13. of *honoring God with the lip, and not with the heart*: but it seems rather to import vain and windy words, and the *lip*, to be opposed here, not so much to the *heart*, as to the *hand*: words without fruit, or effect; and may well be rendered, *matter of lips*, idle talk only: for the word, *word*, in Hebrew, does often signify *matter*; as it is also rendered, Prov. 16.20. and 25.2. So Prov. 14.23. *the word*, or *matter of lips*, is opposed to the *labor of the hands*; and *profit*, or *advantage*, said to come of the one; nothing but *want* to proceed from the other: and, *a man of lips*, Job 11.2. is put for, *a talkative man*; for one that talks much, but proves nothing. Nor can I accord, therefore, with those, who by *a word of lips*, here understand *eloquence*; because *lip* seems to be put, not for *language* alone, as Gen. 11.1. Zeph. 3.9. but for fineness of *language*, Job 12.20. yet so the Geneva version, rendering the text, *I say, surely I have eloquence*; as spoken in the person of Ezekiah: the use of the phrase carries it the other way, rather.

*{I have counsel, and strength for war*} The words thus read, are spoken as Ezekiahs, intimating a conceit, that he should have of his own sufficiency, for such requisites as were needful to wage, and maintain war with. But some of our former versions render the words, thus, *but counsel, and strength are for war*; as spoken by Rabshakeh, (but scoffingly) in way of advice to Ezekiah, not to rely on vain words, that would stand him in no stead; but to consider seriously what want he had, as well of *good counsel*, as of forces and arms, being both alike necessary for war. See Prov. 20.18. and 24.6. Luke 14.31. And there want not those, who read the whole passage in one continued tenor, *Thou sayest* (that is, you think, imagine, with yourself) that *counsel, and strength for war, are but a matter of words*; that is, as easy to be had, as words are; or, as others, that *surely lip-labor* (so say they in scorn, he terms prayer) is *counsel, and strength* sufficient *for war*: as if instead of these, he relied upon prayer. So the Jewish doctors. But these expositions seem over-forced.

*{Now in whom dost thou trust, that thou rebellest against me?*} If you have not a fond conceit of your own sufficiency herein, what other aid or power from abroad, is it, that you rely upon? that you dare offer to withdraw yourself from my obedience, whose predecessors, your father before you acknowledged, 2 Kings 16.7. and 18.7.

**V. 6.** *{Lo thou trustest in the staff of this broken reed, on Egypt; whereon if a man lean it will go into his hand, and pierce it.*} Having endeavored to beat him, or scoff him off, rather, from confiding in any policy or power of his own: he now labors to take him off, from expectation of any sure assistance from abroad. If he think of any foreign forces, it must be from Egypt; but Egypt was more like to hurt, than to help: for that was her wonted guise. Which he sets forth, by a resemblance taken from a bruised, or broken cane, which if a man lay hold on to sustain him when he is in danger of falling, will not only fail him, but maim him, with the sharp toothed shivers of it, running into his hand.

*{in the staff of this broken reed*} Thus he terms Egypt. *a staff*, being an emblem of stay and support, (see chap. 3.1.) because she professed and promised support and succor to other people. See on Chap. 18.1. and 30.2. and 31.1. And *a reed*, or *cane*, rather, (for the Hebrew word here used, is the very same with our English; whence also by the Greek and Latin, it descended unto us) in way of allusion, partly, to those paper-canes; for which Egypt, abounding in them, and supplying other countries, far and near, with them, was famous; (see on ch. 19.6,7.) and partly, also, to such canes, as men commonly used for walking-staves; as we also do, at this day, and the weaker sort, for support. See on ch. 10.20. and 50.10. but withal, to *a broken*, or *a bruised one*, as the word is rendered, where from *broken*, it is distinguished, Chap. 42.3. and therefore unable to help, or uphold, Chap. 20.6. and 30.5,6. For whereas a learned late writer would have rendered it, not *broken*, or *bruised*, but *frail*; though, as we read it *a reed*, it may carry the better color; yet if the word be aright rendered, not *a reed*, but *a cane*; though the Hebrew word comprehend both, (because not of *reeds*, but of *canes*, are staves made) it will appear not so fit: since that the failing of it, as also the maiming of it, is here attributed, not to the matter of it, because *a cane*, which being firm and entire, would afford stay sufficient; but to the affection of it, because *bruised* and battered, and scarce able, therefore, well to sustain itself, much less to support another.

*{so is Pharao King of Egypt to all that trust in him.*} Not only, not helpful, but prejudicial and harmful. So had he been to Samaria, 2 Kings 17.4,5. and so he proved to Gods people, Chap. 30.3. and 31.3. See Ezek. 29.6,7.

**V. 7.** *{But if thou say to me, We trust in the Lord our God: Is it not he, whose high places, and whose Altars Hezekiah hath taken away, and said to Judah and Jerusalem, Ye shall worship before this Altar?*} Having endeavored to take him off from his confidence in man, and in Egypt by name; wherein, a party, at least, among them, had been very faulty, as appears, Chap. 30.1,6. and 31.1,2. he now strives to shake him off from his hold of, and trust in God, as one whom he had exceedingly wronged, in abridging his service, and restraining it to one place, which yet was no other thing than God himself had enjoined, Deut. 12.11,13,14. nor were those high places and altars, that he took away, the most of them, other than high places assigned to idol-service, 2 Kings 18.4. and for those other in which the true God was served, it is noted as a defect in his son Manasses reformation, in his latter, and better days, that they were not utterly removed, 2 Chr. 33.17.

*{But if thou say*} Heb. *And* (which may here well stand) *if* (as Deut. 12.21.) *thou shalt say*: as Jer. 5.19.

*{said to Judah and Jerusalem*} 2 Chron. 32.12. *commanded Judah and Jerusalem*, (that is, the inhabitants of either) *saying*.

*{before this altar*} 2 Chr. 32.12. *before one altar*, to wit, that in the Temple at Jerusalem, Chap. 31.9.

**V. 8.** *{Now therefore give pledges, I pray thee, to my Master the King of Assyria, and I will give thee two thousand horses, if thou be able on thy part to set riders upon them.*} Since that you neither have power sufficient of your own to withstand my masters forces, nor have hope of help, either from God, or man; your best course is to come to agreement with my lord, and give him security for your future fidelity, and performance of what he shall further require of you; which if you do, I will undertake he shall furnish you with more horses, than you can find men to manage: Or, to let you know your own weakness, do but give me good security, and I will deliver you two thousand horse, upon condition, that you shall furnish them with riders, and do the best you can with them; or, if you cannot, that then you re-deliver them, and yourself together with them; or lastly, as others, engage yourself in fight with my masters forces, and I will furnish you with two thousand horse, to come forth with into the field, if you have but as many riders for them, as daring him to fight, and offering him, in scoffing manner, some helps, if he could, and dared undertake it.

*{Now therefore*} Heb. *And now*; as Chap. 30.3. Yet some retain the copulative here.

*{give pledges*} Or, *hostages* Heb. *mingle thyself*; as Ezr. 9.2. Psalm 106.35. Prov. 20.19. & 24.21. and the word, in the original, is very general, and may as well signify *compound*, or *make agreement*. Which some therefore understand of yielding himself into the hands of Sennacherib, on such terms, as he should propound to him, and engaging himself for the making of them good, as ver. 16. Others, of *giving security*, for the horses hereafter mentioned, or *laying a wager* upon them, because of undertaking by suretyship, the word is oft used, Prov. 6.5. and 11.15. and 17.18. and others, of joining battle, wherein two adverse parties are mingled either with other; because another word of the same notion is very commonly so used, Deut. 2.5,19,24. 2 Kings 14.10. Dan. 11.25.
