*{I pray thee*} The word here used, as also that which answers it, the same with it, both in Greek and Latin, is a particle, either of asseveration and assent, Gen. 18.21. or of incitation, and putting on, Psalm 118.2–4. or, of obsecration and entreaty, Gen. 18.30,32. and hereafter, ver. 11. for this place controls those Jewish critics, who affirm, that perpetually it signifies *now*: it is here used, in the second notion, not in the third; for Rabshakeh would scorn to stoop so low, as to pray, or to entreat; and would rather therefore be rendered, *go to*, than *I pray thee*.

*{and I will give thee two thousand horses*} Either my master will furnish you with horse, for your use and honor, if you yield yourself to him: or, I myself, will at present, out of my own troops, afford you such a number of them, to do the best you can with them.

*{if thou be able on thy part to set riders upon them*} Implying, that he was not able to find so many among all his soldiery, that were expert and able riders. And the old Latin therefore renders it in the negative; *and*, or, *but thou wilt not be able to set riders on them*. Which howsoever it is by most interpreters deemed such a thing, as might probably be true; for that, say they, their kings were forbidden to multiply horses, Deut. 17.16. and the land of Judah was not so fit, either for the breed of them; for which cause, they stored themselves much with horse, out of Egypt, and other lands, 2 Chron. 1.16. & 9.28. or for the use of them, being hilly, in war; and few therefore among them had any great skill in horsemanship. Yet it seems rather to be an Assyrian brag and jeer, setting light by Ezekiahs forces, in regard of his masters, and withal, covertly nipping them, for their sending of supply to horses to Egypt, Chap. 31.1. as if he had said, they should not need, if they would be ruled by him, to send so far for horses, he would furnish them nearer at hand, with a greater number than they could well tell what to do with. See ver. 9. for though Egypt might have the greater plenty of horse, and be, in some respects, the fitter for breed of them; yet was the land of Canaan well stored also with them, as appears by the multitude of chariots, there recorded to have been anciently, which could be of no use, without horses. See Josh. 11.4. Judg. 4.3,13. as also by the number of them that Solomon kept, though he had many, also from other parts, as what king or country has not, though never so well stored itself, 2 Chr. 1.14. & 9.25. yea, the land in these very times, is said expressly to have been *full of horses*, and of *chariots in abundance*, chap. 2.7. nor were their kings inhibited to keep store of horse, sufficient for the defense of themselves, and the state: but that they should not give their mind wholly to multiply horses, or heap up treasure (for the charge is, concerning both, the same) as if their chief strength consisted in either, Deut. 17.16,17. Psa. 20.7. & 33.16,17. Prov. 21.31.

*{to set*} Heb. *give*: but so the word is commonly used, for *to put*, or *set*, Exod. 25.12,21,26,30. Jer. 6.27. and it is the rather used here, in reference to the former branch, as if he had said, if you can find riders, I will find you horses.

**V. 9.** *{How then wilt thou turn away the face of one Captain of the least of my Masters servants?*} How then, being so sorrily furnished, are you able to defeat any one of my masters least and lowest commanders? much less to deal with all his forces.

*{How then*} Heb. *And how*; as Dan. 10.17.

*{wilt thou*} Or, *canst thou*: the future is oft potential; see Jer. 2.23. or, *darest thou*, to wit, offer once to attempt it; as ch. 10.14. Jer. 2.23. Zach. 1.21.

*{turn away the face*} Or, *turn back the face*; as, *turn back the battle*, chap. 28.6. and the phrase implies a defeat, a causing to turn back without effect, as in suit, 1 Kings 2.16. Psalm 132.10. so in fight.

*{of one*} Or, *of any one*: *one*, for *any one*, as Job 14.4. Matth. 18.10.

*{of the least of my Masters servants*} As implying, that the least of them was able to command, and to furnish, far more than so. See chap. 10.8.

*{and put thy trust on Egypt for chariots and for horsemen?*} While you rely on them that can do you no good, but much harm. See ver. 6.

*{and put thy trust*} Some disjoin this branch from the former, rendering it, *but thou puttest thy trust*: but it runs better, as we have it, and would yet more smoothly, if it were, *while thou trustest*: for so the particle is used and rendered, Est. 2.21. Psalm 146.2. and so would be, 2 Kings 11.25. *and he vexed Israel, while he reigned over Syria*.

*{chariots*} Heb. *chariot*; see chap. 21.7. & 22.7.

**V. 10.** *{And am I now come up without the Lord against this place to destroy it? the Lord said unto me, Go up against this land and destroy it.*} The more yet to dishearten Ezekiah and his people, by cutting off all hope of help from above, he pretends, that he came by command, and commission from God. And it is true, that such a business was determined, and passed, in Gods secret disposition, ch. 10.6. but that was more than he ever once dreamed of, or had any intent to execute, ch. 10.7.

*{come up*} *Come up*; Or, *go up*: as 1 Kings 22.12,15. military terms: Heb. *ascend*: see ver. 1.

*{without the Lord*} The name *Jehovah*, as we now read and render it, Exod. 6.3. Psalm 83.18. or, that *Son of four letters*, that is, *four lettered* name, as the Jews style it, which that answers to, is here twice used; whereby it appears, that the same (notwithstanding the superstitious conceit, and groundless assertions, of not Jews alone, but some of ours also, to the contrary, concerning it) was in those times in use, and commonly known: and that, not unto Gods people only, but unto other nations also. Rabshakeh names it six several times in his speech, ver. 7. here, and ver. 15,16. see also, Gen. 24.50. Exod. 5.2.

*{and destroy it*} This, concerning the city, God had not determined; much less ever signed him any such commission: see ch. 37.33,35.

**V. 11.** *{Then said Eliakim and Shebna, and Joah unto Rabshakeh, Speak, I pray thee, unto thy servants in the Syrian language, for we understand it; and speak not, in the Jews language, in the ears of the people, that are on the wall*} In these words is related a piece of that submiss and dejected carriage, foretold, chap. 10.4.

*{Then*} Heb. *And*; as ver. 9.

*{said*} The verb is singular, because delivered but by one of them, though in the name of the rest also: See verse 12.

*{I pray thee*} Of this particle (for so only it is) see on ver. 8. and on chap. 38.3. it is rendered *oh*, Gen. 18.30,32. and so would rather be here, than, *I pray thee*; the rather, the speech running as in the person of no one of them, but them all.

*{thy Servants*} Too mean a phrase, for a kings messengers: But so Ahaz himself, before; *I am thy Servant*, 2 Kings 16.7.

*{the Syrian language*} Heb. *Aramite*, Ezra. 4.7. Dan. 2.4. by all which places (this and those) put together, it appears, that this language was in ancient times most generally spoken, being in ordinary use under those three great monarchies, the Assyrian, the Chaldean, and the Persian: and it is that, wherein some part of the Old Testament was penned; which we commonly, but causelessly, now call *Chaldee*, when as the Scripture itself, terms it *Aramit*, or *Syriac*; nor was it indeed more the Chaldean, than the Persian, or Assyrian language, though termed, Dan. 1.4. *the tongue of the Chaldeans*; because spoken with them at Babylon, and in the kings court especially; in regard whereof the Jewish children, being to attend the king there, were to be taught it.

*{we understand it*} Heb. *hear it*; as Gen. 11.7. & 41.15. & 42.23. So chap. 33.19. The courtiers and statesmen understood it, having for, and by negotiations learned it, and been acquainted with it, though the common sort of people then did not, chap. 28.11: & 33.19. howsoever, in process of time, after their return from the Babylonian captivity, and in the days of our Savior, when it was more corrupt, and had further degenerated from the Hebrew, which it had more affinity with before, it grew common among them; and is in that regard called the *Hebrew tongue*, in the New Testament, because then commonly spoken with them, Joh. 19.13,17. Act. 21.40. & 22.2.

*{speak not in the Jews language*} The Hebrew, their native language, Neh. 13.24.

*{in the ears*} For, in the hearing: as Ch. 5.9. & 22.14. Jer. 36.6.

*{of the people*} Herein they bewray overmuch timorousness, and diffidence; thereby occasioning the adversary to be more peremptory with them.

*{upon the walls*} Where the soldiers lay, and whither the people did, in likelihood, upon this occasion flock, many of them, to view the king of Assyria’s ambassadors, and to hear (if they could) also, what their message might be.

**V. 12.** *{But Rabshakeh said, Hath my Master sent me to thy Master, and to thee, to speak these words?*} Upon the discovery of their diffidence, manifested in the request they made to him, he carries himself the more arrogantly and insolently toward them; and endeavors to move the people to mutiny; whom he perceived them to be jealous of; partly by menacing them with a strait siege, and putting them out of hope of being able to hold out; and partly, by promising them very fair conditions, that the king his master would afford them, if they yielded themselves up to him, v. 16,17.

*{But*} Heb. *And*; as Chap. 31.2.

*{to thee*} Hence it appears, that the former request, though conceived, as in the name of them all three, yet was delivered by one of them only, as the foregoing speech was uttered by Rabshakeh alone, though two other were also joined in commission with him: see ver. 2. And it may be surmised, to have been a motion of Shebna’s own contriving of purpose, suspected to comply with the enemy, thereby to give them some hint of the peoples disposition, and occasion, by these means, to work further upon them.

*{Hath he not sent me to the men that sit upon the wall*} Heb. *not to the men?* with the note of interrogation only; the supply is from the former branch; the like whereunto, see 1 Chr. 10.11. Job 14.5. & 22.24. Chap. 10.5. & 30.29.

*{that sit*} That is *are*, or *abide upon the wall*] expecting the issue of the treaty: So Deut. 9.9. 2 Sam. 7.18. (for it is not to be imagined, that David conceived that so humble and solemn a prayer, sitting) Jer. 39.14. & 40.5,6.

*{that they may eat their own dung, and drink their own piss with you*} This he speaks to affright the people with expectation of a strait siege; such as that threatened, Ezek. 4.9,12,15. and as Samaria sustained, 2 Kings 6.25. Not that they were then in any such extremity; but that so they should be compelled to do, unless they yielded up the city.

*{dung and piss*} The Jews, because they account the words here used by Rabshakeh, no very cleanly terms, never read them, but two other in the room of them; in like manner they deal, not with Rabshakehs only, but with the Holy Ghosts language, 2 Kings 10.27. where they substitute another in the room of one; derived from the former of these, importing a common *draught*: Instead of the latter, they read *the water of the feet*: of which form of speech, see on chap. 6.2. & 7.20. from Deut. 28.56,57. and I find the very same used by Pliny, l. 30. c. 7. *the water that runs by*, or *between the feet*.

**V. 13.** *{Then Rabshakeh stood, and cried with a loud voice in the Jews language*} *Then*: Heb. *And*, as ver. 11. *Rabshakeh stood*: lifted himself, as much as he could (for he was standing, before, v. 2.) being not now to parley with them, that stood on even ground with him, but to speak unto them, that were aloft on the wall; *and cried aloud*, together with his body raising also his voice, that it might reach to the whole multitude of them, or to as many, at least, as might be. See ch. 33.7.

*{and said, Hear the words of the great King, the King of Assyria*} See verse 4.

**V. 14.** *{Thus saith the King, Let not Hezekiah deceive you: for he shall not be able to deliver you*} As he dealt before in his speech, addressed to the king, by his messengers, so now in his parley, directed to the people, he labors to persuade them, that neither their king, nor their God, should be able to deliver them, if they stood out against his master.

*{to deliver you*} *Out of his hand*; As it is, more fully, 2 Kings 18.29.

**V. 15.** *{Neither let Hezekiah make you trust in the Lord*} That which he both did himself, 2 Kings 18.5. and endeavored to make his people also so to do, 2 Chr. 32.6–8.

*{saying, the Lord will surely deliver us*} Heb. *will delivering deliver us*; as Exodus 5.23. 1 Samuel 30.8. So also, 2 Kings 18.30.

*{the city shall not be delivered into the hand of the King of Assyria*} This he might well assure them of; for God, by his prophet, had before promised as much, ch. 31.4,5. & 33.20.

*{delivered into the hand*} Heb. *given into the hand*: that is, the power; as 2 Kings 18.29,30. Jer. 15.21. & 26.24. and so, *deliver out of hand*, that is, *from the power*, v. 19. 1 Kings 18.29. Dan. 3.15,17.

**V. 16.** *{Hearken not to Hezekiah; for thus saith the King of Assyria, Make agreement with me, by a present, and come out to me, and eat ye every one of his own vine, and every one of his own figtree, and drink ye every one the waters of his own cistern*} He would bear them in hand, that their condition should be no way impaired, but bettered, rather, by yielding themselves up to his master. For they should quietly enjoy what they were possessed of at present, (which unless they came out, and compounded with him, they could not do,) and when he should see good to remove any of them into some other place, he would seat them in a land, in all respects, as good as their own.

*{make an agreement with me by a present*} Or, *seek my favor by a present*. Heb. *make with me a blessing*; or *deal with me, by a blessing*: *a blessing*, for, *a gift*, or *present*: as Gen. 33.11. Josh. 15.19. 1 Sam. 25.27. 2 Kings 5.15.

*{come out to me*} Yield yourselves up to me. So 2 Kings 24.12. Jer. 38.2,17,18.

*{and eat*} Or, *and ye shall*, or *may eat*. For that is the use of the imperative, in such kind of speeches. So Gen. 42.18. *Do thus, and live*, that is, *if ye do thus, ye shall live*: as Luke 10.28. Romans 10.5. See the like, Psalm 37.25. *dwell for ever*, 2 Kings 18.32. *live, and die not*. You shall freely and quietly enjoy each one his own, if you do, as I advise you.

*{every one*} Heb. *a man*: as ch. 9.20.

*{of his vine, and of his fig-tree*} That is, the fruit *of his vine*, and the fruit *of his fig-tree*: as Jer. 5.17. these plants and fruits mentioned, because most common in those parts for food and refreshing. See 1 King. 4.25. Mich. 4.4. Zachary 3.10. put here for all commodities and conveniences, as well for necessity, as for delight.

*{and drink*} Or, *shall*, or, *may drink*: as before.

*{the waters of his own cistern*} Or, *the water* (see chap. 1.22.) *of his own pit*: as Leviticus 11.36. Jeremiah 14.3. such as they had usually near unto their houses, for receipt of water, that they might have it, upon all occasions, ready at hand, alluded unto, Prov. 5.15.

**V. 17.** *{until I come, and take you away to a land like your own land*} Until I see good to remove you hence, as Salmaneser did your brethren of the other ten tribes, 2 Kings 17.6. and 18.12. This being the manner of conquerors, in those times, to remove the natives of a land conquered, into some other country, placing others in their stead, to keep them the quieter, and to put them out of hope, by rising, to recover their own again.

*{take you away to a land*} Heb. *take you to a land*, for *take you*, and carry you *unto a land*: a defective, or comprehensive speech, including two several notions in one term. So Gen. 29.9. *take me* (for, take, and bring me) *two kids*, Num. 11.16. *take them* (for, take, and bring them) *unto the Tabernacle*, Prov. 25.22. *take coals* (for, take, and heap coals) *on his head*, Ezek. 17.5. *he took* (for, he took, and placed, or set it) *by great waters*, Hos. 11.3. *he took them* (for, he took, and carried them) *on his arms*. So the words would there be rendered. See of the like, chap. 38.17,21.

*{a land of corn and wine, a land of bread, and vineyards*} A land that has plenty of these commodities; as the land of Canaan had, Deut. 8.8,9.

*{wine*} Heb. *new wine*, or, *sweet wine*, Chapter 24.7.

**V. 18.** *{Beware lest Hezekiah persuade you*} A defective speech, See the like Gen. 3.22. Deuter. 8.12. Job 36.18. Jer. 51.46.

*{persuade you*} Or, *seduce you*; or *beguile you*, as Jeremiah 38.22.

*{saying, the Lord will deliver us*} See on v. 15.

*{Hath any of the Gods of the Nations delivered his land out of the hand of the King of Assyria?*} Either this king, or other his predecessors. ch. 37.11,12,19.

**V. 19.** *{Where are the Gods of Hamath, and Arphad?*} What is become of them? See Chapter 37.19. or, *Where were* they, to wit, when they should have saved those that served them; but indeed could not save themselves. See Chap. 47.1.

*{Hamath and Arphad*} Of these places, see ch. 10.9.

*{where are the gods of Sepharvaim?*} See 2 Kings 17.24. whereby it appears, that this place (and so in likelihood the other also here mentioned) was not subdued by Sennacherib, (though he vainly arrogate the subduing of them to himself, verse 20.) but before his time, by Salmaneser, or some other of his ancestors.

*{and have they delivered Samaria out of my hand?*} Or, *or have* the gods of *Samaria delivered* it *out of my hand?* or *could they deliver it*, &c. the copulative in a disjunctive notion: as ch. 17.8. the indicative in a potential: as Job 37.23. v. 9. and a supply from the former branches, as ch. 10.5.

**V. 20.** *{Who are they amongst all the Gods of these lands, that have delivered their land out of my hand, that the Lord should deliver Jerusalem out of my hand?*} He boasts arrogantly of what had been done by others, (see verse 19.) and impiously yokes the living God with dumb idols, as of no more power than they. So Chapter 10.15.

*{have delivered*} Or, *could deliver*: as ver. 19.

**V. 21.** *{But they held their peace, and answered not a word; for the Kings commandment was, saying, Answer him not*} *But*. Heb. *And*: as v. 7. *they held their peace*; both the king’s messengers, and the people also, 2 Kings 18.36.

*{not a word*} Or, *aught*: as Jer. 26.2. not that they said, nothing at all to him; for to what end then went they out, but that they made no answer to these his vainglorious vaunts and blasphemous menaces; the king having beforehand given them instructions to the contrary, as well witting that to debate, and argue thereabout with him, would but incite him to further outrage. See Prov. 9.7,8. & 26.4. Amos 5.13.

*{the Kings commandment was*} Heb. *it*, for, *was*: the pronoun for the verb substantive: as ch. 34.16. & 43.10,13.

**V. 22.** *{Then came Eliakim the son of Hilkiah, that was over the household, and Shebna the Scribe, and Joah the son of Asaph the Recorder, to Hezekiah, with their clothes rent, and told him the words of Rabshakeh*} Heb. *And*: as v. 12. See v. 3.

*{with their clothes rent*} Heb. *rent of clothes*: as 2 Sam. 13.31. & 15.32. Jer. 41.5. See the like syntax, Chap. 63.1. Either in the detestation of the blasphemies uttered by Rabshakeh; as the high-priest on the like pretense, Mat. 26.65. or, out of perplexity of mind, and extremity of grief, arising as well from the consideration of their own distress, as of the dishonor also done unto God: for this renting on such occasions was very usual, Gen. 37.34. 2 Sam. 1.1. & 3.31. & 13.19. Joel 2.13. see ch. 37.1. The Jewish doctors would hence gather, that Rabshakeh was a Jew by birth: because say they, the Jews’ manner was not to rent their clothes, upon the hearing of any blasphemer, unless he were a Jew. But neither does it by the text appear, that they tore their clothes at that very time, when he so blasphemed; but rather afterward, when they were come away from him: nor is there any good ground brought to prove such a restraint of that their demeanor: and the apostles’ practice may seem to control it, Acts 14.14. See of Rabshakeh, further before, on v. 2. and of the heavy plight of these messengers, ch. 33.7.

### CHAPTER 37

**V. 1.** *{And it came to pass, when King Hezekiah heard it, that he rent his clothes, and covered himself with sackcloth, and went into the house of the Lord*} This chapter is the same in substance, with 2 Kings 19. It relates Ezekiah’s carriage upon the report of Sennacherib’s message, delivered by Rabshakeh, ver. 1–5. God’s gracious answer returned thereupon, verse 6,7. A second message of Sennacherib sent in writing, ver. 8–13. what Ezekiah did therewith, v. 14–20. God’s second answer thereupon, v. 21–35. The destruction of Sennacherib’s host, by an Angel, v. 36. of himself, by his sons, ver. 37,38.

*{it came to pass, that*} Heb. *it was, — and*: as Chapter 3.2.

*{heard it*} A defect of the pronoun: as ch. 31.5. v. 9.

*{rent his clothes*} In token of extreme grief: as his messengers before him, ch. 36.22.

*{covered himself with sackcloth*} Heb. *sack*: which God by the present judgment, called for, chap. 22.12. a further expression of inward regret, humiliation, and repentance, 1 King. 21.27,29. Jon. 3.6. this being the usual mourning weed in those times. See Chap. 15.3.

*{went into the house of the Lord*} Unto the Temple, to pray there where God had promised to hear, 1 Kings 8.18,19. & 9.3. 2 Chr. 7.15,16. (as heathen people and princes used in such cases for such purposes, to repair to the temples of their gods, Chap. 15.2. & 16.12.) and to perform that office in person himself, which he required in his behalf, and in the behalf of the whole estate, from the prophet Esay and others, v. 4. So 2 Chr. 20.3,5,6. Est. 4.16. Jon. 4.6,7.

**V. 2.** *{And he sent Eliakim, who was over the household, and Shebnah the Scribe, and the Elders of the Priests, covered with sackcloth unto Esay, the Prophet, the son of Amoz*} He rested not in his own performances, but sends to request the assistance of others, God’s prophet more especially, in prayer. See Jer. 21.1,2. So Paul himself, Rom. 15.30. 2 Cor. 1.10,11. Eph. 6.18,19. Col. 4.3. 2 Thess. 3.1.

*{Eliakim, and Shebna*} Two in chief place about him, See chapter 36.3.

*{the Elders of the Priests*} As those other two of the chief in the civil state; so those in the ecclesiastical, called *the Elders of the Priests*; to distinguish them from *the Elders of the People*, Numb. 11.16. 1 Sam. 15.30. chapter 3.14. called also *the Elders of the Congregation*, Levit. 4.15. and, *of the land*, 1 Kings 20.7. and, *of Judah*, or *Israel*, in general, 2 Chr. 5.4. & 34.29. So the Centurion procured *the Elders of the Jews*, to repair, in his behalf, to Christ, Luke 7.3.

*{covered with sackcloth*} In mourning apparel. See verse 1.

*{Isaiah the son of Amoz*} See chapter 1.1.

**V. 3.** *{And they said unto him, Thus saith Hezekiah, This day is a day of trouble, and of rebuke, and of blasphemy*} *A day*, for, *a time*: as ch. 26.1.

*{of trouble*} Or, *distress*, or *straits*: as chapter 33.2.

*{rebuke*} Whereby God rebukes us for our sins: as Job 33.19. Ps. 39.11. Hos. 5.9. or, *taunting*, and *reviling*, wherewith the enemy taunts and reviles both God, and us, verse 4. Hab. 2.1. and so rather here.

*{blasphemy*} Or, *provocation*, Ezekiah 35.12. or *contempt*, or *reproach*, Neh. 9.18,26. See Chapter 5.24.

*{for the children are come to the birth, and there is not strength to bring forth*} We are in great distress and extreme difficulties, out of which we are by no means able to wind ourselves: resembled here by the condition of a woman that has hard labor, has been long in sore travail, but cannot be delivered, her own strength being quite spent, and that she goes with so feeble, that it cannot work for itself, to procure, or further its own delivery. See ch. 26.17,18.

*{birth*} Heb. *breach*, or *breaking place*: the mouth of the matrice; the nearer whereunto, the fruit of the womb approaches, the stronger and sharper the pains are. So the word I rather suppose to signify, with the most part of the Jewish interpreters, than as some other of them, who would have it to be *the stool*, spoken of, Exod. 1.16. See ch. 66.9. Hos. 13.13.

**V. 4.** *{It may be the Lord thy God will hear the words of Rabshakeh, whom the King of Assyria his Master hath sent to reproach the living God, and will reprove the words which the Lord thy God hath heard*} It may be God, though not in regard of us, who by our sins have deservedly brought these evils upon ourselves, yet in tender regard to his own honor and Majesty, which these wicked wretches thus abuse and insult over, and will do so much more, if they prevail further against us, will be induced to show mercy unto us, and vindicate his own honor, by delivering of us. The argument that God’s own people were wont anciently to plead with, in the like cases: See Num. 14.13–16. Josh. 7.9. Psalm 74.18,23. & 89.50,51. & 115.1,2. and God himself professes oft times to have had special regard hereunto, in the sparing of his people, Deut. 32.26,27,36–38. verse 35. ch. 48.11. Ezek. 20.8,9,13,14,22. & 36.20,21,32.

*{the Lord thy God*} Not only the God whom you worship, or serve, as his servant at large: as Dan. 3.17,18. but the God whom you in a more special manner belong unto, as his prophet. So 1 Sam. 15.21. 1 Kings 17.1.

*{will hear*} Not that he doubted whether God had heard him; for he could not be ignorant (of what he also afterwards implies) that there is in every place, as an eye of God seeing, Prov. 15.3. so an ear of God hearing, as well bad, as good, Psalm 94.7,9. but *to hear*, is here to take notice of, and to make it by some special sign, or work, to appear, that he so does, Psalm 4.1. & 65.5. & 86.17. for when God forbears to right the wrongs offered to his people, and indignities done to himself, he seems, in the eyes of flesh and blood, not to hear, or to regard either, Psalm 22.2. & 44.23,24. & 94.7. ch. 40.27. & 49.14.

*{the living God*} The true God. So called, Psalm 42.2. Jer. 10.10. in way of opposition, to lifeless, dumb, and dead idols, Psalm 116.4–6. Jer. 10.5.

*{and will reprove the words*} Will convince them of folly and vanity, by showing, that he can do, what they say he cannot do, ch. 36.20. as he convinced Nebuchadnezzar’s words, by delivering his three servants, Dan. 3.15,17. so the word is used, Job 6.25,26. And so the Chaldee here takes it, and some of the Jewish doctors. But the words may be referred to the king of Assyria, and his messengers, their language; and read, as thus knit, to the former, *to reproach the living God, and to taunt* us, or *and to taunt*, (simply, to wit, *the living God*, as before,) *with the words that the Lord hath heard*. See verse 3. and this way, besides some of the Rabbins, go, the ancient Greek interpreters, the old Latin, and divers others. So some take the word, as Job 15.3. and so there is a defect, of the particle instrumental; like that, Psalm 17.13,14. so of the other before the verb infinitive, *to taunt*, but supplied from the former branch. Which yet also will not need if with one of the Jewish commenters, whom a learned late writer therein seconds, we render the text, *and hath evinced*, or *demonstrated*, (endeavored at least so to do) *by such words, as the Lord hath heard*. So he supposes the word to be taken, Gen. 24.14,44. and 31.42.

*{wherefore lift up thy prayer for the remnant that is left*} *Wherefore*. Heb. *And*: as ch. 29.13.

*{Lift up prayer*} Because voice, heart, and hand, are wont all to be lifted up in earnest prayer, 2 Chron. 32.20. Psalm 141.2. Lam. 3.41.

*{thy prayer*} Not without good ground required of God’s prophet, whose office it is as well to be the tongue of God’s people, by prayer to God for them, 1 Sam. 12.23. as to be God’s mouth to them, by delivering his word to them, Jer. 15.19. Mal. 2.7. Acts 6.4. a defect of the pronoun. as ch. 30.23.

*{for the remnant*} For a great part of the land was surprised and spoiled by the enemies’ forces already. See Ch. 33.8. and 36.1. over, and besides the ten tribes, gone before into captivity, 2 Kings 17.6. & 18.11. which some suppose also here respected; but see v. 32.

*{that is left*} Heb. *that is found*: that is still in being. So 2 Kings 25.19.

**V. 5.** *{So the servants of King Hezekiah came to Isaiah*} Heb. *And*, (as 2 Kings 3.9.) *the servants of the King*, (as also v. 1.) his courtiers before mentioned, verse 2.

**V. 6.** *{And Isaiah said unto them; Thus shall ye say, unto your Master; Thus saith the Lord, Be not afraid of the words which thou hast heard, wherewith the servants of the King of Assyria have blasphemed me*} *Thus shall ye say*, or *Thus say*: as the imperative for the future, ch. 26.16. so the future for the imperative: as Gen. 32.4. 1 Sam. 11.9. *of the words*] Heb. *from the face of the words*. So 2 Chr. 20.15. c. 30.17.

*{thou hast heard*} By the report of your messengers, v. 1. and I much more immediately by myself, verse 4.

*{the servants*} The word here used, is, in his native sense, a name of age, and signifies *a boy*, or *a youth*, Gen. 37.2. & 41.12. Chap. 3.5. & 7.16. & 8.5. but because such are usually under the government, and the command of their elders, hence both it, and the words in Greek and Latin, answering it, are used as terms of state & condition, for *a servant*, Judg. 7.11. 1 Sam. 9.22. Est. 2.2. Acts 4.25. in both notions together, it is found used of one, and the same person, 2 Kings 9.4. *the young man, the Prophets Servant*, (so the words would there be rendered) one that attended upon Eliseus, as Eliseus did upon Elias, 2 Kings 3.11. In the latter notion it is here taken: yet it may well be here, not without some privy nip; when God uses this term of ambiguous notion, that might as well import *his boys*, as *his servants*, instead of that used elsewhere of them, 2 Chron. 32.16.

*{blasphemed*} Or, *reproached*, as it is rendered, Numb. 15.30. ch. 43.28. & 51.7. or *reviled* because this, and reproaching, are distinctly used, verse 23.

**V. 7.** *{Behold, I will send a blast upon him*} Or, *Behold* (so he begins his doom likewise, ch. 10.33.) *I will put a Spirit into them*. Heb. *Behold I am giving* (as Jer. 5.14.) *a blast on him*, or *Spirit on him*, which some understand of the report brought him, of the Ethiopian expedition. Others rather, because this, and the report, seem here distinguished, of a fear or terror that God would strike into him: for the word, *Spirit*, is usually taken for any strong and efficacious affection and disposition, of what nature or kind soever. See Num. 5.14. Ch. 11.2. & 19.14. & 29.10. and such a fear or affrightment God is read to have stricken into persons and people, either for the restraint or diversion of them, from pursuit of evil intended against his people, or for his people’s more easy prevailing against them, Gen. 35.5. Exod. 23.27. & 34.24. 2 Chr. 14.14. & 20.29. Some conceive it to import only a mind to return, as if it were said only, I will work in him, on such news brought him, a willingness to return: but that seems not so full; though the Rabbins run, as with one consent, that way, and some of ours also after them. Yet of ours, some other again suppose it to be meant of carrying him away headlong, as with a stiff blast, or gust of wind; as Zac. 4.6,7. & 7.14. But this seems too forced.

*{and he shall hear a rumor*} Of this rumor, see v. 9. though some would have it meant, of the tidings brought him of the slaughter made in his army, vers. 36.

*{and he shall return to his own land*} See vers. 37. that which also he began to do, upon the former report. See v. 8.

*{and he shall fall by the sword in his own land*} That is, *be slain with it*: as chap. 3.25. see the complement, v. 38.

**V. 8.** *{So Rabshakeh returned*} Heb. *And*; as ver. 5. Whether he went back with that great army, wherewith he came before Jerusalem, chap. 36.2. some make it a question: there seems to me no likelihood, that he should so do, because it appears not, that he returned to his master, for any other end, save to acquaint him, what issue his parley had with them of Jerusalem, and to receive instructions how to proceed further with them; for which purpose, his own return, with some small retinue, was sufficient: nor was his master’s second message likely to take any effect with Ezekiah, when the forces were withdrawn, that did formerly affright him.

*{and found the King of Assyria warring against Libnah*} This Libnah was a royal city, having a king of her own, before the conquest of Canaan, Josh. 12.15. after the conquest whereof, it fell by lot to the tribe of Judah, Josh. 15.42. & was one of those cities, which out of that tribe were assigned unto the Levites, Josh. 21.13. It had some time revolted from Judah, under Joram, 2 Kings 8.22. 2 Chron. 21.10. but was, it seems, after recovered again, though by what king of Judah, is uncertain. It seems to have been situate not far from Lachish, Josh. 10.31.

*{for he had heard that he was departed from Lachish*} From whence he had before dispatched him, with two other commanders, and a great part of his army, unto Jerusalem: though whether having first taken it (as most conceives, and seems not unlikely) or no, is not expressed. But concerning the occasion of his removal from thence to Libnah, divers conjectural reasons are rendered. Some say, because Libnah stood more towards Egypt, thereby to stop the passage of any aid from thence. Others, that he might make towards Tirhakah, that was coming against him. I suppose rather, to make his approaches nearer to Jerusalem, with the residue of the forces which he retained still with him. So that as Joshuah, moving from Jerusalem-ward, and clearing the coast before him, went from Libnah to Lachish, Josh. 10.29,31. So Sennacherib making onward toward Jerusalem, went from Lachish to Libnah. Meanwhile those of ours are very wide, who make Libnah here to be Pelusium, a city of Egypt, misled by Joseph the Jew, who in the tenth of his *Antiquities*, Chap. 1. misrelates this story, affirming, that Sennacherib having taken all the cities of Judah and Benjamin, save Jerusalem only, sent Rabshakeh, and some other with him, to take in Jerusalem, but went himself, in person, into Egypt, where lying in siege before Pelusium, news was brought him of the Ethiopian forces coming against him, to aid the Egyptians: for fear of whom, breaking up his camp there, and returning into Judea, he found his forces left in those parts, destroyed by the plague. Which relation varies much from the sacred story, as that author too oft does.

**V. 9.** *{And he heard say concerning Tirhakah, King of Ethiopia, he is come forth to make war with thee*} To wit, Sennacherib lying before Libnah, had such tidings brought him, whether true indeed, as those that came to Saul, and diverted him from the pursuit of David, 1 Sam. 23.27,28. or raised upon some vain and groundless surmise, as befell the Syrians sometime at the siege of Samaria, 2 Kings 7.6. is not certain. Whether of the twain it were, certain it is, that it put him into thoughts of leaving Judea, and withdrawing of his forces thence, with what speed he might.

*{Tirhakah*} The Greeks and Latins call him Tharaks, and Tarachus, and Eusebius tells us, that he was an Ethiopian, but king of Egypt, which seems not so well to accord with the words of the prophet in this place; he seems to have been the same with that, Ethiopian king, of whom Strabo speaks in his *Geography*, lib. 2 and 15. by the name of *Tearchon*, or *Tarchon*: for that termination, the Greeks use much in proper names, whence *Jesua, Jason*, 2 Mac. 2.24. and *Sarug, Sargon*, Chap. 20.1. Joseph, more corruptly than any other, unless his copies be corrupted, calls him *Tharsices*, or *Tharsicen*.

*{King of Ethiopia*} Not of Egypt, as Eusebius, and some other from him. Heb. *of Chush*: whereof see, on chap. 11.11.

*{he is come forth*} Or, *gone out*: a term used commonly of warlike expeditions, as 2 Sam. 2.13. & 11.1. Psalm 60.9. cha. 42.14. Jer. 4.7.

*{to make war with thee*} Either by coming to assist the Jews, as chap. 20.5,6. or by invading the Assyrian’s own country in his absence, while his principal forces were in foreign employment; which seems the more likely of the twain, because it put him into thoughts of looking home.

*{and when he heard it, he sent messengers to Hezekiah, saying*} Yet before he would withdraw his forces that lay before Jerusalem, or depart the country, as he was resolved to do, he thought good to make trial whether Ezekiah; whom by the somewhat over-base demeanor of some of his messengers (see ch. 36.11.) and his own former submiss carriage (2 Kings 18.14.) he surmised to be well near utterly quailed, would, upon a second summons, suddenly give all up, or no.

*{and when he heard it, he sent*} Heb. *and he heard, and sent*. The like structure, see Ruth 2.9. chap. 30.30. & 35.4. and the like defect of the pronoun, ver. 1.

*{messengers*} Whether the same, that before, or some other, is not certain: the latter more likely; but the message the same.

*{saying*} Not by word of mouth, but by writing: see ver. 14. as Zachary, yet speechless, *wrote, saying*, Luke 1.63. whence an ancient Father, proves *writing* to be *speaking*, against those of his times, who deemed their subscriptions no denial of their Christian profession.

**V. 10.** *{Thus shall ye speak unto Hezekiah, King of Judah, saying*} The instructions given by him, to his messengers, are related, as spoken to them; but were indeed delivered to them in writing, to be delivered by their hand to Ezekiah, as a letter from him, though not directed to him, as if he scorned to grace him, so much as to write to him; but had sent him only a copy of the instructions, that he had given his messengers, whereby he might sufficiently understand his mind. See ver. 14.

*{Let not thy God, in whom thou trustest, deceive thee, saying, Jerusalem shall not be given into the hand of the King of Assyria*} See cha. 36.14,15.

*{thy God*} As if he were the God of that nation alone, and had a finite and circumscribed power, exercised only among that people. So the Syrians speak of God, 1 Kings 20.23. and some such conceit, the Jewish doctors suppose, that Jonas had, Jon. 1.3.

**V. 11.** *{Behold thou hast heard what the Kings of Assyria have done unto all lands, by destroying them utterly; and shalt thou be delivered?*} See Chap. 36.19,20. & 10.13,14.

*{destroying them utterly*} See chap. 11.15. *them*, that is, their inhabitants: so ver. 18.

**V. 12.** *{Have the Gods of the Nations delivered them, which my fathers have destroyed?*} Or, *Could the Gods of the Nations, whom my fathers destroyed, deliver them?* See on chap. 36.20.

*{as Gozan*} A city of the Medes, so called of the river, beside which it was seated, 2 Kings 17.6. & 18.11. by Ptolomy termed, *Ganzania*.

*{and Haran*} A city of Mesopotamia, called also, *Charran*, Gen. 11.31. Act. 7.4. it is joined with Eden and Ashur, Ezek. 27.23. and by Lucan, is termed, *an Assyrian city*.

*{and Rezeph*} A city of the same region; in Ptolomy, called *Resapha*.

*{and the children of Eden which were in Telassar?*} *Children*, that is, inhabitants, or natives; as chap. 11.14. Jer. 2.16. *of Eden*, a region in Mesopotamia; or, as some, in Chaldea, but the former name, seems sometime to include also the latter. (See Acts 7.2. with Gen. 11.31.) so called from the delightsomeness of it: for the word, itself signifies *delicacy*, or *delight*, Psalm 36.8. Chap. 47.8. in the eastern part thereof was that pleasant garden, or Paradise seated, wherein our first parents at first were placed, Gen. 2.8. See Ezekiel 27.23.

*{Telassar*} Some, with one of the Chaldee paraphrasts, would have this to be *Resen*, a city mentioned, Gen. 10.12. Others, that Seleucia, of which Strabo, lib. 11. Some remains of the ancient name of it, seem to continue in the term, *Thelda*, found in Ptolomy; and *Thilutha*, mentioned by Marcelline, l. 24. a place of great strength, situate on an island, in the midst of the river Euphrates: which yet, whether so called, as some would have it, as if it were *Tell-Ashur*, that is, *a bank*, set to keep out the Assyrian, may deservedly be doubted: nor want those, who suppose it to be the same with *Elassar*, Gen. 14.1. Of the term *Tell*, in the name of this, and divers other towns and cities. see on Jer. 30.18.

**V. 13.** *{Where is the King of Hamath, and the King of Arphad, and the King of the City of Sheparvaim, Henah, and Ivah?*} Before he spoke of their gods, now of their kings; whom their gods, or idols rather, could not save: nor can I accord with that learned critic, who would have *Melec*, here, to be the same with *Moloc*, not a king, but an idol. See Chap. 36.19. and of *Hamath*, and *Arphad*: See chap. 10.9. & 11.11. 1 Chr. 18.9. Jer. 49.23.

*{Henah and Ivah*} These two, though omitted, chap. 36.19. yet were before mentioned also in the first message, 2 Kings 18.34. what places they were is very uncertain, little mention being made of them, save in this Assyrian embassy. Some resemblance of the one of them, to wit, of *Hena*, some deem to be found, in the term *Ingiline* (for the last letter of it, the Greeks express oft by *G*. see on chap. 1.5.) the name of a territory bordering upon Mesopotamia, whence the heretics, called *Angelici*, are by some deemed to have had their denomination. See Epiphanius, *Heresy*, 60. though some other suppose it to be *Ange*, a city of Arabia the fertile, mentioned by Ptolomy. The other of them called *Ivah* here, seems to be the same with that, which is termed *Avah*, 2 Kings 17.24. which some would have to be the land of the *Avits*, who dwelt sometimes in the Philistines’ country, until driven from thence, they seated themselves, as they think, in Arabia, the desert. See Deut. 2.23. for for as those *Avits*, mentioned, Josh. 13.3. divers, both of Jewish writers, and ours, deem them to be no other, than the *Hivits*, Exod. 23.23. one letter being put there for another.

**V. 14.** *{And Hezekiah received the letter from the hands of the messengers, and read it:*} Hence it appears, that the message itself, was sent to him in writing; though it be not unlikely, that the messengers, as occasion was, would, by words of mouth, be pressing the same things. See ver. 9,10.

*{letter*} Heb. *books*; 2 Kings 5.5–7. Jer. 29.1. in the plural, as here, 1 Kings 21.8. 2 Kings 10.1. & 20.12.

*{and Hezekiah went up into the house of the Lord*} See ver. 1.

*{went up*} Because it stood on high, and they went to it by degrees, Chap. 2.3. Ezek. 40.6. or, simply *went* thither, as ver. 1. See Chap. 7.1,6. So Chap. 28.22.

*{and spread it before the Lord*} Not that God might read it, as himself had done; as if otherwise he could not have notice of it, or were not sufficiently acquainted with it already; but that by the tender of it thus, as before God’s face, he might express the earnestness of his desire, that God would be pleased to take special notice of it, and to induce him the rather so to do. A learned interpreter renders it, *and he read it before the Lord*: and a word, almost the same with that here used, differing only in the diverse placing of a point (as *Sibboleth*, and *Shibboleth*, Judg. 12.6.) signifies sometime, *to expound*, Neh. 8.8. whence some have thought, that the *Pharisees* had their name; but neither is that here used, nor is either of them found used for to read.

**V. 15.** *{And Hezekiah prayed unto the Lord, saying*} Heb. *before the Lord*: as Psalm 40.2.

**V. 16.** *{O Lord of Hosts, God of Israel*} See Chap. 1.9. & 17.6. & 45.15.

*{that dwellest between the Cherubins*} Who do in a conspicuous manner, exhibit and manifest yourself, in your Temple, as in your palace, the place of your residence among your people, and in it, more specially, upon your Ark, therein placed, as on your throne, or seat of estate, where you will be convened, and sought unto; and from whence you have promised to hear, and to help, Exod. 25.22. Num. 7.89. 2 Chron. 7.15. Psalm 20.2,6. & 68.28,29. & 80.2.

*{dwellest*} Heb. *sittest*, as on your royal seat, or chair of estate; as 1 Kings 2.12. Psalm 9.4. or *dwellest*, or *residest*; as in your palace, 2 Sam. 7.2. Psalm 132.13,14.

*{between the Cherubins*} Or. *Cherubim*, or *Cherubs*; for one note of plurality suffices. See *Seraphim*. Chap. 6.1. The word *Cherub*, is of doubtful, both original, and signification. Some suppose, that both this, and the word *Seraph*, do in the first place signify those celestial spirits, that minister unto, and attend upon the most High, the Sovereign Lord of heaven and earth; and it seems to be, not improbable, for what other could, or should be those so termed? Gen. 3.24. Ezek. 10.3,8,9. Though I conceive not on what ground it should be affirmed, as by some it is, that either of their *knowledge*, or the *abundance* of it, they should be so termed, there being somewhat indeed in the word, that may signify *abundance*, nothing that has any notion of *knowledge*. But the word here, as also in the story of the furniture of the Sanctuary, and elsewhere, is most commonly used, for certain symbolical images, whereby those celestial ministers, were in a bodily shape represented, Exod. 25.18,19. & 26.1,31. 1 King. 6.23,32,35. That they had a resemblance of some living creature, cannot be doubted. For mention is made of their wings, Exod. 25.20. 1 King. 6.24. And some would have them to have been winged *calves*, or *oxen*; because that which is called, *the face of a calf*, or *an ox*, Ezek. 1.10. is called the face of a *Cherub*, Ezek. 10.14. Others, and so most of the Jewish doctors, suppose them to have been, as we decipher them, like winged boys: and their critics, some of them, would have them so termed, from the particle of similitude; and the word *rabe*, or *rabia*, that signifies *a boy*: for the figure they give them, it is not improbable; but for the notation of the word, there is little likelihood of it: the word though in Chaldee and Syriac, so signifying, yet in Hebrew never so used. Nor do I suppose, that any instance of the like composition can be produced. The first letter seems radical, and the word to have been deduced from some Hebrew root, though now unknown. That seems more probable, that some other have, who suppose, that by a transposition of letters, (whereof many instances may in the Hebrew be given,) the word *Cherub*, may be deduced from the word *Recheb*, that signifies *a chariot*, both, for that the *Cherubs*, or *Angels*, are called *God’s chariots*, Psal. 68.17. and God is said to come riding on a *Cherub*, as a prince, or commander on his horse, or in his chariot, Psal. 18.10. and that the name of *a chariot*, is expressly given to the *Cherubs*, here mentioned, 1 Chr. 28.18. for they are these two that stood fixed on the lid of the Ark, called *the Propitiatory*, Exod. 25.18,19. from whence God spoke to Moses, Num. 7.89.

*{dwellest between the Cherubim*} The word *between*, is not here in the text, nor in any of those places, where this phrase is used, 1 Sam. 4.4. 2 Sam. 6.2. 2 King. 19.15. Psal. 80.2. So that it is no more in the text, than *that sittest the Cherubs*, or, *dwellest* (that is, inhabitest) *the Cherubs; sittest on them*: as he is said, *to stand over them* Ezek. 10.18. or, *to abide among*, or *between them*; as he is said, to speak *from between them*. Num. 7.8,9. a representation of his Majestical presence, among his glorious troops in heaven: and I should choose rather to render it, *that residest*, than (as the Greeks and Latin) *that sittest*, because the Ark, on the lid whereof these *Cherubs* were fixed, is called God’s *footstool*, Psal. 99.5.

*{thou art the God, even thou alone, of all the Kingdoms of the earth*} And, not of ours only, as Sennacherib supposes, ver. 10. Ch. 10.10,11. See Psal. 103.19. and Nebuchadnezzar’s confession, Dan. 4.17,32,34,35.

*{thou art*} Heb. *thou he*: the pronoun for the verb substantive: as Chap. 9.15. & 43.10,13. ver. 19.

*{thou alone*} Deut. 6.4. Psal. 86.10. Chap. 43.10,11.

*{thou hast made heaven and earth.*} The peculiar character of the true God; whereby he is distinguished from all counterfeit gods, Psal. 96.5. & 146.6. Chap. 42.5. & 45.24. Jer. 10.11,12. & 32.17.

**V. 17.** *{Incline thine ear, O Lord, and hear; open thine eyes, O Lord, and see;*} Hear their words, and behold his letter, ver. 14. that is make it by some act and work to appear, that you have heard the one, and seen the other, and take notice of either. So Dan. 9.18. See on ver. 4.

*{Incline thine ear*} A metaphor taken from those, that bow down the head to listen to such as speak to them, from below, and in special manner therefore attributed to God, whom, as sitting aloft in the highest heavens, Chap. 57.15. & 66.1. we speak unto, from here below, Eccl. 5.2. so Psal. 31.2. Dan. 9.18. yet is it used more largely; for as God is said *to incline his ear* unto us, so are we said *to incline our ear*, also, to him. See Chap. 55.3.

*{and hear all the words of Sennacherib, which hath sent to reproach the living God*} Or, *who hath sent*: because it is spoken of a person. Or, and of him, *whom he hath sent*, as some render it, to wit, of Rabshakeh, Chap. 36.2. ver. 4. see 2 King. 19.16. but the former seems the better, because it needs no supply, nor is any defect apparent: for Rabshakeh’s words were his master’s, delivered in his name, ch. 36.4. beside, that Ezekiah in this clause seems rather to have respect to the contents of the present letter, than to the words of the former message, which he laid open to God before, vers. 1.4. The words may be read, *wherewith he hath sent to reproach the living God*, see ver. 4.

**V. 18.** *{Of a truth, Lord, the Kings of Assyria have laid waste all the Nations, and their countries*} Heb. *Verily, Lord*, &c.

*{all the Nations*} Before mentioned. So it is, 2 King. 19.17. but the Hebrew text here has it, *all the lands; lands*, for *nations* of those lands, as it is more fully expressed, 2 Chr. 32.13,17. So ver. 11. See Chap. 66.8. And there is in the words, a sylleptical, or comprehensive form of speech; whereby two divers notions, are in one word comprised; the one expressed, the other implied, and to be supplied, to make the sense up entire; when it is said, *have laid waste nations and countries*, for, *destroyed the nations, and laid waste their countries*. See the like, Exod. 20.18. *they saw the thunderings, and the lightnings, and the sound of the trumpet*, for, *they saw* the one, *and heard* the other, Luke 1.64. *his mouth opened, and his tongue* that *opened*, this *loosed*, 1 Cor. 3.2. *I made you drink milk, not meat*; for, *drink milk, eat meat*, 1 Tim. 2.12. *I permit not a woman to teach, but to be in silence*; *permit not* the one, *command* the other, 1 Tim. 4.3. *forbidding to marry, to abstain from meats; inhibiting* the one, *enjoining* the other.

*{and their countries*} Heb. *country*, or *land*, taken collectively, for *countries*, or *lands*; or distributively rather, for the *country* and *land* of each of them.

**V. 19.** *{And have cast their gods into the fire*} Heb. *giving*, for, *giving have given*: a defective form, as Chap. 59.13. that is, *have surely given*, or *cast*; (as the more usual phrase is, Judg. 1.8. & 20.48. Psal. 7.47. in all which places, yet there is an hypallage, or a kind of transposition) *their gods* (that is, their idols: as Psal. 96.5.) *into the fire*: as David dealt with the Philistines’ gods, 2 Sam. 5.21. *giving into the fire*, for, *casting into the fire*: as Ezek. 15.4,6.

*{for they were no gods*} Heb. *they no gods*, for, *they were no gods*: the pronoun for the verb substantive: as ver. 16. *no gods*, 2 Chron. 13.9. Gal. 6.8.

*{but the works of men’s hands, wood, and stone, therefore they have destroyed them.*} So Psal. 115.4. & 135.15. Chap. 40.19,20. & 44.12–17. Jer. 10.3,4. Dan. 5.4,23. He mentions those, the rather, of the baser matter, because those the enemy less regarded, and therefore burnt them; whereas they made booty of those that were of stuff more precious, chap. 46.1. See Jer. 43.12.

**V. 20.** *{Now therefore, O Lord, our God, save us from his hand*} Heb. *And now*: as Chap. 36.5. *hand*, for *power*: as chap. 36.15,18. do you that for us, that their gods could not do for them, ver. 12.

*{that all the Kingdoms of the earth may know that thou art the Lord, even thou, only.*} Psal. 83.18. Chap. 59.19. See ver. 16. *thou, thou only*: as, *thee, thee only*, Psa. 51.4. the gemination makes the sentence the more vigorous.

**V. 21.** *{Then Isaiah the son of Amoz sent unto Hezekiah, saying*} Heb. *And*: as Chap. 36.22. *sent*, in likelihood, by some messengers, that the king had sent unto him, as before, ver. 2. to understand whether he had any further word of answer from God. See Jer. 37.17.

*{Thus saith the Lord God of Israel*} So styled here, in way of opposition to those sorry gods, of other nations, as before, ver. 16.

*{whereas thou hast prayed to me against Sennacherib King of Assyria*} Or, *What thou hast prayed unto me for, against the King of Assyria*, I have heard: so it is, 2 Kings 19.20. and the word here used, though of more general extent in the use of it, yet in its original, having a notion of *judicature* in it, whence the ambiguity of it, Psa. 106.30. signifies properly, such a prayer, wherein a man, though in all submiss and lowly manner, does as it were debate the case with God, and plead the equity of that, which he sues unto him for. Such are those of Moses, Num. 14.13–19. of Joshuah, Josh. 7.7–9. such are divers in the book of Psalms, Psalm 7. & 10. & 13. & 74. & 88. & 89. & 115. and such is this of Ezekiah; and the word therefore is very significantly here used; as also again, Chap. 38.2. Some join the words thus to the former, *Thus saith the Lord God* *of Israel, to whom thou hast prayed.* See the like syntax, chap. 49.23.

**V. 22.** *{This is the word which the Lord hath spoken concerning him:*} In way of answer to your latter prayer, ver. 15–20. or, as some, *This is the thing* (*word*, for *thing*, as Eccl. 8.3.) *that God commandeth*, to be returned in way of answer, *to him*; but this seems to be over-strained.

*{concerning him*} Or, *against him*; as Jer. 49.1,7.

*{The virgin the daughter of Zion hath despised thee, and hath laughed thee to scorn; the daughter of Jerusalem hath shaken her head at thee*} Or, *the Virgin, daughter of Zion, despiseth thee, and derideth thee; the daughter of Jerusalem shaketh the head at thee.* Some understand the words, as spoken, not of the inhabitants of Jerusalem, scorning and deriding Sennacherib; but of his scoffing and scorning them, thus rendering the text, *He hath despised thee, and mocked thee, O virgin, daughter of Zion, he hath shaken his head at thee, O daughter of Jerusalem.* But the text will not bear it; for the pronouns are masculine, the verbs feminine.

*{virgin daughter of Zion*} Some suppose the term of *virgin* to be here given unto the city of Jerusalem, because she had not hitherto been surprised or forced by any foreign power. But neither is that true; for Joash, king of Israel, took it, and pillaged it in Amaziah’s reign, 2 Kings 14.13,14. nor does it seem to be the true notion of this title, being given to other places, whereof that cannot be said: Howsoever the Jewish critics say, that it is always to be so taken, where it is applied to place or people. Others, therefore, would have it given to the Jewish people, the inhabitants of Jerusalem, as to God’s church, which he had as a chaste virgin espoused to himself, chap. 54.5. Hos. 2.19,20. 2 Chron. 11.2. Rev. 14.4. and had as great care of, as any man or woman had of a darling daughter, abiding yet under their wing, chap. 49.15,16. Zach. 2.5,8. but considering, the same term is given, even by this prophet also, to other people; as to Sidon, chap. 23.12. and to Babylon, chap. 47.1. I suppose, it would rather be rendered, *damsel*, a term given to those states, as in beauty, bravery, stateliness, and delicacy, resembling a damsel of noble birth, and according to her parentage, curiously educated. But of the style, see more, on chap. 1.8. & 23.12.

*{daughter of Jerusalem*} As before of Zion: for the place itself, or the inhabitants of it; as Jer. 2.13. *Sion*, and *Jerusalem*, the same, as chap. 1.27. for as for those, that by *the daughter of Sion*, would have understood the people of the upper city, by *the daughter of Jerusalem*, the people of the lower city, it is over-nice; nor accords with those other places of the prophet, where both terms are likewise used, chap. 3.3. & 4.3,4. & 10.12,32. & 24.23. & 31.4,5,9. as also is that of a learned writer, who by *the daughter of Babel*, Zach. 2.11. would have understood the region or territory of Babylon, whereof Babel was as the mother, because inferior towns are commonly called daughters, in relation to their mother city, Josh. 15.31,36,41.

*{shaken her head*} Heb. *the head*, as Psalm 22.7. *they shake the head*: which yet is more fully, Psalm 109.25. and Lam. 2.15. *they shake their head*: and so is not amiss here rendered, *she shaketh her head*: but then *her* should be in a diverse character, to note a defect of the pronoun, as Deut. 25.12. and as ver. 23. As he sometime shook his hand, in menacing manner, at her, chap. 10.32. so shall she shortly shake her head in scorn and derision at him: see Jer. 18.16. Mat. 27.39.

*{at thee*} Heb. *after thee*: When instead of your hands, wherewith you brag that you would do great matters, verse 24. you shall be glad to betake yourself to your heels, and to turn your back to her; a secret gird at his shameful flight, ver. 37. 2 Chron. 32.21.

*{thee*} Sennacherib it is, whom he speaks unto, but calls not by his name, as not vouchsafing to name him.

**V. 23.** *{Whom hast thou reproached and blasphemed?*} Or, *reviled?* see ver. 6.

*{and against whom hast thou exalted thy voice, and lifted up thine eyes on high?*} Do you well know, and consider with yourself, who it is, against whom you do so insolently advance yourself: see Exod. 5.2. & 9.16,17.

*{and*} Or, *or*; as chap. 36.19.

*{exalted thy voice*} In big words, and presumptuous language: though alluding, it may be, also, to Rabshakeh’s loud crying, chap. 36.13. Heb. *the voice*; as chap. 13.2. a defect of the pronoun, as ver. 4.22. supplied, chap. 40.9. & 58.1.

*{lifted up thine eyes on high*} A lofty look, a sign of an haughty heart, chap. 2.12. see on chap. 10.12. otherwise, the phrase is used in no evil sense. Gen. 19.22. chap. 40.22.

*{even against the holy one of Israel*} In blaspheming his name, taunting his people, and traducing and disgracing his Anointed: so Exod. 5.2. & 9.17. Psalm 2.1,2. & 74.19. and 89.51. of the style given to God here, see on chap. 1.4. Some end the interrogation at voice, and read the rest of the verse, by way of enunciation: as showing either wherein, or against whom he had carried himself so insolently, *in that thou liftest up thine eyes on high*; or, *thou hast even lifted up thine eyes on high, against the holy one of Israel*: and so the insertion of *even*, in our version, should be needless, which yet is very frequent, ver. 16.20. chap. 41.12. & 43.10,11,25. the copulative being put for *that*; as chap. 22.20. or, *even*; as chap. 27.1. But the received reading seems the better, because more agreeable to the manner of our prophet, whose common custom is to express the same thing, by divers notions, laid down in distinct branches, as in this very argument, chap. 10.12. besides, that it suits not so well, to say, *thou exaltest thy voice, in that thou liftest up thine eyes*: or, the question, being of the former, to return answer to it by the latter.

**V. 14.** *{By thy servants hast thou reproached the Lord*} Heb. *By the hand of thy servants*: as Exod. 35.29. chap. 20.2. Jer. 27.3. it is, 2 Kings 19.23. *thy messengers*. See chap. 36.2. and verse 4,14,17.

*{and hast said*} Or, *in that thou sayest*; for that use of the copulative does not amiss here: see on verse 23.

*{By the multitude of my chariots, am I come up to the height of the mountains, to the sides of Lebanon:*} Or, *with the multitude of my chariots*. I have with my chariots, not with my foot forces only, got over the highest mountains that lay in my way, and I have brought them all safe over the tops of the hills, notwithstanding the great number of them (a matter of no small difficulty) partly, by cutting out, and leveling of ways for them, where the grounds were rough and rocky, (a practice alluded to, chap. 40.3,4.) and partly, by felling of such trees as obstructed their passage. So did Xerxes make way for his army through Athos, in his expedition against Greece, Herodote, l. 7. Annibal over the Alps, into Italy, Livy, l. 21. Vespasian in his march towards Jerusalem, over the mountains of Judea, Joseph *of the Jewish war*, l. 3. c. 11. which mountains seem to be by the Assyrian also here specially intended, together with those in his way thither, and chiefly those about Jerusalem, that seemed to make the access thither the more difficult, Psalm 125.2.

*{the height of the mountains*} Or, *the highest mountains*, or *hills*; as Psal. 95.4. and as afterward, *the tallness of cedars*, for *the tallest cedars*: and *the choice of firs*, for *the choicest firs*.

*{the sides of Lebanon*} One of the famousest mountains in those parts, mentioned, as one of the limits of the promised land, Deut. 3.25. & 11.24.

*{and I will cut down the tall Cedars thereof, and the choice fir trees thereof;*} Or, *I will cut down the tallest of his Cedars, and the choicest of his firs*. Heb. *tallness*, as Chap. 10.33. Ezek. 31.5,10.) and *choice*: as Jer. 22.7. either to clear his way for his army to pass, or to furnish him with timber, for works and lodgings. See chap. 14.8. the meaning seems to be, that nothing could, or should hinder him in his passage toward, and his approaches to Jerusalem, which he principally aimed at. Howsoever, as he threatens to hew down Lebanon here; so God threatens elsewhere to hew down his Lebanon. See chap. 10.33,34. and so accordingly did, vers. 36. But the words may well be rendered, in the time past, *I have cut down*, &c. and so the next, *I have entered*, &c. as the foregoing words were; those ensuing, also, ver. 25. so run; for he seems in this whole passage to vaunt of what he had done.

*{and I will enter into the height of his border, and the forest of his Carmel.*} This passage is somewhat otherwise read in the book of Kings, 2 King. 19.23. and the readings compared, will afford us the more light, whereby to find out the right meaning of the text. What is here termed *merom*, that is, *height*, or *high place*, rather: as Chap. 26.5. is there called *malon*, that signifies *an inn*, Gen. 42.27. Exod. 4.24. or, *a lodge*, or *lodging*, Chap. 10.29. Jer. 9.2. by both which terms, is, undoubtedly, the same thing meant; and somewhat it must be, about Mount Lebanon, or, appertaining thereunto: and I conceive it to be no other, than *the tower of Lebanon*, situate on the eastern side thereof, with its prospect towards Syria, Cant. 7.4. called *an high place*; because it stood aloft, and was high built, of purpose, to overlook the country before it: and *a lodge*, or *lodging*, in regard of the garrison, that being a frontier place, was, for the security of the place, lodged in it: though it is not improbable, that the Assyrian might also, in way of contempt, so term it; as a place, in his reckoning, of no more strength, or worth, than a sorry lodge, in a park, or garden. See of Jerusalem, chap. 1.8. and of some other lands, Chap. 24.20. In both places it is said to be *the high place*; or, *lodge, of its end*; (so, rather than *border*; for which the Hebrews have another word) because it stood at one end of the mountain, looking toward Damascus, the head city of Syria, that lay eastward from Judea, Chap. 7.8. & 9.12. our English renders it, *lodgings*; as taken collectively, and intending not some one, but such forts and holds as were on the frontiers thereabout situated, for the better security of the adjacent parts: nor is this interpretation altogether improbable: but admitted there, it should have been accordingly, *high places*, here; the words following, in both places the same, are by divers good interpreters, otherwise rendered, than our version has them, not, *and the forest of his Carmel*, but (as the Hebrew points, though by the Jews themselves, here not observed, lead unto, distinguishing between the two last words,) *his forest, and field*. or *fruitful field*: as the word is rendered, chap. 32.15. it is word for word in the Hebrew; *and I will go*; or, *have gone*, (gotten up) *unto the high place of the end thereof, forest, field*, or *fertile field thereof*: as if he had said, having felled his trees, and so made passage for my army, I will march, or, have marched, with it, to his high garrison tower, and so through his forest, to the fertile fields that lie below it. I am not ignorant, that the Jewish interpreters here understand by *Lebanon*, the land of Judea; so called, say they, because it is the highest ground in the world; (which what ground they have for, I know not: but know it certainly to be untrue) by the tall *cedars* and *firs*, the great men of the land: as Chap. 2.13. by *the high place*, or *lodging*, the Temple, God’s dwelling, Psalm 78.69. & 132.13,14. as also, that divers of our writers tread in the same track; some conceiving the land of Judah to be meant here, likened to *Lebanon*, for height and stateliness; to *Carmel*, for fertility and pleasantness. Others, by *Lebanon*, understanding Judea; by the *forest*, the wilder part of it; by *Carmel*, the manured; by the *lodge*, or *inn*, as they render it, Jerusalem: and that Jerusalem seems, sometime, to be in Scripture called *Lebanon*, or to be likened, at least, to it, appears, Jer. 22.23. Zach. 11.1. But that which I have before delivered, seems to me to be the genuine sense of this place.

**V. 25.** *{I have digged, and drunk water*} The text, 2 King. 19.24. is somewhat fuller, *I have digged, and drunk strange waters*; that is, springs of water, where none appeared, and which had been formerly unknown. He boasts of his power and policy, that could find out means, to furnish with water, such a numerous army, as emptied the pools, and dried up the rivers wheresoever they came. The Jewish doctor, as he widens it too much, so, withal, he extenuates it not a little, when he would have the meaning to be, I undertake no work, but that I finish; as those, that wanting water, dig, till they find what to drink: of *digging for water*, see on Gen. 26.18–22. Num. 21.27,28. Psal. 84.6. and of furnishing with water, beyond expectation where none to be had; that whereby God, at sundry times, has manifested, and is wont to magnify his power, and his providence, and wherein this vain boaster professes himself able to do strange matters; See Exod. 17.1–6. Num. 20.1–11. Judg. 15.18,19. 2 King. 3.17,20. Neh. 9.20. Psalm 74.15. & 78.15,16. & 107.35. & 114.8. Chap. 41.17,18. & 43.19,20.

*{and with the sole of my feet have I dried up all the rivers of the besieged places*} As if his army had been so great, that with their feet alone, they were able to dry up all the pools and rivers wheresoever they came; not unlike the Syrian’s vaunt of his forces, that he brought men more than enough, with him, to carry all the dust of Samaria away in their fists, 1 King. 20.10. as also to what the Greeks report of Xerxes his army, that they should drink whole rivers dry at a dinner. Juvenal, *Satire* 10. See Herodote, lib. 7. and Justine, lib. 2.

*{with the sole of my feet*} as Psal. 57.6. or, *footsteps*, as Psalm 85.14. that is, wheresoever I set footing, as Josh. 1.3. I do with the multitude of men and beasts, that I bring along with me, drink all dry. So some of the Jewish commenters. But other of them, rather, I dry up all with the very footing of them. And he speaks it, as if the rivers were dried up in a trice, so soon, as he set but the sole of his foot on them; as Jordan was divided and dried up so soon, as the plants of the priests’ feet, that bore the ark of God, touched the water thereof, Josh. 3.15,16. For it seems to come far short of the Assyrian’s boasting, that some would have the meaning to be, that he dried up great rivers, enclosed with high and strong banks: as Cyrus did Gyndes and Euphrates, Herod. lib. 1. Jer. 50.38. to make them fordable for his forces.

*{have I dried up all the rivers*} As the Psalmist, of God, *Thou driest up mighty rivers*, Psal. 74.15. See Chap. 42.15.

*{the rivers of the besieged*} Or, *fenced*, or, *enclosed*. Heb. *rivers of session, siege*; or, *enclosure*. See Chap. 19.6. that is, either such rivers and streams, as running beside cities, make them the more difficult to besiege, and the better able to hold out a siege. Or, such waters derived from some river, into pools and enclosures, made for that purpose. Some Jewish critics would by the word here used, understand Egypt; because the name in Hebrew comes near unto it: as if he should brag that he had dried up the rivers of Egypt, which God threatens to do, Chap. 11.15. but that another of them, not undeservedly, controls the whole passage: some render in the future, *I will dig and drink waters, and with the sole of my feet, dry up all the waters of the siege*; as aiming at Jerusalem, and the preparations made by them, to furnish themselves with water, expecting a siege, Chap. 22.9,11. and the courses taken by them to keep his army from water, by obstructing the springs that might afford it them, 2 Chr. 32.3,4. He boasts therefore, that their endeavors, in either kind, should prove but lost labor; he would dry up all their store, and provide water sufficient for his forces, by digging deep, and bringing of springs to light, where none had ever been seen, or dreamed of before. And this so well suiting with the story itself, would not lightly be rejected. Howsoever the words be rendered or read, the scope of this his vain vaunting, is to imply, that no place had been, or could be able to hold out against him, who was able, by his power and policy, to overcome all difficulties, to level mountains, and dry up rivers, for the freer passage of his forces, and yet to furnish them, also, with all necessary provisions, where they were most unlikely to be had.

**V. 26.** *{Hast thou not heard long ago, how I have done it, and of ancient times, that I have formed it?*} Hitherto was Sennacherib brought in vaunting of his own designs and doings; now God turns his speech again to him, controlling him for his folly. And as he told Ezekiah, that he could not but have heard, what his ancestors, the kings of Assyria, and he himself also had done, ver. 11. So God demands of him, whether he had not heard from his prophets, to whom he had revealed it, and by whom he had formerly published it, c. 48.3. That God had in his secret counsel, designed all those things to be done by his progenitors and himself, both concerning other nations, and concerning his own people, which he fondly arrogates to his ancestors, and to himself, Deut. 32.27. Chron. 10.13. Whereas he and they, were all but God’s instruments therein, and had never, without him, been able to do what they did. See Chap. 7.17,20. & 10.5,6,15. & 20.4. So many, both of the Jewish commenters, and ours. But divers other, go another way, reading the words, *Hast thou not heard, that I long ago did it*; or, *made it*, and, or, *that of ancient time I framed it?* Applying the note of time, not to the Assyrian’s ear, but to God’s act & expounding the text, Some, of the works that God had formerly done for his people, such as the Assyrian king, here, vaunted of, in making a passage for them through the red sea, Exod. 14.21,22. and through Jordan, Josh. 2.10. & 3.16. but this seems not so probable. Others, of the city, and state of Jerusalem, which he had founded and established, Psal. 48.8. & 78.68,69. & 149.2. Chap. 14.33. & 22.11. And this seems very probable.

*{long ago.*} Heb. *after from*. It is used sometime of place, 2 Chr. 26.15. Ezr. 3.13. sometime of time past, as here, and 2 King. 19.25. to come: as 2 Sam. 7.19.

*{how*} Or, *that*: a defect of the particle, as Psal. 55.2. Chap. 10.12.

*{I have done*} Or, *I made*: as Chap. 44.2. & 46.4.

*{it*} Or, *this*; as Psalm 109.27. as having reference to the thing, either spoken by Sennacherib, or done by God, Chap. 41.20. or, *her*; that is, the city of Jerusalem. Of which before, ver. 22. though, not naming her here; but speaking of her, as the only *her* that God regarded. So Jer. 33.2.

*{of ancient times*} Heb. *from days of priority*, or, *antiquity*; as cha. 33.7. that is, *from eternity*, say some, understanding it of God’s purpose, Chap. 25.1. In former times; *long since*, say others, understanding it of his work, Chap. 44.2. For those Jewish masters do but trifle here, that tell us of the Messiah, and Jerusalem, made before heaven and earth; and of Tophet, made for Sennacherib on the second day of the world. See Chap. 30.33.

*{formed it*} Or, *framed it*. The word is taken from the potter’s act and art, in framing of earthen vessels; Jer. 18.3,4,6. that is, say some, decreed, determined, that it should be done; as Chapter 14.24,26. Acts 2.23. & 4.2. Eph. 1.11. 2 Tim. 1.9. 1 Pet. 1.20. As the potter conceives in his mind beforehand, the fashion of that which he intends to frame. See Chap. 26.3. & 29.16. Others, framed, and effected by my own might, without help of nature, or human art, or force; as Gen. 2.6,8. Chap. 45.18. But as others, rather, *formed*, or, *framed her*. This city and state, the framer whereof, he is in a more special manner, by this prophet, oft said to be, Chap. 43.1,21. & 44.2,21,24. and 64.8.

*{now have I brought it to pass, that thou shouldst be to lay waste fenced cities, into ruinous heaps*} What I formerly purposed, should be effected concerning those nations and cities, which I would have destroyed, that have I now done by you, Chap. 24.1,10,12. & 25.2. & 26.5. & 27.10. Or, as others, reading the words, by way of interrogation, *And now should I bring it to be laid waste, and fenced cities to be ruinous heaps?* or, to be *ruinous heaps, as fenced cities?* Should I suffer this place, which I so framed, to be laid waste, and destroyed by you, as if I had founded it to no other end? See chap. 45.18. and that you should do with it, or the cities belonging to it, as you have done with some others, verse 18. See Jer. 33.2,6.

*{have I brought it?*} Or, *should I bring her to that pass?* A potential sense: as Chap. 26.9.

*{that thou shouldest be to lay waste*} Or, *that it*, or, *she should be laid waste*. Heb. *and*, (for *that*; as Chap. 16.12.) *thou*, or, *it*, or, *she* (for the second person masculine, and the third feminine, or neuter, are in this form the same) *shall be to lay waste*, or, *unto vastities*, or, *desolations*; (for some make it a noun, as the like word, Psal. 73.19. & 74.3. or, *that thou shouldest be to lay* her, or, it *waste*: for so the words also may well be rendered; and the want of the pronoun is very rife, Chap. 31.5. ver. 22.

*{to lay waste defenced cities into ruinous heaps*} That is, *to lay waste*, by bringing them, or by *laying waste*, to bring them, *to ruinous heaps*: To lay them waste in that manner, that they become ruinous heaps. A defective form of speech; such as ver. 18.

*{ruinous heaps*} Or, *heaps over-grown*; to wit, with grass, weeds, shrubs, and other like trash, as waste places are wont to be. So the word not elsewhere found, save Jer. 4.7. is deemed to imply, from a word of the same notion or of near affinity with it. See Chap. 27.10. & 32.14. 1 Macc. 4.38.

*{defenced cities*} Either of other nations, Chap. 25.2. or, of Judah and Jerusalem; (see Jer. 34.1.) whereof, though he took many, yet he razed them not, Chap. 27.10. or, *as* the *defenced, cities*, to make this city heaps, (Psal. 79.1.) as some other, so served by him; which albeit the Chaldeans were afterward suffered to do, Mic. 3.12. yet the Assyrian never did. The note of similitude supplied, as ver. 27.

**V. 27.** *{Therefore their inhabitants were of small power; they were dismayed, and confounded*} Heb. *And*; as ver. 20. So read, it renders a reason why those cities were by the kings of Assyria, so surprised and ruinated, to wit, because the inhabitants of them had no power of hand, or courage of heart to withstand them: and therefore they were so enfeebled and disheartened, because it was God that brought that evil upon them: so Exod. 23.27,28. Josh. 2.11,12. & 5.1. Howbeit, it may as well be read, *Whose inhabitants. And they*, for, *whose*; as, *and he*, for, *who*; Mal. 3.1. compared with Mat. 11.10. and so it proceeds to relate the condition of the persons, as well as of the places, that had, by the Assyrians, been subdued.

*{of small power*} Heb. *short* or, *shortened of hand*; as chap. 50.2. & 59.1.

*{they were as the grass of the field, and as the green herb on the house-tops, and as corn blasted before it be grown up*} An extreme weakness and feebleness; or a soon and sudden destruction, or both, by divers lively resemblances copiously described.

*{as*} A defect of the note of similitude: very common in Scripture; that yet needed not to have been supplied, save in the first branch. See the like, Psal. 11.1. Chap. 33.11,12.

*{the grass of the field*} Heb. *herb*; as Deut. 32.2. see Psal. 90.5,6. & 102.4,11. & 103.15. Chap. 40.6. Mat. 6.30. that is easily trodden down by the foot, not of wild beasts only, 2 Chr. 25.18. but of the least, and feeblest cattle. See chap. 26.6.

*{the green herb on the house-tops*} Or, *green tender herb*; as it is rendered, Deut. 32.2. Job 38.26. or, *tender grass*; as 2 Sam. 23.4. Prov. 27.25. *grass*; simply, Gen. 1.11,12. Job 6.5. Chap. 15.6. Jer. 14.5. *herb*; as here, Psal. 37.2. Chap. 66.14. It is deemed, properly, to signify the first putting forth of aught that springs out of the ground, as the former, the same when it is come to some growth, *as the green herb*: so Psal. 129.6.

*{corn blasted before it be grown up*} Heb. *blasting before standing*; as *standing*, for, *standing corn*, (of which defect, see on chap. 17.5.) so *blasting*, for, *corn of blasting*; that is, *blasted*. The abstract, for the concrete, as chap. 35.1,7. the word most commonly is supposed to signify arable ground; for which purpose, a dry soil is wont to be preferred before a moist. It is here only used for *blasting*, by the Hebrew critics therefore deemed, through the change of a letter, to descend from another root, that signifies to *blast*, Gen. 41.6,23. and the word indeed used, 2 King. 19.26. is apparently so: Whence it is also manifest, that either the scribe’s pen slipped here in a letter, (the letters of either word being much alike) or, that both words, though differing in a radical letter, were used for one and the same thing. Howbeit, a late learned writer, retains the word here in that other sense, rendering it, *as a land*, or *arable ground, before corn*, to wit, to be sown in it, while it lies fallow. But the other term here used, signifies properly *corn*, not as sown, or sprouting out, but *standing*; got to height, and expecting harvest; and the parallel place in the story, requires to take it the other way.
