**Ver. 28.** *{But I know thine abode, and thy going out, and coming in, and thy rage against me*} I am well acquainted with your doings at home, your enterprises abroad, all your counsels, all your courses; and take notice of your insolent carriages against me.

*{I know*} Not, as I know the ways of the righteous, by way of approbation, acceptation, and care to give a good issue to them, Ps. 1.6. but by a general notice of them; in that they neither are, nor can be concealed from me, Psa. 94.11. & 139.1–4. and by a special notice, also, that I take of them, in due time to deal with you, for them, as, for them, you deserve to be dealt with, Jer. 17.10. & 48.30. Hos. 5.3. Amos 5.12.

*{thine abode*} As Gen. 24.55. or *thy dwelling*; as Jer. 9.6. as we say to one, that takes overmuch upon him; *we know where you dwell, Sir*: or, *thy sitting*: as Psa. 139.2. Lam. 3.63. your abode at home, and what you do there, because opposed to business abroad: so Deut. 6.7. & 11.19.

*{thy going out, and thy coming in*} As Deut. 28.6,19. Psalm 121.8.

*{thy rage against me?*} Heb. *thy raising up of thyself* (in a raging manner) *against me*: the verb is not found anywhere in this emphatical and reciprocal form, save in this argument: the preposition signifying usually *unto*, is used here for *against*, as Chap. 33.11. *el*, for *al*, as Jer. 47.5,7. & 50.7,26,29. & 51.1. So in the next verse.

**V. 29.** *{Because thy rage against me, and thy tumult is come up into mine ears*} Heb. *Thy raging*; or, *raising up of thyself*: as v. 28. the verb infinitive, for the noun.

*{thy tumult*} The word here used, does most usually signify *tranquility*, Job 12.5. chap. 32.11. & 33.20. but here, and 2 Kings 19.28. *tumultuation*, as springing from another stock; whence the word, that signifies *a tumultuous noise*, chap. 13.4. & 17.12. & 66.6. and is framed with a reduplication of the last letter, to imply an intention of the thing thereby signified. Howbeit, some of the Jewish commenters would have the word taken in his common sense, reading the words (which they suppose defective) with supply from the former branch, *and*, or *even*, the rage of *thy tranquility*, that is, thence arising, or thereby procured; as Prov. 1.32. but this seems over-nice, and a nicety needless; not unlike the conceit of those, that would deduce the word in this sense, of *noise* and *tumult*, from that, of *ease* and *tranquility*, because ease and tranquility, is wont to breed pride and insolency, Jer. 48.11.

*{is come up*} So Psalm 74.23. *the noise of thine adversaries; the tumultuous noise of those that rise up against thee, goeth up continually*. See 2 Chron. 28.9. Ezr. 9.6. Jon. 1.2.

*{into mine ears*} It makes so loud a cry, that I cannot but hear it, and take notice of it. So Gen. 18.20. chap. 5.9. Jam. 5.4. See ver. 4.17.

*{I will put my hook into thy nose, and my bridle in thy lips; and I will turn thee back, by the way, by which thou camest.*} Because you rage and rave on this wise, like some great unruly fish, or some fierce wild beast, or some headstrong horse, I will take you with my hook, or, I will ring you, and bridle you, and lead you whither I list; turn you about, and make you go the way you would not, turn you back from the place you principally intend, and with shame and confusion return you to your own home. So chap. 30.28.

*{hook into thy nose*} Alluding either to *a fish-hook*, wherewith fish taken, are drawn which way the fisherman pleases, Job 41.1. Ezek. 29.4. & 38.4. Amos 4.1. or to such *rings* as men put into the noses of bears and buffaloes, to keep them in, and over-master them with; Ezek. 19.4,9. or, to *a chain*, or *collar*, put about the neck of a dog, or some other beast, with a cord, or leash fastened thereunto, whereby to lead him, as some of the Jewish masters would have it; but the mention of the *nose*, seems not well to admit it: and the most of them go to the first way; I should rather the second.

*{my bridle in thy lips*} *My bridle*, or *snaffle*, or *bit*; as it is rendered, Psa. 32.9. where, from *bridle*, it is distinguished; and the Jewish doctors affirm it to be an instrument made of iron to put into beasts’ mouths; *in thy lips*, that is, in your mouth; wherewith to rein and restrain you, and to keep you within compass, as the rider does the horse with bridle and bit, whereby he has him at command, Psa. 32.9. & Prov. 26.3. chap. 30.28. Jam. 3.3.

*{and turn thee back by the way that thou camest*} See verse 34.

**V. 30.** *{And this shall be a sign unto thee;*} God now turns his speech from Sennacherib, whose *dismission*, or *mittimus*, he had now signed, ver. 29. as his *mission*, and *commission* before, chap. 10.6. unto Ezekiah, whose faith to confirm, in the assured expectation of of his speedy delivery, he confirms his prediction and promise of it, with a sign, though of a thing afterward to ensue. See on chap. 9.6. and the like, Exod. 3.12. I am not ignorant, that some, both of the Jewish writers, and ours, suppose, that Sennacherib should upon the report of Tirhakah’s coming against him, withdraw his forces from Jerusalem, go forth to meet him, pass into Egypt, having spent two years in that expedition, return again to the siege of Jerusalem, and receive that fatal discomfiture there, and so it should be, a sign antecedent, not subsequent, to the main matter, to be thereby assured. But these things are spoken without any ground of story, sacred, or other; nor seem to suit so fitly with the relation of the penmen of Scripture, either here, or in the other holy records, 2 Kings 20. and 2 Chr. 32. See ver. 36.

*{ye shall eat this year that which groweth of itself; and the second year, that which springeth of the same; and in the third year, sow ye, and reap, and plant vineyards, and eat the fruit thereof.*} A sign of this nature, God was pleased to assign them, not only thereby, to assure them of further indemnity from the Assyrian, and deliverance out of their present difficulties and distress, but to encourage and comfort them also, against those distracting thoughts, that might arise in their minds, concerning necessary provisions, for them and their families, when the siege should break up, the land being so wasted by the Assyrians, and such spoil made of all, as by an enemy is wont to be, in a country that is not his own, chap. 1.7. for God hereby engages himself, so to provide for them, that from those very returns of their land, that it should of itself yield, notwithstanding the havoc that the enemy had made, and the want of liberty and opportunity to till and manage their grounds, they should have food sufficient, both for the present year, and the next.

*{ye shall eat*} That is, your people, the inhabitants of Jerusalem and Judah, *shall eat*, that is, have food sufficient to sustain them, as cha. 65.3. Heb. *eating*, a defective speech: for *eating*, ye shall eat: see the like, cha. 59.13.

*{this year*} Heb. *the year*, as Jer. 28.16. so, *the day*, for *this day*; or, *today*, as Jer. 1.10,18.

*{that which groweth of itself*} So is the word used, Lev. 25.5,11. where it is enjoined, that in the Sabbatical year, or year of cessation, or intermission, they should not till their grounds, nor prune their trees, nor reap the increase of the one, nor gather the fruit of the other, but let all lie common, and eat out of the field only from hand to mouth, as we say, that which came up of its own accord, either forth of the ground, by grain and seed, the year before, shed; or from off their trees, without any husbandry used about them; God engaging himself, by promise, so to bless them with increase, the foregoing year, that the proceed of it should afford store sufficient, both for that year, and the next also, until the harvest time came, of what had been that year sown, and the gathering of their fruits from the trees, that year dressed, Lev. 25.20–22. Now hence some gather, that the fourteenth year of Ezekiah (for in that year it was that Sennacherib invaded Judea) was a Sabbatical year, and that should be the reason, why that year, they should feed upon such things, as the ground, unmanaged, should yield. Others, that not this year, but the next, was the Sabbatical year; and that this year being hindered from tilling and sowing, by the enemy’s invasion; and the land therefore affording nothing to sustain them, but what the ground of itself yielded; and the next year being a Sabbatical year, wherein, by the law, they were inhibited to ear, or sow aught, they must for that year feed on that which sprang up, from what came of itself the year past. Others drive off the Sabbatical year, one year further, to the sixteenth of Ezekiah, the hindrance from tilling and sowing, say they, being in the fifteenth, from the enemy; in the sixteenth, from the law. To examine strictly those dissenting opinions; and compute exactly the Sabbatical years, from the first observation of them, unto these times, is a matter of much difficulty, and would require a far longer discourse, than these Annotations will admit. Sufficient it is, that God here promises, that for two years together, they should have a competence of sustenance from that, which their land, untilled and unmanaged, should afford them of itself, notwithstanding the great waste that the enemy made of it, and the fruits of it. See Judg. 6.3–5.

*{that which springeth of the same*} This to be the meaning of the word, here used, is generally, in a manner, agreed: howsoever the Rabbins, some of them, add frivolous fables of fruit-trees, by miracle suddenly shooting up again, and bearing fruit, where the enemy had cut them down; and of corn, in like manner, where it had been burnt down by the enemy, as also, Popish commenters, in favor of their old Latin version, of their feeding the second year on *apples*, and the like, only. The word is nowhere else found, but here, and (with a transposition of letters, the like whereunto, is in other words also observed) in 2 King. 19.19.

*{sow ye*} You shall have liberty, without either impeachment from the enemy, or inhibition, otherwise, to sow, and reap freely, and quietly to enjoy the fruits of your lands and labors, Psa. 128.2. of this use of the imperative form, see on chap. 36.16. The words imply a plenty of provisions, that their land, then tilled, should afford them, with much comfort and cheerfulness to be enjoyed by them, Deut. 8.7–10. chap. 65.13. See chap. 4.2. & 30.23–25.

**V. 31.** *{And the remnant that is escaped of the house of Judah, shall again take root downward, and bear fruit upward*} From the promise of a blessing more than ordinary, upon their land, he passes to the like, concerning the state, and themselves; That albeit, they had been much diminished and impoverished, by the Assyrian invasion; yet those that remained of them, having escaped the Assyrian sword, should thrive and prosper; & the state that was thereby so shrewdly shaken, that it seemed ready to fall to the ground, should be settled again, and restored to the same, or to a better and more flourishing condition, than it enjoyed before those broils. See the like promise, chap. 27.6. and the complement of it, 2 Chr. 32.22,23.

*{the remnant that is escaped of the house of Judah*} Heb. *the escaping of the house of Judah that remaineth*, or, *is left*; ch. 4.2. & 10.20. Ezr. 9.15.

*{shall again take root*} Heb. *shall add to root*, as ch. 10.20. & 52.1. *to root*, for *to take root*, as ch. 40.24. Jer. 12.2. a metaphor from plants or trees, that being sorely shaken, and loosened with violent winds, yet settle, fasten, and take firm hold again at the root.

*{downward*} As trees, which the lower they shoot down with the root, become the more firm. See Virgil, of the *esculus*, a kind of oak, in his Poems of *Husbandry*, l. 2.

*{bear fruit upward*} Shall become so conspicuous like a tree laden with fruit, that to other people abroad, their thriving and prosperity shall appear, Chap. 4.2. & 60.21,22. & 61.3,9.

**V. 32.** *{For out of Jerusalem shall go forth a remnant, and they that escape out of mount Zion*} There shall be a certain number of people, who having escaped the Assyrian’s sword and hand, by repairing to Jerusalem, and continuing there in safety, shall, when the siege is broken up, and the enemy gone out of the land, return in peace to their former possessions, and wonted places of abode, and be settled again in them. See the like, Jer. 4.5. & 34.11. & 37.11,12.

*{go out*} Either to view the enemy’s camp, now left, and to gather the spoils of those that came to spoil them: so some, as Cha. 33.23,24. or, rather, to return to their own dwellings again, from which, for fear of the enemy, they had fled; and others of the city, to their lands and possessions abroad, which, for fear of the enemy, before, they dared not do, Chap. 33.17.

*{a remnant*} A small company remaining, in regard of those multitudes that had miscarried in the troubles of the times. Chap. 1.9. & 10.21,22. & 17.6.

*{they that escape*} Heb. *an escaping*: as Ch. 10.20. ver. 31.

*{the zeal of the Lord of hosts shall do this.*} This God will do, out of a due regard to his own glory, and a fervent affection of love to his people: as Chap. 9.7. ver. 35. Ezek. 36.5.

**V. 33.** *{Therefore, thus saith the Lord, concerning the King of Assyria*} Heb. *unto the King of Assyria*: as in the next words, *unto this city*: but so is the particle used, also, ch. 22.22.

*{He shall not come into this city*} Heb. *unto this City*: as Josh. 8.5. though it be used also for *into*, as 2 King. 7.12. but here rather, *unto*, he shall not so much as come at it, much less enter into it, and surprise it, as he made full account to do. For the truth is, Sennacherib never came himself, in person, to Jerusalem, though he sent men and messengers thither. See Chap. 36.1,2. ver. 9,34.

*{nor shoot an arrow there*} Nor shoot so much as an arrow into the city, to annoy, or hurt any there; or to strike down those, that, for defense, might appear upon the walls; though it is not unlikely, that his army lying before it, and near unto it, would be exercising of their archery. Heb. *and he shall not*: and so afterward thrice repeated; adding much vehemency and vigor to the sentence.

*{nor come before it with shields*} Heb. *with shield*: not that his army came thither unarmed; or without shields, for defense, with swords and weapons of offense only: but that either he should not in person so present himself with his guard of shield-bearers, (whereof, see 1 King. 10.16,17. 2 Chr. 9.15,16. & 12.9–11.) or with his forces, so furnished, to make any assault upon the city. Some learned, conceive by *shields*, to be meant, here, a kind of military frame, consisting of a great number of shields joined together, somewhat like the tiling, or shingling of a roof, by the Latins called *testudo*; because their shield resembled a *tortoises shell*, under the covert whereof, being thereby secured against shot of arrows, and stones, that might be cast down upon them, they made their approaches to the walls of cities besieged, or assaulted. Of this see Livy, l. 44. Ammian, l. 26. and Vegetius, l. 2. c. 16. But whether this device were so ancient, as these times, or no, may be doubted.

*{nor cast a bank against it.*} So 2 Sam. 20.15. or, *mount*; as it is sometime rendered, Jer. 6.6. Ezek. 4.2. so the Chaldee here understands it: and the notation of the word may seem to carry it this way. For it comes of a word that signifies *to cast up*: and it is used, commonly, of the casting up of earth; to make *a causeway*; or *cast way*: thence so termed, Chap. 62.10. of the use thereof, in war, and siege of cities, see Hab. 1.10. Howbeit, the Hebrew doctors, (whom divers of ours follow, rendering it, *nor discharge an engine*,) affirm it to be an engine; such as the Romans call *balista*; wherewith they used to cast great stones, with much violence, either against the walls of cities and forts besieged, or into the forts and cities themselves: to this purpose pressing, Jer. 6.6. where mention is, of cutting down wood to make such withal; and Ezek. 17.17. where *towers* are joined with them, from the tops whereof, they used to discharge them. Of the engine, see Ammian; l. 23. and Vegetius, l. 4. c. 22. See of the like, 2 Chron. 26.15. The word is here in the singular number, as those, also, of *arrow*, and *shield*, before; though collectively taken to make the speech more emphatical: *he shall neither shoot arrow into it, nor come with shield before it; nor discharge engine against it*: and it is always joined with a verb, that signifies *to pour out*; which helps to confirm this latter opinion, concerning the right signification of it: it has its original from being *lift up*: its construction, from the use of it, in *throwing*, or *pouring out* stones and the like. See, besides the places already cited, Ezek. 21.27. & 26.8. Dan. 11.15. and there seems to be a defect in the phrase *to cast*, or, *pour out the balist*, for, *to pour out stones* with *the balist*: as, *to throw out*, or *shoot the bow*, for, *to shoot arrows with the bow*. Psalm 78.9. Jer. 4.29. our term of discharging, does very fitly express it.

**V. 34.** *{By the way that he came, by the same shall he return*} So vers. 29. A proverbial form of speech, having in it an intimation of some attempt, without issue, or of labor in vain. He shall go as he came, and lose all his labor: as Jer. 14.3. But it seems here to import somewhat more; to wit an ignominious return, with some few scattered troops, through those countries, by which he had marched in great state, with such a gallant and numerous army, before. See ch. 10.8. & ver. 14,15,37.

*{and shall not come into this city, saith the Lord*} or *unto*: see vers. 33. The same thing is repeated, and God’s own word again given upon it: he began with it, and concludes with it, and firms to it, to give the stronger assurance of it; because it might seem a thing most improbable, almost incredible, that Sennacherib, having so great an host with him at Libnah, not many miles from Jerusalem, and a puissant army before Jerusalem, yet should not so much himself, as come thither: for what could be imagined, that should stay, or hinder him from so doing? And they much diminish the force and weight of God’s words, when they render them, *he shall not come into this city*: besides both the prime and most proper use of the particle, and short of that, which the story itself holds out.

**V. 35.** *{For I will defend this city to save it*} Heb. *I will shield*, (for thereof comes the word *shield*, used, ver. 33.) or, *fence*, (for thereof, also, comes the name of *a garden*, as a place *fenced*, and enclosed, Cant. 4.4.) *this City*, to save it (see 2 Chr. 32.22.) that which no other fence, without him, could effect. See Psalm 5.12. & 32.10. Zach. 2.5.

*{for mine own sake*} In regard of my own glory: which this insolent varlet endeavors so to obscure and debase: so elsewhere; *I wrought for my name’s sake*, Ezek. 20.9,14,22,44. & 36.21,22. See ver. 32.

*{and for my servant David’s sake*} See chap. 29.1. & 38.5. To show thereby his entire and constant affection to David, and high esteem of him, in doing good to, & taking care of, the safety and welfare of his seed, for him, Exod. 20.6. & 34.7. (see Ruth 2.20. 1 Sam. 12.22,23. 2 Sam. 9.3.) and to make his word and promises good unto him, concerning the establishment of his house, 2 Sam. 7.11,15,26. Psal. 89.29,35,36. & 132.11,12. So 1 King. 11.12,13,32,34,36,38. & 15.4,5. 2 King. 8.19. hence the ground of those prayers, 1 King. 8.25,26. Psal. 132.1,10.

*{my servant*} The style that God is wont to give unto those, whom he will thereby show, in more special manner, to affect and respect: as to Moses, Num. 12.7,8. to Job, Job 1.8. & 2.3. & 42.7,8. to David, most frequently, 2 Sam. 7.5,8. 1 King. 11.13,36,38. See the same promise and passage with this, 2 Kings 20.6. Ch. 38.6.

**V. 36.** *{Then the Angel of the Lord went forth; and smote in the Camp of the Assyrians an hundred and fourscore and five thousand*} The complement of that which had been more than once before threatened, Ch. 10.12,16–18,33,34. & 14.25. & 30.27–33. & 31.8. & 33.23.

*{Then*} That is, as many interpreters, some two year after the prayer of Ezekiah, and God’s promise, by Esay, concerning the deliverance of his people, ver. 35. For they suppose, that Sennacherib, having upon Tirakah’s rising against him, withdrawn his forces out of Judea, and spent two years in the conquest of Ethiopia and Egypt, returned back to Jerusalem, to renew the siege of it, and then received this blow. See ver. 30. But these be mere surmises; for which no good record of antiquity, is produced: and the course of the relation being carried on in this manner, by a continued thread, without interruption, both here, and in the sacred history elsewhere, 2 Chron. 32.20,21. seems not to admit any such distance between the one, and the other. Yea, the express words in the book of Kings, puts the matter, in my apprehension, out of all doubt. For the penman of that book, or that part of it, wherein this story is recorded, having related Sennacherib’s first message, together with an army sent unto Jerusalem, from Lachish, 2 King. 18.17. the return of his messengers, back from thence, unto Libnah, whither, from Lachish he had removed, Chap. 19.8. then the tidings brought him of the Ethiopians against him, ver. 9. and his second message thereupon, by letter, unto Ezekiah, ver. 10–14. (all which must needs be, before any expedition into Ethiopia, or Egypt,) Ezekiah’s prayer, presently, upon the receipt of the letter, ver. 14–19. and God’s gracious answer, by Esay, thereunto, ver. 20,34. he subjoins immediately to prevent all mistake in this kind, and excluding all conceit of any long delay in the execution of what God, by the prophet, had promised; *And it came to pass in that night, that an Angel of the Lord went out*, ver. 35. What night, but the very next after the message, by the prophet, sent from God? Thus the links of the story are so close-clasped together, that there is not the least gap, or flaw left, for any such disjuncture of time, to be forced in, without breach made in the chain itself. In the Hebrew, both here, and there, it is, *And*; as ch. 36.3,9,11.

*{the Angel of the Lord*} Or, *an Angel of the Lord*: not an evil spirit; as yet some; they are nowhere so styled: but one of those blessed spirits, that are of God’s soldiery; which he is wont to make use of, as well for the protection of his people, as for the destruction of his and their enemies, Gen. 32.1,2. 2 King. 6.14–17. Ps. 34.7. & 68.17. & 103.20,21. Heb. 1.14.

*{went forth*} From heaven, where these glorious troops attend on God’s Majesty, Matth. 18.10. Luke 1.19. or, from the Lord, that sent him, 2 Chr. 32.21. See chap. 30.27. or, *went forth*, in a warlike manner about this work. For it is a military term, 2 Sam. 11.1. See ver. 9. and so some take it, Gen. 10.11.

*{and smote*} With plague and pestilence, say some: as 2 Sam. 24.15,17. so, not Berosus, as some mistake it; but Joseph the Jew, l. 10. c. 2. says, that Sennacherib returning from the conquest of Egypt, found his army thus consumed with the pestilence: but that seems not so likely, because the noisomeness of such a malady, would have infected the whole country; with thunder and lightning, say other: which is not altogether improbable. See chap. 30.30. or, with an hidden combustion, that scorched and killed them. See ch. 10.16,17. which, say some of the Jewish writers, did so consume their bodies to ashes, that neither the land might be annoyed with their carcasses, nor the people troubled with interring them; & yet neither burnt their garments, (no more than the fire did, that slew Aaron’s sons, Levit. 10.2,5.) nor defaced their ornaments, that the people might enjoy their spoils. See ch. 10.16. & 33.23.

*{In the Camp of the Assyrians*} As some, lying before Libnah, where Sennacherib himself, with a great party of it was, ver. 8. Others, set down before Jerusalem, whither no small body of it had been sent to beleaguer it, while the residue stayed at Lachish, ch. 36.2. there being no mention or probability of the departure of it, as yet, from thence; though it be not unlikely, that some such matter was intended, had not this sudden blow prevented it: & here some proceed so far, as to particularize the place, where this blow was given; some affirming it to have been in *the valley of Jehoshaphat*, 2 Chr. 20.25,26. Joel 3.12. Others in *the valley of Gehinnom*, Josh. 15.8. ch. 30.33. But these are mere uncertainties. I suppose the slaughter was made, as well in the one part of the camp, as in the other; as well in that before Jerusalem, as in that also before Libnah. Nor was the distance of place between the one, & the other; such as could impeach the dispatch of that execution, by an Angel, in an instant, when as within so short a space of time, an Angel, in likelihood, slew all the firstborn, throughout the whole land of Egypt, Compare ch. 30.27,30–32. with this place, & Exod. 12.22,29. with Heb. 11.28. & 1 Cor. 10.10. what God is said to do in the one, an Angel is said to do, in the other: because by the ministry of an Angel it was done. see c. 31.8.

*{an hundred and fourscore & five thousand*} A great slaughter indeed, as it is termed, ch. 30.25. and a slaughter of great ones, there termed *towers*; for so it is said, 2 Chr. 32.21. *The Lord sent an Angel, which cut off all the mighty men of valor, and the Leaders and Captains in the camp of the King of Assyria.* Rabshakeh, in likelihood, with his companions; among the rest. See ch. 10.16,33. where these great ones are called *his glory, his lofty boughs*, and *his tall trees*: as the meaner sort of them, that make up this reckoning, *his thorns*, and *his thicket*, ver. 17,34. for I cannot believe what some of the Jewish masters groundlessly gather from that passage in the Chronicles, that this whole number should consist only of the former. This story and remarkable passage of God’s providence, the Devil has endeavored to obscure and deface, (as many other of the like nature, recorded in Scripture,) partly, by displacing of it, and partly, by blending of it with idle fictions of his own: this to effect, he has made use of the Egyptians, who, therewith, to gain estimation to themselves & their idols, relate, that Sennacherib invading their country, Sethon a priest of Vulcan, who was then their king, being upon some disgust deserted by his soldiery, and in regard thereof, in great distress, betook himself to his idol, before whom having deplored his present condition, he fell into a sleep, wherein his god appearing to him, willed him to arm such of the common people, as were willing to follow him, & go out the next day against the enemy with them, & he should be sure to do well enough. This oracle given him, his god the night following, sent a multitude of field-mice into Sennacherib’s camp, consisting of Assyrians and Arabians that gnawed asunder all their bow-strings, and leather thongs of their quivers and their shields; by which means on the morrow, finding themselves thus disarmed, they were enforced to fly, and by the Egyptian (though raw) forces, fell many of them in their flight. So Herodote, l. 2. from the reports of the Egyptians to him, when he was among them, by whom also he was shown an image, said to be that Sethon’s, with a mouse in his hand, and this motto adjoined to it; *Let men learn devotion, by looking on me.* And thus, as Sennacherib would have ranked the true God among heathen idols: as no more able to save his people, than they were, those that served them: so has the Devil, by them, endeavored to detract from him the honor of this admirable work, and to attribute it to their idols.

*{and when they arose early in the morning, behold they were all dead corpses*} Heb. *and they arose-and behold*. The like syntax, see c. 35.4. v. 7.

*{when they*} To wit, those of the enemy’s party, that had escaped with their lives: as 1 King. 20.29,30. or the people of Jerusalem, that expected to hear further of them.

*{behold*} A note of admiration not without just cause prefixed, before the relation of so sudden, and so stupendous a change. So in the prediction of it, ch. 10.33.

*{they were all dead corpses*} Yet not *all* simply, but *all* in a manner: the main body of the army, and the most of the great ones: for some, with Sennacherib himself, escaped. See ch. 17.14.

**V. 37.** *{So Sennacherib King of Assyria departed*} He was not destroyed then, with the rest of his forces: God reserving him as to be destroyed at home, by his own sons, so surviving the loss, to see the power of that God, whom he had set so light by. The like have some deemed of Pharao, because he is not expressly mentioned, as perishing together with his troops: Exo. 14.18. & 15.4. but we have elsewhere, as well clear Scripture against Pharaoh’s escape, Psal. 136.15. as for Sennacherib’s escape here, see Job 21.30.

*{So*} Heb. *And*; as ver. 8.

*{departed*} With such a sorry remnant of his great army, as was left, ch. 31.8,9.

*{and went and returned*} *with confusion of face, to his own land*, 2 Chr. 32.21. especially being to pass through some of those countries, which he had formerly subdued, and in great pomp and state, marched through before. See ver. 34.

*{and dwelt at Nineveh*} *the strong hold*, that, *for fear of the sword, he fled to*; nowhere staying by the way, as nowhere thinking himself in safety, until he got thither. See chap. 31.8,9. or *and sat down at Nineveh*, 2 Sam. 7.1. & 11.1. kept himself quiet there, and went out to war no more. So some of the Jewish commenters, not amiss: his loss was so great, as he could not soon recover; his shame such, as he had no list to look much abroad. See 2 Chr. 32.21.

*{Nineveh*} The chief city of Assyria, built there by Nimrod, nephew to Cham, by his son Cush: after that out of the land of Shinar, or Chaldea, where he was first seated, he had broken into the country of Ashur, the son of Sem; and is in Scripture constantly termed *Nineveh*, Gen. 10.11,12. 2 King. 19.36. Jon. 1.2. & 3.3,4,6,7. & 4.11. Nah. 1.1. & 2.8. & 3.7. which name, also, is sometime found in profane authors; as in Ptolemy, l. 8. c. 6. Sect. 5. and in Ammian, l. 18. c. 9. Howbeit, the most historians, both Greek and Latin, call it, *Ninos* and *Ninus*, and report it to be so named, from a king of that name, who first founded it, which is directly contrary to the records of holy Writ. And indeed, who sees not that *Ninos*, or *Ninus*; are no other than *Nineveh*, molded into a Greek and Latin form? and it is not improbable, that the *Ninus*, they write of, was no other than Nimrod, for some of them make him the first king of the Assyrians. See Diodore, l. 2. c. 1. who is said to have been the first that, by war, invaded any neighbor country; (see Justine, l. 1.) which is as much in effect, as of Nimrod, Moses reports, Gen. 10.10,11. where the word used, is observed to imply no less. See on ver. 36. Howbeit, the word *Nineveh*, may, to some, seem to come nearer to the Greek *Ninuas*, or *Ninyas*, which they say, was the name of their *Ninus* his son. See Diodore, *ibid.* c. 21. and from him, might Nimrod be deemed to have given Nineveh that name; as Cain called the city that he built, by the name of his son *Enoc*, Gen. 4.17. if it could be made to appear, that Nimrod had any son of that name. But it is more probable, that from the name of the city, the Greeks, at first, forged the names both of the father, and the son. The like whereunto, both they, and other writers are wont to do, when the names of cities and countries, are such, as they find no other certain, or probable ground of, to fasten them on some one man of note, or other, who sometime bore that name, that either founded, or forced them, and so became lord of them; as by a multitude of instances might easily be shown. Nor can I therefore be induced to concur with that learned writer, who presuming, not Nimrod, but Chus, the father of Nimrod to be *Ninus*, supposes, that Nimrod building this city, called it, not by his own, but by his father’s name *Nineveh*, as *Ninaveh*, that is, *Ninus his habitation*, or dwelling place, since, neither is it the manner of those oriental tongues, to put the governing word, after the governed; nor does it appear, that either Cush, or Nimrod, were either of them, so anciently known by the name of *Ninus*. *Nun*, indeed, or *Non*, we read to have been the name of Joshua’s father, Exod. 33.11. Num. 13.9. 1 Chr. 7.27. and, *Nin*, for, *a son*, or for *issue*, we find, Gen. 21.23. Job 18.19. Esay 14.24. but neither do we anywhere find *Nin*, to be a proper name of any one, or other; nor either *Nun, Nen*, or *Nin*, to have been the name either of Cush, or Nimrod, or, of any of Cham’s posterity; and consequently, not of the first founder of *Nineveh*.

**V. 38.** *{And it came to pass, as he was worshiping in the house of Nisroch his god, that Adrammelech, and Sharezer his sons smote him with the sword*} Thus was he reserved, as Pharao, in the slaughter of the firstborn, Exod. 12.30. to see the deliverance of God’s people, and the destruction of his own; and then to be slain at home by the hand of his own sons, in the temple of his god, who was not able to save him, as the God of Israel had his, from the evil that he threatened, and had intended against them; who also had foretold this his end. See ver. 7.

*{And it came to pass, as he was worshiping*} Heb. *And he was bowing himself*: as 2 Kings 5.18.

*{in the house*} The temple. See on Chap. 15.2.

*{of Nisroch*} Of this idol, save in this story, we find no mention in Scripture; nor that hitherto has been observed by those, that have made diligent search into the monuments of antiquity in this kind, elsewhere. It may seem to have been the *Sun*, whom, most of those eastern people, chiefly adored, under divers names, Ezek. 8.16. and may seem to have been so termed from his circular motion, whereby he traverses the heavens, between the two tropics, from a word of that notion, Jer. 2.23. For as for the conceit of a learned writer, who would have it to import *a God of soft*, or *tender, flight*; answering to the Greek *Ζεὺς ὁ Φύξιος*, unto whose temple, therefore, as to a sanctuary, Sennacherib should flee for succor; it neither has ground in story, and is too far fetched; and as little probability carries that of another, who would bring *Nisroc* up to *Rac*, found in *Shadrac*, Dan. 1.7. which (says he, but without proof) in the Babylonian language, signifies, the *Sun*. Joseph, l. 10. c. 2. calls this idol, *Arasce*.

*{Adrammelec*} The name of an idol, which those of Sepharvaim adored, 2 King. 17.31. the word signifies *a magnificent King*; both titles given to the true God, Chap. 33.21,22. and their manner was, as to give unto their idols, the titles of the true God; so to impose the names of their idols, on their children, or on those whom they would honor, and had in esteem. See on Chap. 39.1. Dan. 1.7. & 4.8.

*{Sharezer*} An Assyrian name, composed of *Shar*, and *Etser*; from whom, it grew to be in use, also, among God’s people: as appears, Zach. 7.2. Joseph in his *Antiquities*, corruptly calls him *Selenaar*.

*{his sons*} These words here written, are read, but not written, 1 Kings 19.37. and are very remarkable, much conducing to aggravate the dismal end of this impious and insolent miscreant, having his life taken from him, by those who had received life from him. Divers causes, the Jewish commenters relate of this their unnatural attempt and design: which, because they seem to be but fabulous fictions, such as they are nothing sparing of, I forbear to rehearse. See Chap. 33.1. Joseph says they were his two elder sons; but without ground.

*{smote him with the sword*} That is, slew him; as Deut. 20.13. See ver. 7.

*{and they escaped into the land of Armenia*} So that the murder of the tyrant, by his own sons, for the present, went unpunished; no justice being done on them, for the death of him, that had unjustly, himself, done so many to death. See Judg. 1.5. 1 Sam. 15.33.

*{Armenia*} Heb. *Ararat*; on the mountains whereof, the Ark, wherein the whole stock man and beast was enclosed, rested after its floating so long to and fro, when the deluge was abated, Gen. 8.4.

*{and Esarhaddon and his son reigned in his stead*} Of this Esarhaddon, there is mentioned also, Ezr. 4.2. whence it may appear, that sometime after, he renewed the attempts of his ancestors, against the land of Israel. For he further emptied that country of its natives, by Salmaneser there left, and peopled it with some colonies of his own, who there profess to have been brought thither by him, therein prosecuting what Salmaneser had in part done before him, 2 King. 17.4,24. and it is not unlikely, but it was he also, who after Ezekiah’s decease, by his forces, under the command of others, (for it appears not, that in person he did it,) re-invaded Judea, took Manasses prisoner, and carried him to Babylon, which was, it seems, as yet subject to the king of Assyria, 2 Chr. 33.11. But he is thought to have been the last of that monarchy. Some suppose him to have been the same with him, whom Ptolomy calls *Assaradinus*; and the names, indeed, come very near. Others would have him to be him, whom the Greeks call *Sardanapalus*; because the Assyrian monarchy ended in him: nor are this name and that of *Esar-haddon*, much asunder. For *Sardanapalus*, is no other, than *Esar* (or *Sar*,) *-haddon-pul*; a compound of those three simples; the last whereof, *pal*, or, *pil*, or, *pol*, or, *pul*; (for they come to all one,) is found in those Assyrian and Chaldean names, (for it is common to both,) sometime single, as in *Pul*, 2 King. 17.19. sometime prefixed, as in *Pil-etser*, 2 King. 15.29. sometime inserted, as in *Nabo-pol assar*, mentioned in Ptolomy; sometime annexed, as in *Esar Haddon-Pal*, or, *Pul*, whence *Sardanapalus*.

### CHAPTER 38

**V. 1.** *{In those days was Ezekiah sick unto death.*} This story, of Ezekiah’s sickness and recovery, a remarkable monument, both of the uncertainty of all outward prosperity, and how soon and suddenly our greatest joys may be blasted; as also, of God’s, as well power, as pity, in being able to bring back from the threshold of death, and so doing Psalm 9.13. is recorded also, in 2 King. 20.1–7. 2 Chron. 32.24.

*{In these days*} That is, say the Jewish writers, three days, before that slaughter made in the Assyrian army: for on the third night of his sickness, that, say they, fell out. But if Ezekiah then lay sick of so dangerous a disease, how could he, with Sennacherib’s letter, go up to the Temple? Chap. 37.14. when as it is apparently implied, that by means thereof, he was restrained from access to God’s house, ver. 22. Some of ours would have it to be in Sennacherib’s absence, while he was in employment against the Ethiopians and Egyptians: concerning which, see on Chap. 37.35. from 2 Chron. 32.20,22. and the reason they render is from ver. 6. where deliverance from, and defense against the king of Assyria, is promised: whereby it appears, say they, that this sickness did precede that deliverance. But this may easily be avoided: for the promise there seems to be, and well may be, of a continued preservation and protection, for the future. See on the place. Others, therefore, after Joseph the Jew, in his *Antiquities*, l. 10. c. 3. hold, that this sickness befell Ezekiah, shortly after Sennacherib’s defeat, and departure thereupon. Nor does the computation of Ezekiah’s years and reign, any way control this. For in Ezekiah’s fourteenth year, Sennacherib invaded Judea; and having received a submiss message and moneys, according to his own demand, from Ezekiah, sent notwithstanding his army, a great part of it, unto Jerusalem, supposing it would be suddenly, upon the very sight thereof, delivered up to him. This his army had not long lain there, but that Rabshakeh, who at his access thither, had presently summoned the city, receiving no such answer, as he looked for, returned to his lord, whom he found dislodged from the place where he left him; & upon tidings brought him of the Ethiopian king’s expedition, sending a letter back to Ezekiah, to try what might be done, before his camp were broken up: and Ezekiah, upon receipt of it, seeking by renewed suit unto God, that was from God, by the prophet promised, which, without longer delay, was the very next night performed. Now all this might very well have been accomplished within the fourteenth year of the reign of Ezekiah, especially if the invasion were made about the beginning of the year: but allowing for the dispatch of them some good part of the fifteenth; and this sickness following very shortly thereupon the reckoning of fifteen years ensuing, will well consist with twenty nine of his reign fully complete. Of the phrase itself, see ch. 4.1,2. Jer. 3.16,18.

*{sick*} What kind of disease this was, is not certain: some deem it to be that which we call *the plague*. Thus much only appears, that that it was some disease, accompanied with a malignant ulcer, ver. 21. Much more uncertain it is, for what special cause it was, that God pleased thus to exercise him, about which, many are pleased to deliver their conjectures, some improbable; as those, who suppose it was to chastise him for not marrying before. But neither does it appear, that he was not before married; nor is any set term of time defined in the Law, at which men ought, in those times, to enter into that estate; nor do we read of any, that were chastised for leading a single life. Others, somewhat more probably, to keep him from being lifted up, after so great, and sudden, and strange a deliverance, that which man’s nature is too prone unto (see 2 Chr. 26.16 2 Cor. 11.7.) and Ezekiah himself was, not long after, overtaken with, 2 Chron. 32.25. or to correct him, for coming short in thankfulness, answerable to so high a favor; that which he was sometime after found somewhat defective in, 2 Chron. 32.25. or, thereby further to refine him, and fit him for such favors, as he meant further to confer on him, chap. 1.25. 2 Cor. 4.16. Heb. 12.10,11. or thereby to inure him, to depend constantly upon him, and keep closer to him; considering what need he had of his continual support, 2 Cor. 1.9,10. or lastly, to withdraw his heart and affections from the things here below, and to cause them to mount up, and aspire more unto heaven, 2 Cor. 5.1,2. And these, or some of these, or some other, not unlike these, might God have an aim at, in this passage of his providence: but which, or what, in particular, is no easy matter for any mortal man to divine. See Job 10.2. Rom. 11.33,34. and it is safest for us, therefore, to be sparing in defining aught therein.

*{unto death*} The disease being such as was deadly in its own nature. See Joh. 11.4. Phil. 2.27.

*{and Isaiah the Prophet, the son of Amoz, came unto him, and said unto him; Thus saith the Lord*} being sent unto him from God, not so much to give him a visit, as to deliver him the message hereafter related.

*{Set thine house in order*} *Command*, Or, *Give charge concerning thine house*: as ch. 45.11. & 48.5. As if he had said; make your will, and dispose of your estate, that there may arise no question or controversy about it, after your decease.

*{for thou shalt die, and not live*} Heb. *thou art dead*; no better than a dead man, as sure of this disease to die, as if you were already dead. So Gen. 20.3. Joh. 3.18. Rom. 8.30. Yet a secret reservation there was, though the sentence seemed peremptory, to humble and to try him; as in that of Nineveh, Jon. 3.4. See Jer. 18.7,8. Ezek. 3.18.

*{die, and not live*} As, *live, and not die*, Ezek. 18.21. and, *not die, but live*, Psal. 118.17. an emphatical form of speech, only; not, as some of the Rabbins fondly and falsely expound it; *Thou shalt die*, in this world, *and not live* in the next.

**V. 2.** *{Then Hezekiah turned his face toward the wall, and prayed unto the Lord*} *Then*, to wit, after this message delivered to him, and the departure of the prophet that brought it. See on ver. 4. Heb. *And*; as ch. 37.36.

*{turned his face to the wall*} As he lay in his bed, not out of sullenness and discontent, as Ahab, because he wanted of his will, 1 King. 21.4. nor because he could not endure to behold the face of God’s prophet, that had brought him so sad a message, as Eliseus tells Joram, 2 King. 3.14. (for the prophet departed, when he had done his errand) but, as some conjecture, because the Temple stood from his house on that side, toward which, they used in their private houses to pray, 1 King. 8.35,48. Dan. 6.10. and so the Chaldee paraphrast expressly renders it. As others, that being sequestered from the company of those about him, and having withdrawn himself from such variety of objects, as might in his devotions distract or disturb him, he might with the more privacy, the more intention of mind, and the more freedom and fervency of spirit, address himself unto God. See somewhat the like, 1 King. 18.42. and the contrary, upon a diverse occasion, 1 King. 8.14. where it is rendered, *and the King turned his face about*; and so the word properly signifies. They swerve too much from the simplicity of the text, who by *wall*, would have the *heart* here meant; because *the walls of the heart* are mentioned, Jer. 4.19.

*{prayed*} Of the word here used, See on ch. 37.21.

**V. 3.** *{And said remember now, O Lord, I beseech thee, how I have walked before thee in truth, and with a perfect heart; and have done that which is good in thy sight.*} Thus God’s servants, in an humble and modest manner, dare appeal, even to God himself, for the sincerity and integrity of their hearts, and for their serious care, and sedulous endeavor, to please him and to approve themselves and their courses unto him, Job 10.7. & 23.10–12. Psal. 7.3–8. & 18.22,23. and do plead sometime the same unto God, as expecting, therefore, favor and mercy at his hands; not in regard of any matter of merit in them, or of reward, deservedly for the same due to them; (for they acknowledge all that they do, or can do, to be but duty, and due debt, Luk. 17.10. Rom. 8.12. 1 Joh. 2.6.) but in regard of his gracious promises freely made thereunto, Psal. 5.12. & 7.10. & 33.18,19. & 34.15,19,22. & 37.39,40. & 91.1–16. See Neh. 5.19. & 13.14,31. Ps. 26.1–9. & 86.2. & 119.22,31,38,94.

*{Remember*} So Nehemy, in the places above-cited; and the Psalmist, Psal. 25.6,7. & 18.32. & 89.5. Not that God can forget aught, much less any good, that is done by any, or for any of his, Heb. 6.10. but then he is in a special manner, said to remember either person, or performance, when by some act of mercy, or bounty, exhibited to the one, or for the other, he makes it to appear, that he takes notice of, minds, and accepts of either. So Gen. 8.1. & 18.29. & 30.12. See the like, ch. 37.4,17.

*{now?*} The same word that was used before, ch. 36.11. and might better be rendered, *I pray thee*, here, than there. The words run thus in the text; *I beseech thee, O Lord, remember, I beseech thee.* For the word repeated, is with very little difference the same, *Ana*, and *Na*, and of the same notion usually; and there is the very same repetition found twice in one verse, in the *Hosanna*, Psal. 118.25. whence some, too much addicted to Jewish fopperies, would have *Ana*, to be one of the names of God; because it is joined both here, and there, with *Jehovah*; and the Jews so use it in their prayers.

*{How*} Heb. *that*; as ver. 7.

*{I have walked*} Heb. *I have made* (that is inured, or accustomed) *myself to walk*. I have studiously and carefully applied myself so to live, and so to behave myself. So Gen. 24.40. or, I have constantly so conversed and carried myself; as Lev. 26.12. 1 Sam. 12.2. Ps. 26.3. See of Ezekiah, 2 King. 18.5,6.

*{before thee*} As in your sight, Gen. 5.22. & 6.9. & 17.1. Psal. 16.8. & 119.168. Luk. 1.6.

*{in truth*} In sincerity, 1 Sam. 12.24. 1 King. 2.4.

*{with a perfect heart*} Or, *an entire heart*; when the heart is not divided between God and the creature, or between God, and some false god, but is entirely set upon him; though a man may have his failings in some things, as Ezekiah also, and some others had, to whom yet this commendation is given. See 1 King. 8.61. & 11.4. & 15.3,14. 2 Chron. 25.2. whereas of some other, it is said, that some good things they did, but *not with an entire heart*, 2 Chr. 25.2. See of Ezekiah, 2 Kings 18.6.

*{have done that which is good in thy sight*} Heb. *the good in thine eyes*, as Jer. 26.14. that which has been acceptable and well-pleasing to you, and accepted of you, 2 Chron. 29.2. as that is said to be *evil in God’s eyes*, that he mislikes and disallows, Gen. 38.10. 2 Sam. 11.27. ch. 65.12. so that is said to be *good in the eyes of God*, that he likes and allows, Lev. 10.19. Deut. 6.18. 1 Sam. 3.18. 1 Chron. 18.13.

*{and Hezekiah wept sore*} Heb. *wept with great weeping*; as 2 Sam. 13.36. This grief of Ezekiah, thus manifested, is supposed, to have proceeded, partly, from an apprehension of some displeasure, that God had conceived against him; in regard whereof, he should be taken away so soon, and so suddenly, after so great a deliverance, as one deemed unworthy to enjoy the blessed fruit and comfort of it, as befell that nobleman for his unbelief, 2 Kings 7.2,19,20. partly, from a foresight and forecast of such danger and disturbance, as might befall church and state; much out of frame, both when he came to the crown; and much distracted and disjointed again by the late invasion, should he then be taken away, before either were again well settled; especially, since that he had then no son to succeed him; and the want of an heir-male (many, in regard thereof, taking occasion to pretend title to the crown) might be a means of producing much distraction in the state: for his son Manasses, that succeeded him, was, as yet unborn; as appears by his age, when he came to the crown; for he was but 12 years old at his father’s decease, 2 King. 21.1. whereas his father lived fifteen year after this sickness, ver. 5.

**V. 4.** *{Then came the word of the Lord to Isaiah; saying*} A speedy return of a gracious answer, agreeable to those free promises, ch. 58.9. & 65.24.

*{Then*} Before he was gone out into the city, or unto his own house, while he was yet in the king’s house; for *he was not yet gone out into the middle Court*; or, as some read it, *gone out of*, to wit, the king’s house, which had three courts within the utmost wall, or compass of it; one, next to the chief house; another, next the street; and a third between those other two: (See 1 King. 7.8. & Jer. 36.12. & 37.15.) which Esay had not yet entered, being still in the first, or at least, was not gone out of, when this message came to him, 2 King. 20.4. where the reading is *Court*; but the writing is *City*; because, say some of them, the king’s palace was as a city; and the courts thereof, as the streets of a city. And they render this, as one reason, why God was pleased to return such an answer, by the same messenger, so speedily, ere he were gone out of the king’s court, 2 King. 20.5. that it might not be known and divulged in the city; that a doom of death had, from God, been passed upon their sovereign, which might have produced some evil consequences among the people. This is not improbable. Whereunto we may add, that God hastened his answer, that he might not hold his dejected servant over-long in affliction of mind, anxiety of spirit, and solicitous suspense; and by the same messenger, by whom he had sent the former, to give the stronger assurance of the certainty of it; which might have been more questionable, had the message come by any other: and that the same party might, to others abroad, relate jointly together, both the one, and the other. So dealt he with David: he sent Nathan to him, at the same time, ere they parted, both to convince him of his sin, and the heinousness of it; and withal, upon his humble confession and acknowledgment thereof, to assure him of pardon, 2 Sam. 12. ver. 12,13.

*{Then*} Heb. *And*: as ver. 2.

*{came*} Heb. *was*: as Jer. 1.2,4.

*{the word of the Lord*} By a secret inspiration, a message from God: as 2 King. 1.15. & 3.15. Act. 10.19. & 11.12.

**V. 5.** *{Go, and say to Hezekiah*} *Return*, or, *Go back*, 2 King. 20.5. Heb. here. *Going, go*: as Jer. 13.1. & 28.13.

*{and say*} Heb. *thou shalt say*: as ch. 6.9. & 7.4.

*{Thus saith the Lord, the God of David thy Father,*} For whose sake also, he bears a loving and tender affection to his issue: and to you more specially treading in his steps, 2 King. 18.3. chap. 16.5. See ch. 37.35. Jer. 13.13. & 17.25. & 33.17,21–26.

*{I have heard thy prayer*} see ch. 37.4,21.

*{I have seen thy tears*} Taken special notice of them, and taken them to heart: as Exod. 3.7. see Psal. 56.8. Though the prophet had neither heard the one, nor seen the other; yet God, in heaven, had, Psal. 34.15.

*{behold, I will add to thy days fifteen years*} I will not only recover you of the present disease, so that you shall be able, within three days, to go abroad again, 2 King. 28.5. But I will over and above that, assure unto you a lease of your life, for fifteen years longer: such a favor, as we never read the like, afforded unto any other of his servants, though very high in favor with him. See Gen. 27.2. Psal. 39.4. and no marvel, therefore, if it be ushered in with a note of attention, and serious consideration: *behold* (see ch. 7.14. & 37.7.) and sealed, being an unusual grant, with an unwonted miracle, ver. 8.

*{I*} Who before had passed, by my prophet, a sentence of death on you, ver. 1. Deut. 32.39. 1 Sam. 2.6. Psal. 68.20. Hos. 6.1.

*{I will add*} Heb. *I am adding*: or, I am he, that will *add*: as ch. 29.14.

*{to thy days*} That is, to the days, say some, that were formerly allotted you in my secret purpose, Job 7.1. & 14.5. as if God’s counsels were not fixed, ch. 25.1. & 26.3. to the days; that in the course of nature, he might have attained to, say others, but could not have attained, had he been given up to the violence of this present disease, Job 15.32. Ps. 55.23. See 1 Sam. 26.10. but the meaning is plain, to those years, that he had lived already.

*{fifteen years*} The one half, in likelihood, and it may be precisely, of the whole time of his reign: For this is, not without ground, deemed to have fallen out, about the fortieth year of his age, and the fifteenth year of his reign: for he was full twenty five year old, when he began his reign: and full twenty nine he reigned, 2 King. 18.2. 2 Chronicles 29.1. so that the fortieth of his age, and fifteenth of his reign, are in part, at least, coincident: In part, I say, because they might have divers beginnings, and expirations accordingly. So that half the time of his reign, he enjoyed peace and tranquility, without interruption: see ver. 6,15. chapter 39.6.

**V. 6.** *{And I will deliver thee, and this city out of the hand of the King of Assyria; and I will defend this city*} Hence some infer, that this sickness of Ezekiah befell him, before the dissolution of the Assyrian camp. But of that there is no necessity, in regard of aught here spoken. See on ver. 1. The promise before made to them, in the time of their distress, by the Assyrian forces, chap. 37.35. is again here renewed, to give Ezekiah assurance, not of his life only to be prolonged, but of peace and tranquility to be continued unto him, together with it. For Ezekiah might have some doubt, lest Sennacherib, though having so great a blow given him: yet might in some space of time, recover himself again, and either he, or some of his successors, might return to molest him, and the state again, out of a desire to be revenged for the former discomfiture: and that after his decease appears to have been, in some sort, effected, 2 Chron. 33.11. Now this to meet with, and to ease Ezekiah’s mind of all such misdoubt and dread: God promises to continue this his protection, both of him and his city: and to safeguard them, against whatsoever power any king of Assyria should be able to raise, or make against either. That which Sennacherib made account was more than God could do, Chapter 36.20. & 37.10,11. Ezekiah prayed for, well knowing, that he could, chapter 37.20. and God by promise engaged himself to do, for the present, there, chapter 27.21,25. for the future, also, here. See 2 Chron. 32.22.

**V. 7.** *{And this shall be a sign unto thee from the Lord, that the Lord will do the thing that he hath spoken*} Ezekiah had craved a sign for the strengthening of his faith, vers. 22. and the sign here mentioned, being put to his choice, 2 Kings 20.8,10. Thus is God content, in mercy and goodness, to comply with man’s infirmity, and condescend to his weakness: and as the nurse leading the little child, to stoop down to us, when the short hand or arm of our feeble faith, is not able to reach to his, 2 Chronicles 32.24. See Genesis 15.8–18. Judges 6.36,40. Chapter 7.11,14. and 37.30.

*{that the Lord*} The pronoun relative, for the demonstrative particle: as ver. 3.

*{will do the thing*} Heb. *word*: as Gen. 20.10. & 21.11.

**V. 8.** *{Behold*} See before, ver. 5.

*{I will bring again the shadow of the degrees, which is gone down in the Sun-dial of Ahaz, ten degrees backward*} Heb. *I am bringing*, or *do bring again*: as ch. 3.1. & 44.3. Jer. 29.3,4.

*{the shadow*} Made by the sun: and the sun, consequently, together with it: as in the next branch is expressed.

*{of the degrees*} Marked upon the surface of the dial, to show the progress of the sun, and the process of the day together with it.

*{which is gone down*} Or, by *which it is gone forward*. See more hereof on the next branch.

*{in the Sun-dial of Ahaz*} Heb. *in the degrees of Ahaz*, (that is, in the dial which king Ahaz, Ezekiah’s father, had for public use erected, in some open place, about his palace, marked out with a certain number of lines, or degrees, such as before,) *in the Sun*, or *with the Sun*; on whose motion the shadow with the progress, or the regress of it, wholly depended; the particle may be taken the latter way, as well as the former: as 1 Sam. 1.24. Hos. 5.6.

*{so the Sun returned ten degrees, by which degrees it was gone down*} By the *Sun*, some here would have understood the shadow which the sun made on the dial; because it is said to have gone back by so many degrees, as it had gone forward on Ahaz his dial. And some hence would infer, that the course of the universe was not inverted, or altered; but the shadow, only, upon the dial; called here the sun, as the windows are so called, by which the sunshine is let in, Jer. 15.9. but neither can it well be conceived, how the shadow made by the sun, should go backward, or forward, without the sun; nor could foreign people, in remote places, have taken notice of it, had no alteration been in the course of the universe. See chap. 39.1. nor is any such thing found, as is intimated in that place of Jeremy: nor is it necessarily so implied in the text, that the sun went forward, or backward, on Ahaz his dial, either here, or, 2 King. 20.9–11. where there is no mention of the *Sun*, but of the *shadow* only. Though it be true, that the retrograde motion of the sun, appeared by the shadow upon the dial: for there may well be a transposition of the words in the text, as our English has conceived it, or the text be otherwise expounded, as shall afterward appear.

*{returned*} Or, *went back*; as is more fully before expressed, so many degrees, as it had already gone forward. Which some suppose to have been done in an instant; and then the day so much longer than ordinary, by so much of it, only, as was already spent. Others are of the mind, and so the most, that the sun went back in his ordinary pace, and then the day must be twice so much longer than ordinary: as much time being spent in his return to the point, at which he rose; as much more in his coming back to the point, from whence he had returned.

*{ten degrees*} What space of time was by each of these degrees described and limited out, is uncertain. Some would have them whole entire hours; *ten* of such twelve, as are mentioned, Joh. 11.9. and then should that day have been, if the sun went back suddenly, two and twenty hours long; if an ordinary pace, (as they seem to hold) thirty two hours long. But against this is objected; First, that if it had been of this latter and larger size, it had been longer than that, when the sun stood still in Joshuah’s day: for that was no longer than two days, at most; a day of four and twenty hours, Josh. 10.13. whereas this should be, within four hours, as long as three days: and yet of that day, it is said, that there was none like it before, or after it, Josh. 10.14. 2 Neither size will suit with the choice that Ezekiah was put to, of having the sun go ten degrees forward, or backward, 2 King. 20.9,10. For if they were entire hours, the sun was already within two hours of setting; and could not go, therefore, above two such degrees forward; nor by above two hours (which his going forward must do) hasten the night. Others, therefore, conceive these degrees to have been but half hours; and that is the opinion most received; and so the day should be of seventeen hours, if the sun retired in an instant. And so some define it: or of twenty and two hours, (two only short of Joshua’s day) if he kept to his pace: for ten degrees, that is, five hours of the day were past, what time this miracle was wrought. So that it was about their fifth hour complete, our, eleven. Ten degrees, that is, five hours were spent in his regress, and as many in his renewed progress, unto the point from which he retired. All which put together, make twenty two hours. Yet there want not those, that allow each degree but a quarter of an hour, and so enhance the number of them on the dial; from twenty four to forty eight: so the day should be cut shorter by five hours, at least. But it is not very probable, that the day should be minced into so many small shreds on the dial. The Jewish doctors tell us, (but that is one of their tales) that the day was shortened, just so many degrees at Ahaz his death, as it was lengthened at Ezekiah’s recovery.

*{by which degrees it was gone down*} Heb. *in the degrees*; or, *by the degrees which it had gone down*. And according to our reddition of it, therefore, should be a transposition of the words in the text; *by the degrees which*; for, *by which degrees*. Some following the order of the words, as they lie in the text, render them, *in the degrees*; and expound them, *in the Dial*, thence inferring, what above is related. And it is true, that in the foregoing words, the dial of Ahaz his setting up, is called, *Ahaz his degrees*: by a synecdochical form of speech, whereby the part is put for the whole, because it consisted of *a gnomon*; or, *index*, and *a table*, or *plane*, marked with those degrees. But the word is there without the article: whereas it is here, as in the beginning of the verse, with the article prefixed: and is to be taken, therefore, rather for the degrees themselves, wherewith the motion of the sun was measured, and discovered upon the dial. And the words therefore may well be rendered, *by the degrees which it* (to wit, the sun) *had proceeded*.

*{it was gone down*} This if we take the word strictly, and understand it of the sun: it should imply, that the sun was then in his declination, and that it was past high-noon, or midday, so many hours, as those ten degrees made up. So he should return, not to his morning point, but to his zenith, or meridian, where in Joshuah’s days he stood still, Josh. 10.13. But this seems not so likely. Some understand it of the shadow on the dial; supposing it to have been like our sundials, against some wall, whereon the shadow descends, as the sun gets up, and ascends again, as the sun declines and goes down. So the miracle might commence from some part of the forenoon, according to the degrees spent, and past, from the sun-rising. But the dials seems to have been no mural, or vertical, but an horizontal one. And some of the Jewish writers tell us, that it consisted of an half-circle, whereon those degrees were signed with an *index*, or *style*, situate in the midst thereof; the shadow whereof, falling upon the verge of it, showed, how, by degrees, the day went away. And to meet with such doubts, the plainest way, is, to expound the word rendered, *gone down*, not strictly of declination, or descension, but of *progress*, simply considered, without any notion of ascent, or descent properly so termed. So you may find it used, Judg. 11.37. & 15.11. 1 Sam. 23.6. 2 Sam. 23.21. 2 Kings 8.29. Jer. 18.2. & 22.1. and so it may well be rendered here, *which it had passed*; or, by *which it had gone forward*.

**V. 9.** *{The writing of Ezekiah, king of Judah, when he had been sick, and was recovered of his sickness*} The inscription, or title of the ensuing hymn, declaring the occasion of it; like that, 2 Sam. 22.1. Psalm 18. and 34. their titles. The manner of God’s people, anciently, was, upon some special favors received from God, to conceive, and compose solemn forms of thankful acknowledgment. See Exod. 15. Judg. 5. 1 Sam. 2. Psalm 18. & 30. & 34. Chap. 12. & 25. & 26.

*{writing*} That it might remain upon record, to posterity, Deut. 31.19,22. Psal. 78.5,6. ver. 19.

*{when he had been sick*} Heb. *in being sick*: so Deuteron. 4.46. chap. 5.5.

*{was recovered of his sickness*} Heb. *lived from his sickness*; as ver. 16,21.

**V. 10.** *{I said*} I thought; I made full account; as Psal. 14.1. & 32.5. & 39.1. Lam. 3.18,54.

*{in the cutting off of my days*} When the prophet brought me that message from God, that I must die, ver. 1. Then are things said to be done, in Scripture, when, by God’s messengers, from him, they are either promised, or denounced, Jer. 1.10. compared with Jer. 18.7,9. Hos. 6.5.

*{cutting off*} A borrowed speech, taken from the practice of weavers, who, when their web is wrought out, cut it off from the loom, v. 12–14. Lam. 3.54.

*{my days*} The time of my life, Psal. 39.4,5. & 100.2,24. See on ch. 1.1.

*{I shall go to the gates of the grave*} As *the gates of death*, Psalm 9.13. & 107.18. Of the word *grave*, here used: see on Chapter 5.14. For what the Popish writers, here, some of them, prate of their *Limbo*, not far from hell-gate, wherein some of their own, also, here control them, is ridiculous. I passed a doom of death upon myself; I looked for nothing but death, 2 Cor. 1.9.

*{I am deprived of the residue of my years*} Which I hoped to have lived, and in course of nature, might have done. So Ps. 55.23. & 89.45. & 102.24. Heb. *I am made to miss the residue of my years*: so some; referring us to those places where the same word, but in another form, signifies *to miss*, or, *be missing*, 1 Sam. 20.18. & 25.7,21. Or, as others, *I am bereaved of the residue of my years*; affirming it to be an elegant term, taken from the use of the word in the Kedaren, that is, the Arabic tongue. They seem to strain a little too much, who would read it, *the residue of my years, is failed from me*: though they produce the like defect of the particle, Jer. 10.20.

**V. 11.** *{I said*} As before, v. 9.

*{I shall not see the Lord*} I shall not visit his Temple anymore, among those that there worship, Psalm 27.4. and 42.2. and 84.7.

*{even the Lord in the land of the living*} Among those that survive, ch. 53.8. Ps. 27.13. & 116.9. v. 19. He redoubles the word *Jah*, rendered, *the Lord*; (of which, see on ch. 26.4.) to express his ardent affection to God’s service, and to intimate his desire of life, to that purpose, v. 22.

*{I shall behold man no more with the inhabitants of the world*} I shall no longer converse with men here on earth. See Gen. 27.49. Exod. 18.28. I despaired of life. 2 Cor. 1.8. The state of persons deceased, is described, sometime, by others *not seeing* of them; as Job 7.8. sometime, by their *not seeing* of others: so here.

**V. 12.** *{Mine age is departed, and is removed from me, as a shepherd’s tent*} Heb. *My generation*, (as Jer. 2.31. Acts 13.26.) that is, *mine age*, as ours render it) or, *mine issue*, (my posterity, as others; because he had no male-issue then: see ch. 53.8.) or, *mine habitation*, (as Ps. 84.10.) *is made to go*, (as Job 4.21.) *and is carried away from me*, (in a forcible manner; as one is carried away,) *into captivity*: for so the word properly signifies, in this form nowhere else used. I am bereaved of my continuance, or abode here, by the violence of my disease; as one that is, in hostile manner, forced out of his dwelling place; it being as soon and suddenly thrown down, and I severed from it, as is a shed, that a shepherd sets up for his shelter, and removed, from place to place at pleasure, ch. 24.19. Jer. 4.20. Lam. 2.6.

*{I have cut off like a Weaver my life*} He returns to the borrowed speech before used, verse 10. taken from the weaver’s practice, cutting off his web from the loom, either when the web is woven out, as usually; or, as upon special occasion, at sometimes, before it be finished. So again, ver. 12,13. His meaning is, as some, I have shortened my life, or provoked God to shorten it, by my sins, as Gen. 38.7,10. See ver. 17. or, as some other, *my life is cut off by me*, that is, by God, some occasion, by me, given him so to do, though the doing of it be sore against my will; as of Judas, it is said, that *he purchased a field with the reward of iniquity*, Acts 1.18. though purchased, by the priests, not by him, with the money wherewith they hired him, Matth. 27.6,7. I suppose it is to be referred rather to his estimation and account of himself. I made no other account, but that my life would be so cut off. I should bring it suddenly to an end. See ver. 10. 2 Cor. 1.9. The word rendered, *cut off*, is nowhere else found in Scripture: (though in the Chaldee paraphrast, sometime) only a noun derived from it, that signifies *cutting off*, Ezek. 7.25. and the name of a beast, chap. 14.23. & 34.11.

*{he will cut me off with pining sickness:*} *He*, (that is, God) *will cut me off*, (as Job 6.9.) or, *I shall be cut off*; (the word being taken indefinitely; as ch. 2.19. & 17.13. & 22.8,19.) *with pining sickness*: so some, because the word comes of a root, that signifies, *to attenuate*: whence also this name is given to the poorer and meaner sort of people, Jer. 40.7. & 52.15. but others render it, *from the thrum*; because some Jewish critics hold it, to signify those thin and loose threads, that hang dangling down at the end of the web; whence it is used also for *locks*, because they resemble such, when disheveled especially, Canticles 6,7. and so the metaphor from the weaver’s manner of doing, is still continued.

*{from day, even to night, wilt thou make an end of me.*} Heb. *from day, unto night*: that is, as some, from *morning*, to *evening*, (as Gen. 1.5.) you will continually and uncessantly pursue me, until you have made an end of me; or, this very day, before night come, you will dispatch me. See Job 4.20. there is a passage from person to person; as chap. 21.10. & 25.5,6. & 31.7. Amos 9.1. and some would have inserted, *I said*; as ver. 10,11. but that is needless.

**V. 13.** *{I reckoned until morning*} Heb. *I set*, or *put*, or *propounded* to myself (as the word is used, Psal. 16.8. & 119.30.) I thought within myself, *till morning*, or *while yet morning was*, that is, as some expound it; I made account, overnight, that I might live until morning; as others, rather, I made account, ere the morning were over, that an end would be made of me; that I should not live, either the morning, or the day, at least, (as *morning* is taken, Gen. 1.5.) to an end.

*{that as a lion, he will break all my bones:*} So most interpreters take it, as a relation of what his thoughts were, and what he made full account of, that this would betide him ere morning were over. Yet some render them; *But as a lion he*, or, *it broke all my bones*. Whereas I had conceived some hope of holding out till the next day, my disease, or God by it, did so grievously handle me in the night, as if some fierce lion had crushed all my bones to pieces: that that hope of mine was utterly dashed and quailed. Of the similitude, see Jer. 50.17. Lam. 3.4. sore pains are by the *breaking of bones* oft expressed, Job 7.15. Psalm 6.2. and 51.8. Prov. 14.30. and 17.22.

*{from day, even to night, wilt thou make an end of me*} See the same, ver. 12. From this reiteration of the same thing again, some gather, that Ezekiah was two days in this extremity; that in the former verse, is expressed his first day’s thoughts; in this, his second’s: But this observation is of no great certainty. It may rather intimate the fixedness of his thoughts, and the vehemency of his affection thereupon.

**V. 14.** *{Like a crane, or a swallow, so did I chatter; I did mourn as a dove*} This, some apply to his prayers, as very quick and short, by reason of his pains. Others understand it of his speech, so suspended, with the violence of his disease, and the excess of his grief, that he was not able to utter any articulate voice: as Psalm 77.4. but this his prayer recorded, ver. 2. does sufficiently control. The meaning seems to be, that his pains and grief, both joined together, did wring from him such sighs and groans, in the bemoaning of himself, as might well be compared to such kind of noise, or mournful sounds, as these fowls, or their young ones, or their dams, when their young are taken from them, are wont to make.

*{a crane, or, a swallow*} The connexive particle is not in the text: in regard whereof, the old Latin make them but one fowl, rendering it, *the swallow’s young*, or *young swallow*; and the Greek, likewise one only, *a swallow*: but the defect of the particle, as well in the copulative, as in the disjunctive notion, is frequent. See chap. 5.6. & 17.6,14. & 27.7. & 28.24. and that they are the names of two several fowls, and both such as change their abode with the season of the year, appears from Jer. 8.7.

*{crane*} The word is *Sus*, or *Su*, as the Jewish critics require to have it read, which howsoever most of the Jewish masters affirm to signify *a crane*; some rendering the reason thereof, because it is a tall fowl, and goes upright, like *an horse*, who bears also the former name; Yet there want not, (whom I rather herein accord with) that conceive it, to signify *a swallow*, so termed from her note, or the noise she makes, not unfitly expressed, by the word *Sis*. And I the rather hereunto incline, because of the Egyptians’ fable of their *Isis*, that was turned into *a swallow*. See Plutarch, *of Isis, and Osiris*, and Symachus here so renders it.

*{a swallow*} The Hebrew word is *Agur*, or *Gnagur*, (as some pronounce it) both here, and in Jeremy, not elsewhere found, which some of the Jewish writers would have to be *a swallow*; some, *[unclear]*. Yet others rather suppose it to be *a crane*; which from the Greek *γέρανος*, we so term. whereunto they are the rather induced; because not only the Greek comes near it, but the Latin, *Grus*, comes in a manner full home to it. And again, for that by a transposition of letters, in the holy language very usual, (see ch. 36.16,30.) it seems to come from the word *Arog*, or *Gnarog*, that signifies *to bray*, as *Deer* do when they want food, either pasture, or water, Joel 1.20. to whose voice, which a crane’s, rather than a swallow’s, resembles, does the Psalmist compare his groaning after God, using the same term of either, Ps. 42.1.

*{chatter*} Aloud and apace, as those fowls, in parting with, or missing their young; or *peep*, as their young ones do, when they miss their dam, or want meat. Of the word, see ch. 8.20. and 10.14. and 29.4.

*{mourn as a dove*} So chap. 59.11. Ezek. 9.16. the mournful and doleful tone, that turtles and doves have, is well known. See of the word, rendered *mourn*, ch. 8.20. Ezek. 2.10. and of his mourning, v. 2.

*{mine eyes fail with looking upward*} Toward heaven, to God, for ease and relief, 2 Chr. 20.12. Ps. 123.1,2.

*{fail*} Heb. *are exhaust*, or *spent*: as Job 28.4. ch. 19.6. a metaphor from rivers drawn dry, the vigor of them is wasted; my sight fails. So Ps. 6.7. & 31.10. & 38.10. & 69.3. & 119.82,123. but some of the Jewish commenters render it, *are lift up*; according to a word near unto it, but rising from another root, Prov. 26.7. this, if we admit, there needs no supply: but neither is the word anywhere found so used; nor is that other word agreed on, so to signify, in that place of the Proverbs; nor does the root it comes from, signify *to lift up*, simply, but *to draw up*, used properly of water, out of a well or pit, Exod. 2.16,19. alluded to, Prov. 20.5. & Psalm 36.1,3. compared also, with Psalm 40.2. I choose therefore rather, to stick to our version; only rendering it, as the former, in the time past; *mine eyes failed*, or *were exhaust*, with looking, or while I looked *upward*: a comprehensive, or complicated kind of speech, whereby two diverse notions are enfolded and wrapped up in one word. So Ps. 89.33,34. *thou hast profaned his crown to the ground*; that is, *profaned it*, by *casting it down to the ground*; as it is afterward there expounded: so ch. 14.12. *how art thou cut down to the ground?* for, hewed down, and laid along on the ground; and ch. 21.9. *her Gods hath he broken unto the ground*, for, has he broken and cast down to the ground. See further on v. 17.

*{O Lord I am oppressed*} Heb. *it oppresseth me*; to wit, my disease: it is so strong upon me, that it presses me down beyond my strength, Psalm 32.3,4. & 38.2,4,6. 2 Cor. 1.8. Here I suppose would fitly be inserted, *I said*; oft wanting, and supplied; as Nehem. 9.25. Job 8.18. chap. 22.13. and 26.19. See ver. 10,11.

*{undertake for me*} He compares his disease to a bailiff, or sergeant, that, from death, as a merciless exactor, had so attached him, and taken such hold on him, that unless God would be pleased to undertake for him, as his bail or surety, or to rescue him, at least, there was no means for him to escape. See somewhat the like, Job 17.3. Ps. 119.122. where the same word is used; yet some render it, *ease me*; and the word signifies, indeed, sometime, *to be sweet, pleasant*, or *pleasing*, Psalm 104.34. Prov. 3.24. & 13.19. Jer. 31.26. Mal. 3.4. but never actively, *to sweeten*, nor anywhere, *to relieve*, or *ease*. Others of ours render it, *weave me out*; for, because they find a word of the same family with this, to be used for the *woof*, Lev. 13.51. and some allusions to *weaving*, went before, verse 10,12. they suppose the verb here used, may signify *to weave*; and the former similitude therein prosecuted; as if it had been said: though this disease would cut off the web of my life before it be completed: yet Lord be you pleased to weave it out still, and lengthen it to its due period. But this seems somewhat too far fetched.
