**V. 15.** *{What shall I say? he hath both spoken to me, and himself hath done it*} This passage, some, make part of Ezekiah’s former complaint: but as checking himself therein, and intimating the fruitlessness of his complaint, and the unlikelihood of speeding in his former request: as if he had said: to what end do I thus bemoan myself in vain, and spend words to no purpose? it is God that has passed a doom of death, and what he has doomed, he will do: and there is no either debating the matter with him, or murmuring against him, or restraining him from what he intends to do. So Job 9.12,32. & 11.10. & 23.13,14. Ps. 39.9. c. 29.16. or, to what end, do I seek to him, to undertake for me, when it is he himself that does it? But others, at the foregoing verse, end his complaints, and relations of his sad and forlorn condition, and at this, begin his narration of God’s unexpected mercy and goodness to him, in revoking his former doom, returning a gracious message in the room of it, and, accordingly, accomplishing it: as if he had said, according to some, *what I said, he spake, and did*. What I requested of him, for the prolonging of my life, he promised to do, and accordingly did. Or, as others, *what shall I say?* What shall I make more words, in way of relating my then sad condition? like that of David, to Mephibosheth, 2 Sam. 19.29. Or, how can I sufficiently, in any words, express God’s goodness toward me? like that of David, to God, Psal. 106.2. & 116.12. & 139.17,18. he has both said, and done it: both promised me recovery, and accomplished what he promised, 2 Kings 20.5.

*{he hath both spoken*} Heb. *and he hath said*, as Jer. 17.16. & 32.44.

*{unto me*} Or, *concerning me*, as chapter 36.7. either concerning my death, as some, or, concerning my recovery, as others, rather.

*{himself hath done it*} Heb. *he hath done*, with a defect of the pronoun, *it*. as chap. 44.23. though some, to exclude any such supply, bring in the pronoun, expressed in the text, after the verb: which yet will not so well do here: because the neuter, commonly, is feminine.

*{I shall go softly, all my years, in the bitterness of my soul*} So those that understand the foregoing branch, of the message, or doom, of death: *I shall, hereafter, have no joy of my life*: *I shall go drooping all my life long*. But this seems not to be his meaning. For what hope, or expectation, could he have, of living years, that despaired of holding out a day to an end? See v. 12,13. Others, therefore, render it, *I will be thinking on this favor that God has shown me, all the days of my life, as long as I live*, v. 20. Ps. 34.1. & 116.2. or, *I shall pass the rest of my life peaceably and quietly, after this bitter brunt is once over*, v. 6. ch. 39.8.

*{go softly*} That is, *pensively* say some: as one oppressed with extremity of grief. So Ahab, 1 Kings 21.27. Or, *softly*, that is, *deliberately*, or *considerately*, says a Rabbin, as men use to do, that are seriously thinking on some weighty matter. (to which purpose, the old Latin, *I will reckon up to thee*) As minding God’s mercy herein showed him, and *confessing* to, or praising his name for the same. Or, rather, *softly*: that is, *quietly*, and *cheerfully*: as the word is used, also, ch. 42.4. being nowhere else found: as those are wont to do, that march in state, says one: as a nurse, that leads a child gently by the hand, says another, from the use of it, in the Talmud: rather, as men are wont to walk leisurely, where they fear no danger of surprisal: contrary to the manner of those that are frighted, or possessed with fear, ch. 28.16. Jer. 46.5. & 48.9.

*{in the bitterness of my soul*} Whereof, verse 17. so Job 7.11. and 10.1. or, *after my soul’s bitterness*, when it is past, and gone. So is the particle found used, Chapter 18.4. See Chap. 53.8.

**V. 16.** *{O Lord, by these things men live: and in all these things is the life of my Spirit: so wilt thou recover me, and make me to live*} That is, as those that admit this reading: By your promises and performances of the same, is the life of man prolonged, and mine among the rest, whom you have restored to life and health, Deut. 8.3. Mat. 4.4. See ch. 64.5. And this sense the words will very well bear. Yet they are by divers, divers other ways rendered, by some, thus: Other men may *live beyond these* years, that you have now assigned me, but *among them all the life of my Spirit*, by miracle thus continued to me, has this advantage above theirs, *that thou wilt maintain it in health and life*; that is, in vigorousness to the last. By others, it is thus read: *Beyond those* years, that you by some message, assign them, men may *live, and among them all*, so may *the life of my Spirit* be produced: and I hope, therefore, or entreat you, therefore, *that thou wilt yet, relieve and quicken me*. By others again, *unto all those, that shall live* in time to come, *beyond these* years, shall *the life of my Spirit* be made known, how *thou hast made me to sleep, and quickened me*: brought me to death’s door, and raised me up again. By some lastly to let pass the rest, *In these, yea in all these* troubles of divers sorts, threatening death, ch. 37.3. & 38.1. *Yet, doth the life of my Spirit live: thou hast made me to sleep*, (or, rather, *recovered me*,) *and revived me*. The former require too many supplements to make them up: this last, least of any.

*{by*} Heb. *upon*: as ch. 3.5,6. or, *beyond*: as Job 22.24. & 23.2. or, *by*, as Gen. 27.40. Ps. 9.4.

*{men live*} Heb. *they live*: an indefinite form of speech.

*{in all*} Heb. *unto all*: as most commonly: and so v. 17. or, *in*: as ch. 26.9. & 28.2.

*{the life of my Spirit*} See Gen. 2.7. Chapter 42.5. Psalm 104.29,30.

*{so*} Heb. *and*: or *so*: as Prov. 17.3. ch. 53.7.

*{wilt recover me*} Or, *hast recovered me*: restored me to health and strength: so Job 39.7. is the word used: and as some also, Psalm 1.26.2. Some render it, *thou hast made me to sleep*, understanding thereby, some, (as above) the sleep of death, Psalm 13.3. some, natural rest: as if he had been distempered, through want of sleep, which God had been afterward pleased to afford him, Psalm 127.2. Jer. 31.26. but the word signifies, sometime, indeed, *to dream*, Chapter 29.7,8. and so most take it, Ps. 126.1. never *to sleep*.

*{make me to live*} Or, *made me whole*, as v. 9. or, *kept me alive*: as Exod. 1.17.

**V. 17.** *{behold*} See what a sudden change here was. So Chapter 17.4.

*{for peace I had great bitterness*} Or, *upon my peace* (as chap. 30.6.) or, *after my peace*, (as Jer. 52.31.) came *great bitterness*. Not long after my deliverance from those difficulties, I had been in by the Assyrian king, and his forces, when I made account, that now I should enjoy peace and rest, this grievous affliction then suddenly surprised me. See ver. 1. so Job 29.18. & 30.15. Jer. 8.15. & 14.19.

*{for peace*} That is, instead of it, as Gen. 11.3. or presently *upon* it; or *after* it; as Gen. 7.4. Heb. *unto*; as Gen. 50.21. whence some would expound it, My bitterest afflictions became salvation to me; that is, they turned to my good, Ps. 119.67,71. Rom. 8.28. Heb. 12.11. but the former seems the sounder.

*{peace*} Tranquility and prosperity, Chapter 48.18. and 57.19,21.

*{great bitterness*} Heb. *bitter bitterness*, or, *bitterness bitterness*, for abundance of bitterness, or, bitterness upon bitterness; grief upon grief: so, *justice justice*, for, exact justice, Deut. 16.20. *peace peace*, for, *perfect peace*, ch. 26.3. *bitterness*, for, matter of grief and vexation; as v. 15. 1 Sam. 22.2. Ruth 1.20,21.

*{but thou hast in love to my soul delivered it from the pit of corruption*} Heb. *and* (for, *but*, as chap. 29.13.) *thou hast loved my soul from the pit of corruption*: a concise, or comprehensive form of speech, comprising two notions in one term; whereof, the one is expressed, the other is suppressed; but implied, and to be supplied in the version, that the sense may be entire; so Psal. 118.4. *the Lord answered me in largeness*, for *the Lord answered me*, and set me *in a large place*, or, set me *at large*, enlarged me. Jer. 46.27. *I will save thee from afar*, for, *I will save thee*, and bring you back; or, *in safety* bring you back *from a far* country; Acts 27.44. *they were saved to the shore*, that is, *they were saved*, and brought, or, brought *in safety unto the shore*; so 1 Sam. 7.2. *they lamented after the Lord*; that is, *with lamentation*, they looked, or sought *after* him; 2 Corinthians 5.2. *Ye have not mourned, that he might be taken from among you*, that is, *out of grief*, or *in mournful manner*, endeavored, or taken a course, *to have* such an one *cast out* of your society; as it follows, there, ver. 13. see here, before, ver. 14. and after, v. 21. as also, ch. 1.4.

*{love*} The word here signifies a propension, whereby a man’s soul is strongly carried toward some party, whom he is exceedingly taken with: see Gen. 34.8. it is frequently used, of God’s love to his people, Deut. 7.7. & 10.15. & 21.11. and of them to him. Psalm 91.14.

*{my soul*} For, *me*; as Ps. 3.2. & 116.7,8. & 119.25.

*{from the pit*} The grave, Psalm 32.3. & 103.4. the word here used signifies as well *destruction*, as *a pit*; whence some ambiguity in that latter place; and that which is here called *the pit of corruption*, or *consumption*, is, Psal. 55.23. called *the pit of destruction*; the same word being there used in the latter place, that is here in the former.

*{of corruption*} Or, *consumption*. The word it comes of, signifies *to waste*, and *wear away*; as garments, over long worn, use to do, Deut. 8.4. & 29.5. Psal. 102.26. ch. 50.9. it is applied to men’s bodies also, and the parts thereof, Gen. 18.12. Psalm 32.3. Lam. 3.4. attributed here to the grave: because it wastes and rots men’s bodies, as old clouts and rags rot, or, consumes them, *till they be not*; as the Psalmist speaks, Psal. 72.7. where this very word is used; another term of the same notion, see ch. 10.25. where with that *consumption*, the Assyrian is, in wrath, threatened, from which, Ezekiah is here, out of love, delivered.

*{for thou hast cast all my sins behind thy back*} You have no more minded, regarded, or taken notice of my sins, which might justly have caused you to deny me this favor; than as if you had cast them behind your back; a borrowed speech, taken from the manner of men, who are wont to cast behind their back, such things as they list not to look on, have no regard of, nor desire to mind, or remember, Psal. 16.22. & 50.17. see somewhat the like expressions, Ps. 85.2. Chapter 43.25. Jeremiah 31.34. Micael 7.19. we know the common by-word of the wallets, or, two parts of the wallet; the fore-part, into which we put other men’s faults, and the back-part, into which, our own. But we must set our sins before our face, if we would have God to cast them behind his back, Ps. 50.21. & 51.3.

**V. 18.** *{For the grave cannot praise thee: death cannot celebrate thee*} The deceased cannot perform those offices anymore, whereby you are honored; your name celebrated, and the glory published and propagated here on earth, among the sons of men, Psalm 6.5. & 30.9. and 80.18. and 88.10–12. and 115.17,18. *the grave*, for, the buried; and *death*, for, the dead: as *circumcision*, for, the circumcised, Rom. 15.8. Gal. 2.9. Phil. 3.5. the same thing repeated in divers terms.

*{cannot praise thee*} Heb. *will not*, or, *shall not confess thee*; as Ps. 6.5. & 105.1. Mat. 11.25. and so ver. 19. the indicative form, in a potential notion; as chap. 26.18. so in the next word, and the next branch.

*{celebrate*} Or, *praise*, thence, *hallelujah*; the first, and last word of divers Psalms; Psalm 106. & 146–150. Rev. 19.1,4,6.

*{they that go down into the pit cannot hope for thy truth*} Dead bodies laid up in the grave, can neither see, nor expect: neither take notice of, nor look for your faithfulness and truth, in the performance of your gracious promises, Eccl. 9.4–6,10.

*{they that go down into the pit*} So the word is used, Gen. 37.22,24. Exod. 21.33. ch. 14,15,19. and why some should here render it, *a cistern*, I see not: for the phrase, see Ps. 88.4. Ezek. 26.26. & 31.16. & 32.24,25.

**V. 19.** *{The living, the living he shall praise thee, as I do this day*} They that survive, and they alone can, and each of them should: the repetition is emphatical; as the like, Psalm 51.4. & 76.7. this being the principal end to which men should live, and for which they should desire life, Psalm 80.18. & 102.21. & 115.18,28. and 119.17,88,175. Rom. 14.7,8. Phil. 1.20,21. See v. 22.

*{as I do*} A defect to be supplied, from the former branch; *as I now praise thee*; as Job 14.5. 2 Chron. 10,11. Chapter 30.29.

*{the father to the son shall make known thy truth*} To transmit the memory thereof unto posterity, Ps. 78.3,4. & 145.4. Joel 1.3. The syntax is, as 2 Sam. 3.30. Jer. 40.2.

*{thy truth*} Your faithfulness in the performance of your promises, as v. 18. Ps. 25.10.

**V. 20.** *{The Lord was ready to save me*} Of his readiness, see v. 4. Heb. *The Lord to save*, a defective form: as, *the ears of the people were to the book*, Neh. 8.3. and, *thy servant to thy fear*, or *service*, Psalm 119.38. that is, *attentive* to the one, and *devoted* to the other.

*{therefore we will sing my songs to the stringed instruments, all the days of our life, in the house of the Lord*} As at present he praised God, by his hymn, penned to that end, on purpose; so he does, by solemn promise, further engage himself so to do, as well in public, as in private, as long as he lives: so Psalm 34.1. & 104.33. The memory of God’s mercies should abide with us, when the act of them is over: as the scent of the civet does in the box, though the civet itself be gone, Psalm 105.5. and 119.93. & 145.7.

*{therefore*} Heb. *and*: so ch. 37.20,26.

*{we will sing my songs to the stringed instrument*} Heb. *we will hand my hand-instruments*.

*{we*} He speaks in the plural, as men of some note and repute do, sometime, of themselves; (so Gen. 39.27. Dan. 2.36. Job 18.1. Cant. 1.4.) or, to imply a joining of others together with him, in this sacred and solemn action: as Ps. 34.3. & 142.7. so Num. 22.6. Job 18.3. Cant. 1.4.

*{will sing*} The word properly signifies *to handle*, or play upon such an instrument as is managed by the hand. See on chapter 23.16.

*{my*} Because more specially concerning me: or the song sung to them, composed by me: though some suppose the jod here, to be no pronoun, but a paragogical production of the word only, and then there will be no *my*, in the text. See somewhat the like, Jeremiah 22.24. Lamentation 1.1. and Psalm 50.10. so Hab. 3.19.

*{stringed instruments*} Or, *hand-instruments*, rather: for the word is more general. We find in Scripture, their ancient musical instruments reduced to two heads, the *Nechiloth*, Psalm 5. and the *Neginoth*, Psalm 6. the *Nechiloth*, were *wind instruments*, such as were managed by wind, or breath, as pipes, fifes, flutes, trumpets, cornets, and the like: so called, because they are pierced, or bored through, and made hollow, to receive and transmit the wind, or breath, that produces the sound. See ch. 2.10. & 30.29. The *Neginoth* were *hand-instruments*, such as were managed by the hand, not the stringed only, whether touched with the fingers, as lute, and harp: or struck over with a quill, as the cittern, or with a bow, as the viol, but such, also, as are shaken to and fro, as the cymbal, or beaten, whether with hand, or stick, as the timbrel, so called, from the fore mentioned word, that signifies *to touch, strike*, or play upon any such kind of instrument, whether without song, or singing thereunto, 1 Sam. 16.16,17,23. & 18.10. & 19.9. 2 Kings 3.15. Psalm 68.25. and the word here used, is sometime, therefore put for *a song*, that is sung thereunto: as Job 30.9. Psal. 69.12. & 77.6. Lam. 3.14,63. which may help to justify our version, that here so renders it.

*{all the days*} See on ch. 1.1. no day should pass over his head, without some mindfulness of this mercy, or, so long as he lived, he would be praising God for it, so oft as he should have occasion to repair to his house, Ps. 145.1,2.

*{of our life*} See before, *we will sing*.

*{in the house of the Lord*} The Temple: as Chap. 37.14. which he desired health to repair to, ver. 22. he would praise God for it, as well in public, as in private, that others might be affected also with it, receive spiritual good by it, be incited to serve God, trust to him, and depend on him, with expectation of the like success: and that as many had (no doubt) joined together in prayer for him, so many might return praise to God with him, and in his behalf: this being the end of holy assemblies, as well to bless God for benefits received, as to seek him for them, Deuteronomy 16.15. 2 Chro. 20.26,28. Psalm 9.14. and 22.22,25. and 34.1–6. and 40.10. and 66.13–15. and 111.1. and 107.32. and 149.1. and 150.1. 2 Cor. 1.11.

**V. 21.** *{For Isaiah had said*} The hymn reported, the penman of this part of the book, whether Esay himself, or any other, returns again to the story, annexing two passages of it, not before specified in this verse and the next. Heb. *And Isaiah said*; but well rendered, *had said*: as the like, Gen. 12.1. because done before his recovery, and the hymn before related, penned by him thereupon, v. 9. See 2 Kings 20.7.

*{said*} No doubt, by God's direction and appointment.

*{Let them take a lump of figs, and lay it for a plaster upon the boil*} Whether this plaster, according to God's appointment, by the prophet prescribed, had any power or virtue in it, to help forward the cure intended, is much questioned. Some think that it had not, no more than the clay, that our Savior tempered, to open the man's eyes with, that was born blind, Joh. 9.6,7. used, only, to intimate the cure, and to enhance the miracle, the cure being accomplished by such means, as had, of themselves, no power to produce it. Others suppose, that it might have some natural power, to put forward the thing intended; for that they find in good authors, that figs are held useful, either for the dissolving, or ripening of swellings, and those also, that are with some malignity accompanied. See Celsus, lib. 5. ch. 28. & Pliny, lib. 23. chap. 7. Against which, some except again, that figs are deemed so, where no ulcer is, as here there was. But whether any such efficacy were in the plaster, or no, certain it is, that the cure was miraculous, and the effect, in a way, extraordinary; that Ezekiah brought so low, by so violent a disease, as himself describes it, ver. 13,14. and an ulcer of that malignity, should with the use of so slight a remedy, be so raised up, and recovered, that he should be able within three days, not to rise from his bed, or sit up only, but without danger to go abroad, 2 Kings 20.5. God would have him, and others, hereby, learn, not to neglect the means, when God either enjoins, or affords them, for their good, corporal, or spiritual, that they may not by tempting him, bereave themselves of the benefit that they might have reaped by them. See 2 King. 5.10–14. Mat. 4.6,7. & 22.4,5,8. Luk. 7.29. & 14.16–24. Acts 27.24,25,31.

*{lay it for a plaster upon the boil*} Heb. *bruise it* (for so the word signifies, Lev. 21.20. found in no other place of Scripture, but here, and there) *upon the boil; bruise it upon the boil*, for *bruise it*, and *lay it*, or *lay it bruised upon the boil*. So Prov. 26.7. *can a man take fire* (for, *take*, and *carry*, or *taking fire*, carry it) *in his bosom, and not be burnt*; and Prov. 25.22. where the very same word is, compared with Rom. 12.20. *so shalt thou take coals of fire* (that is, *take*, and heap, or lay, or having *taken coals*, heap, or put them) *upon his head*. Of such concise language, see before on v. 14,17. It is more fully expressed, 2 Kings 20.7. *they took, and laid*.

*{it*} The lump. Or, *them*; the figs: the same defect is, 1 Kings 20.7.

*{upon the boil*} Or, *ulcer*: one of the plagues of Egypt, Exod. 9.9–11. See also, Job 2.7,8.

*{and he shall recover*} Heb. *he shall live*: as ver. 9. so Num. 21.8,9. this shows, that this was done by direction from God. Otherwise, the prophet could not have thus ensured the success of it. The complement whereof, after the thing done, is recorded, 2 Kings 20.7.

**V. 22.** *{Hezekiah also had said*} Heb. *And Hezekiah said*, so before, v. 21.

*{what is the sign*} Or, *what shall be the sign?* as it is rendered, 2 Kin. 2.8. what sign may I have of the certainty of what you tell me?

*{that I shall go to the house of the Lord?*} To wit, so suddenly so soon, being in so low and weak condition, as now I am: for the promise of God was, that he should *on the third day*, go abroad, and repair to God's house, 2 King. 20.5. and the same is repeated in craving a sign, 2 Kings 20.8. so that the sign seems to have been desired not so much to seal the lease of the ensuing term of his life, as the sudden recovery of his health; which seemed to him, a thing so strange, and in a manner incredible, that he desired to have it, by some sign, ensured to him: the rather, in likelihood, encouraged to make that request, because God, of his own accord, had before given him a sign to assure him of delivery, from the king of Assyria, ch. 37.30. And that learned man, that would have the word to be understood, as spoken not by way of request, but in way of wonderment only; *What a miracle will this be, that I shall go to the Lord's house?* considered not the course of the story, whence this is taken: and is controlled by the prophet's answer there recorded, 2 King. 20.9.

*{go up*} To wit, within these three days, 2 King. 20.5,8. *go up*, as, *went up*, ch. 37.15.

*{to the house of the Lord*} The temple: as Chap. 37.15. His first journey, upon his going abroad, was to the temple: partly, to publish his recovery, and to make it known to the people, that hung in suspense, uncertain what was, or would become of their king, whose continuance with them could not, but be earnestly desired by the better part among them: but, principally, to praise God, in public, in the special place of his solemn service, and in the face of his people, therein joining together with him, it being one main cause, for which he desired life, and health. See v. 20. So Ps. 27.4. & 42.1,2,4. & 84.2. & 122.1. Ezek. 46.2,10.

### CHAPTER 39

**V. 1.** *{At that time Merodach Baladan, the son Baladan king of Babylon, sent letters, and a present to Hezekiah*} This story is recorded also, 2 Kings 20.12–19. briefly touched with some aspersion upon Ezekiah, concerning it, 2 Chr. 32.25,26,31. It is here inserted to make way; and give some light unto some ensuing prophecies, concerning the Babylonian captivity, and the deliverance from the same.

*{At that time*} Shortly after Ezekiah's recovery, 2 King. 20.7.

*{Merodach*} This was the name of one of their idols, Jer. 50.2. As it was an usual thing among God's people, to insert some of God's titles into the names of their children; so the manner of the heathen people, was to impose their idols' names on their sons, favorites, and followers. Hence *Merodach*, here, and *Evil-Merodac*, 2 King. 25.27. See Dan. 1.7. & 4.8. As also, Rom. 16.1,14,15. 1 Cor. 1.12. Phil. 2.25. 1 Thess. 1.1. His name at large is supposed to have been, *Merodac-ken-pad*, whence *Mardokempad*, in Ptolomy. So his idol, *Merodach* should be but a part of his name; as *Nebo*, another of them ch. 46.1. of his father's; or as some his grandfather's; *Nabo-nassar*; of his son's, *Nabo-pol-assar*; and of his son's son, *Nabu-chadnatsar*. For that learned man seems to be mistaken, who conceives this *Merodach*, to be *Nabopolassar*, who understanding that so many degrees the sun went back, in Ezekiah's dial, began thereupon to divide the day into hours. Nor do I find, where the author he cites, says aught of the latter; and he is expressly against the former. I might add, that this crosses the relation of the Rabbines, of *Merodac's* being accustomed to eat the third hour of the day, and then sleep to the ninth, and that on the day that the sun went thus back, he found it morning still, when he awoke. But the one seems to be as authentic as the other. He is called *Berodac*, 2 King. 20.12. whether by a slip of the scribe's pen, the letters being much alike; or by a change of the letter, in common speech, is uncertain. But so Dimon, for, Dibon, ch. 15.9. And this man's nephew, as is supposed, commonly called, *Nebuchad netsar*, is in Jeremie's prophecies, oft termed *Nebuchadretsar*, Jer. 25.1,9. & 37.1. & 39.1. Some would have *Merodac*, to be a common name to the kings of Babylon, as *Pharaoh*, anciently, to the Egyptian kings, and *Ptolomy*, in latter times; *Candace*, to the Ethiopian queens, Acts 8.27. and *Caesar*, to the Roman emperors, Act. 25.10,12. But hereof is no great probability, nor any good proof made. See on Jer. 50.2.

*{Baladan*} So called, by his father's name, then added, it may be, to the former, when he came to succeed him. The name is found mentioned, by Berosus, a very ancient writer of the Chaldean affairs, Joseph. antiquities, lib. 10. ch. 3. It is a compound name of *Bel*, or, *Bal*, one of their deities, chap. 46.1. (found also in *Bel-shatzar*, Daniel 5.1.) and *Adan*; found likewise in *Nabuzar-adan*, 2 Kings 25.8.

*{Baladan the son of Baladan*} As *Bartimeus, the son of Timeus*, (if we may compare kings and beggars, together) Marke 10.46. added here, it may be, to distinguish him from some other of that name. His father, or grandfather (*Son* put for *Nephew*, as Dan. 5.18,22. some suppose, to have been *Nabonassar*, mentioned by Ptolomy, from whose reign the chronologers use to draw their computations of those times: yet not to have been so called, until he came to the crown; but *Beladan*, or, *Balada*, by his native name before: contrary to that which is said of his son. They walk by themselves, that would make, either the father, or the son, a Mede. One of the two Baladans, some suppose to be to him, whom Ctesias, calls, *Belitanas*; whose shrine, or sepulcher, at Babylon, was in high estimation, for many after-ages.

*{king of Babylon*} Yet not so absolute a king, as may seem, but that he held, in some sort, from the king of Assyria, *that great king*, as they then termed him, ch. 36.4,13. for out of his country, the king of Assyria drew people to inhabit some part of the dispeopled land of Samaria, 2 King. 17.4. and unto his city, did the Assyrian king's captains carry king Manasses prisoner, 2 Chr. 33.11. Howbeit, about this time, the luster and power of the Assyrian being much impeached and impaired, by the defeat given to Sennacherib, the Babylonian kings growing weary of the Assyrian yoke, began to entertain thoughts of shaking it off, and making themselves more absolute, as not long after they did laying ground for a new monarchy; as large as that other, on whose ruins it was reared.

*{sent letters*} Heb. *books*; as ch. 37.13.

*{and a present*} See 2 Chr. 32.23.

*{for he had heard that he had been sick, and was recovered*} The occasion of this embassage, is, in part, here related, (*he had heard of his sickness*) to congratulate his recovery, 2 King. 20.12. He had heard also of the defeat given by miracle, to the Assyrian forces; and of the miracle granted upon Esay's prayer, for the confirming of Ezekiah's faith, concerning his recovery, 2 Kings 20.11. and in regard of the one of these two, in likelihood, of the latter, he is said also to have sent to inquire, 2 Chr. 32.31. Which yet no way favors their fancy, who would have the shadow only to have gone back on Ahaz his sun-dial, the sun holding his ordinary course still in the sky: for he sent not to inquire, whether such a thing were done or no, (which in his own country they could not but see and observe) but whether, upon such an occasion, it had been done; and at such a one's request. And for the former, the like seems to be implied; where it is recorded, that upon that defeat, presents were, from foreign princes, sent to Ezekiah, 2 Chr. 32.21,23. He sent, in likelihood, therefore, the rather, partly, out of his disaffection to the king of Assyria, of whose overthrow, and power, and repute, thereby clipped, and eclipsed, he was glad; and partly, also, out of a desire to curry favor with Ezekiah, and entertain amity with one, who appeared, hereby, to be highly in favor with so powerful a God, as could, on that wise, command, both in heaven, and on earth. That which one of his lineage, also, was enforced to confess, Dan. 4.35.

*{was recovered*} Heb. *grown strong* again.

**V. 2.** *{And Ezekiah was glad of them*} Being overmuch taken with, and somewhat puffed up with so solemn an embassage, from a prince so remote, and of no small power, with whom he had never had any commerce, or intercourse before. And there may seem to have been two special causes of this his affection; his repute and his profit. For he deemed it, a matter of no small repute and honor to him, that the report of what had befallen him, and God had done for him, should fly so far abroad, and that hereby occasion was ministered, to make his state and wealth further known, to such a potentate, as he was. And again, he might suppose, that compliance with such a one, might turn to his advantage. For the Babylonian might be induced to attempt somewhat against the Assyrian, whom he perceived that he bore no good affection unto, if he should be offering, at any time, to molest him again. Certain it is, that some smatch of elation and sinister affection was in it. See 2 Chr. 32.25,31. and see David's like infirmity, or, as himself terms it, *folly*, 2 Sam. 24.1,10. Instead of what is here said, *He was glad of them*, or *on them*, is read, 2 Kings 20.13. with change of one letter, *he heard of them*, or *on them*: which may minister suspicion of some slip of a pen, in that place; as in *Berodac*, above. See v. 1.

*{and showed them the house of his precious things, the silver, and the gold, and the spices, and the precious ointments, and all the house of his armor, and all that was found in his treasures; there was nothing in his house, nor in all his dominions, that Hezekiah showed them not*} Some of the Jewish writers say, that Ezekiah did this, not of his own accord, but at the request of the Babylonian ambassadors, who desired the sight of them. And therefore understand those words, that are read, 2 Kings 20.13. as they expound them, & ours render them, *He hearkened to them*: he condescended therein to them. This is but a mere conjecture of theirs. But howsoever, by the issue, it appears, that there was some spice of vanity, and ostentation, in it; which afterward he smarted for, 2 Chr. 32.25.

*{his precious things*} Or, *his spicery*: or, *odoriferous drugs*. The same word is found, with little difference, in letters interchangeable, Gen. 37.25. & 43.11. And it seems to be derived, from a word that signifies *to pound*, or, *beat to powder*; because such drugs and spices, are wont to be so dealt with, to make confections of them, Exod. 30.34–36. Howbeit, some of the Jewish doctors would have it a more comprehensive term, and to signify, as ours, in the text, render it, *any precious things*, of what kind soever. Which some, the rather, incline unto, because mention is made, afterward, of spices apart. But the one word, may be here used of odoriferous *drugs*, the other, of *spices*, for other uses. And so the old Latin seems to distinguish them, interpreting the former, *spices*, or *drugs*, the latter, *odors*, as the Greek, *perfumes*.

*{precious ointment*} Heb. *good oil*; as Ec. 7.1. So c. 57.9. Hos. 12.1. *Oil*, for *ointment*: because the ordinary ground of them, Exod. 30.24,25.

*{all the house*} Or, *every house*; for there might be divers of them, so ch. 1.5.

*{of his armor*} Of which see ch. 22.8. Some render it, *jewels*; and it may as well be *wardrobe*: for the word is very general. See ch. 22.24. including all *arms*, 1 Sam. 31.9. *weapons*, Jer. 21.4. *jewels*, Gen. 24.53. *garments*, Deut. 22.5. *instruments*, 1 Chr. 15.16. *vessels* chap. 52.11. *cask*, Jer. 48.11. *household stuff*, Gen. 31.37. Ezek. 12.4. of any kind whatsoever. The first, which our version gives in the text, seems most probable in this place.

*{all that was found in*} For *all that was in*: an usual Hebraism. See ch. 13.15.

*{his treasures*} Or, *treasuries*. For the word is used here, as elsewhere, for places, wherein stores, of all sorts, are stowed, 1 Chr. 26.24. & 27.25. So ver. 4.

*{there was nothing*} Of worth sufficient for the sight of such persons. Heb. *not a word*, for, *not a thing*. So Gen. 19.21. 1 Kings 10.3. Psalm 141.4. so also, v. 4.

*{in his house, nor in all his dominion*} Heb. *and*, or, *or*; (as ch. 36.19.) *in his whole dominion*. The sight whereof, when they were there, and report of what they had seen when they came home, might, in likelihood, prove a bait to the Babylonians, inciting them, in succeeding times, to attempt the gaining of so rich and flourishing a kingdom. For Babylon, in likelihood, was not in those times, so goodly, and stately a place, as afterward: Nineveh, at that time, being the *great city*, Jon. 1.2. & 3.2,3. the chief seat of the Assyrian monarchy, c. 37.37. by the ruin whereof, was Babylon raised.

**V. 3.** *{Then came Isaiah the prophet unto king Hezekiah, and said unto him; what said these men? and from whence came they unto thee*} By these questions, and that other, v. 4. the prophet not coming on his own head, but sent on God's errand, as Nathan to David, 2 Sam. 12.1. would draw from him a relation of his own inconsiderate act, and make way by his answer thereunto, to the message, which, from God he was to deliver unto him.

*{Then*} Heb. *And*; as ch. 28.4. and so ver. 4. & 5. & 8.

*{And Ezekiah said, they are come from a far country to me, even from Babylon*} So it is said of Babylon, Jer. 4.16. And Ezekiah seems the rather to mention the remoteness of the place, from whence they came, as implying, that he could, in common civility, do no less, than show all the kindness, and afford the best and amplest entertainment that might be, to those that had come so long a journey, on so kind and friendly an embassage. *Of Babylon*, Heb. *Babel*; see on ch. 13.1.

**V. 4.** *{Then said he, what have they seen in thy house? And Hezekiah answered, All that is in mine house have they seen: there is nothing among my treasures, that I have not showed them*} An ingenuous confession. See on v. 2.

*{among my treasures*} Heb. *in my treasuries*; see on v. 2.

**V. 5.** *{Then said Isaiah to Hezekiah, Hear the word of the Lord of hosts*} Hear what, for this your oversight, God now says to you: so cha. 28.14.

**V. 6.** *{Behold, the days come, that all that is in thine house, and that which thy fathers have laid up in store unto this day, shall be carried to Babylon*} A sad message, and such as might well quail and quell all the joy that Ezekiah had of this so glossing and well pleasing an embassage, fulfilled, partly, in his son Manasses his days, 2 Chr. 33.11. but principally in the days of Jehojakin, and Zedekiah, 2 Kings 24.12–16. & 25.6–21. God, thereby, showing how deeply he detests pride and vain glory, and how severely he sometime, chastises it in his own, even his dearest, and best beloved. See 2 Sam. 24.10–13. Not that this failing in Ezekiah, was the main cause of this grievous evil, here foretold; but to intimate that what he had unadvisedly done, should help to whet them on to the doing of it; and by the acquainting of him with it, to sad his soul, and give him occasion, thereby, to humble himself for his folly therein: which, accordingly also he did, 2 Chr. 32.26.

*{Behold*} I shall tell you that which you did little think of, when you showed these men all your stores. So chap. 29.14. & 37.7.

*{the days come*} Heb. *coming*; the time is a coming. So Jerem. 7.32.

*{thy fathers*} Your ancestors; the kings, your progenitors. So chap. 37.12.

*{shall be carried to Babylon*} As ch. 8.4. being seized on by the king of Babylon, & his ministers; so the Syrian threatened Ahab, 1 King. 20.5,6.

*{nothing shall be left saith the Lord*} As you concealed nothing from them. See on v. 2.

**V. 7.** *{And of thy sons that shall issue from thee, which thou shalt beget, shall they take away; and they shall be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon*} This is news yet sadder, and more heavy than the former: a man's sons are much dearer to him, than his substance, and their welfare, than his wealth: this was the worst tidings that came last to Job, Job 1.18,19. See also, 1 Sam. 8.11,13. and the prophet delivers it, in variety of terms; (as God to Abraham Gen. 21.1.) *thy sons, that shall issue from thee, and whom thou shalt beget*; the more to move affection, and to make the deeper impression.

*{whom thou shalt beget*} Either immediately, as Manasses, 2 Chr. 33.11. or mediately, as those his issue, and yours by him, of the blood royal, 2 Ch. 36.6,10,20. Dan. 1.3,4.

*{shall they take away*} That is, *shall be taken away*; the verb taken indefinitely: as ch. 8.4. Luke 12.20.

*{and they shall be*} Or, *that they may be*; to make them so: so the particle is oft used, ch. 13.2. & 19.15.

*{eunuchs*} Or, *officers*; for the word is used for either. See Gen. 37.36. ch. 56.3. Jer. 41.17.

**V. 8.** *{Then said Hezekiah to Isaiah, Good is the word of the Lord which thou hast spoken*} A pious speech of an humbled soul, acknowledging all that God wills, or does, to be just and good; & willingly, therefore, submitting himself thereunto. So 1 Samuel 3.18. 2 Sam. 15.26. Job 1.21. Ps. 39.9. & 119.75,137. Lam. 3.22. Mic. 7.9.

*{he said moreover*} Heb. *and he said*; as cha. 30.26.

*{For there shall be peace and truth in my days*} It is yet a great favor, that God has vouchsafed me, in delaying this evil, that it shall not come in my time, (as 1 Kings 21.29.) and in giving me assurance of continued peace and safety, during my life. See Chap. 28.6.

*{For there shall be*} Or, *Yet there shall be*; as ch. 9.1. or, *That there shall be*: as Job 11.6. & 23.3. to wit, *is it not good?* as it is more fully, 2 King. 20.19. See there.

*{peace and truth*} Or, *assured peace*. So Chap. 26.3. and 20.18. Jeremiah 14.13. and 33.6. Howbeit, there seems to be an allusion to the solemn form of salutation, then in use, *peace, and truth*, Est. 9.30.

### CHAPTER 40

**V. 1.** *{Comfort ye, Comfort ye my people, saith your God*} In the foregoing chapter, was an hint given of the Babylonian captivity. And by the subject matter of the ensuing prophecies, it may appear, how fitly the story, therein related, was here inserted. For the subsequent sermons are generally, most, if not all of them, concerning that their captivity, their delivery out of it, and the restitution of their state and church, in after-times; but so, that they rest not in that, but reach still further, unto the spiritual delivery of God's people, from the far more direful thraldom under sin and Satan, by the Messiah typified, the advancement of his kingdom, and enlargement thereof, by the subduing and bringing in of those nations, that had formerly been enemies thereunto. The sermon, in this chapter contained, the prophet makes entrance into, with a promulgation of God's purpose, concerning his people's deliverance; the approach thereof, he commands, for their comfort, to be published to them, by his messengers, ver. 1–5,9–11. and the undoubted certainty of the performance of it, notwithstanding all obstructions and difficulties lying in the way, is confirmed, first, from the stability of God's word, illustrated by the fickleness and frailty of all human excellency, ver. 6–8. Secondly, from the immensity of his power and essence, illustrate by the feebleness and vanity of all creatures, idols especially, ver. 12–20. and concluded with a tart check to idolaters, for their impious presumption, verse 21–26. and a gentle reproof of God's people; for their diffidence of support and deliverance, verse 27–31.

*{Comfort ye*} It is the speech of God by the prophet, directed first to the prophets, that were to live in the time of the Babylonian captivity; as did Jeremy, Ezekiel, and Daniel; and secondly, also, to those holy persons, endued with a prophetical spirit, that lived near our Savior's coming in the flesh; as Zachary, Luke 1.67. Simeon, and Anna, Luke 2.25,26. and to the apostles, likewise, and their assistants, that were to publish the glad tidings of salvation by Christ, not to the Jews only, but to the Gentiles, Acts 13.23,33,46,47. It is redoubled, to add the more emphasis to it: as verse 9. Zeph. 2.1.

*{my people*} Whom I have not utterly cast off, or forgotten; though for the present, I may seem not to regard, v. 27.

*{saith your God*} Heb. *will your God say*; and so divers interpreters, not amiss, as foretelling what charge and instructions God would give, in those times, to his ministers and messengers, for their dealings with his people.

*{your God*} Who will shortly show himself so to be, ch. 14.1. ver. 10. Rom. 3.29,30. & 10.12.

**V. 2.** *{Speak ye comfortably to Jerusalem*} Heb. *Speak to the heart of Jerusalem*; as Gen. 24.3. & Hos. 2.24. *Jerusalem*, that is, God's people, ver. 1. those that sometime dwelt there themselves, or are the issue of them; that have special relation to Jerusalem, either that below, or from above, Galat. 1.26. So verse 9. chap. 51.17.

*{cry unto her*} Publish, proclaim it; as ver. 6. So Dan. 3.4. Jon. 3.2,4.

*{that her warfare is accomplished*} The word here used, does signify, sometime, *a set term of time*, Job 14.14. Sometime, *service* in general, whether military, or other, Num. 4.23. & 8.24. sometime, *a set term of service*, Job 7.1. and so here; *the set term of her service*, or *servitude, is expired*. Heb. *fulfilled*; as Gen. 29.27. Acts 2.1. that the time, which was by God prefixed, for the continuance of her captivity and servitude, under the Chaldeans, is now at an end. See Jer. 25.12. & 27.7. Dan. 9.2. and so that the term likewise prefixed for their servitude, though of another nature, under the law, is now expired, at the bringing in of the Messiah, Gal. 4.1–4.

*{that her iniquity is pardoned*} God's wrath is pacified and appeased towards her, and he reconciled again to her, having for Christ's sake, in whom satisfaction is made for the sins of all God's people, forgiven, and forgotten all those her transgressions, that were the procuring causes of her captivity, Chapter 43.25. Jer. 31.34. Dan. 19.24. Romans 3.25,26. Hebrews 9.15,26. Hebrews *her iniquity is accepted*; or, the punishment of her iniquity: as the word is used, Gen. 4.13. an allusion to those sacrifices, or sacred rites, used for expiation of sin, which being accepted, the sin is said to be expiated, Lev. 1.4.

*{that she hath received of the Lord's hand double for all her sins*} Not that satisfaction was by any of their sufferings made unto God's justice for their sins, that nothing could do, but the blood of Christ alone, Heb. 10.4–10. much less, that they had suffered more at God's hand, than by their sins they had deserved; for they confess, that God had punished them far beneath their iniquities, Ezra 9.13. Lam. 3.22. but that she had in a large measure been chastised by God for her transgressions, endured so much to the full, as he deemed fit to be inflicted, Ps. 80.5. *double*, for, abundantly, as ch. 61.7. Jer. 16.18. & 17.18. Rev. 18.6.

**V. 6.** *{The voice of him that crieth in the wilderness*} Or, This shall be, or, Let this be *the voice of him, that crieth in the wilderness*. This shall be, or, Let this be the subject matter, that shall then be proclaimed. Yet the prophet may seem here to speak of it as if in a prophetical rapture, at present, he heard it. So ch. 13.4. & 66.6. Jer. 4.15,19,21,31. & 31.1,5.

*{of him that crieth*} Collectively, of those that are sent out to publish the return of God's people from Babylon, unto their own country again; and of those, likewise, that give warning of the Messiah his coming, of John the Baptist more especially, Mal. 4.5. Matthew 11.14. Mark 1.2,3. Luke 1.76,77. John 1.22,23.

*{in the wilderness*} The wastes that lay between Babylon and Judea; as implying the place where this cry should be made; to the people, that dwelt near at hand thereabout; and so the text runs, both in the ancient Greek version, and in the evangelists, who seem to have followed the same, Mat. 3.3. Mar. 1.3. Luke 3.4. John 1.23. which yet, as it respects the appearance of the Messiah; so it has a more special relation unto, the wilderness of Judea, where John Baptist's father lived, and wherein he began his preaching, Luke 1.39,40,80. Mat. 3.1. Mark 3.1,4. Howbeit, some, regarding the points of distinction in the Hebrew, refer this clause to the words following, and making them part of the cry, read the text in this manner.

*{In the wilderness prepare ye the way of the Lord*} It is a figurative speech, borrowed from the practice of great princes and potentates, who when they are to remove from place to place with their train and attendants; or to lead military forces into foreign parts, are wont to send their harbingers before, to survey the coasts, and with the help of pioneers going along with them, or the inhabitants of places adjacent summoned in to assist them, to clear the way from obstructions, and facilitate their passage. See on Chapter 37.24. and see the like, Chapter 62.10.

*{In the wilderness*} Because in such places, there being ordinarily no beaten roads, the ways are usually overgrown, and uneven, and the passages commonly obstructed. And it has an eye to those waste and desert places, that God's people were to pass by, in their return from Babylon, into their own country: as Chapter 41.18,19. and 43.19,20. but withal, alluding to their traveling in former time, through the wilderness, from Egypt, to Canaan, Num. 10.33.

*{Prepare ye the way*} Not that the people of the countries, by which God's people were to pass, in their return from Babylon, should be called in, to clear and fit the way for them: but that their passage home, should, by God's providence, and his good hand upon them, be made as easy and expeditious for them, as if such a thing had been done. See Cyrus his proclamation, how well it suits herewith, Ezra 1.3,4. and the effect of it there, ver. 5,6. See also, Ezra 7.7–28. & 8.21–3,31,32. Spiritually, the way is prepared for Christ's coming, by ridding men's hearts of those mystical thorns and thickets, briers and brambles, of evil concupiscence and corruptions, wherewith they are either by inbred vitiosity, or by practice and custom of sin, wholly overgrown, Jer. 4.4. Hos. 10.12. Heb. 6.8. that which in a special manner was performed by the ministry of John, Mal. 4.5,6. Mat. 3.1,2,7–12. Mark 1.4.

*{of the Lord*} By which God's people may pass under his conduct, as formerly, to the land of Canaan, Exod. 13.21,22. Num. 9.17–23. Ps. 68.7. ch. 58.8.

*{make straight in the desert a highway for our God*} The same thing in other forms repeated.

*{make straight*} Or, *even*, or both; make it straight, and lay it level, that they may not be compelled to fetch tedious compasses about, and wind to and fro, to avoid the unevenness of the way. See ch. 26.7.

*{a highway*} Or, *causeway*, a way cast up for the more convenient passage. See ch. 35.8.

**V. 4.** *{Every valley shall be exalted, and every mountain and hill shall be laid low; and the crooked shall be made straight, and the rough places plain*} Luk. 3.5. The way shall be made even and easy, for their more convenient and commodious passage, all impediments & obstructions being remedied and removed, ch. 41.15,16. & 42.16. & 45.11. Zach. 3.7. The words may be read, as spoken by way of injunction, that so they may run in one tenor with the former, ver. 3. *Let every valley be raised, and every mountain and hill taken down*, or *laid low*, made even and level with the other, as much added to the one, as is taken from the other, that there may be an equality; as 2 Cor. 8.14. (because hill and dale make the passage more troublesome and tedious) *and let the crooked way*, or place, *be made a straight one, and the rough places plain*. Howbeit, what God wills to be done here, he says, he himself will do, that is, cause to be done, Chapter 42.16.

*{the crooked*} To wit, place, way or passage: a defect of the subject: as ch. 34.4. Ezek. 13.15. the word may signify *perverse*, as we render it, Jer. 17.9. or *crooked*, as our version has it; and as another word, in a parallel place, ch. 42.16. and so both the Greek, and the evangelist, Luke 3.5. Yet the word, in its native notion, signifies a *supplanting* place, or passage (for so the verb it comes of, is constantly found used, Gen. 27.36. Hos. 12.3. Jer. 9.3.) such a way, as men are subject to trip and stumble in, as rough and stony ways commonly are; see ch. 62.10.

*{straight*} Heb. *straightness*; Psalm 45.6. or *evenness*, as Psalm 26.12. for the word most commonly signifies a *plan*, Deut. 3.10. & 4.43. Josh. 13.9,16,17. the abstract for the concrete, or a defect of the regent: *straightness*, or *evenness*, for a place of *straightness*, or *evenness*, that is, a *straight*, or *even* place, a *plan*: so also, chap. 42.16. Zach. 3.7.

*{rough places*} A defect of the subject, as before: the word here used, comes from a verb, which, as most think, signifies *to lift up*, Exod. 28.28. & 39.21. where alone it is in Scripture found: whence a noun commonly rendered *elation*, or *pride*, Psal. 31.20. and another used by the Jewish doctors, for a *stone*, or *pebble*, that lying higher than the ground, or path, makes the way rough and uneven; and the Jewish doctors therefore expound the word here, of places rough or rugged with hillocks, clods, stones, or other eminences, that make it uneven and troublesome to travelers. Only one of them would have the verb in Moses signify, *to join*, or *bind* together, and the substantive, in the Psalm, *a combination*, and the adjective, *hills joined* one to another. But the former, as the more received, so seems the more probable.

*{plain*} Or, *a plain*, as we use the word substantively: for the word signifies properly, *a vale*, or *a plain*, Genesis 11.2. Deuteronomy 11.11. Chapter 41.18. & 63.14. this clause may well be the same, in effect, with the branch next before-going: the sum of all is, that all impediments and encumbrances, great or small, should be removed.

**V. 5.** *{And the glory of the Lord shall be revealed, and all flesh shall see it together*} Or, *That the glory of the Lord may be revealed, and all flesh may together see it*. So some, as rendering a reason, why all this preparation is required, that the Lord may generally be seen coming in pomp and state. But the clause annexed, confirms the received version. The meaning is, that God's power manifested in the deliverance, reduction, and restitution of his people, shall be so conspicuous, that not they alone themselves; but others also of all sorts, shall see it, and take notice of it, Psal. 126.2. A typical resemblance of God's majesty, and glory manifested in Christ, for the salvation of all his, Joh. 1.14. See Psal. 97.6. ch. 33.13. & 66.18.

*{all flesh*} That is, all the elect, say some, as *all flesh*, for the whole Jewish nation, Jer. 45.5. but the word seems more general; and to import all nations, as well Gentiles, as Jews as Joel 2.28.

*{see it*} A defect of the pronoun; as Jer. 17.6. and so in the next clause.

*{for the mouth of the Lord hath spoken it*} And it shall certainly therefore be effected, how improbable, or impossible soever, it may seem in man's sight. So Chapter 1.20. and 58.14.

**V. 6.** *{The voice said, cry.*} Heb. *A voice saying*. which some render in the future, *A voice shall say*, which they understand of a voice of Christ, speaking to his apostles, and suggesting unto them what they should preach. Others, in the present: *There is a voice, that saith*, which yet they expound, as spoken prophetically of the time to come. But we need not decline the received version; the prophet relating a charge, that God had by an inward voice, in vision given him. Howbeit, I shall rather render it, *A voice*, than *The voice*, partly, because there is no article in the text; and partly, to distinguish it from the voice before-mentioned, ver. 3. See the like, Rev. 14.13.

*{And he said, what shall I cry?*} He, that is, the party unto whom the voice came, and that charge was thereby given, demanding what it might be, that he was to proclaim: the prophet Esay himself, as I conceive it: for the prophets' manner is to speak in the third person, of themselves. So chap. 2.1. Howbeit, the conceit of that Jew is most frivolous, who supposes the prophet, as repenting him of his over-forwardness in offering to be sent, before he knew what his errand would be, chap. 6.8. was now grown more wary; and would first know what it was, that he was thus to publish. But this vain conceit of so unsuitable a disposition to so heroical a spirit, as this our prophet was endowed with, I should not mention, but that I find it, to have taken with some great ones.

*{All flesh is grass, and all the goodliness thereof is as the flower of the field*} The subject matter of that which he was to proclaim: which to make the text, therefore, the more clear and entire, some insert, *And he*, or *it* (to wit, the voice) *said, Cry*. The like supplies, see Neh. 13.25. Job 8.18. Psal. 27.8. But the question is, to what end, or upon what occasion this sermon of man's frailty, is here enjoined to be made. Some would have it done, for the fitting of men to receive Christ, and the doctrine of salvation, by Christ. And, indeed, the serious consideration of man's own infirmity and impotency, notwithstanding all his natural endowments and excellencies, to save himself, or to afford aught that may conduce thereunto, is a special means to induce, yea, enforce him, to go out of himself, and to make him willing to seek for salvation by Christ. But the scope of God, by the prophet, in this place, seems rather to arm and confirm the hearts and minds of God's people against such doubts and distrustful thoughts as might arise within them, or be suggested to them, in the time of their captivity, concerning the impossibility of the foregoing promise, of the releasement & restitution, especially, considering the great power of the Babylonians, under whom they were captives: which to remove and blow away, the prophet is willed to proclaim, that not the Babylonians alone, but all the men in the world, were they put all together into a body, were but grass, and all their might and excellency, no other, than as some goodly and beautiful, to look upon, Mat. 6.28,29. but tender and fading flower, that cannot endure so much as the least puff of wind; such as God is able, with a word of his mouth, to defeat and destroy, yea, with the least blast of his breath, to disperse and blow clean away. And so it has reference to the close of the foregoing discourse; *for the mouth of the Lord hath spoken it*, ver. 5. that which also it returns unto, in the end of this passage, as being the main end intended in it; *but the word of our God shall stand for ever*, v. 8.

*{All flesh is grass*} So Ps. 37.2. & 90.5,6. & 92.7. & 103.15. ch. 37.27. 1 Pet. 1.24.

*{flesh*} Man, or mankind, Gen. 6.12,13. so verse 5. But in the word here, is an intimation of man's infirmity and frailty; as Gen. 6.3. Ps. 78.39. ch. 31.3. Jer. 17.5. and so it is used of Christ, Rom. 8.3. Heb. 5.7.

*{is grass*} That is, is like grass, is as grass; as in the next branch, is as a flower: a defect of the note of similitude; as Chapter 28.1. and 33.4,11. but it is that, that makes the sentence more emphatical; as if he should say, he is not like grass only, he is no other than grass, with God especially. So, not like vanity only, Psalm 144.3. but vanity itself, Psal. 39.5. & & 63.9. not *as a wind*, but *a wind that passeth away, and returneth not*, Psalm 79.39. See the like, Job 7.7. and 8.9,14. So verse 7.

*{and all the goodliness thereof*} The Hebrew word properly signifies, *benignity, bounty*, or *goodness*, Proverbs 20.6. and because that is a thing, that usually makes men desirable, and to be had in estimation and repute, Prov. 19.20. hence it comes to pass, that the same word is used for *grace*, or *gracefulness*, or *glory*, as it is here rendered in the ancient Greek, and by the apostle, 1 Pet. 1.24. See Exod. 33.19,22. where the one is deemed to be expounded by the other; and there appears, therefore, no necessity of altering the text, as some would do. The word seems to import, whatsoever natural endowments, may make men to be had in admiration, or estimation, with others, as persons of eminency, and ability to effect great matters. And one of the great Jewish masters observes it, to be ordinarily used for *any excellency*, or *eminency*, either in good, or in evil. See Psal. 16.3. See also of man's vanity, ch. 2.22. Those, that pressing the propriety of the word, understand it to be meant of *piety*, or *moral goodness*, I conceive to go beside the intendment of the prophet, in this place: as well as the Jewish commenters, who expound it of the Gentiles, the enemies of God's people especially, all whose goodness, say they, is but sin; (not unlike that, Rom. 14.23.) or, if they had done any good, yet it perished, & was not regarded, in regard of the wrongs that they did to God's people, Ezek. 18.24. or the good that they intended, or do to any, dies with them, when they die. Ps. 146.4.

*{as the flower of the field*} Or, *as a flower of the field*: as any one of them, the tenderest, and of least continuance or vigor so Job 14.2. Ps. 103.15.

*{The grass withereth*} Psalm 37.2. and 90.6. and 102.4. Chapter 15.6.

*{The flower fadeth*} Chap. 28.1,4. James 1.10. and so does man and all his excellency, together with him, Ps. 49.17. & 73.19,20. & 146.4.

*{because the Spirit of the Lord bloweth upon it*} Or, *when the breath of the Lord bloweth upon it*: The flower fades, if but the wind blow upon it, Psalm 103.16. James 1.11. called *God's breath*, Psalm 147.18. whence some of the ancients do so understand that, Gen. 1.2. man, and his excellency, is all likewise blasted, if God do but blow upon it, ver. 24. Hab. 1.9. who, as with a word, with a breath, he made and created all things at first, Gen. 1.2. and 2.7. Psalm 33.6. and when they are ruined, can raise and renew them again, Ps. 104.30. so with a bare blast of his breath, he can much more dissipate, & blow clean away, both the creature itself, and whatsoever might or power it is able to make, Job 34.14,15. Ps. 104.29. Dan. 2.34,35. Zach. 4.6,7. Some expound it of the Spirit of God, discovering the vanity of all human excellency. But that seems not so much intended in this place.

*{surely the people is grass*} Or, *surely all people*, (as *all flesh*, before, v. 6. supplied, as 1 Sam. 30.8. & chap. 30.17. and as the like, chap. 58.13.) *are grass*. And the Babylonians therefore and your mightiest adversaries whosoever. So Ps. 39.5. *surely every man*, or *all men, in his best*, or *surest*, his most settled estate, is *all*, or altogether *vanity* see ver. 6. Some restrain it to God's people; as if the meaning were, that even in them, by nature there is no preeminence above others: but if they have any, it is of God's free grace only, Rom. 3.9. but this seems to narrow the text overmuch, and to be beside the scope of the prophet.

**V. 8.** *{The grass withereth, the flower fadeth; but the word of our God shall stand for ever*} This some understand of the Jewish people: that, howsoever through human frailty and mortality, many of them might die, during the time of the captivity, and so perishing, not partake in the promised delivery; yet God's promise, should be fulfilled, and remain firm to the residue, Rom. 3.3. & 9.6. & 11.1,5. But the meaning, rather, seems to be, that men being but frail and infirm creatures, their plots and projects might miscarry, and their attempts and designs be frustrate; but God's word and purpose, in whatsoever he spoke or promised, should be sure to stand firm, and take place, maugre all the oppositions that man might make against it, Ps. 33.10,11. & 119.89,91. ch. 14.26,27. & 55.10,11. Dan. 4.35. Mat. 5.18. Mar. 13.31. The apostle Peter applies it to the work of regeneration, wrought in the soul by the ministry of the word, 1 Pet. 1.23,24,25. So John 8.51. 2 John 2.

*{stand*} Firm. See chap. 7.7.

**V. 9.** *{O Zion, that bringest good tidings, get thee up into the high mountain*} Or, *O thou that bringest*, or *tellest good tidings to Zion, get thee up into an high mountain*. The former reading some of the Jewish commenters follow; and the most of ours understanding the text; they of Jerusalem, as being the head-city, from whence these good tidings were to be divulged unto the whole country, round about: ours, also, of the glad tidings of salvation by Christ, from thence to be published unto other people abroad, Chap. 2.3. Luk. 24.47. Rom. 10.18. But they consider not that the message, or tidings, concerning the dissolution of the Jewish captivity by Cyrus, at Babylon, was not to come abroad from Jerusalem, but to be carried from Babylon thither. The latter reading, after the Chaldee paraphrast, some of the Jewish doctors, and after the old Greek and Latin, some of ours also admit and approve. And according to it, those are called upon, that were by public authority to be employed about the divulging of the edict made by Cyrus, for the freedom of God's people from their long and tedious captivity, and the liberty granted them for return into their own country, as 2 Chron. 36.22,23. Ezra 1.1,2. or any other that were to go upon the like errand, to get up into places of eminency, from whence they might best be heard, to acquaint as many, as might be, with this comfortable news. So chap. 52.7. Nah. 1.15.

*{Zion*} The same here with Jerusalem; as chapter 1.27. and 37.32.

*{that bringest good tidings*} The word, here used, is in a feminine form. That which seems to have misled many, in applying it to Sion; because the names of cities are, in Hebrew, feminine. But the feminine form is used, in Scripture, sometime with a masculine notion; Eccl. 1.1,12. *The Preacher* (a feminine form) *the son of David, king of Jerusalem*: and this very word, Psalm 68.11. *The Lord gave the word, and great was the company* (not of women-preachers, though the form be feminine, but) *of those that published it*. And so the Greek, in the masculine, renders it here. For the reason of the phrase; there is a twofold figure in it; a threefold, I might say: there is, first, an *ellipsis*, or a defect of the subject: as, *standing* for, *standing corn*, Chap. 17.5. *fading*, for, *a fading plant*, ch. 28.4. And the word wanting, to be supplied, is a feminine, to wit, *nephesh*; howbeit, not simply, as it signifies, *a soul*; but as by a *synecdoche*, or comprehensive form of speech, it is put, and that very frequently, for *a person*, Gen. 12.5. & 14.21. & 46.26. Rom. 13.1. 1 Pet. 3.20. This supplied, there will appear to be a *periphrasis*, or a circumlocution in it, as *a preaching person*, for, a *preacher*: so *a publishing*, or, *reporting* party, or person; for, *a publisher*, or, *reporter*. The word *good*, is not in the text, nor, necessarily, implied in the word; though it be in that which the Greek here uses; for the word signifies simply and indefinitely, to *report*, or, *publish* aught, without any special notion of good or evil, 2 Sam. 18.19,20. Yea, it is used of one that brought very bad tidings of the loss of the ark, 1 Sam. 4.17. Howbeit, because it is more frequently used of gladsome messages, 1 Sam. 31.9. 1 King. 1.42. Jer. 20.21. And it must of necessity be so rendered, 2 Sam. 4.10. the reading may well be here retained; though, *thou that bringest tidings*, were sufficient: the subject matter of the message, being not, in the present passage, expressed; as it is, chap. 52.7. The word here is singular as there also, but taken collectively; and so comes home to that in the Psalm.

*{get thee up*} Heb. *ascend thee*. A redundant elegancy, yet having some emphasis in it; as Gen. 12.1.

*{into the high mountain*} Or, *into an high mountain*. Alluding as some, to the situation of Sion, ch. 2.2. & 14.13. But that was formerly rejected. Others therefore conceive, that there is a respect had to their sentinels that were seated, commonly, (as our beacons) on the top of some high hill, which such as brought tidings of public concernment, were wont to repair unto; and there having by some sign, set up, called people together, to publish to them what news they brought, or message they came with. So chap. 42.11. & 52.7. Apparent it is, that men use to get up into some eminent place, that desire to be heard of many, Deut. 27.12,13. Judg. 9.7. 1 Samuel 26.13,14. Jerem. 20.22. so did our Savior, Matth. 5.1.

*{O Jerusalem, that bringest good tidings,}* Or, *O thou that bringest good tidings to Jerusalem*, as before.

*{lift up thy voice with strength*} Or, *strongly*, Psal. 29.4. 1 Chron. 25.5. Jon. 3.5. Cry with all your might, as loud as you can, that as many as may be, may hear you, having a double advantage from the height of the place, from whence you speak, and from the shrillness of your voice: so ch. 58.1.

*{lift it up*} A reduplication emphatical; as ver. 1. and a defect of the pronoun: as ver. 5.

*{be not afraid*} Make no scruple or doubt of publishing it, though the tidings you bring may seem never so unlikely to be credited; for it is certainly true, and shall be undoubtedly made good, chapter 35.4.

*{Say unto the cities of Judah,}* The sometime inhabitants of them (as Jer. 11.12.) though, at present, driven from them, and dispersed here and there: but to the cities, the rather, because they were to be repaired, and re-edified, upon their return to them. See ch. 44.28.

*{Behold your God*} Your God with whom the heathen have so oft, and so long twitted you, during this time of your captivity, as unable to relieve you, Deut. 32.37,38. Psal. 42.3. & 115.2. Ezek. 36.20. and of whom yourselves have had some doubtful thoughts, as if he did not regard you, but had clean forgotten you, ver. 27. chap. 49.14. is now at hand, ready to show forth himself, to their conviction, and your comfort, Deut. 32.39. So chap. 12.2. & 25.9. & 41.27. & 52.6. As it has reference to the Messiah, Behold he that was so long before promised, and has so long been expected, is now, at length, exhibited, Hag. 2.7. Zach. 9.9. Mal. 3.1. Luk. 2.15,30. Act. 13.32,33. or, as some, behold that Jesus, whom you denied, and crucified, but is risen again from the dead, received into heaven, and set there at the right hand of the Father, the same is your God, Act. 2.23,32–36. & 2.14,15,20,21. But the former seems to sort better with the type here first intended.

**V. 10.** *{Behold*} As ch. 35.4. & 62.11. Zach. 9.9.

*{the Lord God will come with strong hand*} As chap. 8.8. Exod. 13.3. Ezek. 20.33,34. and so there should be such a defect of the subject as before, ver. 9. and so most of the Jewish commenters on the place take it. Howbeit, because the word here is masculine, whereas the word for *an hand*, in Hebrew is feminine; (howsoever one of them would salve that incongruity, by a place, Ezek. 2.9. where a masculine relative has reference to it) the text is by one, (that herein dissents from the rest, whom some of ours also follow) read; *The Lord God will come against the mighty*, or *strong* one; that is, taking the word collectively; as the like, Jer. 9.23. Amos 2.14. against the mightiest, and most powerful enemies of his people, whether temporal, as the Babylonian, or spiritual, as Satan; so is the particle used, Exod. 14.25. and 20.15. Num. 12.1. See chap. 49.24,25. Luk. 11.21,22. Col. 1.13. Heb. 2.14. 1 John 3.8. But a late writer supposing the particle to be here redundant, as elsewhere, reads the words, *The Lord will come strong*. See on ch. 26.4.

*{and his arm shall rule for him*} Or, *his arm shall rule over him*; that is, prevail against him; to wit, *the mighty* one before-mentioned; his power, Chap. 51.5. & 53.1. of itself sufficient fully to effect his own work and will, Psal. 115.3. & 135.6. chap. 59.16. shall overcome and oversway all opposition, chap. 41.2. & 59.16. Rev. 6.2. I suppose the term *lo*, that is, *him*, or *to him*, may well be here an elegant redundancy, as oft it is, Exod. 18.27. *he went to him*. See ch. 59.16. and before ver. 9.

*{his reward is with him*} So chap. 62.11. he comes with a recompense of mercy and bounty, unto all those that have faithfully adhered unto him, constantly depended upon him, and patiently expected his appearance; for their delivery from their forepassed thraldom, Psal. 9.18. & 58.11. chap. 28.16. & 30.18. & 61.7. Jer. 31.16. and of wrath and fury unto those, that have been the afflicters and oppressors of them, chap. 35.4. & 59.18. & 66.15. Psal. 31.23. The apostle has the like of Christ's coming to judgment at the last day, Rev. 22.12.

*{his reward*} This some refer to the rewarder, the Lord, called his, because to be given or rendered by him, Ps. 62.12. Rom. 2.6. Others, to the rewarded, *the mighty*, or, *strong*, before spoken of, as called *his*, or *their* reward; because to be received by him, or them, Ps. 28.4. But the parallel place to this, ch. 62.11. not admitting this latter, carries it strongly for the former.

*{with him*} He comes furnished with rewards of either kind, to be presently rendered without further delay, Mal. 3.17,18. & 4.1,2. Howbeit, I suppose that over-nice, that one of the Jewish doctors has, who expounds this passage of God's freeness in working for his people, that he is not like other shepherds (for a shepherd he is compared to ver. 11.) that keeps sheep for hire, Hos. 12.12. Zach. 11.12. but he feeds his freely, *his hire is all with himself*, he brings it with him, he demands nothing from them, Chapter 43. ver. 25.

*{and his work before him*} This some refer to the mighty ones, as before; whose wicked works for which God will recompense them with wrath, are said to be, in God's sight, known to him, and observed by him, whatsoever they may surmise to the contrary, Psal. 94.5–11. Chap. 66.18. Others, to the persons to be rewarded in general; but by *work*, understanding recompense for *work*, as Chap. 49.4. & 65.7. Psal. 28.4. Jer. 25.14. and so this passage should be the same with the former. But others, lastly, refer it unto God himself; *his work*, that is, the work he comes to effect for the deliverance of his, *is before him*, it lies open to him, ready to be accomplished by him, there lying nothing in his way, that may any way impeach his free passage to it, or progress in it. See the like phrase, Gen. 13.9. & 47.6. Ps. 5.8.

**V. 11.** *{He shall feed his flock like a shepherd*} The office that God in Scripture does usually make choice of, whereby to decipher his sedulous and tender care of the good and welfare of his people, Ps. 23.1. & 77.20. & 78.52. & 80.1. applied in more special manner to the Messiah, Ezek. 34.23. and owned by him, under the title of the *good shepherd*, Joh. 10.11,14. called also the *great shepherd*, Heb. 13.20. and the *chief shepherd*, 1 Pet. 5.4.

*{he shall*} Or, *will*; as before, *will come*: and so after, *will gather, will lead*.

*{feed*} Under the term of *feeding*, (being of large extent) is comprised all necessary attendance and accommodations, conducing to the safety and welfare of a flock; as provision of pasture, protection against rapine, preventing of straying, cure of such maladies, relief of such infirmities as sheep are wont to be subject unto, and the like. See Psalm 23.1–4. Ezek. 34.3,4,11–16.

*{his flock*} His people, Ps. 100.3. Ezek. 34.31.

*{he shall gather the lambs with his arm*} Or, as some, *into*, or *in his arm*; that is, *bring them together*, and *take them up in his arm*: a concise speech, such as ch. 38.17,21. Jer. 13.6. & 36.21. and, *arm*, for *arms*; as Ps. 10.5. he will have a special care of dealing charily with weak and feeble ones, supporting their infirmity. So Chap. 42.3. Matthew 11.28.

*{and carry them in his bosom*} Or, *lap*: as chap. 49.22. when they are wearied with traveling: a defect of the pronoun; as chap. 30.2.

*{and shall gently lead those that are with young*} So some of the Jewish critics take the word here used, as signifying such as have been covered by the male, from a word, used, Gen. 31.12. Some other of them, *that give suck*, 1 Sam. 6.7,10. Psalm 78.71. because hence the word signifying *a sucking-child*, Chap. 49.15. & 65.20. the same is found used, and likewise diversely rendered: as 1 Sam. 6.7,10. Psalm 78.71. So Gen. 33.13. where, see Jacob, how chary of over-driving such; and as chary a hand would God cause to be had, in bringing his people home to their own country, fitted with all convenient accommodations, for their safety by the way, Chapter 60.4,9. and 66.20. Ezra 1.6. See how chary, also, Christ was of over-charging his novices with aught, that they could not yet well brook, Mat. 9.14,17. Joh. 16.12. and Paul therein imitating him, 1 Cor. 3.1,2.

**V. 12.** *{Who hath measured the waters in the hollow of his hand?*} Because it might be suggested, or supposed, that though no power of man were able to hinder God from working so strange, unexpected, and as little believed a work, for the delivery of his people; yet their gods might be able to cross him, in that his intending design; the prophet invites them to the serious consideration of God's infinite and inconceivable power and essence, such as neither any counterfeit deity is able to imitate, nor any creature's skill is able to express. See the like, Proverbs 30.4.

*{who hath measured the waters in the hollow of his hand?*} Or, *who can measure the waters* (that is, the sea, Gen. 1.10.) *in his fist?* the word is used for a *handful*, 1 Kings 20.10. Ezek. 1.3.19. and the indicative is oft used potentially, in Hebrew. See Num. 23.8,10. Jer. 2.23,32. Dan. 3.15. with 17. *who can?* he, and he only, *in whose hand are the depths of the earth*, which together with the water, make but one globe, Ps. 95.4. and *in whose fist*, the whole air, that environs either, is enclosed, as Agur, Prov. 30.4.

*{and meted out heaven with a span*} Or, *or* (as ver. 13.) *can* (as before) *mete out heaven with his span?* a defect of the pronoun; as Job 39.21. the word is used, 1 Sam. 17.4. Ezek. 43.13. It is a borrowed speech, taken from builders and carpenters, that use to mete out their work, sometime by rule, and sometime, also by hand, ch. 44.13. See ch. 48.12.

*{and comprehendeth the dust of the earth in a measure?*} Or, *or can comprehend* (as before) *the dust of the earth* (that is, the main body of it, as cha. 26.19. Dan. 12.2.) *in a measure*, or in *a tierce*; as the Hebrew word intimates, derived from a term, that signifies *three*, for notation correspondent to the Latin *triental*: it seems by the use of it, Ps. 80.5. to have been a drinking, or quaffing cup, as well as a measure; of what capacity it was, our Jewish masters tell us not: some of them say, it was a great measure, and cite the Psalmist, not improbably, to that purpose, so termed, because it contained as much as three lesser. Other of them say otherwise, that it was no great measure; but it was so termed, because it contained a third part, only, of a greater vessel, or cask: and the one sort, therefore, would have it, there, to comprehend the three captivities, Jehojakim's, Jehojacin's, and Zedekiah's; the other, to resemble their abode in Babylon, as but a third part of their sojourning in Egypt. Thus they leave us in mere uncertainties. I suppose it to have been used for a cup, with the former, of capacity more than ordinary; and by the notation of it, *a cup of three*, as containing so much, as might well make three draughts or so much as three of those cups, that they were ordinarily wont to drink at one draught: but for a measure, or vessel, to mete out materials, whether liquid, or solid with; to have been among those that were reckoned of the least ordinary size; that might well be deemed a sorry measure to deliver earth out by, or other like trash, yea, or matter of more worth, that yet might be reputed of a deep and large size, either to offer a man to drink of, or to enforce him to take down, when the liquor is very unpleasant, and such as he likes not: it must here, of necessity, to import no such great vessel, that it may, with some proportion, answer the *fist*, and the *span*. Nor can I, therefore, so easily accord with that learned man, who would have it to signify the third part of an Epha, as the *Seah* is said to do; (see Chap. 27.8.) because by a word near unto it, that measure is in the Ethiopic language expressed, Mat. 13.33. The old Latin renders it, *with three fingers*: which would suit well with the former, if there were any good for it; but none appears.

*{and weighed the mountains in scales, and the hills in a balance*} Or, *and weigh out the mountains by a beam, and the hills in scales*, or *in a balance?* there are two words here used, which, say our Jewish masters, signify two sorts of engines, or instruments, used for the weighing out of commodities, or wares, the one for greater quantities, the other for less: but that is somewhat too general. And I suppose they have no other ground for it, save because the *mountains* are said to pass the one, and the *hills* the other. They are both found together, Prov. 16.11. Where the words are rendered, *a just weight and balance*, but would rather be *a just beam, and balance*: the former word, save in those two places, nowhere else found, is, by some of them, said to signify (and that not improbably,) such *a beam*, as is used to weigh commodities, by hanging of a stone, or other weight at the one end, and the material that is to be weighed, at the other, it being marked with certain notches, or figures, whereby the certain stint of the weight may be discerned, such, I am told, that they use oft with us, to weigh hay in the field: the latter word more common, and used after again, verse 15. seems to answer the Latin *bilanx*; whence our *balance*, and is so termed, from the two *scales*, hanging at either end, which from the similitude of them, the Latins call *dishes*, the Hebrews, *ears*. The meaning is, that God can as easily lift up the highest and greatest mountains that are, yea, all of them together, great or small, as a man can do any ordinary weight, at a beam, or in a scale.

**V. 13.** *{Who hath directed the Spirit of the Lord; or being his counselor hath taught him?*} Or, *who directed the Spirit of the Lord: or taught him?* As there is none that can do aught of the things before mentioned: so was there none assistant to him by way of aid or advice, in the creating and constitution of these creatures at the first, nor needs he any such help or direction, for the contrivance or execution of aught that he determined to do.

*{directeth the Spirit of the Lord*} The word signifies, sometime, *to mete out*, as ver. 12. sometime, *to direct*, or carry a thing evenly, as men's works are, when they are cut out by rule, and squared by line and level.
