But the verse seems to consist of two propositions, joined; though much to the same, in effect, with a discretive; the name of Jacob, annexed, to the one, of Israel, to the other, but both signifying the same people: as verse 1. chapter 44.1.

**V. 23.** *{Thou hast not brought me the small cattle of thy burnt offerings, neither hast thou honored me with thy sacrifices:*} You have not offered them to me, but to strange gods, to idols, which you chose, rather than me, and preferred before me, Deuteronomy 32.17. Judges 2.12,13. and 5.8. and 10.6,13,14. Psalm 106.35–39. Jer. 2.11,13,28. Amos 5.25,26. or, as some other, you have offered them, indeed, as to me, but so, as no way pleasing to me, because without true piety, or sincere repentance: See chapter 1.11–15. But this seems here, not so natural.

*{the small cattle of thy burnt offerings*} Or, *thy burnt offerings of small cattle*, that is, *kids*, or *lambs*, as Exodus 12.5. Of the phrase, see chapter 2.25.

*{burnt offerings, and sacrifices*} See chapter 1.11.

*{I have not caused thee to serve with an offering, nor wearied thee with incense*} I have not exacted of you such abundance of these kind of oblations, that you should deem it to be such a burden to you, or to make you weary of me and my service; and so it has reference to that, verse 22. or, it is not I, but your idols, that have been at so much cost with you, and have made you a slave to them, tiring you out with such services, as they have from time to time exacted from you: See chapter 57.5,10. Jer. 3.24. and this I take to be the genuine sense of the place. Though most interpreters go another way, to wit, that these things God had not required of them, being performed by them in such manner, and for such ends as they did them. See chapter 5.11,12,13. of *offering*, or *oblation*, and *incense*, see also there. Some of the Jewish commenters refer all this to the time of the captivity, wherein the Temple being destroyed, the only place where they might sacrifice, Deut. 12.13,14. these were neither done by them, nor required of them. Others, restrain them to Achaz his time, 2 Chr. 28.24. but the one seems impertinent, the other too narrow.

**V. 24.** *{Thou hast bought me no sweet cane with money; neither hast thou filled me with the fat of thy sacrifices:*} This goes on in the selfsame notion with the former, verse 22,23.

*{sweet cane*} Heb. *cane*, or *canel*, as it is usually termed (for *sweet* is not in the text) or, *calamus*, as it is rendered, Ezek. 27.19. but, *sweet cane*, as here, so Jer. 6.20. either for the composition of the sweet ointment, Exodus 30.34. or, for the incense, Exodus 30.7. there is an elegant consonancy in the original, between *buy*, and *cane*, which our English cannot express.

*{money*} Heb. *Silver*: as chapter 55.1.

*{filled me*} Heb. *made me drunk*, or, *made me drink*; or *moistened me abundantly*: for the word does not only signify, *to be drunk*, or *make drunk* (if at least, it do at all so signify, which to me does not yet appear, nor can I light on any place that does necessarily evince it) but sometime *to bedew*, as chapter 16.9. or, *to bathe*, as chapter 34.5. or, *to soak*, chapter 54.7. Jer. 46.10. or, *to water plentifully*, Psalm 65.10. chapter 55.10. whence it is applied to beneficence, Prov. 11.25. and so it may have reference to God's altar, that was patiently bedewed with the blood, and the fat of the beasts that were sacrificed thereon, Lev. 3.13–17. sometime, *to drink largely*, or, *liberally*; or, *to full satisfaction*; and the word that is commonly used for *drunkenness*, does sometime import the like; as, of Joseph's brethren, Genesis 43.34. for it is not to be thought, that they would so far forth forget themselves, as to be drunk in his presence; and the Greek word, in like manner, that answers thereunto, John 2.10. also, 1 Cor. 11.21. for it is scarce imaginable, that any of them were so extremely profane, as to be drunk openly in the congregation at such times, nor does the opposite member of hunger intimate any more: And by consequence also, the word here used, does signify, *to take one's fill of aught*, or, *to take large or full satisfaction, or delight, in aught*, Proverbs 5.19. and 7.18. Psalm 36.8. where the term of *watering*, is not so suitable: and in the active form, *to satiate, refresh*, or *cause to drink*, or *feed liberally*, even to full contentment, Jer. 13.14,15. or, to make one drink, or take in largely of that, which yet they take little delight or contentment in, Lam. 3.15. Thus, here, respecting God, it implies a large or liberal expense in sacrifice, for the supply of his service at the altar, which is called his Table; as the sacrifices offered on it, his meat, Ezek. 41.22. Mal. 1.7,12. Yet withal, not without some hint of that gross conceit, which some heathen had, that their gods fed on the steam that ascended from their sacrifices, which some among the Jews might have, also, some taint of. See Deut. 32.38. Psalm 50.13.

*{but thou hast made me to serve with thy sins; thou hast wearied me with thine iniquities*} Hitherto he had minded them of their failings, in performance of duty; he now tells them of their faults. They had not only neglected him, as weary of his service, which they esteemed of no better, than as some slavish condition, verse 22,23. but had also so vexed and grieved him with their sins, that his bearing with them, and enduring of them, was as grievous and burdensome to him, as an hard service, under some harsh and rigorous master, chapter 7.13. and 63.10. Jer. 44.22. Ezek. 6.9. Amos 1.13. And this latter, especially, was it, that he took to heart. To which purpose it is, that God says elsewhere, that he did not so much command the former, Jer. 7.22. or, complain of the want thereof, Psalm 50.8. as well because he regarded not so much their failings in the one, as in the other: and again, because they were sometime free, and forward enough in the one, when they were wholly regardless of the other, Mic. 6.6–8. All this, to show, that the deliverance of them from their thraldom, was of his own free favor and mercy; not from any matter of merit, or desert, on their part, verse 25.

**V. 25.** *{I, even I, am he, that blotteth out thy transgressions,*} Or, *I, even I*, (a passionate and emphatical expression, as Gen. 6.16. verse 11.) *do blot out*; (Heb. *he blotting out*, or, *am blotting out*; the pronoun, for the verb substantive: as verse 13. for there is no article prefixed before the participle,) and there is in the term of *blotting out*, a metaphor taken from the blotting of some thing out of a book, as Exodus 32.32,33. and more especially, of a debt out of a debt book, Col. 2.14. and our *sins* are as *debts*, Matthew 6.12,14,15. and 18.24,27,33. Luke 7.41–43,47,48. and 11.4. which being once blotted out, and done away, neither are we any more charged with them, Ezek. 18.22. nor God any more wroth with us, for them, chapter 54.9. See chapter 44.22.

*{for mine own sake*} Heb. *for myself*; as Job 18.4. Proverbs 16.4. out of a respect to his own honor, chapter 52.5. Ezek. 20.14,22. and 30.9. and 36.20–23. his mercy, Deut. 4.27. Jer. 3.12. his fidelity, Psalm 106.45. chapter 1.27. and 56.1. and his free love and affection to them and their ancestors, Deut. 7.7,8. verse 4. Jer. 31.3. Mal. 1.2. not in regard of any desert of theirs, who had so extremely, from time to time, both neglected and wronged him, chap. 44.8,9. Ezek. 36.22,23.

*{and will not remember thy sins*} As that which is blotted, or razed out, cannot now be read, or repeated, and consequently, is not regarded, nor remembered, Exodus 17.14. Psalm 9.5,6. and so a debt, when the bond cancelled, or the book crossed, is then no more thought on, or looked after. In like manner, God having remitted the sins of his, does no more now regard them, than as if he had forgotten them; (for so is the term of *forgetting*, or, *not remembering*, frequently used, both in Scripture, and common speech, Psalm 45.10. Phil. 3.13.) see Psalm 25.7. and 79.8. Jer. 31.34. Hosea 4.6.

**V. 26.** *{Put me in remembrance:*} If I have omitted, or not taken notice of aught, that you suppose might make for your justification, mind me of it.

*{let us plead together*} See chapter 1.19.

*{declare thou, that thou mayst be justified*} Or, *cleared*, or, *clear thyself*; as verse 9. Say what you can for yourself, you have liberty so to do, as Acts 26.1. The ancient Greek renders it, *Remember, that we may be judged, tell thy sins first, that thou mayst be justified*: and this the Greek Fathers commonly produce, and press, to prove, that confession and acknowledgment of sin goes before justification, and is the way to remission, Luke 18.13,14. a point not unsound, but a place impertinent, for the version forces that into the text that is not there.

**V. 27.** *{Thy first father hath sinned*} This some understand of Adam, from whom all mankind is descended, and from whom sin was propagated unto all his issue; yea, of whose actual sin, as most hold, all men stand guilty: and to this purpose, they apply that, chapter 48.8. Rom. 5.12. and that all men, for that corruption traduced to them from Adam, stand guilty of sin, and liable to God's wrath, cannot be denied, Psalm 50.5. Rom. 5.12. and 6.23. Ephes. 2.2,3. But this charge seems to be more special, and such, as in a more peculiar manner concerns this people. Others, of Abraham, the principal Patriarch, with whom God entered into a special covenant, sealed up with that solemn right of circumcision, Genesis 17.2,7,11,13. Rom. 5.11. named, as the head and root of their stock, chapter 41.8. and 51.2. and the sin of his here hinted, some make the denial of his wife, chapter 12.15. and 20.2. Others, the doubting of God's promise, in demanding a sign, Gen. 15.8. Or, because these may seem to have been slips of human frailty: the most, therefore, conceive it to have been his idolatry, before his call, which they ground upon Joshua 24.2,3. But of Abraham, no such thing is there said, and the Jews' traditional story, of Abraham's escaping the fire, that he was thrown into, because he would not worship idols, (which they build on the word *ur*, that signifies *fire*, Neh. 9.7.) tells us a contrary tale: but the truth is, the one is as groundless as the other. Others, Terah, Abraham's Father, the first, say they, of that line, that fell off to idolatry; which circumstance, though uncertain, yet, that sometime an idolater, is apparent, Josh. 24.2. Others, Jeroboam, who set up idolatry among the ten Tribes, 2 King. 12.28,30. But this seems to concern Judah, as well as Israel, which that did not, 2 Chron. 13.10,11. Others, Ahaz, 2 Chron. 28. and others, Manasses, 2 Kings 21. & 23.26. & 24.3. Now kings, say these last, as are Fathers to their people. But how or, why, either of these should be termed their *first father*, after so many foregoing them, they show not. I suppose, therefore, that *thy first father*, is no more here, than *thy forefathers, thine ancestors*. The word *father*, is sometime taken collectively: so Ezek. 16.3. *Thy father*, for *thy fathers*; and the word *first*, is frequently used for *former*: so, *the first age*, for *the former age*, or the age foregoing, Job 8.8. and, *the first things*, for *former things*, verse 9.18. and so would it be rendered, 1 Tim. 5.12. Rev. 2.4. So the meaning is, not you alone, but your forefathers, also, have been grievous transgressors, as well as yourselves; and there is no cause, therefore, why I should do so great a favor for you, as this is, in regard either of yourselves, or of them. See chapter 1.4. Psalm 78.8. and 106.6,7. Jer. 3.24,25. and 7.22–26. Zach. 1.4. Mal. 3.7.

*{and thy teachers have transgressed against me*} Heb. *thine interpreters*, Genesis 42.23. Job 33.23. or *ambassadors*, 2 Chronicles 32.31. Their priests and prophets, so termed; because they are as ambassadors between God and his people; and their office is, to open and make known God's will and pleasure unto them, Deuteronomy 33.10. Jer. 15.19. Mal. 2.7. and are called his ambassadors, because sent by him; their ambassadors, because sent to them, 2 Cor. 5.19,20. They that should have taught others, better, have been, themselves, as bad as any. See 2 Chron. 39.24. Jer. 5.30,31. and 8.10,11. and 23.13,14. Dan. 9.8,11.

**V. 28.** *{Therefore*} Heb. *And*; as verse 4.

*{have I profaned the Princes of the Sanctuary*} Or, *of holiness*, as chapter 62.9. that is, *the holy Princes*; as their land was termed *the holy land*, chapter 63.19. Jerusalem, *the holy city*, Neh. 11.1,18. the people, *an holy seed*, Ezr. 9.1. the sanctuary, *an holy place*, Psalm 5.7. and 68.5. Either the rulers of the Temple, Jer. 20.1. Or, their kings anointed with *holy oil*, Psalm 89.20. and Princes, governors of the holy people, because taken into special covenant with God, Deut. 26.19. Psalm 114.2. these God is said to have profaned, because he had rejected, abhorred, destroyed them, exposed them to a curse, to shame, to reproach, Psalm 44.13,14. Jer. 23.40. and 24.9. or dealt with them, as with profane and common persons, not regarding the dignity of their places, Psalm 89.39. ch. 47.6. Jer. 22.18,19,24–28. and 39.6,7. Lam. 2.2. For they seem to step aside here, who expound the words, as if God should not say, that he had so done, but that he might justly deal so with them.

*{and have given Jacob to the curse*} Or, *made Jacob a curse*; or, *an accursed thing*, chapter 65.11. caused him to be destroyed, as an accursed thing, Joshua 6.16,18,21. for that is the word here used.

*{and Israel to reproaches*} Exposed them, by their servitude and bondage, to most shameful reproach, Zeph. 2.8. Jer. 24.9. *Jacob* and *Israel*, the same, as verse 22.

### CHAPTER 44

**V. 1.** *{Yet now hear*} This chapter depends upon the next foregoing, as that on the next before it; God signifying unto his people, that though they, and their forefathers, had deserved so evil of him; and that he had therefore, therein intending, as well the chastisement, as the amendment of them, given them up into their enemies' hands, and suffered them to endure a long and tedious captivity; yet he would now, at length, relieve and refresh them, restore them, and cause them to thrive and prosper again.

*{Yet*} Heb. *And*; as ch. 43.1.

*{O Jacob, my servant; and Israel, whom I have chosen*} See chapter 41.8.

**V. 2.** *{Thus saith the Lord, that made thee, and formed thee*} See chapter 43.1,7,21.

*{from the womb*} From your nativity, say some; as Psalm 22.9,10. and 71.6. before you were able to do, much less to deserve aught, Rom. 9.11. But rather from your first beginning, to be a nation severed from others, an entire people of yourself. It is a metaphor, taken, not so much from the forming of the body in the womb, Psalm 119.73. and 139.13–16. Job 10.8–11. Jer. 1.3. as from the practice of midwives, that receiving the birth from the womb, do compose and frame it, and each limb of it, unto its due posture; and so did God with this people, when he molded them up, into a proportionable frame of church and state: So verse 24. chapter 46.3. See, also, chapter 48.8. Jer. 2.2.

*{which will help thee*} A defect of the relative; as chapter 42.1,5. Or, as the words may well be read, *Thus saith the Lord, he that made thee, and formed thee from the womb, will keep thee.* See chapter 41.10,13,14.

*{Fear not, O Jacob, my servant*} Chapter 41.8,10.

*{and thou Jesurun, whom I have chosen*} Heb. *Jeshurun*: a name given to Israel and his posterity, in regard of the uprightness that was in him, and ought to have been in them, Deut. 32.15. and 33.26. *chosen*; as verse 1.

**V. 3.** *{For I will pour water on him that is thirsty*} That is, as some, the spiritual water of grace, in abundance, upon those, that finding, and feeling the want of it, in themselves, do hunger and thirst after it; and so the metaphor should be taken from water, or drink, that a man is supplied with, for the slaking of his drought, and the quenching of his thirst, as chapter 12.3. and 55.1. Jer. 31.25. Matthew 5.6. John 4.14. and 7.37,38. Rev. 22.17. But neither will the word, of *pouring out*, well admit that metaphor here, no more, than in other the like places, to the like purpose produced, Joel 2.28. Acts 2.18. (which rather seem to allude to the pouring out of the oil, upon the head of king, or Priest, Leviticus 8.12. Psalm 133.2. 1 Samuel 10.1. 2 Kings 9.3.) since that we use not to pour water, or drink, upon men, or beasts either, when they are thirsty, but rather pour it out to them, or for them, 2 King. 4.20. chap. 58.10. and the tenure of the text carries it to such water, rain, or other, wherewith dry and parched grounds are wont to be watered, to refresh them, and make them fertile and fruitful: and I conceive it ought not to be rendered, *him that is thirsty*, but, *the thirsty place*; as, after, *the dry*, for *the dry land*: a defect of the subject in either. By a like metaphor, is *a land of thirst and dryness*, or, *a thirsty and dry land*, chapter 35.7. and Ezek. 19.13. for, a land that is dry, for want of water, as a man athirst for want of drink, Psalm 63.1.

*{and floods upon the dry ground*} Heb. *dry*: as Genesis 1.9. a defect of the subject, as before; *floods*, for abundance of water: as chapter 30.25. Psalm 119.136. an allusion here, partly, to rain, that the clouds pour down, Psalm 77.17. and partly, to such rivers, as overflowing the lands that lie near them, make them fertile. See on chapter 19.5,6. and 23.3.

*{I will pour my spirit upon thy seed, and my blessing upon thine offspring*} *My spirit*, that is, *my blessing*, (the one expounds the other) whereby they and their state should thrive and flourish, and multiply, and increase, that had been almost clean exhaust, and exceedingly impaired, in a manner, beyond all hope of recovery, before, chapter 26.19. Ezek. 37.3,11–14. So of their land, chapter 32.15. and of their seed, chapter 61.9. he follows still the comparison taken from grounds well watered, as chapter 58.11. and the seed sown in such soil, chap. 32.10. A type of that spiritual growth, and increase of God's church, and the members of it, under the Messiah, by the graces and comforts of his Spirit, Acts 9.31. Eph. 4.12–15. Col. 2.19. 2 Peter 3.18. See chapter 27.6. and 37.31. and 61.9,21.

**V. 4.** *{And they shall spring up as among the grass, as willows by the watercourses*} Heb. *in among*; and then there seems a defect of the note of similitude, to be supplied from the latter clause: but some rather read it, *as among*; and then there is no defect. Howbeit, there want not, that read it in a continued sentence, but with some transposition of the words, *They shall spring up*, or *shoot up*; or, *That they may shoot up* (as chapter 41.20.) *as willows beside the streams*, (as it is rendered, chapter 30.25.) or, *watercourses amidst the grass*; that is, as willows, that shoot up speedily in watery places, and soon overtop the grass among which they grow. See chapter 15.7. Job 40.22. Ezek. 17.5. the trees here mentioned, are reckoned up among those fair, shroudy, and flourishing ones, that they used to make booths of, in the Feast of Tabernacles, Leviticus 23.40. Howsoever we read the text, a prosecution it is of the former resemblance. See the like, Numbers 24.6. Psalm 1.3. Jeremiah 17.8.

**V. 5.** *{One shall say, I am the Lord's; and another shall call himself by the name of Jacob; and another shall subscribe with his hand to the Lord, and surname himself by the name of Israel*} The future increase of God's people is intimated, not only by his blessing, in making them fruitful, and multiplying their issue, chapter 60.22. and 61.9. Jer. 31.27. as he did sometime in Egypt, Exodus 1.12. but by addition, also, of many proselytes, from other parts, to them, who should give up their names to God, to be entered into his muster roll, and registered in his church book, among the faithful, that belong to him, and are listed for his service. See the like, Psalm 87.5,6. See also, chapter 40.26. This, in likelihood, was, in part, fulfilled, upon the dissolution of the Babylonian captivity; many thereupon adjoining themselves to God's people; as the like was sometime done on the like occasions, both before, and after, upon their departure out of Egypt, Exodus 12.38. and upon their deliverance from Haman's mischievous plot against them, Est. 8.17. But more fully, in the conversion of the Gentiles, by the preaching of the gospel. See chapter 2.3.

*{I am the Lord's*} Soldier, or servant; as, *the Lord's, and Gideon's*, for, *the sword of the Lord, and of Gideon*, Judges 7.18. and 20.

*{subscribe with his hand*} A defect of the particle instrumental, as Psalm 17.13,14. a metaphor from such volunteers, as do, of their own accord, under their handwriting, list, and enroll themselves, for service, Psalm 110.3. or, as some render it, *write on his hand, unto the Lord*: or, *I am the Lord's*: and so the ancient Greek has it: as, *I unto thee*, Psalm 119.94. that is, *I am thine*; or, belong to you; which they conceive to allude unto the manner of soldiers, or servants, that did bear the Captain's, or Master's name, to whom they belonged, imprinted on one of their hands, which, though it might be alluded unto, Revelations 3.12. and 14.9. yet I doubt, whether that custom was so ancient as Esay's days.

*{surname*} Shall take on him that name, instead of that which he had from his original; or, shall assume it, as an additional unto it. Heb. *shall entitle himself*. See chapter 45.4. thereby intimating, that he is one of *the Israel of God*, Gal. 6.16. a member of God's church; a subject of that kingdom whereof he is *King*, ver. 6. cha. 33.23.

**V. 6.** *{Thus saith the Lord; the King of Israel, and his Redeemer:*} See chapter 43.14,15.

*{the Lord of hosts*} See chapter 1.9. One, as willing to deliver you; so, able to do it.

*{I am the first, and I am the last*} Chapter 41.4. and 48.12. Rev. 1.3,17. and 22.13. *the first*, say some, from whom all things are; and *the last*, unto whom, all is to be referred, Romans 11.36. But I conceive God's eternity, only, to be here implied, Psalm 90.2.

*{and besides me there is no God.*} Or, more concisely, *no god, besides me*, Deuteronomy 4.35,39. and 6.4. and 32.39. chapter 43.10,11. and 45.6,21. verse 8. John 17.3. 1 Cor. 8.5,6.

**V. 7.** *{And who, as I, shall call, and shall declare it, and set it in order for me, since I appointed the ancient people? and the things that are coming, and shall come? let them show unto them.*} Or, *Who is like unto me*, (Psalm 35.10. and 89.8. to wit among the gods that the heathen so account, Psalm 89.6.) *that can call, and declare it, and set it me in order, since I appointed a people of old? or, let them* (that is, their idols) *show unto them* (to wit, that take them for their gods) *the things to come, and such as issue from them*; to wit, if they will be accounted gods, chapter 41.23.

*{shall call*} Or, *can call*, potentially, as ch. 40.12. and 41.26. and 43.8. This, some expound of God's calling of the Israelites to be his people, chap. 41.9. Others, of calling and designing certain of persons, as Cyrus and his forces, to deliver his people, chapter 44.28. and 45.1,4. I suppose the former here intended.

*{and shall declare it*} Or, *and declare it*, that is, tell beforehand what shall, in future times, befall that people: or, as some other, who shall tell me, or direct me, how I should, in the managing of these affairs, proceed? as chapter 40.13. and 45.11.

*{and set it in order for me*} Or, *set it me in order*, or, *set it in order to me*: relate it to me, in a constant course and tenor, what shall, from time to time, betide them, as I have done with my people, both concerning the Egyptian bondage, with the bringing them out from thence, and the settling of them in the land of Canaan, Gen. 15.13,14,16. as also concerning the Babylonian captivity, together with their deliverance out of it, and the restoring them to their own land again, Chap. 39.6,7. & 40.2. & 43.5,6,14. 45–47. See also, Jer. 25.9,11,12.

*{since I appointed the ancient people*} Or, *an ancient people*, that is, the lineage of Abraham, in the posterity of Jacob, to be a numerous nation, and my peculiar people; which long since he both foretold, and fulfilled, Gen. 13.16. & 15.5. & 22.17. Num. 1.45,46. Deut. 1.10. Heb. *a people of antiquity*, or, *of perpetuity*, or, *of eternity*, for the word is used (as the Latin *olim* also, supposed, by some, to come from it,) as well of the time past, chap. 42.14. Jer. 48.8. as of the time to come: in which latter sense, also, some here taking it, expound the text of God's elect, from the world's beginning, yea, from all eternity, chosen, and set apart, and in time, culled out, and called to inherit eternity, Gen. 3.15. Rom. 8.29,30. Eph. 1.4,5. 1 Pet. 1.3,4. Rev. 13.8. and 17.8. but I suppose the former here, principally intended, because God here points unto such conspicuous evidences of his divine power, as lay open, even to any natural man's eye, chapter 41.20. Nor do they seem to conjecture aright, who refer it to the creation of mankind, at the first. See chapter 40.21. and 41.4.

*{things that are coming, and shall come*} *Things to come*, as (chap. 45.11.) *such as shall come to pass*, the copulative for the relative; as chapter 3.6. & 5.4. or, *things to come, and such as shall proceed*, or *spring*, from them. See chapter 43.19. a defect of the relative; as verse 2. that is, things to come, in a continued course, from the first to the last, like links of a chain, hanging one upon another. See chapter 41.22,23,26. and 46.10. and 48.14.

**V. 8.** *{Fear ye not, neither be afraid*} As if, either I were not able to fulfill what I foretell, verse 6. or, any counterfeit deity were able to overpower me, in what I foretell, and intend: the vanity of whom he lays forth, at large, in the words following, together with the senseless sottishness of those that are bewitched with them, ver. 9–20.

*{Fear not*} Ver. 2.

*{have I not told thee from that time, and have declared it?*} Remember that these things were told you before, John 16.1. Matthew 26.6,7. Luke 24.6–8. whereof you see some part already fulfilled; and the residue shall, in their due time, be accomplished. So Luke 1.31,36,37.

*{told thee*} Heb. *made thee to hear*: as chapter 41.26.

*{from that time*} At that time, when I appointed you to be a people, verse 7. or, in a more large sense; *formerly*, or, *in time past*. Heb. *from then*: as chapter 16.23. and 48.3.

*{declared it*} A defect of the pronoun *it*: as chapter 42.21,25.

*{ye are even my witnesses*} Or, *and ye are my witnesses* hereof: See chapter 43.10.

*{Is there a god besides me?*} The interrogative affirmatively delivered, does more vehemently deny: as Job 7.1. See verse 6.

*{there is no god*} That is, *no other god, no god besides me*, to be supplied from the former branch. Heb. *no rock*, Psalm 19.14. no such rock, as is able to protect and secure those that repair to, it for shelter and safety, as God does those, that betake themselves to him, Deut. 4.35,39. & 32.4,32,39. 1 Samuel 2.2. Psalm 18.31. Prov. 18.10,11. chapter 26.4. & 43.11. & 45.5. & 46.9. it is a metaphor taken from such caves, or places of receipt, in rocks; that either men in distress and danger, or, the feebler sort of creatures, for better security against the ravenous kind of them, are wont to resort unto, or to make their constant abode in, Judges 15.8. & 20.47. Psalm 104.18. Proverbs 30.26. Canticles 2.14.

*{I know not any*} Who yet should, if any such were. Howbeit, some read the words of the text, as a continued sentence; *that is no God, that I know not*; and there should then be a defect of the relative; as before, verse 7. but the former reading seems the more probable.

**V. 9.** *{They that make a graven image, are all of them vanity*} See cha. 41.29. some read the words, *They that frame a graven image, are all of them framers of a vain thing*: The word in the latter part supplied from the former; as 2 Chronicles 10.14.

*{and their delectable things shall not profit:*} The Hebrew word signifies as well *delectable*, or *delightful*, as *desirable*. See Chapter 64.11. their idols, which they so dearly affect, and delight so much in, (see Chap. 1.29. and 57.5. Jeremiah 17.1,2.) *shall not profit*, or *cannot profit*: as Chapter 30.5,6. they shall not stand them in any stead, when they need their help, Chapter 45.20. Jeremiah 2.28. or, they are altogether unprofitable, they are good for nothing, ch. 41.29. verse 10.

*{and they are their own witnesses; they see not, nor know; that they may be ashamed*} Or, *even themselves are their own witnesses to their shame that they never see, nor know aught*; a defect of the particle *that*: as Chapter 37.26. The maker of them, who know whereof they are made, and how handled in the making, are the best witnesses, that can be, against them, to testify that they have neither sight, nor sense; and may justly therefore be ashamed of adoring such trumpery, as they, of all others, cannot but know them to be, Ps. 97.7. v. 11. or, they cannot but see their own sottishness and senselessness, if they had the wit to consider it, in worshiping those as gods, whom they see and know to be such, verse 18,19. But the former seems the better.

**V. 10.** *{Who hath formed a god, or molten a graven image, that is profitable for nothing?*} Who, but a madman, would deem aught that man makes, or that himself has made, to be god? or account that to be God, that is good for nought? verse 9. Hosea 8.6. Hab. 2.18. See Jeremiah 16.20.

*{or*} Heb. *and*: as Chapter 43.9.

*{molten a graven image*} Cast materials, or metals, in a mold, to frame thereof an image, that may, by graving, afterward be polished, and perfected. See ch. 49.19. such images put here, for all of all sorts; as ch. 41.29.

*{that is profitable for nothing*} Heb. *not to profit*: as Jeremiah 7.11. and how then fit to be laymen's books? being unprofitable, Habakuk 2.18. abominable, Chapter 41.24. the fruit of errors, Jeremiah 10.15. and lying teachers, Jeremiah 10.8. & 16.19. Habakuk 2.18.

**V. 11.** *{Behold all his fellows shall be ashamed; and the workmen, they are of men*} Or, *and the workmen, they more than any*. See the like phrase, chapter 52.19. Heb. *Adam*; *a man*, for, *any man*, or *any one*; as verse 15. and as *ish*; Jeremiah 5.1. the whole society, or fraternity of them, that have aught to do about them, or dealings with them, may justly be ashamed of them; as they shall also be confounded; when they expect help from them, Psalm 97.7. chapter 1.29. & 42.27. and 45.16. and none more than the workmen, (of which term, see on Chapter 40.19.) the makers of them, that have been best acquainted with them, and the nature and condition of them. See on verse 9.

*{Let them all be gathered together, let them stand up, yet they shall fear, and shall be ashamed together*} Let them convene, and combine, as Demetrius and his fellows, Acts 19.24–29. stand stoutly to it, and make all the power they can, yet shall they never be able to maintain their forged deities, nor to acquit themselves from fear and shame, in seeking to support them. See chap. 41.1,5,21,22.

*{stand up*} As parties to be tried at the bar, Num. 35.12. or, as patrons to plead for their clients, Acts 24.1.

*{yet*} A defect of the discretive; as Psalm 119.8,9. Job 14.9.

**V. 12.** *{The smith with the tongs both worketh in the coals, and fashioneth it with hammers, and worketh it with the strength of his arms*} See chapter 40.19. & 46.6. Jeremiah 10.3.

*{smith*} Heb. *workman of iron*: as 2 Chr. 24.12. He speaks first of the smith, that makes idols of metal; then of the carpenter, that frames them of wood. verse 13.

*{with the tongs*} The word here used, seems rather to signify *an ax*. See Jer. 10.3. and so the Jewish masters commonly expound it, *an ax*, or *an hatchet*, nor is the particle *with*, in the text. Others, therefore, read the words, *The smith maketh an ax*, to wit, say they, for the carpenter, to use for the same purpose, for the framing of such idols of wood, as he does of iron; or, as some other, He makes his idols, as he does *an ax*, or *an hatchet*, or any other instrument for ordinary employment. Others, lastly, expound the whole verse of the making of *an ax*, simply, as describing what pains he takes about the forming of an ax only, which the hewer of wood, or feller of trees, taking from him, or buying of him, makes use of, for matter to make an idol, with, Jer. 10.3. this may seem the more probable, because elsewhere, speaking of molten, or metal images, he mentions gold and silver only, passing by those baser metals, as pointing to the goldsmith, or silversmith, rather than to the iron workman, or, the blacksmith, ch. 40.19. & 46.6. Jer. 10.4,9. Howbeit, they had, even the greatest of them, gods also, as well of brass and iron, as of gold and silver, Daniel 5.4. and much art and curious workmanship may be showed, as well in the one, as in the other.

*{both worketh in the coals*} Heb. *coal*; taken collectively: as we do oft use it; *coal*, for *coals*: and it is used, sometime for *coal*, simply, or dead *coal*, as Prov. 26.21. sometime, for quick *coal*; as chap. 54.16. and so here: either, *he worketh in the coals*, to wit, the metal, to make his idol, verse 10. or, *which he worketh in the coal*, to wit, the ax before mentioned; the copulative, for the relative, in this latter, as verse 7.

*{and fashioned it*} Either the idol, or the ax. See verse 9,10. Chapter 41.7. and the text may be read, without any supply, *The smith an ax both worketh in the coals, and fashioneth it with hammers*: a trajection of the copulative; such as is found, Genesis 22.4. Chapter 17.14. 2 Kings 2.14. Job 23.12. Proverbs 23.4. & 24.27.

*{with hammers*} So the word signifies, as appears, Judges 4.21. joined with *nails*, Jeremiah 10.4. which it cannot therefore signify; though it come from a word, that signifies *to bore*, or *to pierce*; which is not the proper, or principal use of an hammer: but to that is answered, that the *hammer* thereby signified, was somewhat like the *twibil*, sharp, to strike through with, at the one end; and flat, to beat out with, at the other: *hammers*, in the plural; because several sorts of them: some to beat out; and some to polish, Chapter 41.7.

*{with the strength of his arms*} He puts all his might to it, either in regard of the toughness of the metal he works upon; (see somewhat the like, Eccl. 10.10.) or, out of an earnest desire to make him an idol.

*{yea, he is hungry, and his strength faileth; he drinketh no water, and is faint*} This some, also, refer to their eagerness upon the work they are about, that it makes them forget the necessities of nature, out of devotion even to their yet unmade idols, verse 20. Others, to show the unusefulness and inability of their idols, whom they take so much pains about, to relieve them; they may work, and fast, until they faint, for aught they are able to do for them, verse 10. they cannot refresh them, or renew strength to them, when they are tired out, and ready to faint, as God can do, and does, to his, chap. 40.29. they cannot supply them with food, as God did his people, with manna from heaven, Exodus 16.13–15. nor with drink, as with water from the rock he did his, Exodus 17.6. Heb. *and is hungry, and his strength faileth; he drinketh no water, and is faint*. Which some therefore thus render, *when he is hungry*, (wanting bread) *his strength faileth, and if he drink not water, he is faint*; that is, if he want bread and water, he may faint, and his strength fail him, for any provision his idol is able to afford him. See the like construction, chapter 30.20. & 35.4. & 37.9,26. and of *fainting*, and *failing*, Chapter 40.30,31. for, *his strength faileth*; the Hebrew has it, *strength is not* to him: as 2 Chr. 20.12. Or simply, he labors hard at the forge, and about the fire, until he be faint, and his strength fail him, for want of refreshing; as in that employment workmen, the meaner sort of them especially, oft do.

**V. 13.** *{The carpenter stretcheth out his rule*} From the smith, he passes to the wright. Heb. *The workman of trees*, or, *wood*, or *timber*; as 1 Chron. 14.1. & 22.15. *carpenter, cutter*, or *carver*. See Chapter 40.20.

*{stretcheth out*} Upon the piece of timber, whereof he means to make his idol.

*{rule*} Heb. *line*. So the word properly signifies: nor is *a rule* so properly said to be *stretched out*. See chap. 28.17.

*{he marketh it with the line*} The word say the Jewish doctors, signifies *vermilion*; though for that, another word seems used, Jer. 22.14. and it may, peradventure, rather be *ocher*: but by a metonymy, *a string*, or *thread*, therein dipped, or therewith colored: not unlike the same, that our workmen use: the word is no where else found in Scripture: but so *a scarlet string*, or *thread*, Cant. 4.3. for that which is rendered, *a scarlet thread*, Gen. 38.28. & Joshua 2.18. seems to have a far other notion, somewhat the same with that, Prov. 31.21. The same thing in effect, is this with the former, for he stretches a line over it, therewith to mark it, where, and how far, to cut of it.

*{he fitteth it with planes*} Heb. *he maketh it with planes*; or *to work it with planes*: that being the end of his marking the timber, to direct him, and show what is to be taken away of it; the word comes from a root, that signifies *to scrape*, or *pare away*, Leviticus 14.41. the verb found in that notion there, and the noun in this, only here: and it is used here, in the plural number, because they used two sorts of *planes*, a bigger, and stronger, to fetch off the rougher and more rugged matter first, and a less, or finer afterward, to smooth and polish the more exactly the remainder.

*{and he marketh it out with the compass*} The word comes from a verb used, Job 26.10. the verb there only, and the noun here.

*{and maketh it after the figure of a man, according to the beauty of a man*} Or, *to make it after the model* (for the word is properly, of *buildings*, Exod. 25.40. 1 Chr. 28.12.) *of a man, according to the comeliness*, (comely proportion) or *goodliness of a man*, with such outward limbs and lineaments, as a man has, Psalm 115.5–7. & 135.16,17. or, *according to the excellency of a man*, as some; referring it to that which follows. Of the word, see on chap. 4.2. But I conceive it, rather to be here taken the other way, because it is the word *Adam*, that is here used; which usually goes for an ordinary man. See on ch. 2.29. Howsoever, that is the end of using the compass about his idol; as the planes before, to smooth and polish, so this, to give it its due proportions and lineaments.

*{that it may remain in the house*} Heb. *to sit*, or *dwell*, or *stay*, or *abide, in the house*; for all these, the word of *sitting*, imports, in Scripture, Deut. 9.9. 2 Sam. 7.18. Psalm 23.6. chap. 13.20. to dwell in some Temple, as some king in his Palace, or some great man in his house, Dan. 1.2. or to stay and abide in some house, either public, or private, Deut. 27.15. Judges 17.5. because it is not able to stir out, ch. 41.7. Jer. 10.4,5.

**V. 14.** *{He heweth him down cedars, and taketh the cypress and the oak*} Such trees as afford timber of longest continuance. See chap. 40.20. Heb. *to hew down*, as Deut. 19.5. 1 Kings 5.6. which may well be retained, and the text thus read, *He taketh courage also to himself, among the trees of the forest*, or *he useth his strength upon the trees of the wood, to hew him down cedars, and to take the cypress*, or *the oak*, or, to wave all the trajections, and take the words, as they lie in the text, *In hewing he heweth him down*, (as Jer. 3.1.) that is, *He is busy in hewing him down* (see on chap. 59.13.) *cedars; he taketh also the cypress and the oak*, or *the cypress, or the oak*: Or, as a learned late writer, *cedars are to be cut down by him*. See on chap. 41.1.

*{cypress*} The name of this tree is no where else found; and our Jewish masters say little of it, but that it is the name of a fruitless tree. Some of ours would have it, to be a *pine*: so the Greek seems to render either this, or that, in the last clause mentioned. Some, a kind of *oak*, that which is usually called the *holm*; so the old Latin. Some, a kind of *cedar*, because the name of the *cedar*, and this, differ but in one, and that a servile letter: it may well be the *cypress*, partly, because some remarkable places of pleasure seem to have had their name of *Thirsah*, from it, as being planted with pleasant groves of it, 1 Kings 16.9. Cant. 6.4. now the *cypress* is a very graceful tree; and the timber of it, both for the beauty, and the durableness of it, much used in times past, for images. See on chap. 40.20. Howbeit, some are of the mind, that *Gopher*, which Noah built the Ark with, Gen. 6.14. to be the *cypress* tree, and the names come very near; and this then some other. See Bochart in his *Phaleg*, l. 1. c. 4.

*{and the oak*} Or, *or the oak*, as v. 10. of the tree, see on ch. 2.13. and 6.13.

*{which he strengtheneth for himself among the trees of the forest*} So reading the words, the copulative is put for the relative; as ver. 7. But the trees of the forest are not of any man's planting; nor is man's care usually employed about them, to further their growth. See Psa. 104.16. Besides that those trees, as they are of long continuance, so of slow growth, beyond a man's ordinary age, ere they come to be fit for timber. I suppose therefore, the marginal reading to be the better; *and he taketh courage to himself*; or, *he employeth his strength among*, or *upon, the trees of the forest*: or, if we admit the former change, that would be more probable that some other have, *Which hath lift up itself*, or *strengthened itself, among the trees of the wood*. See of Ashur, Ezek. 31.5.

*{he planteth an ash*} Either he seeks out some fair tree in the forest, or takes some one of his own planting, (the original whereof, therefore, he cannot but well know,) that is now, what by his own industry about it, and what by the rain from above, Deut. 11.10,11. grown to some bulk, that may well afford matter for such a purpose.

*{ash*} The name of this tree, likewise, is no where else found in Scripture; and the Jewish masters leave us here, also, at a loss; telling us only, that it is a good timber tree. The old Latin, and so it may be the Greek also, render it, *a pine*. But many, in regard of the identity of the name, conceive it to be a kind of *ash*, that has leaves broader than ordinary, by the Latins called *ornus*, which comes full home to the Hebrew; though I suppose that consonancy between the two words, *oren*, and *ornus*, to be but casual; and that this latter came rather from the Greek *ὀρεινὸς* and was by the Latins so termed, because it thrived best on hills: as Pliny reports of it, l. 16. c. 18. it seems, that chests or, arks, were usually made of it; for the names of either, this, and that of a *chest*, or *ark*, in Hebrew are of the same stock, and differ not much, *Oren*, and *Aron*.

*{and the rain doth nourish it*} Or, *which when the rain hath brought up*] Heb. *made big*, or *great*: as ch. 1.3. Ezek. 31.4. of the syntax, see ch. 37.9,36.

**V. 15.** *{Then shall it be for a man to burn*} Heb. *And*: as ch. 30.20. and 35.4. & 40.18. when it is thus grown up, it serves any one for fuel: *a man*, for *any one*, as ver. 11.

*{for he will take thereof, and warm himself*} Heb. *and he will take* (as ver. 14.) Or, *yea, he will take* (as Chap. 29.23.) Or, *even he himself will take* (as Chap. 40.30.) *of them*, (of any one of those trees before mentioned, or of chips that he hews off) *and be warm*, that is, *that he may be warm*, as chapter 53.2. or, *wherewith to warm himself*, as Job Job 34. ch. 47.14. he himself makes fuel of part of that, whereof, afterward, he makes him a god, Verse 17.

*{yea, he kindleth it, and breaketh bread*} Or, *he kindleth it, also, to bake bread*: he makes use of it, as well for the oven, as for the chimney: the same syntax, as before, and Josh. 24.9. a defect of the pronoun *it*; as ver. 8,13.

*{yea, he maketh a god, and worshippeth it, he maketh it a graven image, and falleth down thereto*} Or, *he maketh also* (as 2 Kings 2.13.) Or, *yet* (as chap. 44.10.) *he maketh of it a god, to bow himself down to*, (as Exod. 20.5.) *he maketh it a graven* (or, *carved*, as chap. 40.20.) *image, to fall down to*: the prophet uses of purpose, as some think, a Chaldee term, both here, and again, v. 17,19. and ch. 46.6. It is found eleven times, in the Syriac of Daniel, chapter 3.

**V. 16.** *{He burneth part thereof in the fire; with part thereof he eateth flesh; he roasteth roast, and is satisfied; yea, he warmeth himself, and saith, I am warm, I have seen the fire*} See verse 15,19.

*{part*} Heb. *half*; as Zach. 14.14. and so both the ancient Greek and Latin, and our former English: which needed not have been altered; the one half of the timber lightly goes away, in hewing, squaring, planing, fashioning, and the like.

*{with part thereof he eateth*} Or, as some, *on part thereof he eateth*, having made him a table, or trenchers of it: but the prophet seems throughout this whole passage, to intend fuel only. I read the words, therefore partly, as in the text, and partly, as before, *with half thereof he eateth flesh*: that is, he dresses flesh, or meat, to eat. See the like comprehensive forms of speech, cha. 38.17,21. to which add, because it comes near to this, that, Prov. 12.27. *the slack*, or *the deceitful man shall not roast his venison*: that is, he shall not roast and eat it: see ver. 19. not, that he spends one half of his materials, in roasting, or dressing him, a joint of meat only: But that which he had before, in the first branch, laid down in general, of burning the one half, that he now repeats after his wonted manner, illustrated by a more particular enumeration of the several employments, whereabout, for fuel, he makes use thereof; to wit for dressing of his meat, his roast, especially, and for the warming of himself. See verse 19.

*{he roasteth roast, and is satisfied*} Or, *with half of it* (I say) *he eateth flesh, having roasted roast, to his fill*. So Psalm 22.26. *The meek shall eat, and be satisfied*, that is, *shall eat to their fill*.

*{yea, he warmeth himself*} Or, *he warmeth himself also*, as ver. 25. Heb. *he is warm*: but those neuters, and passives, have oft a reciprocal sense, as this before. See on ver. 15. and the word *himself*, therefore, need not be in a different character, being included in the verb. See ch. 45.8.

*{and saith, aha*} An interjection, intimating joy and comfort, Ps. 35.25,26. & 70.3.

*{I have seen the fire*} I have been at a good fire; I have felt the fire: *to see*, for *to feel*, as Psalm 34.8. and so for, *to enjoy*, as Psal. 34.12. and *to suffer*, or *endure*: as Ps. 89. ver. 48.

**V. 17.** *{And the residue thereof he maketh a god; even his graven image*} Of the one half of that stuff which he burnt of before, v. 15,16.

*{he falleth down unto it and worshippeth it*} Or, *he falleth down* (before it) *and boweth to it*, v. 15. to his own workmanship, c. 2.8.

*{and prayeth unto it, and saith, Deliver me, for thou art my god*} See Jer. 2.27,28. Hos. 14.3.

*{Deliver me*} He seeks for safety to them that are not able to save, either him, or themselves. See chapter 46. verse 1,7.

**V. 18.** *{They have not known, nor understood*} Or, They have no knowledge nor understanding: they neither know, nor understand aught, as Psalm 14.4. Ch. 27.11. See ver. 19,20. ch. 45.20. Jer. 10.8,14.

*{for he hath shut their eyes, that they cannot see, and their hearts, that they cannot understand*} Heb. *he hath daubed* (as Ezek. 13.10,13.) *their eyes from seeing, their hearts from understanding*. Of which form, see on Chap. 5.6. & 23.1. He, that is, the idol, say some; God, in just judgment, say others, ch. 6.9,10. But more simply, the verb being taken indefinitely, *Their eyes are daubed up*, or *shut*. See the like: Gen. 41.13. 2 Sam. 24.1. Luke 6.38. & 10.10.

**V. 19.** *{And none considereth in his heart*} Or, *So that* (as Psal. 78.5. Jer. 14.19.) none considers in his heart. Heb. *sets it on*, or *returns*, or *reduces it to his heart*, as ch. 46.8.

*{neither is there knowledge, nor understanding*} See verse 18.

*{to say*} To reason and debate the matter, thus, with themselves.

*{I have burnt part of it in the fire; yea, also, I have baked bread upon the coals thereof; I have roasted flesh and eaten it*} See verse 15,16.

*{baked bread*} That is, baked dough; to make bread. So Levit. 26.26. *grind meal*, for grind grain, or corn, whereof to make meal; or, that by grinding, may produce meal, Chapter 47.2.

*{part*} Heb. *half*; as v. 16.

*{roasted*} Or, *I have roasted flesh* therewith, *and eaten* thereof. See v. 16. the like defects are, ch. 27.9. & 30.27.

*{and shall I make the residue thereof an abomination?*} A most abominable thing: so Deut. 27.15. ch. 41.24.

*{shall I fall down to the stock of a tree*} And that one of mine own planting too: ver. 14. Heb. *to that which cometh of a tree*: as Job 40.20. See ver. 15. Jer. 2.17. Hos. 4.12.

**V. 20.** *{He feedeth on ashes*} He is grossly deluded, like one that would feed on ashes, to slake his hunger; or his idol feeds and entertains him with nothing but ashes, matter of sorrow and mourning, Psal. 16.4. as Psa. 102.9. or, he feeds himself with foolish hopes of benefit, from a thing of no worth, no better than ashes; from a piece of wood, that may easily be turned to ashes, Cha. 37.19. See somewhat the like, Hos. 12.1. *ashes* is here, what *wind* there. Howsoever, there seems an allusion to the *ashes*, that the one moiety of his stuff made, showing of what worth the other half was, whereof his god was made.

*{a deceived heart hath turned him aside*} Or, *a deluded heart*, (as Judg. 16.10,13. Job 17.3.) *hath seduced him*. See Hos. 4.12. & 7.11. 2 Thes. 2.11.

*{that he cannot deliver his soul*} Heb. *and he will not*, or *shall not deliver his soul*; *and*, for, *so that*: as ver. 19. the verb taken potentially, as ver. 7. *his soul*, for *himself*: as Ps. 3.2. he is not able to wind himself out of this foolish error, and superstitious conceit, he is so bewitched and besotted with it, Rom. 1.21–25,28.

*{and say*} Think within himself: as Psal. 14.1. & 39.1.

*{Is there not a lie in my right hand*} Is not this mine idol, which I hold in mine hand, a bare figment, a mere fancy and falsehood? Do not I see it, and feel it, and find it to be such? See Jer. 10.8. Romans 1.25.

**V. 21.** *{Remember these (O Jacob and Israel) for thou art my servant*} An admonition to God's people, advising them to consider, seriously, the sottishness of those persons before mentioned, and to learn wisdom, by their folly; that which they are the rather engaged to do, and shunning, carefully, such vanities and abominations, to keep close to the true God, because he has taken them in special to himself, and has dealt very freely and bountifully with them, above others, as well in settling their estate, and his church among them, as in passing by, and pardoning their manifold defections, and restoring them, after a long and tedious captivity, unto their former state again. The words, in the translation, are not so distinguished, as they are in the text: they lie there thus, *Remember these, O Jacob: and Israel, for thou art my servant.*

*{these*} Either things, or persons, or both; for the term is common to either. See ch. 45.7. & 60.8.

*{Jacob, and Israel*} The same, as before, verse 1,23. Psalm 14.7.

*{thou art my servant*} Ch. 41.8.

*{I have formed thee, thou art my servant, O Israel; thou shalt not be forgotten of me*} The words should, rather, according to the stops and points in the Hebrew, be thus distinguished, *I have formed thee, thou art a servant, to me, O Israel, thou shalt not be forgotten of me.* Of the former branch, see ch. 43.1. ver. 1,2. Of the latter, Chapter 48.15.

*{thou shalt not be forgotten of me*} Or, *thou art not*, or, *canst not be forgotten by me*. I neither do, nor can, forget you, though, for a time, I may so to do, Chap. 49.14,15.

**V. 22.** *{I have blotted out, as a thick cloud, thy transgressions; and, as a cloud, thy sins*} Or, *I blot out*: as chap. 43.25. As the sun, when it breaks forth, dispels the mists and clouds with his bright beams, Job 37.11. Psal. 18.12. Or, as the wind disperses them, be they never so thick, Psalm 68.2. Prov. 25.23. or, as a cloud, or vapor, vanishes and appears no more, than if it never had been, Job 7.9. & 30.15. Hos. 6.4. & 13.3. Jam. 4.14. so do I put away your sins, that rise up as a cloud between you and me, Chap. 59.2. hindering the light of my countenance from shining forth upon you, ch. 57.17. and your prayers from finding access unto me, and acceptance with me, Lamentations 3.44. Chapter 1.15. Howbeit, Some render the words another way, on this manner; *I wipe away, as with a thick cloud, thy transgressions, and as with a cloud, thy sins*: the preposition being omitted, as ch. 34.15. & 35.4. & 42.21. So the sense should be; I wash away your sins and your pollutions, chap. 4.4. as the clouds, by pouring down showers of rain, Eccl. 11.4. do wash away the filth and slime of the earth, Ezek. 22.24. and so it might have some reference to the general deluge. Of which, the word is used, Gen. 6.7. & 7.4. But the former seems the fitter.

*{return unto me; for I have redeemed thee*} And have therefore best right unto you: so Psal. 31.5. 1 Cor. 6.19,20. See chap. 43.1,3,4. They seem to strain the text, needlessly, that render it, *return unto me, that I may redeem thee*; as Chap. 45.22. But the syntax is not the same.

**V. 23.** *{Sing O ye heavens, for the Lord hath done it: shout ye lower parts of the earth; break forth into singing, ye mountains, O forest, and every tree therein: for the Lord hath redeemed Jacob, and glorified himself in Israel*} As the whole world, heaven and earth and all the creatures in either, are invited to rejoice, upon the ruin and destruction of Babel, chapter 14.7,8. Rev. 18.20. so are they likewise here incited all to the like, upon the redemption and deliverance of God's people, ensuing thereupon, c. 14.1. & 35.1. 42.10,11. & 45.8. & 49.13. & 52.9. See the like rhetorical expressions, Psal. 96.11. and 98.7,8. All implying such abundant matter of joy, as might well affect the whole creation, were it all sensible of it. See somewhat the like in another kind, Rom. 8.21,22.

*{lower parts of the earth*} Heb. *low*; a defect of the subject, for low parts or places; as Psal. 63.9. & 139.15. or, *lower*; as Eph. 4.9. that is the *earth* below, opposed to the heavens, before, as there; or here, the *valleys* opposed to the *mountains*, in the words ensuing. See Chap. 24.15.

*{the Lord hath done it*} A defect of the pronoun; as Mal. 3.17. Or, the Lord has been working. See ch. 48. v. 11.

*{redeemed Jacob*} Ch. 45.20.

*{glorified himself*} As well in the destruction of his enemies, as in the deliverance of his people, ch. 49.3. & 60.21. & 61.3. Heb. *show himself gallant*: for the word properly imports *bravery*, or *gallantry*, cha. 3.18.

**V. 24.** *{Thus saith the Lord thy redeemer*} Chapter 43. v. 14.

*{and he that formed thee from the womb*} See v. 2.

*{I am the Lord that maketh all things*} Or, *that made all things*, as before, *that formed thee*, Gen. 1.1. & 2.1. John 1.3. Heb. 3.4.

*{that stretcheth out the heavens alone*} Or, *stretched out*; see ch. 42.5. Jer. 10.12.

*{alone*} Without help of any; as in the next branch.

*{that spreadeth abroad the earth by myself*} Or, *spread*. See chap. 42.5.

**V. 25.** *{That frustrateth the tokens of the liars, and maketh diviners mad*} Or, *That frustrate, and make mad*; make them at their wits' end, by crossing them in their predictions: those, especially, whereby they promised long continuance to the Babylonian Monarchy. See of these, ch. 47. ver. 12–14.

*{liars*} The word signifies, first, *lies*, ch. 16.7. Jer. 48.30. then *liars*; that is, men of *lies*; as *wine*, for a man of *wine*, that is, given to wine, a drunkard, Prov. 20.1. it is given to *wizards*, here, and Jer. 50.36. and it seems to come from a word, that signifies, *to invent*, or *devise*, 1 Kings 12.33. or, *feign*, Neh. 6.8.

*{that turneth wise men backward*} Or, *turn*: by confounding them in their counsels and courses, in their plots and projects, Job 5.12–14. & 12.12,13,16,17. Psalm 2.1–4. & 10,11. & 37.12–15. ch. 19.3,11,13,14.

*{and maketh their knowledge foolish*} Or, *make*, as before, 2 Sam. 15.31. ch. 29.14. 1 Cor. 1.20. & 3.19.

**V. 26.** *{That confirmeth the word of his servant, and performeth the counsel of his messengers*} Or, *Confirm the word of my servant, and perform the counsel of my messengers*. For the persons do oft interchange. See ch. 1.29. of Esay, and other of his prophets; as Jeremy, Ezekiel, and the rest, that foretold the downfall of Babylon, and the deliverance of God's people.

*{That saith to Jerusalem, Thou shalt be inhabited; and to the cities of Judah, ye shall be built; and I will raise up the decayed places thereof*} Or, *That say*; that give my people, by my prophets assurance of these things, to be undoubtedly effected. For what God says shall be, shall undoubtedly come to pass: Much more what he says himself will do, whose Word is his Will, and his will his Work. What he will have done, no power or policy of man, can prevent, avert, or avoid. He can frustrate all their designs; none can defeat his, Psal. 33.11,12. & 115.3. & 135.6.

*{inhabited*} Zach. 2.4.

*{cities of Judah*} Psalm 69.35.

*{decayed places*} Heb. *wastes*; as Neh. 1.5,8. & 2.1,2.

**V. 27.** *{That saith to the deep, Be dry; and I will dry up the rivers*} Or, *That say*: and so ver. 28. who with a word of my mouth, can dry up the sea, and his streams. He seems to have an eye to what he did at the Red Sea; as ch. 43.16. & 51.10,11. and, withal, to allude unto Cyrus his draining of Euphrates, at the taking of Babylon, Jer. 50.38. & 51.32,36. See Rev. 16.12.

*{Be dry*} A word of authority and ability conjoined, producing, irresistibly and instantly, an effect answerable to either. See the like of our Savior, Mark 4.39. to the sea likewise, *Be still*. The argument seems to run thus, for the confirmation of God's people. He that can with a word only lay the deep dry, Psalm 106.9. can as easily set his people free, and remove all obstructions that may hinder them, either in their way homeward; or their settling there. See ch. 40.3,4. Zach. 4.6,7.

**V. 28.** *{That saith of Cyrus, He is my Shepherd*} Or, *That say to Cyrus*, (for the particle is the very same that was, before) *Thou art my shepherd*: for in the text, there is no more, than, *my shepherd*. See the like concise form of speech, Chapter 41.26. and 43.9.

*{Cyrus*} To assure them of deliverance, he names the party by whom it should be effected, about two hundred years before he was born. See chap. 13.22. and the like, 1 Kings 13.2. This name he had from a Persian word, in that language said to signify the *Sun*; which they honored as a God; and some suppose that this word *Cores*, or *Cyrus*, was derived from the Hebrew *Cheres*, or *Chares*, that is used sometime for the *Sun*, see on chap. 16.11. and Jeremiah 19.2. it being not unusual with the Persians and Arabians, as some learned affirm, to turn the Hebrew *chet* into *Caph*. That the Sun is by the Persians so called, Plutarch, in the life of *Artaxerxes*, from Ctesias, and upon his credit, relates. But Joseph Scaliger, in his *emendation of times*, l. 6. supposes that Ctesias, being a Greek, was mistaken, by the similitude of sound, between *Corshed*, which, in Persic, signifies the *Sun*, and *Coresh*, which, in that language, says he, signifies *food*. Yet from the nearness of these two, some other learned seek to confirm the truth of the former. Howbeit, it may not unjustly be questioned, whether either of those words, *Coresh*, or *Corshed*, had such use, or signification, in those ancient times, that in the vulgar Persian, they have at this day; any more, than the word *Aphtab*, which now, also, they are said to use for the *Sun*. One main cause of my doubt is, because the Sun was among the ancient Persians, commonly known, called, adored, and attested, by the name of *Mithra*, or, as the Greeks are wont to pronounce it, *Mithras*, and *Mithres*; which appears by records undeniable, out of Strabo, l. 15. Plutarch, in the *life of Alexander*, and *of Artaxerxes*, his *discourse of Isis, & Osiris*, and oft elsewhere. Hence the *Mithriaca*, or feasts and rites, held and performed in honor of the Sun, and the name *Mithridata*, or *Mithridates*, common among them, Ezra 1.8. & 4.7. whereas of either of those two, or of any of those three names above mentioned. I find no such ancient and authentic record produced. If it be said, that the Sun might have more names than one or two, either among them, in those times, as in the Hebrew text of Scripture it has; that is true indeed; but some solid proof must be brought for particulars; whereby it may appear, that these were then names thereof with them. But see further, on chap. 45.4.

*{Shepherd*} Heb. *Pastor*. or *Feeder*, a title given usually to rulers and sovereigns, both in church and state, ch. 56.11. & 63.11. Jer. 2.8. & 23.1–4. Eph. 4.11. that which may admonish them of their office and duty; not *to rule*, only, as the word sometime signifies, Psa. 78.71,72. Mic. 1.14. but *to feed*, also, Chap. 40.11. Jer. 3.15. & 23.14. Ezek. 34.2,23. 1 Peter 5.2. And if the word *Coresh*, did in the Persic tongue, anciently, signify *food*, the name of *Cyrus*, might have a notion of feeding in it, answerable to that title that is here given him in the Hebrew.

*{my shepherd*} Nor as David, of God, Ps. 23.1. but as God, of Christ, Zach. 13.7.

*{and shall perform all my pleasure*} Both concerning Babylon, chap. 48.14. and concerning Jerusalem, and his Temple there, in the next words. God will do all his pleasure himself, Chapter 46.10. but not in these particulars, *by himself*, as he spread the earth, verse 24. but by Cyrus, chap. 13.3,17. & 45.13. & 46.11. Jer. 51.20–24.

*{even saying to Jerusalem*} Heb. *and saying*, or, *and that saying, say*: that say confidently, giving good assurance of what I say. See the like before, ver. 14. & Jer. 3.1.

*{Thou shalt be built*} Ch. 46.13. 2 Chron. 36.22,23. Ezra 1.1–3.

*{and to the Temple, Thy foundation shall be laid*} Ezra 3.10,11.

### CHAPTER 45

**V. 1.** *{Thus saith the Lord*} This chapter is also of the same subject with the former, and may not, without good probability, seem to be part of that prolix sermon, or prophecy, that began with the fortieth chapter, and ends with this; apparent it is, that this chapter begins, where that next before ended, Chap. 44.28.

*{to his anointed to Cyrus*} Among the people of God, two sorts of persons were anointed: kings, 1 Samuel 10.1. and 16.13. 2 Sam. 2.4. 1 Kings 1.39. 2 Kings 9.6. & 23.30. Psalm 89.20. and priests, Lev. 8.12. & 16.32. Num. 3.3. & 35.25. Psalm 133.2. as for the anointing of prophets, with material oil, there is no record extant in Scripture. Elias is willed to anoint Eliseus, prophet in his stead, to succeed him; but that he put in execution, only, by casting his mantle on him, 1 Kings 19.26,29. So that there to anoint, as it concerned Eliseus, yea, and Hazael too, for aught we find in the story, and comparing 1 Kings 19.25. with 2 Kings 8.13. signifies no more than to assign or design one to some special office or function, though no drop of material oil be shed on him to that purpose: so is Absolon said to have been *anointed*, by the people, for their king, 2 Sam. 19.10. though we read not, that that ceremony was used about him; and Christ is said to have been *anointed*, though not with any such material, Chap. 61.1. and so Cyrus, here, though no such custom of oiling kings were in his country. But he is called God's *Anointed*, because he was, as certainly, as sufficiently, and as efficaciously designed by God, and enabled unto the execution of those offices that God had appointed to be done by him, as if he had, at God's command, in the solemnest manner, been anointed by the hand of the highest Priest, or holiest prophet. For those Jewish masters are wide and wild here, (whom yet some Christian writers seem fondly to abet,) by his *anointed*, understanding not *Cyrus*, but *the Lord's Messiah*, or, *the Lord Messiah*, peculiarly so termed, *Christ*; as if the meaning were, *Thus saith the Lord, to his Messiah, concerning Cyrus*. But the text is plain, *to his Messiah*, or, *to his anointed, to Cyrus*, as *to his Messiah*, or *to his anointed, to David*, Ps. 18.50. there is an emphasis in it; here especially: to him, whom I now name, so long before he is in being. See ch. 44.28. and vers. 4.

*{whose right hand I have holden*} Or, *strengthened*; or, *I do*, or *will hold*, or, *strengthen*; for the word signifies; sometime, *to hold*, chap. 41.6,13. & 42.6. sometime, *to strengthen*, 2 King. 15.19. Dan. 11.1. But the particle, here used, carries it rather to the former as chap. 64.7. Yet so, as the latter is also implied; as if it were said; *whom I by holding his right hand* strengthen, or enable, *to subdue nations*. Of such concise and comprehensive manner of speech, see on ch. 38.17,21. Of the metaphor, Ps. 73.22. & 89.21. Ch. 41. ver. 10.

*{to subdue nations before him*} Or, as a late learned writer, *nations are to be overthrown*, or, *laid along before him*: that, says he, is the frequent use of the particle here used, as Chap. 44.14. But the received version may well stand. *Nations*, that is, the Babylonians, and others, that either lay in his way thither, or were assistant unto them, Jer. 50.21. & 51.9. So Psalm 144.2. & ch. 41.2. where the same word is used.

*{and I will loose the loins of Kings*} Or, *and that I may loose the loins of Kings*; or, *when I shall have loosed the loins of Kings*, or, *of their Kings*. See the like use of the copulative, Psal. 99.8. chap. 8.21. & 33.1. & 43.12. Neh. 2.13. Job 11.3. and the defect of the pronoun possessive; chap. 40.31. and 43.14. and 49.22. Heb. *open them*; as if their joints opened, and so were loosed one from another. Either by striking with the sword, through the loins, where wounds are deadly, Deuteronomy 33.11. and where the seat of strength is, Job 40.16. Nah. 2.1. or, by smiting them with terror, and with pains and anguish, thence proceeding, Ezek. 21.6. Dan. 5.6. ch. 21.3. or, as some of the Jewish commenters, by loosing the girdle from their loins, the emblem of strength and authority, Job 12.18. ch. 11.5. & 22.21. & 23.10. See ver. 5.

*{to open unto him the two-leaved gates*} Or, *that doors*; such as great men's houses and palaces are wont to have, Deut. 3.5. Ezek. 41.24. Mal. 1.10. See chap. 13.2. *may be opened to him*; or, *doors are to be opened to him*, as before, *nations to be subdued*.

*{and the gates shall not be shut*} Or, *that the gates may not stand shut*. The gates of great towns and cities: for of them is the word most commonly used, Josh. 2.5. 2 King. 7.1,3,10. put oft times also, therefore, for the city itself, Exodus 20.10. Deut. 16.11. & 28.51. no gates, or bars, shall be able to keep him out: all shall fly open before him, as Acts 12.10. See ver. 20. The whole passage may thus be rendered. *Whom holding by the right hand*, I will enable *to subdue nations before him, when I have loosed the loins of Kings; and to open the two-leaved doors unto him, so that no gates shall shut*. Or, *Whom I hold by my right hand, to subdue nations before him, whose Kings' loins I have loosed*: the copulative for the relative; as Chap. 4.6. & 17.2. *and to open the two-leaved doors unto him, so that no gates shall stand shut*: Of this use of the copulative, see Chap. 44.20. *Be shut*, for stand shut; as, *be open*, for stand open, chap. 60.11. and *be built*, for, stand built, Dan. 9.25.

**V. 2.** *{I will go before thee, and make the crooked places straight*} Or, *uneven ways, even*; the word rendered *crooked*, is no where else found, and ambiguous, therefore: the root it should come from, has a notion of *goodliness*, and *gloriousness*: nor want there those, who not improbably conjecture, that it signifies hilly places: two letters, *resh* and *daleth*, being in shape so near the one to the other, that they may easily be taken, and so are, sometime, the one for the other; *Diphath*, and *Rodanim*, for *Riphath*, and *Dodanim*, 1 Chr. 1.6,7. with Gen. 10.3,4. See, also, Chap. 40.15. Jer. 2.20. & 31.40. So the sense should be; *I will lay the hilly places level*: for the verb does manifestly signify, *to level*, or make plain and even, chap. 28.25. I will go before you to conduct you (as Exod. 13.21. ch. 58.8.) and to clear all your passages for you. See ch. 40.4. & 42.16. ver. 13.

*{I will break in pieces the gates of brass, and cut in sunder the bars of iron*} No strength shall be able to withstand you, or keep you out, Psal. 107.16. and 147.13. Prov. 18.19.

**V. 3.** *{And I will give thee the treasure of darkness, and hidden riches of secret places*} The rich treasures, as of other Kingdoms, so of Babylon, especially, Jer. 50.37. and 51.13. that have a long time been laid up, and lain out of sight; but you shall now seize on, and receive as a reward for your work done, for me and my people. See the like of Nebuchadnezzar, Ezek. 29.18–26.

*{that thou mayst know, that I the Lord, who call thee by thy name, am the God of Israel*} Or, *that it is I the Lord, who call thee by name, even the God of Israel*. Heb. *I have called thee by thy name*. See before, on ch. 44.28. and ver. 4. See also before, ch. 43.1.

**V. 4.** *{For Jacob my servant's sake, and Israel mine Elect*} See on ch. 41.8. it is out of God's love to his Elect, that he does all this, ch. 14.1. & 43.4,14.

*{I have even called thee by thy name: I have surnamed thee, though thou hast not known me*} That is, I have taken special notice of you, say some; as Exod. 34.12,17. Chap. 43.1. John 10.3. but it seems to intimate withal, a special denomination of him; because it is here more fully, than before, ver. 3. *I have called thee*, or, *call to thee, by thy name*, Exod. 31.2. and because there is mention of *a name*; and, *a surname*; some refer it unto that, which, of Cyrus, say they, is reported by Herodot, lib. 1. and by Justine after him, that being cast out by his grandfather's command, he was found sucking a bitch, and was thereupon called *Spaco*, which in the Persic tongue, signifies *a dog*; but after, coming to years, and to place of command, withal, was then called *Cyrus*, a name, that has a notion of power and authority in it, as they suppose may appear, by the Greek *Κῦρος*, that signifies *authority*; thence derived, and from it, *Κύριος*, *a Lord*, so that his first name should be *Spaco*, and his surname, *Cyrus*, before mentioned, in the last of the foregoing chapter, and the first of this. But of these fables, rather than stories, antiquity yields us not a few: as of Telephus, nursed by an hind or a doe, Romulus, and Remus by a female wolf, and the like. Howbeit, the truth is, that the authors produced do not so report, as is related; for the former says only, that the herdsman's wife was called *Spaco*, which in the Median tongue, answers the Greek *Cyno*, so termed, of a word that signifies *a dog*, or *bitch*, and that thence arose the idle figment, of his being suckled by a bitch, because he had been nursed by her, as from Romulus, and Remus his nurse, called *Lyco*, or *Lupa*, the like report was raised: and the latter, though he tell the tale, as a truth, yet he affirms the name *Cyrus*, to have been given him, while he lived in the herdsman's house: nor indeed is it so certain, what the name *Cyrus* imports: and much less, that those Greek terms had their original from the Persic: nor seems it so safe, to build expositions of Scripture, on such sandy ground: nor, lastly, does the word here used signify that which we usually call a *surname*. The word signifies, properly, *to extitle*, or *entitle* one, to give him some eminent, or honorable, title: so Elihu tells Job, that he could not, nor durst, give titles, as in way of flattery, men use to do, Job 32.21,22. & Chap. 44.5. it is said, *one shall entitle himself by the name of Israel*: call himself one of those that belong to Israel: as our Savior calls Nathanael, *a true Israelite*, John 1.47. and two of his apostles, James, and John, *the sons of thunder*, Mark 3.17. the word therefore, here, has no reference to the term *Cyrus*, (for that was his proper, and peculiar name,) but to those other high, and honorable titles, that God here gives him, and would rather be rendered, *I have extitled*, or *styled thee*; or *I have given thee an honorable style*, or *title*, to wit, in calling you *Cyrus my shepherd*, Chap. 44.28. and *Cyrus, mine anointed*; for that is the style, and those the titles, that God here fastens upon him. The words may be rendered, either by connection with the former verse, *That thou mayst know, that it is I the Lord, that call thee by name, the God of Israel, for Jacob my servant's sake, and Israel mine Elect* (for so the verses, sometime, break, in the middle of a sentence: as Psalm 96.12,13. & 98.8,9. chap. 64.1. Jer. 41.18. and 50.13.) *I both call thee by thy name, and give thee honorable titles.* So is the copulative oft used, Psal. 76.7. Jer. 17.26. howsoever, the latter part of this verse, seems most fitly, either thus rendered, or *I then called thee*, &c.—*when thou knewest not me*: as Chapter 31.3. & 44.14.

*{though thou hast not known me*} Heb. *and thou knowest me not*: or *when thou knewest me not*: as Chapter 33.1. and 43.12. before ever you had any notice at all of me; but were, by means thereof, afterward brought thereunto. See Ezra 1.1.

**V. 5.** *{I am the Lord, and there is none else; there is no God besides me*} Ch. 43.11. & 44.6,8.

*{I girded thee with strength, though thou hast not known me*} I gave you power and might, (as Psal. 18.32.11,5. a metaphor from persons *girt*, who are in that regard, both more active and stronger. See on v. 1.) or, I stirred you up, to gird, and get on your armor, to make warlike preparations, and set upon an expedition, (as 1 King. 20.11. 1 Sam. 24.13. Psal. 45.3,4.) though you then little thought on me, or who it was, that did set on work, or that did so prosper and strengthen you, ver. 1,2. or, *when as yet, thou wast* altogether *ignorant of me*: as verse 4. See also, Chapter 13.3–5,17. and 10.6,7.

**V. 6.** *{That they may know from the rising of the Sun, and from the west, that there is none besides me; I am the Lord, and there is none else*} Or, *That it may be known*: as Chap. 59.19. See Mal. 1.11. That by the deliverance of my people, which I will effect by you, my name, and renown, may pass through the whole world, and men in all parts, come to the notice of it, by occasion of your proclamations concerning it, & your acknowledgment thereof therein published, Ezra 1.1,2.

*{the West*} Heb. *evening coast*: as Psalm 113.3. Chapter 43.5.

*{I am the Lord*} Or, *that I am the Lord*: as Chapter 41.7. & 43.17.

**V. 7.** *{I form the light, and create darkness*} Heb. *Framing light, and creating darkness*; or, *That frame light, and create darkness*. That send prosperity, and adversity; the one, at some times; the other, at other times: and the one, to some; the other, to others, Ester 4.3. & 8.16,17. Psalm 97.11. & 112.4. Eccles. 3.1,4. as by the motion of the celestial bodies, I make the air, either lightsome, or dark, Gen. 1.2–5. Psalm 19.1,2. & 74.16. & 104.20. Jer. 31.35. & 33.20. for thereunto he here alludes.

*{I make peace, and create evil*} Heb. *making*, or, *that make*; and *create*, or *that create peace*, that is, prosperous success and safety; as Judg. 18.6. Ch. 48.18. as to Cyrus and his forces; so to his own people by him, and them, Chapter 26.3. & 57.18,19. *Evils*, that is, calamities to the Babylonians, and their complices, Chapter 47.9,11.

*{I the Lord do all these things*} Or, that (as before) *I the Lord do*, or that it is, *I the Lord, who do all these things*; as ch. 44.21. See Lam. 3.37,38. Amos 3.6.

**V. 8.** *{Drop down ye heavens from above; and let the skies pour down righteousness; let the earth open, and let them bring forth salvation, and let righteousness spring up together*} These words are diversely expounded. Some understand them, as a calling upon heaven and earth, the whole world, to rejoice, upon the deliverance of God's people; as chap. 44.23. So the ancient Greek, and those that follow it; Though some suppose that this reading came there by a mistake of the transcriber. Others, of their concurring, and conspiring together, in carrying on that work, that God was now, by Cyrus, setting on foot for the destruction of Babylon, and the deliverance of God's people, according to his judgment, the one, to his faithfulness, the other. See Josh. 10.13. Judg. 5.20. 1 Sam. 7.10. Psalm 18.9–14. & 85.11. Others make it a description of Cyrus his prosperous and plentiful reign, accompanied with justice, clemency and bounty: in regard whereof, the Persians were wont to call *Cyrus* a *father*; *Cambyses*, his son, a *Lord*, and *Darius*, his successor, a *Merchant*, or *a Trader*: so Herodote, lib. 3. And indeed somewhat after this manner, is Solomon's reign described, Psalm 72.6,7. Some draw it all to a spiritual sense, as a promise from God, that holiness and righteousness, should abound as plentifully among them, after their return from captivity, (the people being thereby refined, and reformed, chap. 48.10.) as the earth is wont to abound with fruit, when it has been liberally watered with rain from above, Psalm 65.10–13. & 68.9. For they seem to dive overdeep, that find Christ, and the Virgin Mary, here: as many also do the like, Psalm 72.6. & 85.11. Those seem to come near to the true sense of the text, who suppose, therein to be intimated an abundant blessing of God upon his people, in their state now again to be restored; and that set forth in certain metaphorical phrases, borrowed from those means, whereby lands are wont to become fertile and fruitful, and the benefits of plenty, peace, prosperity and safety, that unto people from thence accrue. See the like, Psalm 72.3,6,7,16. & 85.9–12. chap. 35.1,2,9. Hos. 2.21–23. Howbeit, I conceive the genuine sense of the place to be this, That God's mercy and goodness, should so manifestly, and plentifully appear, in the deliverance of his people, and disposing all things for their behoof, as if the heavens rained down whole showers of it upon them, and the earth, having received it, should return a plentiful improvement of it, that it seems to be the proper intendment of the like passages, in those places, Ps. 85.11. & ch. 61.11.

*{Drop down*} Not a prayer for a blessing, as some would have it, by man: but a command, rather, of blessing from God, Deut. 28.8,12. Psalm 78.23. Ezek. 34.26. Mal. 3.10. as a countermand on the other side, cross thereunto, Chap. 5.6.
