*{pour down righteousness*} Or, *in righteousness*; as Psalm 72.3. & Joel 2.23. two parallel places: that is, in a due, just, and full measure: or, showers of *righteousness*; as *rain of liberalities*, Psalm 68.9. and *showers of benediction*, Ezek. 34.26. for large and plentiful rain; or, of *righteousness*; that is, of mercy, bounty and goodness: for so the word is, in Scripture, very frequently used, Ps. 112.3,9. 2 Cor. 9.9,10.

*{let the earth open*} Or, *open itself*; for such verbs, neutrally taken, have oft a reciprocal sense: see Ch. 44.16. So *to be hard*, or *to harden*; (as the form of the verb carries it) for, *to harden one's self*, Job 9.4. & 39.16. or *open*, by a defective form, for, *open its mouth*, as it is at full, Genesis 4.11. and Numbers 16.30,32. But so it is also, Ps. 106.17. *the earth opened*; to wit, her mouth; as, *I opened*, to wit, the door, Cant. 5.6. *open*, to receive, and take in, what comes down upon it from above, Deut. 11.11.

*{let them bring forth salvation, and let righteousness spring up together*} That is, say some, *Let* the things on earth, *bring forth salvation*. Others, *that salvation and righteousness, may spring forth*; and *it*, (to wit, the earth) *may produce, them together*. But I find not where the former verb is so used, as may well warrant this version. I suppose the text may not, amiss, be thus rendered, *That* (as verse 1.) *they* (that is, heaven and earth, as it were between them) *may bring forth salvation*; (that is, *deliverance*, or, *safety*: as chap. 16.1. & 60.18. to my people) *and it* (that is, the earth, as Gen. 3.18. Deut. 29.23. so watered from above) *may cause righteousness to sprout forth together* with it, either God's goodness, or his faithfulness, therein manifested, and magnified. See these two joined, Chapter 56.1.

*{I the Lord hath created it*} Or, as some, *God will create it*: as ch. 41.20. That God, who has an absolute command and power over heaven and earth, has appointed these things to be done, or, is he that will do them: as Ps. 109.27. But others rather (because the pronoun is a masculine,) *I have created him*, to wit, Cyrus: I have fitted & furnished him with parts and abilities, for this purpose, to deliver my people, and to do execution on their enemies, ch. 44.28. So chap. 43.7.

**V. 9.** *{Woe unto him that striveth with his Maker*} This passage is here inserted, as some think, to curb and restrain the impatience of some spirits among God's own people, who growing weary of their long continuance in captivity, began to murmur against God, and complain of him, as if he dealt not so equally with them, nor so advisedly, in delivering them up to the will, and detaining them so long in the hands of those that thereby took occasion to blaspheme his name, Chap. 52.5. Ezek. 36.20. and refusing, withal, to await God's leisure, and abide his pleasure, either for their continuance, in that dejected estate, or their deliverance out of it; as by him, in his wisdom, should be deemed meet. See Chap. 28.16. As others, to check and control the pride and presumption of their enemies, the Babylonians especially, who made account to keep God's people in an everlasting slavery, chap. 14.17. Yea, to make their part good against God himself, if he should attempt to rescue them out of their hands. See Chap. 10.11. & 37.10. Dan. 3.15. It may well intend either, or both rather, with many other passages of God's providence, concerning the affairs of those times; which flesh and blood would be overprone to be quarreling with God about, and controlling his carriage of them. See chap. 40.27. and 49.14.

*{striveth with his Maker*} Either by opposing his intentions, or by controlling his dispensations. Some taint whereof, in heavy pressures, takes hold sometime, even of the godly, though they check, recall, reprove, and recover themselves, eftsoons, again. See Job 21.7–13. Psalm 73.1–22. Jeremiah 12.1,2. Habakuk 1.2–4,13,14.

*{his Maker*} Heb. *his potter*, or *him that framed him*, Chapter 44.24. and 64.8. an allusion to the matter, and manner, of man's first creation, where the same term is used, Genesis 2.7.

*{let the potsherd strive with the potsherds of the earth*} That is, *with earthen potsherds*, like itself: as if he had said, if frail man, who is but an earthen pot, 2 Cor. 4.7. made out of the earth, Gen. 2.7. & 3.19. will needs be contending, let him pick out his match to contend with, let him cope with man like himself; but let him take heed how he attempt to be dealing with his Maker, how he enter into the lists with him, who is infinitely stronger than himself, Eccl. 6.10. 1 Cor. 1.25. & 10.22. See Jer. 18.3,4,6. or, as some render the words, *as the potsherd, with earthen potsherds*; as if it were said, that contends with his potter, as if he were, being but an earthen pot, at the best, contending and quarreling with some other such as himself: the defect of the note of similitude is frequent. See ch. 21.8. & 28.1,4. and the supply of the verb from a former passage, no less usual. See ch. 44.11,18. Some would render it, *the potsherd with the workers of the earth*: that is, with some one of the potters. But I find not the word any where so used: that for *a workman*, Chapter 44.12,13. differs from this, as *Shibboleth*, from *Sibboleth*, Judges 12.6.

*{shall the clay say to him that fashioneth it, what makest thou?*} What is it, that you intend to make? as controlling his intentions, either as not fit or, as not feasible: or, why did you frame me in this, or that manner, in other manner than I would have had you to have done? See Jer. 18.4,6. Rom. 9.20. and somewhat the like, ch. 10.15.

*{or thy work, it hath no hands*} That is, you have not sufficiently polished your work, you have not done it so exactly, as you should: it has not yet the last hand, as we say, put to it. But the words may rather be read, *or*, Heb. *and*: as Chap. 44.10.) *For thy work there are not hands*; you want hands, that is, power and ability, to go through, with what you intend; you foretell, or promise, more than you are able to perform, or bring about. See 2 King. 7.2. But I rather here incline to that late learned annotator, who, from the former branch, renders the words, *or* shall *thy work* say, (to wit, of the workman,) *he hath not hands?* shall it deny him to have hands, by whose hands it was made.

**V. 10.** *{Woe unto him, that saith to his father, what begettest thou? and to the woman, what hast thou brought forth?*} Another similitude, whereby God illustrates the unreasonableness of those, that will take upon them, to control, or quarrel, with their Maker; either charging him with impotency, or challenging him of indiscretion: as if the child should quarrel with his parents, about the breeding of him, in such and such times, or in such and such manner; (see Job 3.3–12. Jer. 15.10. & 20.14,18.) or rather, (and so it answers fitly to the latter branch of the former verse, (to what end do you breed, or attempt to breed; you will never be able to bear, or bring forth, much less to bring up; and you were best, therefore, to forbear. See Chapter 66.9. the issue is introduced by an allegory, speaking to the parents here, as the clay to the workman, there.

*{the woman*} *woman*, for, *mother*; as chap. 49.15. and this term is the rather used here; because the speech is conceived, as with some kind of scorn, as our Savior also used it, to his mother, in somewhat a tart reproof, for her a little overmuch presumption, John 2.4.

**V. 11.** *{Thus saith the Lord, the Holy One of Israel, and his Maker*} Chap. 43.15. & 44.2.

*{Ask me of things to come concerning my sons: and concerning the work of my hands, command ye me*} Or, as some, somewhat allaying the harshness of the term, *commend unto me* (to wit, by prayer) *my children and the work of my hands*; that is, yourselves, Chap. 60.21. my new creatures, 2 Cor. 5.17. my workmanship in Christ, Eph. 2.10. Seek you to me, for the accomplishment of my promise, concerning my children themselves, my handiwork, or concerning those works that are to be wrought for them; and you shall find me as ready to do you service, as if you had me at command, (see Josh. 10.14.) you shall not fail, to obtain whatsoever you request, 1 John 5.14. But the words seem spoken rather by way of reproof, directed unto the idolaters, and enemies of God's people. And some therefore would thus read them; *Ask me of things to come, and concerning my children, and the work of my hands enjoin me*; as if it were said, seek for information concerning things to come, to me the true God, who am able to foretell them, Chap. 42.9. & 43.12. & 44.7. and not to your idols, who are not able to foretell you aught, Chap. 41.22,23,26. & 43.9. & 44.7. See the like, Jer. 33.3. Zach. 10.1,2. and try, withal, if you can countermand, inhibit, or hinder me, in those things, that I intend to do, concerning my people. So the word of *enjoining*, is used sometime, in a notion of *inhibition*; as Deut. 2.37. Chap. 5.6. But I suppose the words may well be read, as spoken by way of interrogation, and thus rendered, *Do ye question me* (as Chap. 41.28.) *concerning the things to come?* (concerning those things that I intend to do,) *concerning my sons*, (or, *children*) *and concerning the work of my hands, will ye enjoin me?* or, *order me?* as the word is used, chap. 38.1. will you presume to appoint, and direct me, what I shall do, and how I shall carry matters concerning the disposition of my people? See chap. 40.13,14. Rom. 11.33,34. so it agrees very fitly with v. 9. & 10. and speaks more plainly what these similitudes there intimate; to wit, that it is overmuch boldness for man to take upon him, to teach, or control God in aught.

**V. 12.** *{I have made the earth, and created man upon it*} See Gen. 1.1,27. Psalm 102.25. chap. 42.5. & 48.13. ver. 18. I framed at first, this vast universe, without advice, or aid of any; and have, by mine infinite power and wisdom, supported, and ruled it, ever since, to this day: and want not, therefore, either ability to go through with; or skill, to manage whatsoever I undertake. See chapter 41.24.

*{I even my hands have stretched out the heavens*} Ps. 8.3. & 104.2. ch. 42.5.

*{and all their host have I commanded*} Or, *do I command*; have I continually at command, ch. 40.26.

**V. 13.** *{I have raised him up in righteousness*} Cyrus, he means, Ezra 1.1. to manifest the faithfulness of his promises, in the deliverance of his people; ver. 3,4. See chap. 41.2. & 42.6. or, *in truth*, as ver. 23. See chap. 41.26.

*{and I will direct all his ways*} Heb. *make straight*, or, *make even*. I will level all his ways: I will give him free passage, and ready success, in all his undertakings; I will facilitate for him all his designs. See ver. 2. & ch. 26.7.

*{he shall build my city*} Ch. 44.28. that is, give order for the building of it; the Temple especially, the principal part of it, Ezra 1.1. as the like is said of Solomon, Acts 7.47.

*{and he shall let go my captives*} Heb. *captivity*: as ch. 20.4. my people remaining in captivity under the Chaldeans.

*{not for price, nor reward, saith the Lord of Hosts*} Freely, without ransom, or any consideration. An argument of a royal mind, and of a right generous disposition. See Chapter 13.17.

**V. 14.** *{Thus saith the Lord; the labor of Egypt, and merchandise of Ethiopia, and of the Sabeans, men of stature shall come over unto thee*} Before, he told of their deliverance out of captivity, and the setting of them at liberty, now, he proceeds to show how, and by whom, they should be furnished with a rich and plentiful supply of such commodities, as should be requisite for the convenient settling of them, in their land again, and the furtherance of them, in those works, that were there to be wrought by them, fulfilled, as most imagine, in the contribution that these people, being tributary to Cyrus, should, at his command, plentifully afford unto God's people returning home from exilement, into their land, and towards the building of God's Temple, Ezra 1.4. & 7.21,22. See chap. 60.5–7. Howbeit, some other, not without some show of probability, expound this whole passage of Cyrus himself; of whom he spoke before, ver. 13. to wit, that because he had dealt so freely with God's people, as was before intimated; God would therefore give him, as a reward, of this his generous carriage, the wealth of those rich Kingdoms and countries, which, together with Babylon, of whom they formerly held, at the fall of that state, fell also into his hands. See vers. 3. Against which is objected, that the pronoun is in the feminine gender; which those, therefore, that stand for the former interpretation, refer either to the word *captivity*, in the former verse; or to the word *city*; but neither is needful: for of states does the Scripture speak usually, as of women, damsels, ladies, wives, or widows, Chap. 47.1,7,8. & 52.2. & 54.1. & 60.4–7. where the like promises are made unto the Jewish state, restored, with those here: which seems to carry it with the former. The transition from person to person, which either exposition presumes, is not unusual: See verse 17. Chapter 31.6,7. and 32.11,12. and 34.5,6. and 42.13,14.

*{the labor*} That is, the fruit of their labor, their wealth thereby gotten; as Psalm 128.2. Jer. 3.24.

*{Egypt*} A very rich Kingdom, 1 Kings 10.28,29. and so the other two rich countries. See Job 28.19. Psalm 72.10,15. of them, see on chap. 43.5. where, because the selfsame people are mentioned, some would have these two places parallel; and refer both to the diversion of Sennacherib: but of that, see there. Sure it is, that it can have no place here.

*{men of stature*} Heb. *measure*, or, *dimension*; as Num. 13.33. 2 Sam. 21.20. 1 Chr. 11.23. & 20.6. So Jeremiah 22.14. Men, tall, and big. Such are the Sabeans reported to have been, Agatharchides, l. 5. c. 50.

*{they shall come over unto thee*} Yield themselves unto you, whether to Cyrus, or to the church, and to Christ (of whom Cyrus a type,) in his church. See Ps. 45.12. & 68.31. & 72.9,10,11,15. ch. 18.7. and 19.21. Zeph. 3.9.

*{and they shall be thine*} Your subjects. See Chapter 19.23–25.

*{they shall come after thee*} As captives are wont to follow a conqueror, in triumph.

*{in chains they shall come over;*} As prisoners, or, captives, Job 36.8. 2 Chr. 36.6. which concerning those, that were by Cyrus subdued corporally, is literally plain enough, but applied to those, that are brought in, by the ministry of the gospel, unto Christ, and his church, must be spiritually understood Ps. 45.5. and 149.6–8.

*{and they shall fall down unto thee*} After the manner of adoration, in use among the Eastern people; which yet Callisthenes, in Arrian, lib. 4. reports, not to have been received in Persia, before Cyrus his days. See chap. 49.23. & 60.14. Psal. 72.9,11.

*{they shall make supplication unto thee*} So Psal. 45.12. and 72.15.

*{saying*} A defect of the participle; as Psal. 105.15. Chapter 26.19.

*{surely God is in thee*} Either *in thee*, or *with thee*; O Cyrus showing it so to be, by giving you such success: as some. See Ver. 1,2. or, in a peculiar manner, in, and with Christ, of whom Cyrus a type, Exod. 23.21. Joh. 1.2. & 14.10. & 16.32. & 17.23. Acts 10.38. Col. 2.3,9. and both God and Christ, in his church, Ezek. 48.35. Zach. 8.23. 1 Cor. 14.15.

*{and there is none else, there is no god,*} That God, who is the only true; and besides whom there is none, ver. 6,21. Chapter 44.6.

**V. 15.** *{Verily thou art a God that hidest thyself*} The prophet's words, admiring the hidden depths of God's dispensations; as if he had said, You Lord do, for some time, seem to hide and withdraw yourself, to stand aloof off in your people's afflictions, Psal. 10.1. Chap. 57.17. and they must, therefore with patience, wait for their deliverance, though for a while it be delayed, Chap. 8.17. and 28.16. for they that so do, shall not repent them of their patience, but shall be delivered, when the wicked idol worshipers shall fail of their expectation, and be destroyed, ver. 15. chap. 30.18. and 44.23. Or, you do carry yourself so closely and covertly, in your dispensations, and in the passages of your providence, that your ways and judgments are unsearchable, and your intentions oft times undiscernible; and men ought not, therefore, to control and censure those things, that are past their shallow reach, Ps. 77.19. Rom. 11.33,34. and so it has reference to ver. 9,10,11.

*{O God of Israel, the Savior*} Chap. 43.3.

**V. 16.** *{They shall be ashamed, and also confounded all of them; they shall go to confusion together that are makers of idols*} Or, *The workmen of images shall be ashamed, and even confounded all of them; they shall go together to confusion*, Psal. 97.7. & 115.8. Chapter 44.11.

*{Idols*} So called, either of a word that signifies *pains* and *throes*, Chap. 13.8. & 21.3. because they procure to men nothing but sorrow and distress. See Chap. 10.10. & 46.1. or, from another, that signifies the figure and fashion of aught, Psal. 49.14. Ezek. 43.11. See Chap. 44.13. Ezek. 8.10.

**V. 17.** *{But Israel shall be saved in the Lord with an everlasting salvation*} *in the Lord*, ver. 25. or, *By the Lord*, as Psal. 33.16. and Chap. 30.15. Heb. *with a salvation of ages*, or, *perpetuities*, or *eternities*, as Chap. 26.4. Dan. 9.24. See Chap. 54.6,8.

*{ye shall not be ashamed, nor confounded, world without end.*} Heb. *unto ages of perpetuity*, Psal. 25.3. Joel 2.26,27. Rom. 9.33. See the like passage from person to person, Chap. 1.29. & 46.1.

**V. 18.** *{For thus saith the Lord, that created the heavens*} Gen. 1.1. ver. 12.

*{God himself, that formed the earth, and made it*} Or *that God*, as (2 Chron. 28.22.) or, *the same*, (as Psal. 102.27.) *that fashioned the earth, and made it*,) who (not made it of nothing, but) out of that rude mass, which at first it was, wrought it into that, fashion, that now it bears, Gen. 1.1,2,9,11.

*{he hath established it*} Or, *he that established it*, Psal. 93.1. and 119.90,91. Eccl. 1.4. or, *that prepared*, or, *fitted*, or, *furnished it* as Ps. 119.73. *Thy hands have made me, and fitted me*, or *furnished me*, with abilities, for employment: So the word is frequently used, Exod. 19.11,15. Josh. 8.4. Job 8.8. Psal. 7.12. and 21.12. fitted it for man's use, by laying it dry, and furnished it with all necessaries for his support, Gen. 1.9,11,29.

*{he created it not in vain*} Or, *who created it, not in vain*. The same word is here used, that is found, Gen. 1.2. as if he had said, who though of nothing he made it a rude mass, and misshapen lump, or a vast and waste body, at first, yet did not intend that it should so continue: the same term is used, Chap. 24.10. and 34.11. and 44.9. A defect of the relative; as Ch. 44.2.

*{he formed it to be inhabited*} Or, *who formed it to be inhabited*: by man principally, Psal. 119.16. and of mankind, chiefly, for his church, 1 Cor. 3.22,23. Heb. *to inhabit*, for man *to inhabit*, or, *to be inhabited*. See Chap. 13.20. Some apply this, more especially, to the land of Judea, which he had assigned for his people, and fitted and furnished it accordingly for them. Gen. 12.7. and 13.15. and 15.18. Deut. 11.10. Psal. 136.21,22. But the text seems larger.

*{I am the Lord and there is none else*} Ver. 14,21,22.

**V. 19.** *{I have not spoken in secret, in a dark place of the earth*} I have delivered my oracles, from time to time openly in public, and that plainly and perspicuously, for the most part, as I now also do, Deut. 4.11,13,14. and 5.22. and 30.11–14. chap. 48.16. Jer. 3.12. Joh. 18.20. not as your false gods, that deliver their oracle in dark caves and corners, from under the ground, places fit for deceit; and in obscure and ambiguous terms, such as may bear contrary senses, that their fraud and ignorance may not be discovered, chap. 8.19. and 29.4.

*{in a dark place of the earth*} Heb. *in a place of the earth of darkness*, for some *dark place of the earth*; as Psal. 74.20.

*{I said not to the seed of Jacob, Seek ye me in vain:*} Or, *I have not said*, &c.

*{the seed of Jacob*} All whose issue God took to be in covenant; that which he did not with the whole issue, either of Abraham, or Isaac, Psal. 22.23. so ver. 25.

*{Seek ye me*} Psal. 27.8. & 105.4.

*{in vain:*} The same word used before, ver. 18. *Not in vain*, because I perform what I promise, and do not frustrate their expectations, being both able to do for them, what they seek to me for; and faithful to keep touch with them, Psal. 9.10. & 22.4,5. whatsoever worldlings think of me, Job 21.15. & 22.17. Mal. 3.14. that which the heathen gods are not able to do for those that seek to them, ver. 20. chap. 46.7.

*{I the Lord speak righteousness; I declare things that are right.*} Or, *I am the Lord* (as chap. 44.24.) *that speak righteousness*, (that is, *righteous things*, as chap. 56.1. or, *in righteousness*, (as ver. 13. that is, righteously, faithfully, firmly, See chap. 63.1.) or, *that speak truth*, (as chap. 41.26. ver. 23.) *that declare things equal*. Heb. *even*, or *right*, and *straight*. See chap. 26.7. & 33.15. I neither require, nor deliver aught, but what is just and equal, Psal. 19.7–10. and 111.7,8.

**V. 20.** *{Assemble yourselves, and come; draw near together, ye that are escaped of the nations.*} This some understand of the Jews returned from the Babylonian captivity, having escaped the Chaldean sword, chap. 43.6. and 66.19. Jer. 50.28. Others, of proselytes converted to Judaism, upon the dissolution of the Jewish captivity, chap. 44.5. or, converted to Christianity, by the ministry of the gospel, Zach. 8.21,22. Eph. 2.12,13,19. Col. 1.21. But I concur rather with those, who expound it of those Chaldeans, or, rather, nations, that had escaped the sword of Cyrus, and were now, having by experience been taught it, able to see, how much God was able to do for his people: how little their idols, for those that them served. Jer. 51.50. See chap. 43.9.

*{they have no knowledge, that set up the wood of their graven image*} *That set up* (alluding either to the posture of their images, or to the bearing of them in pomp on their shoulders, chap. 46.1,8. Jer. 10.13.) their wooden idols, or their graven or carved (see chap. 40.20.) images of wood, Dan. 5.4,23. But the phrase is emphatical; that set up a piece of wood for their god, as a piece of *brass*, or, *brazen stuff*, 2 King. 18.4. and *bricks*, or *brick stuff*, chap. 65.3. See chap. 44.15–20.

*{and pray unto a god that cannot save*} Heb. *to a god, will not*, or *shall not save*: as *to a people, will not*, or, *shall not save*, Lam. 4.17. and, *to a people, will not* or, *shall not profit*, chap. 30.5,6. a defect of the relative; and a future taken potentially. See chap. 44.17. Jer. 2.27. Hos. 4.12.

**V. 21.** *{Tell ye, and bring them near: yea, let them take counsel together.*} Or, *Declare, and draw near*, (there is an elegant consonancy in the words) or, *approach*: (so is the word used, Amos 9.10.) *yea, let them consult together*, as, Psal. 71.10. Some expound it, of coming home to God, and bringing of others with them: as chap. 2.3. Zach. 8.23. but that follows, ver. 22. this is rather of coming to debate. See chap. 41.22,23,28. & 48.14.

*{who hath declared this from ancient time? who hath told it from that time?*} Heb. *who hath made to hear this?* (as chap. 41.22.) or *caused this to be heard*, (as ver. 18. *to be inhabited*) *from antiquity?* or, *from before?* (of old, as Psal. 68.33. & 74.12. Hab. 1.12.) *hath told it from then?* as chap. 44.8. See chap. 41.26. and 48.14. he utters this, as spoken in those times, when Cyrus had won Babylon, and set God's people free.

*{Have not I the Lord? and there is no god else, besides me, a just god and a Savior, there is none beside me.*} Or, *have not I the Lord, beside whom there is no god else, a just and a saving god; beside whom* (I say) *there is none*: the pronoun indicative, for the relative: as chap. 37.27. nor need, *there is*, be in a different character, because that negative, of course, includes the verb substantive. See chap. 43.12.

*{no god else*} Ver. 5,18.

*{a just god, and a savior*} Chap. 43.11. and 63.1.

**V. 22.** *{Look unto me, and be ye saved all the ends of the earth:*} Considering the issue of these things, and how therein, as well my power & deity, as the imbecility & vanity of your idols, has most evidently appeared: leaving them out of all parts, as far as the world is wide betake yourselves to me, who am the only true God, and able to afford you that safety which your idols cannot. See Verse 16,17.

*{Look unto me*} As to a place of safe receipt, and sure refuge, Psal. 34.5. chap. 17.7,8. or as the Jews, sometime, to the brazen serpent, Numb. 29.8,9. Joh. 3.14,15. and 6.40.

*{be ye saved*} Or, *ye shall be saved*: the imperative, for the future: as *do this, and live*, Gen. 42.18. that is, *ye shall live*, Luke 8.28. so Psal. 37.27. chap. 36.16.

*{all the ends of the earth*} All the inhabitants of the world, from one end to another, Psal. 22.27. & 65.8.

*{for I am God, and there is none else.*} Ver. 22. and that you are now convinced of, by what you have seen, ver. 26.

**V. 23.** *{I have sworn by myself,*} Gen. 22.16. having no greater to swear by, Heb. 6.13. So Jer. 22.5. & 49.13.

*{the word is gone out of my mouth in righteousness,*} A defect of the preposition, as chap. 41.2. *in righteousness*, that is, justly, upon good ground, and agreeable to right and equity: one of the conditions required in an oath, Jer. 4.2. in righteousness, that is, righteously, firmly, and faithfully: so as what I say, shall be certainly fulfilled, and this sense, the words next following, confirm; See chap. 63.1. some read it, *out of my mouth*, a mouth *of righteousness*, (as *right hand of righteousness*, chap. 41.10.) that is, *out of my righteous*, or, *out of a most righteous mouth*, Psal. 119.172. ver. 19. and some, by *righteousness* here understand *truth*: as, also, chap. 41.26.

*{and shall not return:*} What I have uttered, shall not be revoked or reversed, being, especially, bound thus with a solemn oath, Ps. 89.34,35. & 132.9. or, it shall not return without effect; but shall most surely and certainly be performed and fulfilled, ch. 48.3. & 55.10,11. See Josh. 8.26. and 2 Sam. 1.22.

*{that unto me every knee shall bow, every tongue shall swear.*} That the knowledge, and acknowledgment of me, by submission to me, and worship done me, shall pass through the whole world: and it is your wisest course, therefore, to come willingly in unto me, ver. 22. Psal. 2.8–10. & 22.27–31. and 86.9. 110.2,3. Phil. 2.10. Rom. 14.11. where the apostle applies it to the last judgment, and Christ's power and authority, that then shall be manifested and exercised by him; which though it be not the main drift of God's speech, in this place: yet is it therein necessarily included.

*{every knee shall bow*} They shall not have me in reverend estimation and serve me inwardly in heart only, Chap. 59.19. Mal. 1.11,14. but shall manifest it by outward expressions, and profession also. See 1 King. 19.18.

*{tongue shall swear*} Swear by me, or swear allegiance to me. See ch. 19.18. & 48.1.

**V. 24.** *{Surely, shall one say, in the Lord have I righteousness and strength*} Or, *Surely, shall he say of me*, (so is the particle used, Gen. 20.13. Chap. 41.7. (*In the Lord is righteousness.* Heb. *righteousnesses*; as Judges 5.11. Psal. 103.6. Dan. 9.6. Mic. 6.5. that is, all righteousness, or abundance of righteousness) and strength. The faithful shall find, feel, and acknowledge all faithfulness and righteous dealing, with strength all sufficient, to be found in God, Job 12.13,16. Psal. 36.5,6. & 145.3,11,12,17. or, their righteousness and spiritual ability to come from him, Zach. 12.5. John 15.5. 2 Cor. 3.5. Phil. 2.13. & 3.9. & 4.13.

*{shall one say*} Heb. *shall he say*, each one *shall say*, or, *it shall be said*, as chap. 25.9.

*{even to him men shall come, and all that are incensed against him shall be ashamed*} Most men read these words, as two distinct sentences; the former, concerning those, who perceiving all power and faithfulness to be in the true God alone, shall voluntarily repair unto him, and adjoin themselves to his people, embracing the advice given them, verse 22. Psalm 65.2. Jer. 16.19. The other, concerning those, that (obstinately stand out against him, and provoke him thereby to wrath, that such shall be put to everlasting shame and confusion, verse 16. Jeremiah 17.13. Yet some, in regard of some distinctions in the original, make them, in effect at least, but one; and these render them two ways. Some, as spoken of persons reclaimed, and affected with a religious shame, arising from the consideration of their former follies. *To him shall they come, and be ashamed, all that have been incensed against him*, Jer. 31.18,19. Others, as spoken of the obstinate and impenitent wicked, and those only, *To him shall they come*, (that is, before his tribunal they shall appear, Rom. 14.10,11. 2 Cor. 5.12.) *and shall* (there, and then) *be ashamed*, (and confounded, chap. 1.29–31. & 2.19–21. Rev. 6.15–17.) *as many as are incensed against him*, Psal. 2.1,2,12. & 21.8–12. & 92.9. For as for those, that understanding the words of the same persons, do thus read them, as a speech of the former parties, speaking on still of God, *Let him come to him, to bicker with him; they shall be ashamed, all that are in heat against him*. It seems to me, to force the text too much; as, also, some other do, whom I therefore let pass.

*{shall men come*} Heb. *he shall come*, as before, *he shall say*: *there shall be coming to him*, to wit, by such as were before spoken of. See on ch. 2.19.

*{that are incensed against him*} See the like of God's people, chap. 41.11.

**V. 25.** *{In the Lord shall all the seed of Israel be justified*} Or, *By the Lord shall all the seed of Israel be justified*: as, *by myself*: v. 23. That which most interpreters expound of justification, and discharge of their sins, by faith in Christ, Acts 10.43. & 13.37,38. Rom. 5.24,25,28. & 5.1. Gal. 2.16. chap. 53.11. as the righteousness, before spoken of, verse 24. of the righteousness by faith, Rom. 1.17. & 3.21,22. 2 Cor. 5.21. Phil. 3.9. drawing hither, what was before said, of blotting out, and doing away their sins, ch. 27.9. & 33.24. & 43.25. & 44.22. Howbeit, I suppose it may be understood of God's justifying of his people, by approving their sincerity, as he did Job's, against Satan's calumnies, and the groundless surmises of his friends, Job 2.3. & 13.18. & 23.10. and declaring their innocence and unjust sufferings, in regard of those, at whose hands they suffered: as he justified David, against the false charges and suggestions of Saul, and his flatterers, 1 Sam. 24.9.18. Psal. 7.3–5,8. so chap. 50.8. *He is near, that justifieth me*, to wit, against the false aspersions, and wrongful imputations of mine adversaries. To clear this a little more, because most, if not all, run the other way; The enemies of God's people pretended, that they had just cause, and good ground, to deal with them, as they did; they are lawful prize said they, and we may justly keep them: and there is no just cause, or reason, that we should be compelled to part with them, chap. 49.24. Jer. 40.33. yea, they took occasion to justify their extreme cruel dealing with them, chap. 47.6. by a pretense of doing justice, in God's behalf, on them, *We offend not* (say they) *in destroying, and devouring them; for they have trespassed grievously against their God*, Jer. 50.7. But God tells both his people, and them, that he would plead the cause of his people against them, and both clear their innocence, by discovering the vanity of these their frivolous pretenses, and do them right on them, as well by rescuing them out of their hands of those that held them; as by taking vengeance on them, for the wrong done to his people, chap. 46.13. & 49.25,26. & 51.5,22,36. Thus God's people presume, that God would clear the righteousness of their cause, as the light, Mic. 7.9,10. compared with Psal. 37.6. and upon the dissolution of the captivity, they acknowledge that God had so done, Jer. 51.10,24. And this I take to be the genuine sense of the place.

*{all the seed of Israel*} See verse 19. either the main body of them delivered out of captivity; (for even a wicked man may be justified, when he is wronged in aught,) or all the faithful, and truehearted among them, Ps. 24.6. John 1.47. Rom. 9.6. & 11.26. Gal. 6.16.

*{and shall glory*} In him, and not in themselves, v. 24. Psal. 56.4. and 106.4. Jer. 9.24. Rom. 3.27. & 5.1. 1 Cor. 1.30,31. Gal. 6.14. shall glory, in that salvation, either spiritual, or temporal, that he has wrought for them, Ps. 34.2. & 105.3. & 106.5. as one that is not cleared only, but righted, enlarged, and avenged on his malicious adversaries, Ps. 64.9,10. ch. 41.16.

### CHAPTER 46

**V. 1.** *{Bel boweth down, and Nebo stoopeth*} In this chapter, and the next to it, (as in the thirteenth, and fourteenth before,) is laid down a very pregnant prophecy against Babylon, containing in it, a prediction of her utter and unavoidable overthrow, together with a general deliverance of God's people, that had been long in thraldom under her. Wherein, also, by the way, is inserted, an assertion of God's incomparable divine power, therein manifested, illustrate by the vanity and imbecility of the Babylonian idols, that should fall, and come down together with that state. In regard whereof, some interpreters deem this to be but a part of the precedent prophecy, and make them one continued context. This chapter begins with the ruin of their idols, as the next with the ruin of their state; which their idols were not able to support, being unable to keep up themselves.

*{Bel*} *Bel*, and *Nebo*, were idols of much note among the Babylonians; and *Bel* seems to have been their chiefest and choicest god. See Jer. 50.2. & 51.44. The name, divers writers of special note, suppose to be the same with *Baal*, conceived in a different dialect. And that this title, signifying *Lord*, was sometime given to the true God, as *the Lord of heaven and earth*, Matth. 11.25. in like manner, as the Phenicians called their god, *Baal-samen*, that is, *the Lord of heaven*, as out of Sanchuniathon, and Philo, his translator, Eusebius relates in his *Gospel-preparative*: but that afterward, God refused so to be styled, because the name had been so commonly given unto idols, Hos. 2.16. and true it is, that the name of *Baal*, as it signifies a *Lord*, does, in regard of God's absolute sovereignty, best agree unto God, but in that regard, he is in Scripture rather termed *Adonai*. Whereas that of *Baal*, both in the term itself, there paralleled with *Ish*, that signifies an *husband*, as also, in the use of the word from whence it comes, is attributed to God, not so much in regard of that his general dominion, which he has over the whole creation, Psalm 103.19. as in regard of that special relation which he has to his church, as he has contracted her to himself, in a conjugal bond, and she stands so espoused, and united unto him. See chap. 54.5. & 62.4. Jer. 3.14. & 31.32. though it be not denied, that the name *Adon*, or *Lord*, is sometime also given to the husband, Gen. 18.12. 1 Pet. 3.6. Howbeit, apparent it is, that this name of *Baal*, (though whether taken up from the use of God's people, uncertain, who are not read, to have called God, usually, by that name,) was very anciently given by the Moabites, Ammonites, Canaanites, Philistines, Sidonians, Phenicians, and other neighboring nations, as also by the idolatrous Israelites themselves, treading in their steps, to such idols, as both the one and the other adored, Num. 22.41. 1 King. 16.31,32. whence the mention of many *Baals*, Judg. 3.5,7. & 10.6,10. and those oft times distinguished, either by the places where their Temples stood, or by some peculiar attribute; as *Baal-Zephon*, Exodus 14.2. *Baal-Peor*, Num. 25.3. *Baal-Zebub*, 2 King. 1.1. *Baal-Meon*, Joshua 17.17. see on Chap. 15.2. and the like: as also names imposed as well on persons, as on places, from those their idols, as *Ethbaal*, the King of Sidon, Jezebel's father, 1 K. 16.31. *Baal-hanan* Ge. 36.38. the same, in a manner, with *Hannibal* reversed; & *Hierombal* the Priest, of whom, out of Porphyrie Eusebius, in the place before mentioned, the same, it may be with *Jerub-baal*, Jud. 6.32. as *Ambakum*, for *Abakkuk*: and *Ambuba* for *Abuba*, or as some, with *Hierombal*. That *Baal* therefore was a name common to many forged deities, is a thing undeniable; and from thence, divers learned men deem, that the name *Bel*, here used, did at first descend, being the same in notion, the one with the other, not differing but in manner of pronunciation, not as two divers words, but two dialects of one word, as *Zen*, and *Zan*, in Greek; for that, say they, which the Phenicians, following the Hebrews, pronounced *Baal*; that the Babylonians, after the Chaldean guise, pronounced *Bel*. Howbeit, some difference I observe between those great ones, that enforces me here to make a stand; for some of them, say, that *Baal* and *Bel* are written with the selfsame letters, בֵּעל the one; and בְּעֵל the other: Which if it be true, then the בֵּל֙ here mentioned, wanting the middle letter, seems not the same with *Baal*, in the Chaldee dialect. Other of them say, that the middle letter in *Bel*, is cast away, after the manner of the Chaldee dialect: but albeit, of the manner of the Chaldean, or Babylonian pronunciation, in some other words, some examples are produced, and in Greek and in Latin, it be a common course, to clip off, or cut out that letter, because they want one whereby fitly to express it, as in other words *Ozias*, Mat. 1.9. *Esaias*, Rom. 10.20. *Pharao*, Rom. 9.17. and the like; so in this: yet neither is there any the like necessity of so doing, in the Chaldee dialect; which is so far from ordinary cashiering of it, that it changes other Hebrew ones, oft, into it. Neither do I meet with any instance, given out of any monument of that language, of *Baal*, thus contracted; the contrary rather does appear, by those portions of Scripture, penned in the Syriac, (which we commonly call the Chaldee,) Ezr. 4.8,9,17. where the word בְעֵל without any such contradiction, is found. Nor do I find, either in the Targum, or Chaldee Paraphrase, as it is commonly called,) of the Old Testament, or in the Syrian version of the New, either the name of *Baal*, in any place, without that letter, or the name of *Bel*, with it. It seems to me, therefore, not improbable, that *Bel* and *Baal*, are two several names, though by Greek and Latin writers, commonly confounded: and that *Bel* was a proper name, in ancient times not unusual; as *Bela*, Gen. 36.32. & 46.21. and other the like, & that of that name, some eminent persons, in divers places had after their decease, been deified. Whence it came to pass, that as there were divers *Herculesses*, in several countries and those of several ages, and several breeds; See Tully *of the deity*, lib. 3. and Herodote, *Lb.* 2. so were there likewise, sundry *Bels*, or *Belusses*; the Egyptian, the Tyrian, the Assyrian, and many more, whose pedigrees are related in Apollodorus, lib. 1. Diodore, lib. 1. Eusebius his *preparative*, lib. 1. & 9. from Phylo Byblius, his version of Sanchuniathon; & others: yea, therefore, many the more, because *Bel*, and *Baal*, are both by Greek and Latin writers, as is not denied, so commonly confounded. Again, that which has been suggested concerning this *Bel*, or, *Belus*, as being sometime a great potentate, and after his decease deified, may receive further strength from hence: in that as the Tyrian *Belus*, is acknowledged to have been no other, than an ancient king of that country, whose cup therefore, the Poet says, Dido drank in, to Aeneas, *Aeneid.* l. 1. so is the like also averred, of the Babylonian *Belus*; whom Nebuchadnezzar, therefore, called his progenitor, in that speech of his uttered in a fit of rapture, from Megasthenes reported by Abydenus, in his *Assyrian History*, and by Eusebius recorded out of him, in his *Gospel preparative*, l. 9. wherein he foretells his Babylonians, of an evil that should befall them, which says he, *neither Belus my Progenitor, nor Queen Beltis, are able to induce the Fates to avert*. Thus he, whereby it appears, that this Belus had been a king, one of his ancestors; and Beltis, in times past, a Queen. This *Bel*, therefore, whom the prophet here mentions, is not unlikely to be that *Belus*, unto whom ancient writers attribute the building of Babylon; though about that, there be no good agreement among them. But in regard thereof, some conclude *Bel*, or *Belus*, to be Nimrod, so called, at first, say they, for his rebellion against his superiors, or his peers; afterward, *Baal*, or *Lord*, when he was settled in his Empire; and that the Chaldeans kept the latter name of him, in their records, suppressing the former, as containing matter of reproach. Yet seem not these things altogether so clear, as is conceived. For however it be certain, that Nimrod, at first built Babylon, Gen. 10.10,11. and it be very probable, that this *Bel*, whom the Babylonians thus adored, was some such great one, as Nimrod, in his lifetime; yet it is well known, that the name of the first founder of a city, is in continuance of time, oft lost, and devolved from those that first began it, unto those, that in succeeding ages repaired its ruins, or raised it to more flourishing and glorious condition. So it is said of a later Pharao, after Joseph's death; that by the Hebrews he built *Rameses*, Exod. 1.11. though it appears, that it was built by some other before, Gen. 47.11. and *Hiel* is said to have *built Jericho*, which he reedified, 1 King. 16.34. and of Babylon itself, Nebuchadnezzar says, that he *built it*, that is, did so beautify and enlarge it, that it might well seem a new city, Dan. 4.30. See Joseph's *antiquities*, l. 10. c. 11. and so might this *Belus*, or *Bel*, have done many ages after Nimrod's days; as of Semiramis also the like is related, to whom many authors therefore ascribe the building of Babylon, as Ctesias, Diodore, l. 2. Strabo, l. 16. and others, not a few: albeit, some again say, that she only performed some works about it: nor does Abyden, one of the ancientest authors, whose remains we have, say any more of Belus, in Eusebius his *preparative*, l. 9. but that *he encompassed Babylon with a wall*. Besides that, as it may justly be doubted, whether Nimrod were upon any such occasion, at first, so called, (which is not very likely, though not much to the present purpose:) and not by his father, upon some other ground, so named from his birth; so there seems as little likelihood, that from the Hebrew *Baal*, this name was given either to him, or any other, whom the Scripture so terms; it being not the manner of Scripture, to corrupt names, as other languages are forced to do, for the reason before expressed. But the Scripture constantly styles this idol, neither בֵּעל nor בְּעֵל but בֵּל֙ simply; nor do we ever find, either this, or that name, in Scripture, ever given unto Nimrod. But whosoever he was that bore the name, or upon what ground soever the name was given him, certain it is, that this *Bel* was a principal god with the Babylonians: under which name, some tell us, that they adored the Sun. Howbeit, the ancientest authors, of whom we find some few fragments, in relations of former writers, as Abydenus, and Megasthenes, (of whom, some remains are found here, and there, in Josephus his *Antiquities*, and Eusebius his *Preparative*,) tell us of two counterfeit deities, King *Bel*, or *Belus*, and Queen *Beltis*, that seem to have been unto them, as *Jupiter*, and *Juno*, unto the Latins and Greeks: the former of them we find in the name of *Belshatsar*, Dan. 5.1. the latter, in the name of *Beltshatsar* Dan. 4.8. nor is that which they say concerning this latter, contrary to what is there said by the Babylonian Monarch, that Daniel was so called *according to the name of his God*; for the name of *God*, with them, might well comprehend deities, such as those were, of either sex, as well, as *Θεός* does in Greek: nor is *it* in the one, any more, than a syllabical adjection: as *os*, or *us*, is in the other: nor does this Babylonian *Beltis* seem to be the same with that Phenician *Baaltis*, whom they make the daughter of Celus, and sister to Astarte, or Venus, by the Greeks termed Dione. See Phylo Bybliensis in Eusebius his *Preparative*.

*{Nebo*} Another of their idols, whose name is found in the appellations of many of their kings and Nobles, mentioned as well in Scripture, as in other writings. Of this sort, are *Nabonassar, Nabo-polassar, Nabuchadnetsar, Nabuzaradan* his chief Marshal, Jer. 39.1,9. and many other. As the former seems to have been some martial man, or great Monarch; so this latter, to have been some famous false prophet, from whom, after his death, deified, they expected oracles by his priests, for his name imports *Prophecy*: and as among both Greeks and Latins, though *Jupiter* were deemed their chief god: yet not he, but *Apollo*, was the god, whom they repaired most to, for answer by oracle: so it seems, that with the Babylonians, albeit, *Bel*, were their *Jupiter*; yet *Nebo* was their *Apollo*: whose oracle that may well be, which Stephen the Byzantine says, was among the Chaldeans, in like request, as Apollo's at Delphos, was among the Greeks. Howsoever, I am not ignorant that some learned understand him, of the oracle of *Belus*: whereof Arrian, in *the life of Alexander*, lib. 7.

*{boweth down*} Or, *is bowed down*: not only failing those that expected help from them; but being pulled down, and carried away, either to be borne about, as a conquest being made, as well of their gods, as of the people themselves, and their persons; or to make monuments of them, or money of the rich metals whereof they were made. See Chap. 10.10,11. Jer. 43.12,13. & 50.2.

*{their idols were upon the beasts, and upon the cattle: your carriages, were heavy laden: they are a burden to the weary beast*} Or, *their idols were for the beasts, and for the cattle*. So the words are in the Hebrew; as if he had said, they went to the brute beast, as fittest companions for them; on whose backs the Medes and Persians bestowed them, to carry them away with them, into their own country, among other their carriages, or they that had wont to be borne about in procession, on men's shoulders, or in chariots, with much pomp and state, are now packed up, and laid as luggage on the backs of beasts, without any respect, or regard. See Chapter 15.7. Heb. *beasts*, and *cattle*, collectively; as Genesis 7.21. Ezek. 33.27.

*{idols*} The word in the first notion, signifies *pain* and *sorrow*. See on Chap. 10.10. & 45.6. used the rather, here, as hinting what they were; not to those only, that had adored them, but to the beasts also, that did now bear them. Though some expound it of the heavy burdens, that they had formerly been to the beasts, that used either to bear them about, or to draw the chariots, wherein they had wont to be borne; like that, Chap. 14.7,8. but the former seems the better.

*{your carriages*} He turns his speech, as some, to the Medes and Persians, that carried them away with them; as relating how heavy their carriages would be, with the weight of them: As others, to their idols, as in way of derision, telling them, that they were heavy gods indeed, heavy burdens both to man and beast. See the like change of the person, Chap. 45.17.

*{heavy laden*} With the weight of them. See v. 3. & of the massiness of their idols, Daniel 3.1.

*{they are a burden*} Or, were; that it may agree with the former.

*{the weary beast*} Tired with the carriage of them; a defect of the subject; as ch. 28.12. & 40.29. and that taken collectively, as before.

**V. 2.** *{They stoop, they bow down together*} Either the Babylonians themselves, that looked so big, and strutted it so before, do now hang the head, and go with dejected looks. See the like, ch. 3.16. & 10.3,4. & 51.23. or, the images of their gods all alike, in the pillaging of their Temples. For the words are the same, that were before used of them, v. 1. and there is an elegant consonancy in the words, which our English cannot so fitly express, as if it were said, *they droop they stoop*, or the like.

*{they could not deliver the burden*} That was carried away upon the beasts, ver. 1. The Babylonians were not able to save their idols, that should have saved them, chap. 44.17. nor could their idols save themselves that ought to have saved others. See ver. 7. The words may well, be rendered, *the burden could not be delivered*; either by others, or themselves: for the verb is indefinite. See the like, ch. 2.19. & 45.24. Mal. 1.4.

*{but themselves are gone into captivity*} To wit, their idols, or gods themselves. See Jer. 48.7. Heb. *and*; as ch. 29.13.) *their soul went into captivity*; as Ps. 105.18. *his soul went into iron*: and the word *soul*, is sometime metaphorically applied, even to things not endued with any sensitive faculty; as ch. 10.18.

**V. 3.** *{Hearken unto me, O house of Jacob*} God, by the prophet, turns his speech to his people, minding them of his divine power manifested in his support of them, from their very first original; thereby to strengthen their faith, in the assurance of his deity, and in a constant expectation of deliverance from captivity; and withal, laying before them, the vanity of idols, and extreme folly of idolaters; partly, to dissuade them from the practice of any such fond fopperies; and partly, to arm them against the fear of them. See the like, ch. 41.8,9. & 43.1,10. & 44.1,8,21.

*{house of Jacob*} See ch. 2.5.

*{and all the remnant of the house of Israel*} That yet survive after the Chaldean invasion, and Babylonian deportation, c. 10.21,22. & 11.11,12. & 28.5.

*{which are borne by me from the belly, which are carried from the womb*} Or, *which have been borne, and have been carried*; because he speaks of the time past: Which from your first original, have been supported, and tenderly tended by me: A metaphor from parents, or nurses, that carry younglings, not yet able to go well, in their arms, or in their lap, chap. 63.9. See Psal. 92.12. Hos. 11.3. and he uses both the terms of bearing and carrying, before used of their idols, v. 1. as thereby purposely to difference the true God, from those counterfeit gods, in that they needed bearing, & were borne by those that worshiped them, v. 7. whereas the true God did himself support and bear those that adored him; and depended on him, Exod. 19.4. Deut. 32.11. ch. 40.11. where by other resemblances, also, is the same thing set forth.

*{by me*} A defect of the pronoun; as Job 16.8,9.

*{from the belly*} See ch. 44.2,24. and somewhat the like; even that, from whence this seems borrowed, Ps. 22.9–12. & 71.6.

**V. 4.** *{And even to your old age, I am he, and even to hoary hairs will I carry you: I have made, and I will bear; even I will carry, and will deliver you*} *I am he*; or, *I am the same*; as; Chron. 28.22. Psal. 102.27. See Mal. 3.6. Jam. 1.17. He promises the like tender affection toward them, constant care for them, and support of them, as he had formerly afforded them, and used about them, (therein surpassing the wonted practice of parents and nurses) even to the last, Gen. 28.15. Josh. 1.5. Jer. 32.40. Joh. 13.1. Heb. 13.5. See Ps. 48.14. & 71.9. the pronoun, both positive, and possessive, is wanting; as ch. 1.15. & 30.3.

*{I have made, and I will bear*} A faithful Creator, 1 Pet. 4.19. Another difference between the true God, and the false; he is the maker of those that worship him, Ps. 100.3. ch. 44.2. whereas, they are made by those that worship them, verse 6. chapter 44.15.

*{I will deliver*} The main scope of all, to ascertain them of deliverance out of their thraldom at Babylon, Chap. 43.14. and 45.13.

**V. 5.** *{To whom will ye liken me, and make me equal, and compare me, that we may be like?*} Or, *To whom will ye make me like, or equal? or compare me, that we should be like?* To wit, the one to the other. Heb. *and we shall be like*. The copulative, for the disjunctive; as cha. 45.9. and for the finitive; as chap. 43.12. See chap. 40.18,25. and v. 9.

**V. 6.** *{They lavish gold out of their bag, and weigh silver in the balance, and they hire a goldsmith, and he maketh it a god*} Having laid before them his own approved power, he proceeds to lay open the silly and sorry condition of those idols, whereon the Babylonians their enemies, relied; and these to render the more, both detestable, and despicable to them, he minds them, both of the original of them, and their inability to help, either others, or themselves. See the like, Chap. 40.19,20. and 44.12–19. Jeremiah 10.3–5,9.

*{lavish gold*} The word here used, signifies properly, *to waste*, or, *spend riotously*, more peculiarly, *flesh*, and dainty fare: whence the term *zolel*, for a *glutton*, or a great waster of flesh: as *sove*, for a *drunkard*, or deep drinker of wine, joined oft together, Deut. 21.20. Prov. 23.20,21. and to *waste* it, whatsoever it be, as some matter of no worth: For that notion, also, the word includes, as appears, Jer. 15.19. Lam. 1.8,11. where it is used. The meaning is, they spare no cost in making them idols, but spend wastefully, as if they set light by their treasure, upon that that is, in truth, of no use or worth, save what the metal gives it. Of their lavish wastefulness in this kind, see in that vast colossus, Dan. 3.1.

*{bag*} Or, *purse*: such as they used to put, keep, or carry money about them in, Prov. 1.14. It is also used for such bags as they kept their weights in, Deut. 25.13. Prov. 16.11. Mic. 6.11.

*{weigh silver*} As in payments they used to do, Jer. 32.9,10. The whole text may thus be rendered, (because the verbs are indefinite, as those, also, ver. 7.) *Gold is lavished*, or, *wastefully spent*, and, *silver is weighed*. *Gold*, whereof to make the idol, and silver, wherewith to pay the workman, or either, to make an idol of it, chapter 30.22.

*{in the balance*} Or, *by the beam*, or, *at the beam*. Heb. *reed*, or *cane* whereof it was oft made: the *beam*, put for the balance, a principal part of it, for the whole. And thence it may be the Hebrew word, *to buy*, Chap. 43.24. because they used to buy and sell by it. Of their several sorts of beams, and scales, or balances. See on chapter 40.12.

*{they hire a goldsmith*} Heb. *Founder*, or *Finer*, ch. 40.19,20. and 41.7.

*{and he maketh it a god*} Or, *to make it a god*, as verse 5. or, *to make a god of it*, of that silver, or that gold, that they deliver him to work upon, Chap. 2.20. or, as before, *a goldsmith is hired, that may make it a god*, as chap. 44.14. as if the workman were able to make a god of that, which was nothing less before, Jer. 10.3,9. and 16.20.

*{they fall down, yea, they worship*} *It*, the idol so made, See cha. 44.17. or, *which they may fall down to, and worship*, a defect of the relative as Ch. 42.1. & 44.2.

**V. 7.** *{They bear him upon the shoulder*} Or, *he is borne upon the shoulder*, on men's shoulders; either unto the place where he is to stand, or from thence sometime, abroad to be seen. See on ver. 3.

*{they carry him, and set him in his place*} Or, *and carried, and set*. See ch. 44.13. Thus have their gods need of help from them, as they had their being from them at first, Jer. 10.3–5.

*{and he standeth*} Or, *there he standeth*, Jer. 10.5. or, *that he may abide there*, as before, v. 6. *to make it a god*: *To stand*, for, *to abide*, or *stay*; as Deut. 5.31. ch. 66.22. so, *to sit*, ch. 44.13.

*{from his place shall he not remove*} Or, *can he not stir*, ch. 40.20. & 41.7. Jer. 10.5. the indicative, in a potential notion; as in those other places, and so in the next clause.

*{yea, one shall cry unto him, yet can he not answer*} Or, *yea, though one cry unto him, yet can he not answer*, because he can neither hear, nor speak, Psal. 125.6,7. Heb. *yea, he shall cry, and he shall not answer*; *and*, for *yet*, as Neh. 5.18. Ps. 44.18. ch. 29.2. and the verb potential, as before.

*{nor save him out of his trouble*} Or, *from his straits*, because he can neither do good, nor evil, he can neither help, nor hurt, cha. 41.23,24. Jer. 10.5. Heb. *he shall not save*: so ch. 45.20.

**V. 8.** *{Remember this*} Ch. 44.21.

*{and show yourselves men*} Not beasts, like those idolaters, cha. 45.20. Jer. 10.14. or, not womenlike, timorous, for fear, to comply with them, or, to stand in awe of aught from their idols, Jer. 10.1,11. So 1 Cor. 16.13.

*{bring it again to mind, O ye transgressors*} Heb. *bring back to heart*: That is, consider well of it, you of my people, that have in this kind gone astray: a defect of the particle *it*, as ch. 44.19. Yet some read the text, *reduce to wisdom such as have transgressed*, and the verb signifies, commonly, *to reclaim*, or *reduce*, Jer. 31.18. Lam. 5.21. Ezek. 18.30. and the *heart* is likewise put, as usually, for *wit*, or *wisdom*, Prov. 6.32. & 7.7. Hos. 7.11. Howbeit, this form of speech is most frequently used, in the former notion, Deuteronomy 4.39. and 30.1. So somewhat the like form, Chap. 41.22. Hagg. 1.5,7. and 2.15,18.

**V. 9.** *{Remember the former things of old*} Ch. 42.9. & 48.3. what things I have in former ages, from time to time, done among you, whereby I have evinced my power, and my deity, v. 3. Psal. 77.11,12. ch. 40.21,22. & 43.16,17. & 44.7,8.

*{for I am God, and there is none else*} Or, *that I am God, and none else* whereby it so appears, cha. 45.5,6,21,22.

*{I am God*} Or, that, *I am God*, that supplied from the former branch, as ch. 45.6.

*{and there is none like me*} Or, as some, *nothing like me*. See ver. 5. Acts 17.29. But here, rather, the former, as ch. 43.7. because of that which follows, ver. 10. that can both foretell, and effect things, as I have done, and still do.

**V. 10.** *{Declaring the end from the beginning, and from ancient times, the things that are not yet done*} Foretelling the issue of things, long before they come to be executed, and the proceedings or passages of them, in a continued course and progress, from the first to the last, and such things, at present, which though, as yet, they are not in being, yet shall surely in their due time, be effected, that which no other than myself can do, chap. 41.22,23. & 42.12. & 45.5,6. & 48.2.

*{saying, my counsel shall stand*} Ps. 33.11. Prov. 19.21. & 21.30. ch. 14.21,26.

*{and I will do all my pleasure*} Ps. 115.3. & 136.5. Dan. 4.35. applied, in particular, to God's will and pleasure, accomplished by Cyrus, in the destruction of Babylon, the deliverance of his people, and settling them in their land again, ch. 44.28. So v. 11.

**V. 11.** *{Calling a ravenous bird from the east*} Cyrus from Persia, lying to the east of Babylon, ch. 41.2,25. who should come swiftly, and seize upon Babylon, as an eagle, or vulture, upon his prey, Job 9.26. By either of which also, Cyrus might be resembled, in regard of his hooked nose like an eagle's, or vulture's beak; which was in him so notable, that it brought men so marked, into much repute among the Persians. See the like similitude of an eagle, Ezek. 17.3,10. Jer. 48.40. & 49.22. Hos. 8.1. Hab. 1.8.

*{a ravenous bird*} Heb. *a fowl*; but the word coming from a root, that signifies, properly, *to flee*, or *fall forcibly* (as a Greek word also fetched from it) upon prey: so used, 1 Sam. 14.33. and metaphorically to fall foul upon a man with bad language, 1 Sam. 25.14. it is more specially used for wild fowl, and those of prey. See instances, on ch. 18. v. 6.

*{the man that executeth my counsel*} Heb. *the man of my counsel*; as ch. 40.13. yet not whom he takes counsel of for aught; for, such God has none, chap. 40.14. But whom he intends to make use of, for the execution of his counsels and purposes concerning the destruction of Babylon, and the deliverance of his people, chap. 44.28. Jer. 50. v. 45.

*{from a far country*} For Persia lay far off, both from Babylon, (Assyria, and some other provinces lying between them) and from Judah. See ch. 13.5.

*{yea, I have spoken it, I will also bring it to pass; I have purposed it, I will also do it*} Or, *as sure as I have spoken it, I will bring it to pass; as I have contrived it, I will also do it*. See v. 10. ch. 14.21,26. a defect of the pronoun *it*, as ch. 44.13,15.

*{purposed*} Heb. *framed, formed*, or, *molded*; not only as the potter does the clay with his hands, Gen. 2.7. ch. 63.8. but as either he, or any other workman, also, is wont to contrive, and conceive in his mind, the fashion of that work, which he intends to produce, for thereunto, also, it is oft applied, Gen. 6.5. & 8.21. 1 Chron. 28.9. ch. 26.3.

**V. 12.** *{Hearken unto me ye stouthearted*} Or, *men of great stomachs*, Psal. 76.5. He seems to speak, rather, to the enemy, that out of the pride of their heart, and height of their stomach, thought to carry things, as they listed themselves, contrary to God's predictions and purposes; (as chap. 10.12.) than to those of God's people, who, either out of imbecility, or incredulity, made doubt of, or denied the truth of God's promises: the term does not so well fit these.

*{that are far from righteousness*} That is, say some, *the transgressors* among God's people; who by their impenitency, and contumacy, made themselves altogether unworthy of the favor, by God, intended them, ver. 8. Chap. 43.22,24. But I suppose it, rather, meant of their adversaries, who had dealt most unjustly and cruelly with his people, whatsoever they pretended, Chap. 47.6. Jer. 50.7,33. and 51.35.

**V. 13.** *{I bring near my righteousness*} Heb. *make to approach*, as chap. 41.21. *my righteousness*, that is, as some, *the righteousness*, which my people receive from me, for their justification, and acquittal from their sins, Chap. 33.24. & 43.25. & 45.24,25. As others, *my faithfulness*, my fidelity, in keeping my word, in making good my promises, chap. 1.27. & 41.2. & 45.8. & 51.5. which no might, malice, or unbelief, of any, shall hinder from taking effect, Rom. 3.3. 2 Tim. 2.13. Or, as I conceive, *my righteousness*, which I shall show, in executing judgment on the oppressors of my people, and righting the wrongs that by their adversaries have been done them; as if he had said, though you have been far from all justice and equity, in those things that you have done unto my people; yet I will deal justly with you, and cause my justice speedily to approach, and take hold on you ere long, Psalm 146.7–9. chap. 59.14–18. Jer. 51.35,36. See on chap. 45.25.

*{it shall not be far off*} See on ch. 13.22. & 60.22.

*{and my salvation shall not tarry*} The deliverance of my people, depending upon, and conjoined with the destruction of their foes. See ch. 14.1. these two go together, as here, so Psal. 98.2. ch. 56.1. & 59.16,17.

*{and I will place salvation in Zion, for Israel my glory*} I will make Jerusalem a place of safety, chap. 26.1,2. & 33.20. Zach. 2.5. for my people: by whose deliverance and restitution, I will gain to myself much glory. So Exod. 15.1,6,11. chap. 60.21. & 63.14. & 66.18. or, as some read the words, *and in Israel my magnificence*; as ch. 4.2,5. & 24.23. & 60.7,19. but the change of the particle carries it rather the former way.

### CHAPTER 47

**V. 1.** *{Come down, and sit in the dust; O virgin daughter of Babylon*} In this chapter is prosecuted the denunciation of Babylon's destruction, entered upon in the beginning of the chapter before going, with a relation of the ruin and captivity of their idols; and after some windings, and occasional digressions, now returned unto again. In this chapter, is her dejected and despicable condition, upon her overthrow, together with the procuring causes, the suddenness and unavoidableness of it, very pithily and pregnantly described.

*{Come down*} From your throne, from your former height and state. So Jer. 13.18. & 48.18. & 51.25. Lam. 1.14.

*{sit in the dust*} Sit on the ground, as one of low and mean condition, having neither throne, nor seat, to sit on, Psal. 113.7. But that in the next branch; here rather, sit in dust and ashes, after the manner of mourners, on special occasions of great and solemn mournings, much used in those times, Job 2.8. & 42.6. Mat. 11.21. See ch. 52.2. Jer. 13. v. 18.

*{O virgin daughter of Babylon*} Or, *O virgin daughter Babylon*: you Babylon, say some, that have hitherto been unsubdued, chap. 23.12. but rather, that are like unto a beautiful young damsel, tender and delicate, in diet and dressings, gorgeous in attire, sumptuous in furniture, and priding yourself in the goodliness of your glorious estate, Jer. 46.11. See on ch. 1.8. & 23.12.

*{sit on the ground*} As before: so Lam. 2.10.

*{there is no throne*} For you to sit on, in state: your government is gone; *throne*, for *government*, as Psal. 89.14,29. & 122.5. so of Tyre, ch. 23.10. *there is no girdle*: there is no power, or trade, left you; your might, or merchandise, is gone.

*{O daughter of the Chaldeans*} O you Babylon, the beauty and glory of the Chaldean state, ch. 13.19. So ver. 5.

*{for thou shalt no more be called tender, and delicate*} Heb. *thou shalt no more add, they shall call thee*: or, *that they shall call thee*; a form of speech, in other languages, unusual; but, in Hebrew, very common, so 1 Sam. 2.3. ver. 5. chap. 23.12. *to be called*, for, *to be*, simply; or, *to be accounted*; such, as chap. 4.3. & 54.5. & 56.7. you shall no longer enjoy that delicacy and daintiness, that formerly you did. See a description of such, and of such an alteration, Deut. 32.56,57. See, also, ver. 8.

**V. 2.** *{Take the millstones, and grind meal*} Prepare and fit yourself for all servile offices; of which, the turning of, or grinding at the mill, as accounted one of the meanest, assigned commonly, as in many countries at this day, instead of beasts, unto the sorriest sort of slaves and captives, Exod. 11.5. Judg. 16.21. Job 31.10. Lam. 5.13. and was ordinarily women's work, Exod. 11.5. Job 31.10. Mar. 24.41. Luke 17.35.

*{take the millstones*} Betake yourself to the mill, as we use to say, take your bed; when our meaning is, betake yourself to your bed.

*{the millstones*} The word here used, and so also, Exod. 11.5. Num. 11.8. and elsewhere, is of a dual form; because the mill consists of two stones, the upper, and the lower: the former called, in Hebrew, *receb*, or, the *rider*, as in some places, with us, *the runner*, because it rides, or runs about, upon the lower, Deut. 24.6. the latter, in the writings of the rabbines (for in Scripture it is not found) is called *sheceb*, the *bedstead*, or *the rester*, because it stirs not, but lies down, and rests under the former. In the law forbidding the taking of the millstones to pledge, it might be deemed by our translation, where the word *rachajim* here used, stands in the first place, and the word *receb* in the second, that the former should signify the upper millstone only, and the latter, the lower: but the former comprehends the whole *mill*, consisting, as of two principal parts, of both: the latter, the upper only: the intent of the Lawgiver, being to inhibit any to take, for pledge, either the whole mill, both stones, or the one of them only; yet, by name, expressing only the uppermost, because that lying loose, might the more readily be taken off, and carried away upon any such occasion, whereas the other being ordinarily fixed, could not so easily be removed; and without it, the other would be altogether unusual. That of grinding, some of the Jews' doctors, both here, and in other the places above cited, writhe, and wrest, to an obscure sense not worthy to be related.

*{grind meal*} That is, grind grain or corn, whereof to make *meal*, or by grinding of it, make meal; as in that proverbial speech running elegantly, in Hebrew, *their bud shall make*, or *yield no meal*, Hos. 8.7. So, *he baketh bread*, for *he baketh dough*, therefore to make *bread*, chap. 44.19. there is a kind of prolepsis, or anticipation, in it, metal, whereof a graven image is afterward to be made; otherwise, the founder no more melts the one, than the miller grinds the other.

*{uncover thy locks*} That is, say some, shave yourself, as mourners use to do, Job 1.20. See chap. 22.12. or, as slaves and captives are wont to be used. See on chap. 3.24. But that were rather to uncover the head, than the hair, or the locks; to make the head bare, by taking away of the hair: and the like exception may be taken against the exposition of those, that by the word here used, would have to be understood, certain rich or curious fillets, wherewith the hair is wont to be wound, and bound up, among great ones especially. The word rather signifies the *locks*, or *tresses* that the hair of such uses to be made up in, their *forelocks*, especially, on either side of their temples, as appears, by Cant. 4.1,3. & 6.7. now those of note and state, queens and princes, especially, had goodly rich tires and diadems, which did not only cover and adorn their heads; but did bind in also, and keep up these their locks, from falling down upon their faces: of which, see ch. 3.21. & 62.3. Est. 1.11. & 2.17. Jer. 13.18. The meaning therefore is, that being stripped of, or having cast off, her costly and stately head-tire, and headbands, she should go barehead, with her hair hanging down about her ears, as captives and drudges are wont to do. See Ezek. 21.16. Lam. 5.16. So ch. 3.24.

*{make bare the leg; uncover the thigh, pass over the rivers*} Truss up your clothes about you, not as those that are to travel, only, Exod. 12.11. 1 King. 18.46. but higher than ordinary, as those that are to wade through deep waters, to pass through thick and thin, Psa. 66.12. & 69.1,2. *the leg, and the thigh*, for, *the legs, and thy thighs*: a defect of the pronoun; as Chap. 37.4,23. and the nouns collective; as chap. 20.2. the former whereof, I suppose, might better be rendered *foot*, than *leg*; as the plural is *footsteps*, or *paths*, Psalm 77.19. Jeremiah 18.15. the latter, *knee*, rather than *thigh*, because it is expressly distinguished from the *thigh*, Judges 15.8. where it is rendered *hip*, as I conceive, not so fitly: but if it be so taken here, it should intimate a further degree of disgrace, of which, Chap. 3.17. and 20.4. but of that, the prophet speaks in the next verse: and the last clause leads rather to the former sense, as spoken unto one that was to wade up to the knees. Some suppose an allusion in it, to the river Euphrates; over whose streams the Babylonians should pass captive into Media and Persia: which it may be, is somewhat too nice, and to me seems needless.

**V. 3.** *{Thy nakedness shall be uncovered, and thy shame shall be seen*} Either you shall want wherewith to cover those parts that womanly modesty abhors to have seen, and to lie open to common view; or, you shall, in scorn and derision, be so disgracefully used, as women prisoners, taken captive, oft times are, by those uncivil & inhumane persons into whose hands they fall. See, besides the places pointed to, on the former verse, Jer. 13.21,26. Ezek. 16.37. & 23.29. Nah. 3.5.

*{I will take vengeance*} To wit, on you, to be supplied from the latter clause; as ch. 48.9. as if he had said, it is not so much Cyrus, as God by him, that comes to take vengeance upon you, ch. 13.3–5,9,11,17. & 14.22. Jer. 50.9,15,21–25,28. & 51.6,11,14,24,25,44. for the wrongs done to his people, ver. 6. Jer. 51.35,36. See chap. 34.8. and 46.13.

*{and will not meet thee as a man*} But in full wrath, without any pity, or commiseration, such as men are wont to show; sometime, unto the weaker sex. I will deal with you, as you have dealt with mine, ver. 6. 2 Chr. 36.17. Judg. 8.18–21. Jer. 50.15. Jam. 2.13. Or, in full power, as God, one of might unconceivable. See Ps. 90.11. ch. 31.3. To this purpose, the Latin, and those that follow it, read the words, *and man shall not withstand me*; but that sense the words will not admit. Again, some of the Jewish doctors, as also of ours, treading in their steps, incline much to the former notion, and render it, *I will not admit any man's intercession for thee*; for the word here used, say they, signifies, sometime, *to intercede*, sometime, *to admit intercession*; and in the former sense, indeed, it seems taken, Gen. 23.8. Jer. 7.16. & 27.18. but for the latter sense, it is not so easy to find a place, that may fit it: they allege, ch. 64.5. but that seems not so clear to this purpose.

*{as a man*} A defect of the note of similitude; as Chapter 40.6. & 41.15.

**V. 4.** *{As for our Redeemer, the Lord of hosts is his name, the holy One of Israel*} Or, *Saith our redeemer*, (for *As for*, is not in the text, nor does so well fit here; and *saith*, or *saying*, is oft suppressed, but to be supplied, as 1 Kin. 20.34. Ps. 27.8. & 105.15. c. 5.9. & 26.19. 45.14. Na. 2.8.) *our redeemer* (our rescuer out of dangers, difficulties, and distresses, Gen. 48.16. ch. 43.14.) *whose name is the Lord of hosts*, (as ch. 48.2. & 54.5. the positive for the relative; as chap. 33.21. & 42.1. ver. 11.) *the holy one of Israel*. See ch. 1.4. Spoken in the person of God's people acknowledging all this done, by God, for their deliverance, out of God's free favor and mercy unto them, Chap. 14.1. & 43.14. & 45.4.

**V. 5.** *{Sit thou silent, and get thee into darkness*} Having broke off his speech to Babylon wherein he had begun to tell her what she must do, and what should betide her, to give her to understand, who it was that spoke it, and would enforce her to do it, ver. 3,4. he returns in this verse again to her; enjoining her further, for shame, and confusion, to be mute, and to get into some dark corner out of sight. *Sit silent*, or *Sit dumb*, (for that is the very word in the Hebrew; as also, Lam. 3.23.) as one confounded, and not able to speak, Ps. 77.4. & 107.42. Mat. 22.12. *and go into the dark*, (the abstract for the concrete; as Job 3.3.) as one ashamed of yourself, and not enduring to be seen, in such sorry condition, as you shall be in shortly, v. 3. Lam. 1.9. & 2.10.

*{O daughter of the Chaldeans*} See on v. 1.

*{for thou shalt no more be called the Lady of kingdoms*} As the state of Judah, sometime, *the Princess of Provinces*, Lam. 1.1. and as Babylon itself also, *the glory of kingdoms*, ch. 13.19. not only, as a most stately and glorious one among them, but as one that ruled over them, Jer. 27.7,8,9. Dan. 2.37,38.

**V. 6.** *{I was wroth with my people, I have polluted mine inheritance, and given them into thine hand: thou didst show them no mercy, upon the ancient hast thou very heavily laid the yoke*} One cause of Babylon's overthrow, before hinted, ver. 4. their extreme cruelty exercised upon God's people; which howsoever, through the just judgment of God, it befell them for their sins, chap. 10.5,6. Jer. 1.15,16. yet it did no more excuse them, who intended nothing less, than the execution of God's just designs, Chapter 10.7. than God's counsel, and purpose, concerning the giving up of his Sons, for the salvation of his elect, did acquit any of those from *wicked hearts*, and *hands*, that had aught to do, either as procurers, or actors, in the putting of him to death, Acts 2.23. & 4.27,28. See on cha. 45.24,25.

*{I was wroth with my people*} Ch. 57.17. & 64.5. Zach. 1.15. of the term, see on ch. 34.2.

*{I have polluted mine inheritance*} Or, *I polluted*; that it may run in the same tenor with the former; as in the original it does. I dealt with my people, whom I had adopted, and taken unto myself, for a peculiar, Exod. 19.5. Deuteronomy 7.6. and was as dear to me, as to an heir his inheritance is wont to be, 1 King. 21.3. ch. 19.25. as with some profane, or unclean thing, Chap. 43.28. Lam. 1.17.

*{and given them into thine hand*} Or, *gave them* (as before) *into thine hand*, that is, *into thy power*: as verse 14. Jer. 12.7. Lam. 1.14.

*{thou didst show them no mercy*} Instead of pitying, and compassionating their misery, you did exceedingly aggravate it, by your extreme, hard, and cruel usage of them, 2 Chr. 36.17. Psal. 69.26. Heb. *thou didst set them no bowels*: *bowels*, for *mercy*, or *tender mercy*: as chap. 54.7. Dan. 9.9. Zach. 1.16. So Luke 1.78. Philip. 2.1.

*{upon the ancient*} Who for age should have been pitied; but with you found no mercy: you deal unmercifully, with old and young alike, Deut. 28.50. Lam. 2.21. & 5.12,13.

*{hast thou very heavily laid the yoke*} Or, *didst thou*, as in the former branch. Heb. *make thy yoke very heavy*: for the pronoun expressed in the Hebrew, should not be omitted: *thy yoke*, not that you did yourself wear, or bear: as 1 King. 12.4. Jer. 2.20. but that you laid upon, and did compel them, to bear, and wear: as Jer. 27.7,10. a metaphor taken from such yokes, as beasts are wonted to draw in. See Jer. 28.48. Lam. 1.14.

**V. 7.** *{And thou saidst*} Thought with yourself, as Ps. 10.11. & 94.7. ch. 10.10. See also, ver. 8.

*{I shall be a Lady forever*} Another cause of her ruin, her insolent, and confident presumption, imagining her power and settlement to be such, as she never should, nor could, by any means, be pulled down, or dismounted, from the top, or height of her state. So Ps. 10.6. Rev. 18.7. See the like presumption of Edom, Obad. 1.3. of Ammon, Jer. 49.6. of God's own people, Jer. 21.13. yea, some tang of it, in one after God's own heart, Ps. 30.6.

*{So that thou didst not lay these things to thine heart*} Heb. *hitherto*, or, *as yet, thou hast not set these things upon thine heart*: as chap. 57.1. you little thought of any such matter, as is now befallen you. See on ch. 46.8.

*{nor didst remember the latter end of it*} Heb. *nor hast remembered her latter end*; as Lam. 1.9. that is, *thy latter end*, as Job 18.4. a permutation of persons, or passage from person to person, the like whereunto, see ch. 1.29. & 31.7. & 34.16. Jer. 17.1. You little thought what would be the issue of these things, or what would, at length, befall you, Deut. 32.29. the clause, likewise, of the [ruin] of God's own people, Lam. 1.9.

**V. 8.** *{Therefore hear now this, thou that art given to pleasures, that dwellest carelessly*} Heb. *And now hear this*: *and*, for *therefore*, the copulative, for the illative: as chapter 42.25. or, *But now hear this*: the copulative, for the adversative; as chap. 40.31. *thou delicate*, or *delicious one*: it comes from that root, from which the land, or garden of *Eden*, had its name, Gen. 2.15. See ver. 1. *that dwellest carelessly*, or *sittest securely*, or *confidently*, Judg. 18.7. Jeremiah 49.31.

*{that sayest in thine heart*} See v. 7.

*{I am, and none else beside me*} The like, see of Nineveh, Zeph. 2.15. An insolent & arrogant expression, of proud and presumptuous persons imitating what God is wont to say of himself, Chap. 41.4. & 43.10,11,12,13. & 44.6. & 45.5,6,22. Some supply it; *I am a Lady*, (the peculiar one, ver. 5,7.) *and there is none* (no Lady worth speaking of) *besides me*; as ver. 10. But the words here next following, carry it rather to the former, as spoken, rather of her unmovable subsistence, than of her matchless magnificence. See verse 7.
